title: Spanish A2
description: The second step in Latin American Spanish, from A1 to CEFR level A2, the level of the Instituto Cervantes DELE A2 exam. Lessons cover telling stories in the past with the preterite and the imperfect, past habits with soler and antes, the present perfect and the preterite as Mexico uses them, time expressions with hace and desde, direct and indirect object pronouns and putting them together (se lo), reflexive and reciprocal verbs, estar + gerund, describing and comparing people and places, indefinites and double negatives, the future tense beside ir a, por and para, commands with pronouns, the conditional for polite requests and advice, reporting what people say, and writing the messages and short texts the exam asks for. About 600 new words build on the roughly 920 from Spanish A1 for about 1,500 in all, with Mexican usage as the standard and Spain's words noted. Conjugation drills add the imperfect, the future, the conditional and the gerund to the A1 forms, and a reading list suggests graded readers for this level. Unlocks when Spanish A1 is complete.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Your life story: the preterite in full
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Spanish A1 ended with a first step into the past. You learned the **[[preterite]]** (*el pretérito
indefinido*), the past tense for finished events: *Ayer comí tacos* (Yesterday I ate tacos),
*Fuimos a la playa* (We went to the beach). You met the regular endings, *fui* for both *ser*
and *ir*, and a handful of irregular forms such as *tuve, estuve, pude, vine, hice*.

That is enough to say what you did last weekend. It isn't yet enough to tell a life: where
someone was born and grew up, when they graduated, got married, moved or retired, what they
said and what they brought with them. This lesson completes the preterite so that you can
read and write a short biography, one of the text types the DELE A2 exam uses, and answer the
classic first-conversation questions: *¿Dónde naciste? ¿Dónde creciste? ¿Cuándo llegaste?*

The next lesson adds a second past tense, the imperfect, for what life *was like*. For now,
everything in this lesson is a finished event.

## A quick review: the regular preterite

| | -ar: *casarse* (to get married) | -er: *crecer* (to grow up) | -ir: *cumplir* (to turn, an age) |
|---|---|---|---|
| yo | me casé | crecí | cumplí |
| tú | te casaste | creciste | cumpliste |
| él, ella, usted | se casó | creció | cumplió |
| nosotros | nos casamos | crecimos | cumplimos |
| (vosotros) | (os casasteis) | (crecisteis) | (cumplisteis) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | se casaron | crecieron | cumplieron |

- The written accents on *-é, -ó, -í, -ió* carry the meaning: *hablo* (I speak) but *habló*
  (she spoke); *me caso* (I'm getting married), *se casó* (she got married).
- Verbs used with *me, te, se, nos* keep the pronoun before the verb, exactly as in the present:
  *Me mudé a Monterrey* (I moved to Monterrey), *¿Cuándo te graduaste?* (When did you graduate?).
- In the *yo* form only, *-car, -gar, -zar* verbs change their spelling to keep the sound:
  *busqué, llegué, empecé*.

## The strong preterites, all together

A group of very common verbs doesn't follow the table above. Each one takes a new stem, and
all of them share one set of endings with no written accents: *-e, -iste, -o, -imos,
-ieron*. These are the **[[strong preterites]]**. There are only a dozen or so you need, and you
already know most of them.

![A chart of the strong preterites in three colored groups. The u group: andar to anduv-, estar to estuv-, tener to tuv-, poder to pud-, poner to pus-, saber to sup-. The i group: venir to vin-, querer to quis-, hacer to hic- (hizo). The j group: decir to dij-, traer to traj-, conducir to conduj-. Arrows lead to a box of shared endings: yo -e, tú -iste, él -o, nosotros -imos, ellos -ieron, with no written accents. A dashed box says the j group has the same endings, but -eron after j: dijeron, trajeron, condujeron. At the bottom: anduve, anduviste, anduvo, anduvimos, anduvieron.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| infinitive | stem | yo | él, ella, usted | ellos, ustedes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *andar* (to walk, to go around) | anduv- | anduve | anduvo | anduvieron |
| *estar* | estuv- | estuve | estuvo | estuvieron |
| *tener* | tuv- | tuve | tuvo | tuvieron |
| *poder* | pud- | pude | pudo | pudieron |
| *poner* | pus- | puse | puso | pusieron |
| *saber* | sup- | supe | supo | supieron |
| *venir* | vin- | vine | vino | vinieron |
| *querer* | quis- | quise | quiso | quisieron |
| *hacer* | hic- | hice | hizo | hicieron |
| *decir* | dij- | dije | dijo | dijeron |
| *traer* | traj- | traje | trajo | trajeron |

The full table for one of them: *anduve, anduviste, anduvo, anduvimos, anduvieron*.
Two details to watch:

- *hizo* is written with *z*, because *hico* would sound like *k*.
- After a *j*, the *ellos* ending loses its *i*: *dijeron, trajeron*, never *dijieron*.

*Andar* is the only new verb here. It means "to walk" or "to go around", usually without a
fixed destination: *Anduve por el centro toda la tarde* (I walked around downtown all
afternoon). In Mexico you'll often hear it for how someone is doing: *¿Cómo andas?* (How are
you doing?, informal). Its present is regular (*ando, andas, anda*); only the preterite is
strong.

Verbs ending in *-ducir* work like *decir*: *conducir* (to drive) gives *conduje, condujo,
condujeron*, and *traducir* (to translate) gives *traduje, tradujeron*. Mexicans usually say
*manejar* for "to drive" (A1), so you need *conduje* mainly to recognize it in reading.

Examples:

- *Mis papás vinieron a México en 1990.* — My parents came to Mexico in 1990.
- *¿Qué te dijeron en la entrevista?* — What did they tell you in the interview?
- *No quise ir a la boda.* — I refused to go to the wedding. (*no quise* = I didn't want to,
  and didn't)
- *Mi abuela trajo su máquina de coser de Guadalajara.* — My grandmother brought her sewing
  machine from Guadalajara.

### *hubo*: there was, for an event

The preterite of *hay* is *hubo*. Use it when "there was" means something happened:

- *En la boda hubo música hasta las tres de la mañana.* — At the wedding there was music until
  three in the morning.
- *Hubo una fiesta muy grande para su jubilación.* — There was a very big party for his
  retirement.

*Hubo* never changes for a plural: *Hubo dos bodas en mi familia el año pasado* (There were two
weddings in my family last year). For "there was" describing a scene (*There were a lot of
people*), Spanish uses another form, *había*, which the next lesson teaches.

## Two smaller patterns, in full

The conjugation drills test these, so learn them now.

### i becomes y: *caer, leer, creer, oír, construir*

When an *i* would land between two vowels in the *él* and *ellos* forms, it's written *y*:

| | *leer* | *oír* | *construir* (to build) |
|---|---|---|---|
| yo | leí | oí | construí |
| tú | leíste | oíste | construiste |
| él, ella, usted | leyó | oyó | construyó |
| nosotros | leímos | oímos | construimos |
| ellos, ustedes | leyeron | oyeron | construyeron |

*Creer* (*creyó*) and *caer*, to fall (*cayó, cayeron*), follow *leer*. Notice the accents on
*leí, leíste, leímos*: they show that *e* and *i* are separate syllables (*le-Í-mos*).
*Construir* doesn't need them (*construiste*), because *ui* is already pronounced as one
syllable.

- *Mi bisabuelo construyó esta casa en 1940.* — My great-grandfather (*bisabuelo*) built this
  house in 1940.
- *¿Leyeron la biografía de Frida Kahlo?* — Did you all read the biography of Frida Kahlo?

### -ir stem changers: only *él* and *ellos* change

You know **[[stem-changing verbs]]** from A1: *pedir → pido, dormir → duermo*. In the preterite,
-ar and -er stem changers are regular (*pensé, volví*). The -ir ones change, but only in the
*él* and *ellos* forms, and only by one step: e → i, o → u.

| | *pedir* | *sentir* (to feel) | *dormir* | *conseguir* (to get) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| yo | pedí | sentí | dormí | conseguí |
| él, ella, usted | pidió | sintió | durmió | consiguió |
| ellos, ustedes | pidieron | sintieron | durmieron | consiguieron |

*Morir* (to die) does the same: *murió, murieron*. *Preferir* gives *prefirió*, and *repetir*
gives *repitió*.

- *Mi abuelo murió en 2015, a los noventa años.* — My grandfather died in 2015, at ninety.
- *Mi hermana consiguió trabajo en Canadá.* — My sister got a job in Canada.

*Conseguir* (to get, to obtain, to manage to) is new in this lesson. Its present also changes:
*consigo, consigues, consigue, conseguimos, consiguen*.

## Years, ages and decades

A biography is full of dates. Spanish reads a year as one big number, never split into pairs
the way English does:

- *1958*: *mil novecientos cincuenta y ocho*
- *2018*: *dos mil dieciocho*
- *2026*: *dos mil veintiséis*

The patterns to use:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *en 1998* | in 1998 |
| *a los 18 años* | at 18, when (he) was 18 |
| *Cumplió 30 años en 2020.* | He turned 30 in 2020. |
| *en los años noventa / en la década de 1990* | in the nineties, in the 1990s |
| *de joven* | as a young person, when (I was) young |
| *en su juventud* | in his or her youth |
| *dos años después* | two years later |
| *después de la boda* | after the wedding |

Two things to notice: "at 18" needs *los* (*a los 18 años*, or just *a los 18*; never *a 18*), and
*cumplir* is the verb for turning an age: *Mañana cumplo 40* (Tomorrow I turn 40).

## The events of a life

![A timeline titled "La vida de Rosa Medina", with six points and a picture above each. 1958: a baby, nació en Puebla. 1964: a school building, entró a la primaria. 1980: a graduation cap, se graduó de la universidad. 1983: two wedding rings, se casó con Arturo. 1990: a moving box with an arrow to a house, se mudó a Monterrey. 2018: a rocking chair, se jubiló.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Most of the verbs for life events take *me, te, se*:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *nacer* (A1): *nací* | to be born: I was born |
| *crecer*: *crecí* | to grow up: I grew up |
| *graduarse*: *me gradué* | to graduate |
| *casarse (con)*: *me casé con…* | to get married (to) |
| *separarse*, *divorciarse* | to separate, to get divorced |
| *mudarse (a)*: *me mudé a…* | to move (house) (to) |
| *jubilarse*: *me jubilé* | to retire |
| *morir*: *murió* | to die |

The nouns that go with them: *el nacimiento* (birth), *la boda* (wedding), *el matrimonio*
(marriage), *el divorcio*, *la muerte* (death). For studies: *la carrera* is a university
degree course (*Estudió la carrera de derecho*, She studied law), and *el título* is the
degree or diploma you get at the end. For people in biographies: *el pintor*, *el escritor*,
*el científico* (*la pintora, la escritora, la científica*), and *la obra*, a work of art or a
play.

*Graduarse* stresses the *u* in the present (*me gradúo, te gradúas*), with a written accent. In the
preterite it's regular: *me gradué, se graduó*. In Mexico people *se jubilan*, and you'll also
hear *pensionarse*, to start drawing a pension.

### Asking about someone's life

- *¿Dónde naciste?* — *Nací en Mérida.* (Where were you born? — I was born in Mérida.)
- *¿Dónde creciste?* — *Crecí en Cancún, pero estudié en Mérida.* (Where did you grow up? — I
  grew up in Cancún, but I studied in Mérida.)
- *¿Qué carrera estudiaste?* — *Estudié ingeniería.* (What did you study? — I studied
  engineering.)
- *¿Cuándo te graduaste?* — *Me gradué en 2016.* (When did you graduate? — I graduated in 2016.)
- *¿Cuándo llegaste a México?* — *Llegué hace tres años.* (When did you come to Mexico? — I
  came three years ago.)

## Text: a short biography

Elena Ríos is an invented painter; the text is written the way short biographies in magazines
and on museum websites usually are.

> Elena Ríos nació en Oaxaca en 1951. Creció en un pueblo pequeño, con sus abuelos.
>
> De joven anduvo por todo el país con una mochila y un cuaderno. En 1970 se mudó a la Ciudad
> de México y estudió la carrera de artes. Consiguió su título en 1975.
>
> Ese mismo año se casó con Julián Mora, un escritor, y dos años después tuvieron una hija.
>
> En los años ochenta pintó sus obras más famosas. En 1986 hubo una exposición de su obra en
> Nueva York, y Elena viajó por primera vez fuera de México.
>
> Julián y ella se separaron en 1992 y se divorciaron dos años después, pero siempre fueron
> amigos.
>
> Elena dio clases en una escuela de arte hasta 2016, cuando se jubiló. Murió en 2021, a los
> setenta años. Su hija dijo: "Mi mamá vivió como pintó: con muchos colores".

Translation:

> Elena Ríos was born in Oaxaca in 1951. She grew up in a small village, with her grandparents.
>
> As a young woman she traveled all over the country with a backpack and a notebook. In 1970
> she moved to Mexico City and studied art (as a degree). She got her degree in 1975.
>
> That same year she married Julián Mora, a writer, and two years later they had a daughter.
>
> In the eighties she painted her most famous works. In 1986 there was an exhibition of her
> work in New York, and Elena traveled outside Mexico for the first time.
>
> Julián and she separated in 1992 and got divorced two years later, but they were always
> friends.
>
> Elena taught at an art school until 2016, when she retired. She died in 2021, at seventy.
> Her daughter said: "My mom lived the way she painted: with lots of colors."

Notes: *pintar* is "to paint" (*pintó* = she painted). *La exposición* is an exhibition (a
word from lesson 15), and *fuera de* means "outside". *Por primera vez* (for the first time)
comes in lesson 04. *Dar clases* is "to teach (classes)". *Tuvieron una hija*:
with a child, *tener* in the preterite means "to have" in the sense of "give birth to, get".

## Pronunciation

- Strong preterites are stressed on the stem: *an-DU-ve, an-DU-vo, TRA-je, DI-jo, HU-bo*.
  Don't put the stress on the end (*andu-VO*): that's the regular pattern, and these verbs
  don't follow it.
- *-ió* is one syllable: *con-si-GUIÓ, sin-TIÓ, mu-RIÓ*. In *consiguió* the *u* after *g* is
  silent; it only keeps the *g* hard.
- *gra-DÚ-o, gra-DÚ-a* in the present, but *gra-DUA-mos* and *me gra-DUÉ*.
- *divorciarse* doesn't stress the *i*: *me di-VOR-cio*.
- Years: *mil no-ve-CIEN-tos cin-CUEN-ta y O-cho*.

## Common mistakes

- Accents on strong forms: ~~anduvó, hizó, pusó~~ → *anduvo, hizo, puso*.
- Treating *andar* as regular: ~~andé, andó~~ → *anduve, anduvo*. (*Andé* is heard in some
  casual speech, but it isn't standard.)
- An extra *i* after *j*: ~~dijieron, trajieron~~ → *dijeron, trajeron*.
- A plural *hubo*: ~~Hubieron muchos invitados~~ → *Hubo muchos invitados* (There were many
  guests).
- Changing the stem in every person: ~~pidí, durmí~~ → *pedí, dormí* (only *pidió, durmió,
  pidieron, durmieron* change).
- *Casarse* with the wrong preposition: ~~Se casó a Luis~~ or ~~Se casó Luis~~ for "She married
  Luis" → *Se casó con Luis*.
- Ages without *los … años*: ~~a 25~~ → *a los 25 años*.
- "To move house" as *moverse*: *moverse* is to move your body. Use *mudarse*: *Me mudé a
  Puebla.*

## Key points

- Regular preterite: *-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron*; *-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron*. Pronouns
  stay in front: *me casé, se graduó*.
- Strong preterites take a new stem and *-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron* with no accents: *anduve,
  estuve, tuve, pude, puse, supe, vine, quise, hice (hizo), dije, traje*.
- After *j*: *dijeron, trajeron, condujeron*.
- *Hubo* = there was / there were (an event); it never becomes plural.
- i → y in *leyó, oyó, cayó, construyó, creyó* (and their *-yeron*).
- -ir stem changers change only in *él* and *ellos*: *pidió, sintió, durmió, murió, consiguió*.
- Years are one number (*mil novecientos noventa*); *en 1998*, *a los 18 años*, *cumplir 30*,
  *en los años noventa*, *de joven*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. The past tenses reference sheet has the strong-preterite table and the
other changes in one place.

lessons.title: When I was a child: the imperfect and past habits
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 01 you used the preterite for the events of a life: *nació, se mudó, se casó*. But
when people remember their childhood, they mostly don't list events. They describe what things
were like and what used to happen: the house was small, we played in the street, my teacher was
strict, every summer we went to the coast.

For that, Spanish has a second simple past, the **[[imperfect]]** (*el pretérito imperfecto*).
English has no single form for it. It uses "used to", "would", "was …ing" or just the simple
past:

- *De niño vivía cerca del mar y nadaba todos los días.* — As a child I lived near the sea and
  (used to) swim every day.

Both verbs are in the imperfect, because both describe how life was, not something that
happened once. This lesson teaches the forms, which are the easiest in Spanish, and three uses:
habits, descriptions, and age and time. The theme is childhood and school, a topic that calls for
the imperfect at every turn. Completing the lesson also opens the imperfect in your
conjugation drills.

## The forms

There are only two sets of endings: one for -ar verbs, and one shared by -er and -ir verbs.

| | -ar: *jugar* | -er: *tener* | -ir: *vivir* |
|---|---|---|---|
| yo | jugaba | tenía | vivía |
| tú | jugabas | tenías | vivías |
| él, ella, usted | jugaba | tenía | vivía |
| nosotros | jugábamos | teníamos | vivíamos |
| (vosotros) | (jugabais) | (teníais) | (vivíais) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | jugaban | tenían | vivían |

![A chart of the imperfect in three boxes. The -ar box shows hablar: habl-aba, habl-abas, habl-aba, habl-ábamos, habl-aban. The -er and -ir box shows com-ía (and viv-ía), com-ías, com-ía, com-íamos, com-ían. The third box lists the only three irregular verbs: ser (era, eras, era, éramos, eran), ir (iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, iban) and ver (veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veían). A note at the bottom says the accents are on -ábamos and on every -ía form, and that the yo and él forms are the same.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Things to notice:

- Accents. In -ar verbs only the *nosotros* form has one: *jugábamos*. In -er and -ir verbs
  every form has one on the *í*: *tenía, teníamos*. It shows that *í* and *a* are separate
  syllables (*te-NÍ-a*).
- yo and él are the same: *yo jugaba, ella jugaba*. Add the pronoun or a name when it isn't
  clear who you mean.
- No stem changes. The verbs that change in the present don't change here: *quería, podía,
  dormía, pedía, jugaba, empezaba*. Irregular *yo* forms disappear too: *tenía, hacía, salía,
  conocía, decía*.
- Verbs with *me, te, se* keep the pronoun in front: *me portaba bien* (I behaved well), *nos
  levantábamos a las seis*.

### Only three irregular verbs

| | *ser* | *ir* | *ver* |
|---|---|---|---|
| yo | era | iba | veía |
| tú | eras | ibas | veías |
| él, ella, usted | era | iba | veía |
| nosotros | éramos | íbamos | veíamos |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | eran | iban | veían |

That's the whole list. *Ver* is only half irregular: it keeps the *e* of the infinitive (*veía*,
not *vía*).

- *Mi abuelo era muy alto.* — My grandfather was very tall.
- *Íbamos a la escuela a pie.* — We used to walk to school (go on foot).
- *Los sábados veíamos caricaturas.* — On Saturdays we watched cartoons.

### *había*: there was, there were

The imperfect of *hay* is *había*. It describes what existed or was there, and like *hay* and
*hubo* it never becomes plural:

- *Había un columpio en el patio.* — There was a swing in the yard.
- *En mi calle había muchos niños.* — There were a lot of children on my street.

Compare it with lesson 01's *hubo*: *había* sets the scene (what was there), while *hubo*
reports something that happened (*Hubo una fiesta*).

## Use 1: habits and repeated actions

The imperfect describes what used to happen again and again. Words of frequency go well with
it: *siempre, todos los días, cada verano, los domingos, a veces, normalmente, nunca*.

- *Cada verano íbamos a Veracruz.* — Every summer we went to Veracruz.
- *Los domingos comíamos en casa de mis abuelos.* — On Sundays we would eat at my grandparents'
  house.
- *En el recreo jugábamos a las escondidas.* — At recess we used to play hide-and-seek.
- *Mi mamá nos castigaba cuando no hacíamos la tarea.* — My mom used to punish us when we didn't
  do our homework.

Careful with English "would". In *On Sundays we would eat at my grandparents' house*, "would"
means "used to", so Spanish uses the imperfect (*comíamos*).

## Use 2: describing people, places and states

When you say what someone or something was like, or how someone felt, use the imperfect:

- *La casa era pequeña, pero tenía un patio con muchas plantas.* — The house was small, but it
  had a courtyard with lots of plants.
- *Mi maestra de primaria era muy estricta.* — My elementary school teacher was very strict.
- *Yo era muy travieso; mi hermana era más obediente.* — I was very naughty; my sister was more
  obedient.
- *De niña tenía miedo de los perros.* — As a girl I was afraid of dogs. (*el miedo* = fear)
- *Me gustaban mucho las caricaturas.* — I really liked cartoons.

## Use 3: age and time in the past

Age and clock time in the past are background, so they take the imperfect:

- *Tenía ocho años.* — I was eight.
- *Eran las tres de la tarde.* / *Era la una.* — It was three in the afternoon. / It was one
  o'clock.
- *Era sábado y hacía calor.* — It was Saturday and it was hot.

Often an event in the preterite happens against that background: *Tenía ocho años cuando nació
mi hermano* (I was eight when my brother was born). Lesson 03 is all about mixing the two.

## *soler*: usually, used to

*Soler* + an infinitive means "usually" in the present and "used to" in the imperfect. Its
present changes o → ue:

- *Suelo levantarme temprano.* — I usually get up early.
- *¿A qué hora sueles cenar?* — What time do you usually have dinner?
- *De niño solía jugar en la calle.* — As a child I used to play in the street.

*Solía jugar* means much the same as *jugaba*. Both are correct; in everyday conversation you'll
often hear the plain imperfect, or *normalmente*. *Soler* is used almost only in the present
and the imperfect, so those are the forms to learn.

## *antes* and *ahora*, *ya no*

*Antes* on its own is an adverb meaning "before, in the past, formerly". With the imperfect it
gives "used to", and it pairs naturally with *ahora* and the present:

- *Antes vivía en Puebla; ahora vivo en Mérida.* — I used to live in Puebla; now I live in Mérida.
- *Antes no había metro en esta ciudad.* — There didn't use to be a metro in this city.

Don't confuse it with A1's *antes de*, which needs a noun or an infinitive after it: *antes de
la cena, antes de salir*.

*Ya no* means "not anymore". It goes before the verb:

- *Ya no juego futbol, pero de niño jugaba todos los días.* — I don't play soccer anymore, but as a
  child I played every day.

*De niño* (*de niña* for a girl) means "as a child, when I was little", like *de joven* from
lesson 01. You'll also see *en mi infancia* (in my childhood).

## School in Mexico, then and now

In Mexico, children go to *la primaria* (elementary school) for six years and then to *la
secundaria* (middle school) for three. Many schools have a uniform (*el uniforme*). *El recreo*
is recess, usually spent in *el patio*, the schoolyard. *Un compañero* or *una compañera* is a
classmate. A child who *se porta mal* (misbehaves) gets *un castigo* (a punishment); one who
does pranks (*travesuras*) is *travieso*.

![A schoolyard at recess in front of a building marked ESCUELA PRIMARIA. On the left, a child sits on a swing (el columpio). A boy in a white shirt, tie and navy trousers (el uniforme) kicks a ball (la pelota). A girl holding a small doll (la muñeca) stands by a bench. A teacher (la maestra) stands near the school door. The ground is labeled el patio.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: *¿Cómo era tu escuela, abuela?*

Sofía is doing a school project on *las costumbres de antes* (the customs of the past). She
interviews her grandmother Carmen, who grew up in a small town in the 1960s.

> Sofía: Abuela, ¿cómo era tu escuela cuando eras niña?
>
> Carmen: Era una primaria muy pequeña. Había solo tres salones y un patio con dos columpios.
>
> Sofía: ¿Llevaban uniforme?
>
> Carmen: Sí. Las niñas llevábamos un vestido azul, y los niños, pantalón gris.
>
> Sofía: ¿Y qué hacían en el recreo?
>
> Carmen: Jugábamos a las escondidas o con la pelota. Yo no tenía muchos juguetes, solo una
> muñeca de trapo.
>
> Sofía: ¿Eras traviesa?
>
> Carmen: ¡Uy, mucho! Mi hermano y yo siempre hacíamos travesuras. La maestra era muy estricta
> y nos castigaba sin recreo.
>
> Sofía: ¿Y veían caricaturas?
>
> Carmen: No, en el pueblo no había televisión. Los domingos íbamos al cine de la plaza. Ese
> cine ya no existe.
>
> Sofía: Antes todo era más tranquilo, ¿no?
>
> Carmen: Sí, mija. Pero los niños también se portaban mal, ¡como ahora!

Translation:

> Sofía: Grandma, what was your school like when you were a girl?
>
> Carmen: It was a very small elementary school. There were only three classrooms and a yard
> with two swings.
>
> Sofía: Did you wear a uniform?
>
> Carmen: Yes. We girls wore a blue dress, and the boys wore gray trousers.
>
> Sofía: And what did you do at recess?
>
> Carmen: We played hide-and-seek or ball. I didn't have many toys, just a rag doll.
>
> Sofía: Were you naughty?
>
> Carmen: Oh, very! My brother and I were always getting up to mischief. The teacher was very
> strict and she punished us by keeping us in at recess.
>
> Sofía: And did you watch cartoons?
>
> Carmen: No, there was no television in the town. On Sundays we went to the movie theater on
> the square. That movie theater doesn't exist anymore.
>
> Sofía: Everything was calmer in the past, wasn't it?
>
> Carmen: Yes, sweetheart. But kids misbehaved too, just like now!

Notes: *de trapo* means "made of cloth" (*el trapo* = rag). *Existir* is "to exist". *Las niñas
llevábamos*: Spanish can say "we girls wore" with a noun and the *nosotros* form. *Mija* (from
*mi hija*) is an affectionate way to address a girl or young woman in Mexico. Every verb in the
dialogue is in the imperfect except *existe*, which is about the present.

## Pronunciation

- Stress the ending in -ar verbs: *ju-GA-ba, ju-GÁ-ba-mos*. The accent in *jugábamos* keeps the
  stress where the other forms have it.
- In -er and -ir verbs the *í* is stressed and is its own syllable: *te-NÍ-a, vi-VÍ-an*. Don't
  run it together as *ten-YA*.
- *veía* has three syllables: *ve-Í-a*. *iba* is *I-ba*, *era* is *E-ra* (a tap *r*).
- *Soler*: *SUE-lo, SUE-les*, but *so-LÍ-a* in the imperfect (no *ue*).

## Common mistakes

- Missing accents: ~~comia, teniamos~~ → *comía, teníamos*. And none in the other -ar forms:
  ~~jugába~~ → *jugaba*.
- Regular forms for the irregulars: ~~seía, ía, vía~~ → *era, iba, veía*.
- Translating "used to" with *usar* (to use): ~~Usaba jugar~~ → *Jugaba* or *Solía jugar*.
- A plural *había*: ~~Habían muchos niños~~ → *Había muchos niños*. (*Habían* is heard in casual
  speech in many countries, but the standard is *había*.)
- The imperfect for one finished event: *El sábado pasado iba al cine* means "Last Saturday I was
  going to the movies" (and something interrupted). For "I went", say *fui*.
- *De niño* for a woman: a woman says *De niña…*.
- *Soler* in the preterite: it has no useful preterite. Say *solía* or just the imperfect.

## Key points

- The imperfect describes what life was like: habits, descriptions, feelings, age and time.
- -ar: *-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -aban*. -er/-ir: *-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían*.
- No stem changes, and only three irregulars: *era, iba, veía*.
- *Había* = there was / there were (background); it doesn't become plural.
- *Soler* + infinitive: *suelo* = I usually, *solía* = I used to.
- *Antes* + imperfect vs *ahora* + present; *ya no* = not anymore; *de niño, de niña*.
- A single finished event still takes the preterite (lesson 03 puts the two together).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Telling a story: preterite or imperfect?
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You now have two past tenses. Lesson 01 gave you the preterite for events (*se mudó, se casó*);
lesson 02 gave you the imperfect for habits and descriptions (*vivía, era, había*). A real
story needs both at once: the scene, and what happened in it. This lesson shows how to choose
between them, how to join them with *cuando* and *mientras*, and how to tell an anecdote and
react to one. The theme is the small dramas people tell their friends about: a fall, a scare, a
stolen wallet, a crash on the way to work.

## Two jobs in one story

Think of a story as a scene in a movie. The imperfect is the set and the lighting: what time it
was, what the weather was like, who was there and how people felt. The preterite is the action:
each thing that happened, one after another, moving the plot forward.

> Era viernes y llovía. Yo estaba en la parada y había mucha gente. De repente, un perro se
> escapó de una casa y corrió a la calle. Un señor gritó, el perro se asustó y regresó a su
> casa.

It was Friday and it was raining. I was at the bus stop and there were a lot of people. Suddenly a dog
escaped from a house and ran into the street. A man shouted, the dog got scared and went back
to its house.

| imperfect: the scene | preterite: the events |
|---|---|
| *era viernes, llovía* | *se escapó, corrió* |
| *estaba en la parada* | *gritó* |
| *había mucha gente* | *se asustó, regresó* |

A quick test: if a verb answers "And then what happened?", it's the preterite. If it answers
"What was it like?" or "What was going on?", it's the imperfect.

![A story timeline. Above, a long shaded band labeled "imperfect: what was going on" contains the words caminaba por el parque, hacía frío, había poca gente. Below, a timeline with four points labeled "preterite: what happened, one event after another": vi a un hombre, me robó la bolsa, grité, se escapó. Arrows go up from each point into the band. At the top, the sentence Caminaba por el parque cuando vi a un hombre, with its translation.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## An action in progress, interrupted

The most common way the two meet: something was going on (imperfect) when something else
happened (preterite). *Cuando* joins them.

- *Caminaba por el parque cuando vi a un hombre muy raro.* — I was walking through the park when
  I saw a very strange man. (*raro* = strange)
- *Dormía cuando sonó el teléfono.* — I was sleeping when the phone rang. (*sonar* = to ring)
- *Cuando me caí, iba a la escuela.* — When I fell, I was going to school.

English often uses "was …ing" here, and so can Spanish: *Estaba caminando por el parque* means
the same as *Caminaba*. That form (the imperfect of *estar* + a verb ending in *-ando* or
*-iendo*) is lesson 09's; for now, just recognize it.

Watch how the choice changes the meaning after *cuando*:

- *Cuando llegué, mis amigos cenaban.* — When I arrived, my friends were having dinner (they
  had already started).
- *Cuando llegué, mis amigos cenaron.* — When I arrived, my friends had dinner (they started
  after I got there).

## *mientras*: two things at the same time

*Mientras* (while) usually takes the imperfect, because it describes something going on:

- *Mientras yo cocinaba, mi hermano ponía la mesa.* — While I was cooking, my brother was
  setting the table. (two backgrounds side by side)
- *Mientras esperaba el metro, me robaron la cartera.* — While I was waiting for the metro, my
  wallet was stolen. (background + event)

*Me robaron la cartera* is literally "they stole my wallet from me". Spanish often uses this
"they" form where English uses "was stolen".

## Words that push the story forward

Some words announce an event, so in a story the verb after them is usually in the preterite:
*de repente* (suddenly), *en ese momento* (at that moment), *entonces* (then), *luego, después*,
and *al final* (in the end). (*Entonces* can also mean "back then", and then it describes:
*Entonces vivíamos en Puebla*, We lived in Puebla back then.)

- *De repente oímos un ruido en la cocina.* — Suddenly we heard a noise in the kitchen.
- *En ese momento llegaron los bomberos.* — At that moment the firefighters arrived.
- *Al final, nadie se lastimó.* — In the end, nobody got hurt. (*lastimarse* = to get hurt)

Words of frequency (*siempre, todos los días, cada verano*) point to the imperfect, as you saw
in lesson 02. But a number of times or a closed period means the preterite: *Fui a Cancún tres
veces* (I went to Cancún three times), *Viví en Puebla cinco años* (I lived in Puebla for five
years, and then left).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Preterite or imperfect?
  accDescr: A decision chart for a past verb in a story. First question: is it the scene, meaning the time, weather, age, a description or a feeling as a state? If yes, use the imperfect, for example era, hacía frío, tenía miedo. If no, second question: was it a habit, something that happened again and again? If yes, imperfect, for example siempre íbamos. If no, third question: was it in progress when something else happened? If yes, imperfect, for example caminaba cuando vi. If no, it is a single event that moves the story forward: use the preterite, for example vi, gritó, se escapó.
  A["Is it the scene: time, weather, age, a description, a feeling (a state)?"] -- yes --> I1["Imperfect: era, hacía frío, tenía miedo"]
  A -- no --> B["A habit, something that happened again and again?"]
  B -- yes --> I2["Imperfect: siempre íbamos"]
  B -- no --> C["In progress when something else happened?"]
  C -- yes --> I3["Imperfect: caminaba cuando..."]
  C -- no --> P["A single event that moves the story: preterite (vi, gritó, se escapó)"]
```

A feeling can also be an event. *Tenía miedo* (I was afraid) describes a state, but a reaction
that happens at one moment of the story takes the preterite: *el perro se asustó* (the dog got
scared), *me asusté* (I got scared).

## Verbs that change their meaning

A few verbs mean something slightly different in each past, because the preterite shows a
single moment and the imperfect a state:

| verb | imperfect (a state) | preterite (a moment) |
|---|---|---|
| *conocer* | *conocía a Ana* = I knew Ana | *conocí a Ana* = I met Ana (for the first time) |
| *saber* | *sabía la verdad* = I knew the truth | *supe la verdad* = I found out the truth |
| *querer* | *quería ir* = I wanted to go | *quise ir* = I tried to go; *no quise ir* = I refused |
| *poder* | *podía nadar* = I could (was able to) swim | *pude salir* = I managed to get out; *no pude* = I failed |
| *tener que* | *tenía que trabajar* = I was supposed to work | *tuve que trabajar* = I had to work (and did) |

- *Conocí a mi esposo en una boda.* — I met my husband at a wedding.
- *Supe que me mentía.* — I found out he was lying to me. (*mentir* = to lie, *mintió* = he lied)
- *No quise decir la verdad.* — I refused to tell the truth.
- *Tenía que ir al banco, pero se me olvidó.* — I was supposed to go to the bank, but I forgot.
  (*se me olvidó* = I forgot, a set phrase)

You don't need to master this table now. Recognize it, and when a sentence in the preterite
seems odd, try the "moment" meaning.

## More words for small dramas

- *Hubo un choque en la avenida: un taxi chocó con un carro. Fue un accidente pequeño.* — There
  was a crash on the avenue: a taxi hit a car. It was a small accident.
- *Mientras dormíamos, hubo un incendio en el edificio de enfrente. Los bomberos llegaron muy
  rápido.* — While we were sleeping, there was a fire in the building across the street. The
  firefighters came very quickly.
- *Iba al banco cuando me encontré con mi maestra de primaria.* — I was going to the bank when I
  ran into my elementary school teacher.
- *Me apuré, pero perdí el autobús.* — I hurried, but I missed the bus.
- *Rompí la ventana sin querer.* — I broke the window by accident.
- *¿Qué ocurrió?* — What happened? (*ocurrir* is a slightly more formal *pasar*)

In Mexico *la bolsa* is a handbag (and also a pocket); *la cartera* is a wallet, also called *la
billetera*. *El testigo* (*la testigo* for a woman) is a witness.

## Telling an anecdote, and reacting

To start: *¿Sabes qué me pasó?* (You know what happened to me?), *Te cuento…* (Let me tell
you…), *Resulta que…* (So it turns out that…).

To move it along: *De repente…, En ese momento…, Entonces…*. To finish: *Al final…,
Afortunadamente… (Fortunately…), Desafortunadamente… (Unfortunately…)*.

The listener reacts:

| reaction | meaning |
|---|---|
| *¿En serio?* | Really? |
| *¡No me digas!* | No way! You're kidding! |
| *¡Qué susto!* | What a scare! |
| *¡Qué mala suerte!* | What bad luck! |
| *¡Qué bueno!* | Good! I'm glad. |
| *¿Y luego? ¿Y qué pasó?* | And then? And what happened? |

*¡No me digas!* is literally "Don't tell me!", but it's a set phrase showing surprise; learn it
as a chunk.

## Dialogue: *¿Sabes qué me pasó?*

Lupe tells her coworker Andrés about her trip to work.

> Lupe: ¿Sabes qué me pasó ayer?
>
> Andrés: No. ¿Qué te pasó?
>
> Lupe: Iba en el metro a la oficina. Había mucha gente y yo estaba muy cansada.
>
> Andrés: ¿Y?
>
> Lupe: Mientras buscaba mi celular en la bolsa, sentí algo. Me di la vuelta y vi a un muchacho
> con mi cartera en la mano.
>
> Andrés: ¡No me digas! ¿Te robó la cartera?
>
> Lupe: Sí. Grité "¡Un ladrón!", pero en ese momento las puertas se abrieron y el muchacho se
> escapó.
>
> Andrés: ¡Qué susto! ¿Y luego?
>
> Lupe: Corrió por el andén, pero se cayó en la escalera y la cartera salió volando. Una señora
> que fue testigo de todo me la trajo.
>
> Andrés: ¡Qué suerte! ¿Y el ladrón?
>
> Lupe: Se levantó y se fue. Pero yo ya tenía mi cartera, y eso era lo importante.

Translation:

> Lupe: You know what happened to me yesterday?
>
> Andrés: No. What happened to you?
>
> Lupe: I was going to the office on the metro. There were a lot of people and I was very tired.
>
> Andrés: And?
>
> Lupe: While I was looking for my phone in my bag, I felt something. I turned around and saw a
> young man with my wallet in his hand.
>
> Andrés: No way! Did he steal your wallet?
>
> Lupe: Yes. I shouted "Thief!", but at that moment the doors opened and the young man got away.
>
> Andrés: What a scare! And then?
>
> Lupe: He ran along the platform, but he fell on the stairs and the wallet went flying. A lady
> who had seen it all brought it back to me.
>
> Andrés: How lucky! And the thief?
>
> Lupe: He got up and left. But I had my wallet back, and that was what mattered.

Notes: *me di la vuelta* = I turned around; *el muchacho* = young man; *salir volando* = to go
flying. *Me la trajo* (she brought it to me) uses two pronouns together, which lesson 07 teaches;
take it as a chunk. *Fue testigo* = she was a witness (a finished role in the story, so the
preterite). *Eso era lo importante* = that was the important thing.

Look at the tenses: the scene (*iba, había, estaba, buscaba*) is in the imperfect; every step of
the action (*sentí, vi, grité, se abrieron, se escapó, corrió, se cayó*) is in the preterite.

## Pronunciation

- *se ca-YÓ* and *se ca-YE-ron*: the *y* sounds like the *y* in "yes". *Me ca-Í*, with the
  stress on the *í*.
- *la-DRÓN*, but *la-DRO-nes* with no written accent: the stress stays on the same syllable.
- Say *¡No me digas!* with rising surprise on *DI*, and *¡Qué SUS-to!* with the stress on *SUS*.
- *mientras* is two syllables: *MIEN-tras*.

## Common mistakes

- Telling a whole story in one past. With only the preterite it sounds like a list of facts;
  with only the imperfect nothing ever happens.
- The preterite for the scene: ~~Fue viernes y llovió cuando salí~~ → *Era viernes y llovía cuando
  salí.*
- The imperfect for the interrupting event: ~~Dormía cuando sonaba el teléfono~~ → *Dormía cuando
  sonó el teléfono.*
- *Conocer* in the wrong past: "I met Ana in 2019" is *Conocí a Ana en 2019*, not ~~Conocía~~.
- *Me caí* vs *me caía*: *Me caí* = I fell (once). *Me caía* = I kept falling, or I was falling.
- *Chocar* with a person: *chocar con* is mostly for vehicles and objects. For running into a
  friend, use *encontrarse con*: *Me encontré con Ana*.

## Key points

- Imperfect = the scene (time, weather, age, descriptions, feelings), habits, and actions in
  progress. Preterite = the events that move the story forward.
- Imperfect + *cuando* + preterite: *Caminaba por el parque cuando vi…*
- *Mientras* + imperfect for things going on at the same time.
- *De repente, en ese momento, entonces, al final* + preterite.
- *Conocí* = I met, *supe* = I found out, *no quise* = I refused, *pude* = I managed, *tuve que* =
  I had to (and did).
- Tell it: *¿Sabes qué me pasó?* React: *¡No me digas! ¡Qué susto! ¿Y luego?*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: How long and since when: the perfect, the preterite and time expressions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Spanish A1 introduced a third way to talk about the past: the **[[present perfect]]** (*el pretérito
perfecto*), made with *he, has, ha, hemos, han* + a **[[past participle]]**: *he comido* (I have
eaten), *¿Has estado en Oaxaca?* (Have you been to Oaxaca?). You used it for experiences and
with *ya* and *todavía no*.

This lesson gives you the fuller picture of how Mexicans divide the work between the perfect and
the preterite, which differs from Spain, and then teaches the other half of "time up to now":
how long you have been doing something and since when (*Hace tres años que vivo aquí, Vivo aquí
desde 2023*). The theme is starting a life in a new country or city: settling in, missing home,
and reaching your goals.

## The perfect and the preterite in Mexico

A quick reminder of the form: *haber* + the participle, which never changes (*ella ha comido,
ellas han comido*). Irregular participles include *hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito,
abierto, vuelto, roto*; *caído* (from *caer*) and *leído* keep an accent.

Mexican Spanish uses the preterite much more than the Spanish of Spain does. Here is the pattern
to produce, with what you'll read in books from Spain:

| situation | Mexico | Spain (to recognize) |
|---|---|---|
| a finished event, even today | *Hoy comí tarde.* | *Hoy he comido tarde.* |
| a finished event, finished time | *Ayer fui al banco.* | *Ayer fui al banco.* |
| "already" with *ya* | *¿Ya comiste? — Sí, ya comí.* | *¿Ya has comido?* |
| life experience up to now | *¿Has estado en Oaxaca?* | *¿Has estado en Oaxaca?* |
| "not yet" | *Todavía no he terminado.* (also *Todavía no termino*) | *Todavía no he terminado.* |
| something going on lately, up to now | *Últimamente he dormido mal.* | *Últimamente he dormido mal.* |

So in Mexico the perfect mainly does three jobs:

1. Experiences in your life so far, with or without *alguna vez, nunca, jamás*: *¿Has
   probado los chapulines?* (Have you tried grasshoppers?) *Nunca he visto la nieve.* (I've never
   seen snow; *la nieve* = snow.)
2. Not yet: *Todavía no he terminado* or *Aún no he terminado* (I still haven't finished).
   In Mexico you'll also hear it with the present: *Todavía no termino*, which means the same.
3. Something that has been happening and still is: *Últimamente he trabajado mucho* (Lately
   I've been working a lot). Linguists who study Mexican Spanish note that its perfect tends to
   describe situations that reach into the present like this.

Everything finished takes the preterite, including this morning and *ya*: *Esta mañana fui al
banco*, *Ya llegué* (I'm here, I've arrived). Spain would often use the perfect for both.
Neither is wrong; they are two standards. Produce the Mexican one, and recognize the other when
you read texts from Spain, including some of the DELE exam's.

## *aún, jamás* and words for recent time

- *Aún* means the same as *todavía* (still, yet): *Aún no he comido* (I still haven't eaten),
  *Aún vivo con mis papás* (I still live with my parents). Without the accent, *aun* means
  "even", which you'll meet in reading.
- *Jamás* is a stronger *nunca*. Like *nunca*, it goes before the verb, or after it with *no*:
  *Jamás he visto algo así* = *No he visto algo así jamás* (I've never ever seen anything like
  it).
- *Últimamente* (lately) goes with the perfect or the present: *Últimamente he dormido poco*.
- *Hace poco* (a short time ago) and *recientemente* (recently) point to a finished moment, so
  in Mexico they usually take the preterite: *Hace poco me mudé* (I moved a little while ago).
- *Hoy en día* (nowadays) and *actualmente* (currently) go with the present. Careful:
  *actualmente* is a false friend. It means "at present", not "actually" (that's *en realidad*).
  *Actualmente vivo en Querétaro* = I currently live in Querétaro.

## How long? *hace … que*, *desde* and *desde hace*

English says "I've been living here for three years", in a perfect form. Spanish uses the
present, because you still live here. There are three ways to say it:

| pattern | example | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *hace* + time + *que* + present | *Hace tres años que vivo aquí.* | I've been living here for three years. |
| present + *desde hace* + time | *Vivo aquí desde hace tres años.* | (the same) |
| present + *desde* + a starting point | *Vivo aquí desde 2023.* | I've lived here since 2023. |

- *Desde hace* takes a length of time (*tres años, seis meses, mucho tiempo*).
- *Desde* alone takes a point in time (*2023, marzo, el lunes, la boda*).
- The negative works the same way: *Hace un año que no veo a mis papás* (I haven't seen my
  parents for a year).

To ask:

- *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que vives aquí?* — How long have you been living here?
- *¿Desde cuándo estudias español?* — Since when have you been studying Spanish? / How long have
  you been studying Spanish?

Don't mix this up with A1's *hace* = ago, which goes with the preterite and a finished event:

- *Llegué hace tres años.* — I arrived three years ago. (finished)
- *Hace tres años que vivo aquí.* — I've been living here for three years. (still true)

![A timeline from 2022 to 2026, with "today: 2026". A point at 2023 is labeled llegué and a point at 2026 is labeled hoy; a bracket between them says tres años. Below, four colored rows: Llegué hace tres años (a point in the past: hace = ago, with the preterite); Vivo aquí desde 2023 (desde + the starting point, with the present); Vivo aquí desde hace tres años (desde hace + the length of time, with the present); Hace tres años que vivo aquí (hace + time + que + the present).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: hace, desde or desde hace?
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question: is the situation still true now? If no, it is finished: use the preterite with hace meaning ago, as in Llegué hace tres años. If yes, second question: are you giving a starting point such as 2023, marzo or el lunes? If yes, use the present with desde: Vivo aquí desde 2023. If you are giving a length of time instead, use the present with desde hace, or hace plus the time plus que plus the present: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años, or Hace tres años que vivo aquí.
  A["Is it still true now?"] -- no --> AGO["Finished: preterite + hace (ago). Llegué hace tres años."]
  A -- yes --> B["Are you giving a starting point (2023, marzo, el lunes)?"]
  B -- yes --> D["Present + desde: Vivo aquí desde 2023."]
  B -- "no, a length of time" --> E["Present + desde hace, or hace + time + que + present: Vivo aquí desde hace tres años."]
```

You'll also hear one more way, with *llevar* + time: *Llevo tres años en México* (I've been in
Mexico for three years). Recognize it for now; you don't need to produce it.

## Settling in: words for a new life

- *Cuando llegué, todo era diferente. La diferencia más grande era el clima.* — When I arrived,
  everything was different. The biggest difference was the climate.
- *Al principio no fue fácil, pero me adapté.* — At first it wasn't easy, but I adapted.
- *Ya me acostumbré a comer tarde.* — I've gotten used to eating late now.
- *Extraño a mis amigos y extraño la comida de mi país.* — I miss my friends and I miss the food
  from my country. (*a* before a person)
- *Mi vida cambió mucho.* — My life changed a lot.
- *Intenté aprender español en mi país, pero aquí logré hablar con la gente.* — I tried to learn
  Spanish in my country, but here I managed to talk to people.
- *Por primera vez tengo amigos extranjeros.* — For the first time I have foreign friends.
- *La última vez que fui a mi país, todo me pareció muy caro.* — The last time I went home,
  everything seemed very expensive to me. (*me pareció* = it seemed to me)
- *Mi meta es encontrar un trabajo mejor. Mi sueño es abrir un restaurante.* — My goal is to find
  a better job. My dream is to open a restaurant.
- *En el pasado, pocos extranjeros vivían aquí.* — In the past, few foreigners lived here.

*Último* (last) usually goes before its noun: *el último día, la última vez*. For "last week" or
"last year" keep using *pasado* (*la semana pasada*). *El sueño* is a dream, and also
sleepiness: *Tengo sueño* (I'm sleepy). *La oportunidad* is an opportunity or chance.

## Text: a podcast interview

Paola hosts a podcast called *Nuevos en México* (New in Mexico). Today she talks with Mark, an
American engineer who lives in Querétaro.

> Paola: Mark, ¿cuánto tiempo hace que vives en Querétaro?
>
> Mark: Hace tres años que vivo aquí. Llegué en 2023 por una oportunidad de trabajo.
>
> Paola: ¿Y ya te acostumbraste a la vida en México?
>
> Mark: Más o menos. Me adapté rápido al trabajo, pero todavía no me acostumbro a la comida tan
> picante.
>
> Paola: ¿Has viajado mucho por el país?
>
> Mark: Sí, he estado en Oaxaca, en Chiapas y en Yucatán, pero aún no conozco el norte. La
> última vez que viajé, fui a Mérida con unos compañeros del trabajo.
>
> Paola: ¿Extrañas algo de tu país?
>
> Mark: Extraño a mi familia, claro. Hace un año que no veo a mis papás, pero hablamos por
> teléfono casi todos los días.
>
> Paola: ¿Y cuál es tu meta ahora?
>
> Mark: Actualmente estudio español con una maestra, desde hace seis meses. Mi sueño es aprobar
> el DELE B1. Hace poco tuve mi primera conversación de una hora en español con mi jefe. ¡Jamás
> pensé que iba a poder!
>
> Paola: ¡Felicidades, Mark! Hoy en día muchos extranjeros viven en Querétaro. ¿Qué es lo más
> importante para adaptarse?
>
> Mark: Hablar con la gente todos los días. Al principio da miedo, pero cada día es más fácil.

Translation:

> Paola: Mark, how long have you been living in Querétaro?
>
> Mark: I've been living here for three years. I came in 2023 for a job opportunity.
>
> Paola: And have you gotten used to life in Mexico yet?
>
> Mark: More or less. I adapted to the job quickly, but I still haven't gotten used to such spicy
> food.
>
> Paola: Have you traveled around the country much?
>
> Mark: Yes, I've been to Oaxaca, Chiapas and Yucatán, but I still haven't been to the north. The
> last time I traveled, I went to Mérida with some coworkers.
>
> Paola: Do you miss anything from your country?
>
> Mark: I miss my family, of course. I haven't seen my parents for a year, but we talk on the
> phone almost every day.
>
> Paola: And what's your goal now?
>
> Mark: I'm currently studying Spanish with a teacher, for the last six months. My dream is to
> pass the DELE B1. Not long ago I had my first hour-long conversation in Spanish with my boss. I
> never thought I'd be able to!
>
> Paola: Congratulations, Mark! Nowadays lots of foreigners live in Querétaro. What's the most
> important thing for adapting?
>
> Mark: Talking to people every day. At first it's scary, but every day it gets easier.

Notes: *¿Ya te acostumbraste?* and *todavía no me acostumbro* are the Mexican pattern: *ya* +
preterite, and *todavía no* + present for "not yet". *Aún no conozco el norte* = I haven't been
to the north yet (*conocer* a place = to have been there). *Iba a poder* = "was going to be
able to". *Da miedo* = it's scary (*el miedo* = fear). *Lo más importante* = the most important
thing.

## Pronunciation

- *a-ÚN* has two syllables; the accent separates *a* and *u*. *Aun* without the accent is one
  syllable.
- *ja-MÁS*, with the stress at the end.
- Long adverbs in *-mente* keep the stress of the adjective and add a second one: *ÚL-ti-ma-MEN-te,
  ac-TUAL-MEN-te, re-CIEN-te-MEN-te*.
- *extrañar*: *ex-tra-ÑAR*, with *x* as "ks" and *ñ* as in "canyon".

## Common mistakes

- A word-for-word "have been …ing for": *He estado viviendo aquí por tres años* is understood,
  but it sounds translated from English. Say *Vivo aquí desde hace tres años* or *Hace tres años
  que vivo aquí*.
- *Desde* with a length of time: ~~desde tres años~~ → *desde hace tres años*.
- *Hace … que* with the preterite when it's still true: ~~Hace tres años que viví aquí~~ → *Hace
  tres años que vivo aquí*.
- *Actualmente* for "actually": ~~Actualmente, no me gusta~~ → *En realidad, no me gusta*.
- *Extrañar* without *a* before a person: ~~Extraño mi hermana~~ → *Extraño a mi hermana*.
- A double negative with *jamás* first: ~~Jamás no he ido~~ → *Jamás he ido* or *No he ido jamás*.
- *Ya he comido* isn't wrong, but in Mexico it sounds like Spain. Mexicans usually say *Ya comí*.

## Key points

- In Mexico, finished events take the preterite, even today and with *ya*: *Hoy comí, ¿Ya
  comiste?* Spain often uses the perfect for these.
- The perfect is for experiences (*¿Has estado…?*), "not yet" (*Todavía no he ido*), and what
  has been going on lately (*Últimamente he trabajado mucho*).
- *Aún* = *todavía*; *jamás* = a stronger *nunca*.
- "I've been … for/since" uses the present: *Hace tres años que vivo aquí*, *Vivo aquí desde
  hace tres años*, *Vivo aquí desde 2023*. Ask *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que…?* or *¿Desde cuándo…?*
- *Hace* + time + preterite = ago: *Llegué hace tres años*.
- *Actualmente* = currently, not "actually".

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Mexico's history told in the past tenses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 03 showed that a story needs two pasts: the imperfect for the scene and the preterite for
the events. History is the biggest story of all, and history books, museum signs and
documentaries use exactly the same system. This honors lesson tells five moments of Mexican
history, from the founding of Tenochtitlan to the Revolution, in short texts you can read with
the grammar of this module.

A warning before you start: this is one simplified telling, written for language learners.
Each event took years, involved many people and is still discussed by historians, and some
dates (especially the oldest) are traditional rather than exact. The dates used here were checked
against Mexican government and university sources, which are listed in the course notes. If you
want the history itself, read a history book; here the history is a way to practice the past.

## How history texts use the two pasts

- Imperfect for the situation: what things were like, who ruled, how people lived. *La ciudad
  era enorme. Había mercados y templos. Mucha gente era pobre.*
- Preterite for the events, usually with a date: *En 1519 llegaron los españoles. La guerra
  duró once años.* A long period that is now over, seen as a whole, also takes the preterite:
  *México fue parte de la Nueva España durante tres siglos.*
- *Hubo* reports something that happened (*hubo una guerra*), *había* what existed
  (*había muchos pueblos indígenas*).

You'll also meet a third option in timelines, school books and headlines: the present, used
for the past to make it vivid (*En 1521 cae Tenochtitlan*, In 1521 Tenochtitlan falls). The
timeline below uses it. When you retell history yourself, use the two pasts.

Centuries are written in Roman numerals and read as ordinary numbers: *el siglo XVI* = *el siglo
dieciséis* (the sixteenth century, the 1500s), *el siglo XX* = *el siglo veinte*. Full dates
are read *el trece de agosto de mil quinientos veintiuno*.

![A timeline titled "Mexico from Tenochtitlan to the Revolution (not to scale)". Seven points: 1325 se funda Tenochtitlan; 1519 llegan los españoles; 1521 cae Tenochtitlan; 1810 el Grito de Dolores; 1821 termina la guerra de Independencia; 1910 empieza la Revolución; 1917 nueva Constitución. Below, a bar from 1521 to 1821 labeled la Nueva España, and a bar after 1821 labeled México independiente. A note says this is one simplified telling.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 1. Tenochtitlan

> Los mexicas, también llamados aztecas, llegaron al valle de México desde el norte. Según su
> tradición, buscaban una señal: un águila sobre un nopal. Encontraron la señal en una isla del
> lago de Texcoco y allí fundaron su ciudad, Tenochtitlan. La fecha tradicional es 1325. En el
> siglo XV, Tenochtitlan era la capital de un imperio muy grande. La ciudad tenía templos,
> mercados y canales, y mucha gente viajaba en canoa.

The Mexica, also called the Aztecs, came to the Valley of Mexico from the north. According to
their tradition, they were looking for a sign: an eagle on a cactus. They found the sign on an
island in Lake Texcoco and founded their city there, Tenochtitlan. The traditional date is 1325.
In the fifteenth century, Tenochtitlan was the capital of a very large empire. The city had
temples, markets and canals, and many people traveled by canoe.

*El águila* is an eagle (feminine, with *el* like *el agua*) and *el nopal* is the prickly-pear
cactus; the eagle on the cactus is on Mexico's flag today.

## 2. The conquest

> En 1519, unos barcos españoles llegaron a la costa del golfo de México. Hernán Cortés y sus
> soldados caminaron hacia Tenochtitlan. Muchos pueblos indígenas, enemigos de los mexicas, como
> los tlaxcaltecas, lucharon junto a los españoles. El 8 de noviembre de 1519, Cortés y el
> gobernante mexica, Moctezuma, se encontraron en la ciudad. Moctezuma murió en 1520; las
> fuentes no están de acuerdo sobre cómo. Ese mismo año llegó una epidemia de viruela, una
> enfermedad que los indígenas no conocían, y murieron muchas personas. Después de una guerra
> muy dura, el último gobernante, Cuauhtémoc, se rindió el 13 de agosto de 1521, y la ciudad
> cayó. Así, los españoles y sus aliados conquistaron Tenochtitlan.

In 1519 some Spanish ships arrived on the coast of the Gulf of Mexico. Hernán Cortés and his
soldiers walked toward Tenochtitlan. Many Indigenous peoples who were enemies of the Mexica,
such as the Tlaxcalans, fought alongside the Spanish. On 8 November 1519, Cortés and the Mexica
ruler, Moctezuma, met in the city. Moctezuma died in 1520; the sources don't agree on how. That
same year an epidemic of smallpox arrived, a disease the Indigenous people didn't know, and many
people died. After a very hard war, the last ruler, Cuauhtémoc, surrendered on 13 August 1521,
and the city fell. That is how the Spanish and their allies conquered Tenochtitlan.

New words in passing: *el golfo* (gulf), *el soldado* (soldier), *el gobernante* (ruler), *junto a* (alongside), *la fuente* (source, also
"fountain"), *la viruela* (smallpox), *la enfermedad* (disease, from lesson 20), *los aliados* (allies).

## 3. New Spain

> Después de la conquista, durante tres siglos, México fue parte del virreinato de la Nueva España. Sobre las ruinas de
> Tenochtitlan, los españoles construyeron la Ciudad de México. El rey de España mandaba desde
> muy lejos, y un virrey gobernaba en su nombre. La sociedad era muy desigual: los españoles
> tenían el poder y la tierra, y los indígenas trabajaban para ellos. Pero en esos siglos
> también nacieron muchas cosas que hoy son mexicanas: comidas, fiestas y palabras que mezclan
> lo indígena y lo español.

After the conquest, for three centuries, Mexico was part of the viceroyalty of New Spain. On the ruins of
Tenochtitlan, the Spanish built Mexico City. The king of Spain ruled from very far away, and a
viceroy governed in his name. Society was very unequal: the Spanish had the power and the land,
and the Indigenous people worked for them. But in those centuries many things that are Mexican
today were also born: foods, festivals and words that mix the Indigenous and the Spanish.

*Mandar* here means "to be in charge" (you know it as "to send"). *Las ruinas* = the ruins. *Desigual* = unequal; *el
poder* = power; *lo indígena, lo español* = what is Indigenous, what is Spanish.

## 4. Independence

> El 16 de septiembre de 1810, en el pueblo de Dolores, el sacerdote Miguel Hidalgo llamó a la
> gente a luchar contra el gobierno español. Ese llamado se conoce como el Grito de Dolores.
> Miles de personas se unieron a su ejército. En 1811 las autoridades españolas capturaron a
> Hidalgo y lo fusilaron, pero la guerra continuó. En 1821, el militar Agustín de Iturbide y el insurgente
> Vicente Guerrero se pusieron de acuerdo, y el 27 de septiembre de 1821 su ejército entró a la
> Ciudad de México. La guerra de Independencia duró once años.

On 16 September 1810, in the town of Dolores, the priest Miguel Hidalgo called on the people to
fight against the Spanish government. That call is known as the Grito de Dolores (the Cry of
Dolores). Thousands of people joined his army. In 1811 the Spanish authorities captured Hidalgo
and executed him, but the war went on. In 1821 the army officer Agustín de Iturbide and the rebel Vicente
Guerrero reached an agreement, and on 27 September 1821 their army entered Mexico City. The War
of Independence lasted eleven years.

*Lo fusilaron* = they executed him (by firing squad). *Se unieron* = joined; *el militar* = army
officer; *se pusieron de acuerdo* = reached an agreement.

Mexico celebrates its independence on 16 September, the anniversary of the Grito, not on the
date the war ended. On the night of the 15th, the president repeats the Grito from the balcony of
the Palacio Nacional, and towns all over the country do the same in their main squares.

## 5. The Revolution

> A principios del siglo XX, Porfirio Díaz gobernaba México desde hacía unos treinta años. Había
> trenes nuevos y fábricas, pero la mayoría de la gente era pobre y muy pocas familias tenían
> gran parte de la tierra. En 1910, Francisco I. Madero llamó a la gente a levantarse en armas el
> 20 de noviembre: así empezó la Revolución. Díaz renunció en mayo de 1911, pero la lucha no terminó: Emiliano Zapata
> luchó en el sur por la tierra de los campesinos, y Francisco Villa ganó batallas importantes
> en el norte. El 5 de febrero de 1917, el país tuvo una nueva Constitución, que con muchos
> cambios sigue vigente hoy.

At the start of the twentieth century, Porfirio Díaz had been ruling Mexico for about thirty
years. There were new trains and factories, but most people were poor and very few families had
a large part of the land. In 1910 Francisco I. Madero called on the people to rise up in arms on 20
November: that is how the Revolution began. Díaz resigned in May 1911, but the fighting didn't end: Emiliano Zapata fought in the
south for the peasants' land, and Francisco Villa won important battles in the north. On 5
February 1917 the country got a new Constitution, which, with many changes, is still in force
today.

*Gobernaba desde hacía unos treinta años* is lesson 04's *desde hace* moved into the past: "had
been ruling for about thirty years". *Levantarse en armas* = to rise up in arms; *renunciar* = to
resign (lesson 17); *el campesino* = peasant, farmworker; *sigue vigente* = is still in force.
Historians don't agree on when the Revolution ended: officially in 1917 with the Constitution,
but some place the end in 1920 and others even later.

### Example 1: background or event?

Take five verbs from part 5 and decide why each tense was used.

1. *gobernaba*: imperfect. It describes the situation at the start of the century, a state that
   had lasted for years.
2. *Había trenes nuevos*: imperfect *había*, because it says what existed (background).
3. *llamó*: preterite. Madero's call is one event with a date (1910).
4. *renunció*: preterite. A single event: Díaz resigned in May 1911.
5. *tuvo una nueva Constitución*: preterite. The moment the country got it (5 February 1917).

Now try *la mayoría de la gente era pobre*: imperfect, a description of how things were.

### Example 2: from a timeline to a story

Timelines give bare facts in the present or as nouns. Turn them into a story by choosing a past
for each piece.

Timeline notes: *1325: fundación de Tenochtitlan. La ciudad está en una isla. 1521: Cuauhtémoc
se rinde.*

1. A founding is an event with a date: *En 1325 los mexicas fundaron Tenochtitlan.*
2. Where the city was is a description: *La ciudad estaba en una isla.*
3. The surrender is an event: *En 1521 Cuauhtémoc se rindió.* (*rendirse* changes like *pedir*:
   *me rindo*, *se rindió, se rindieron*)

Put together, with a linking word: *En 1325 los mexicas fundaron Tenochtitlan. La ciudad estaba
en una isla. Casi dos siglos después, en 1521, Cuauhtémoc se rindió y la ciudad cayó.*

### Example 3: reading dates aloud

- *1325*: *mil trescientos veinticinco*
- *el 16 de septiembre de 1810*: *el dieciséis de septiembre de mil ochocientos diez*
- *el siglo XIX*: *el siglo diecinueve* (the 1800s)
- *a principios del siglo XX*: at the beginning of the twentieth century; *a finales del siglo
  XV*: at the end of the fifteenth century.

## Common mistakes

- The imperfect for dated events: ~~En 1521 la ciudad caía~~ → *En 1521 la ciudad cayó*.
- The preterite for long-lasting background: *Tenochtitlan fue una ciudad enorme* isn't wrong
  (it sums up its whole existence), but when you are setting the scene before an event, use
  *era*: *Tenochtitlan era una ciudad enorme cuando llegaron los españoles*.
- Reading centuries as ordinals: *el siglo XVI* is *el siglo dieciséis*, not ~~el siglo
  decimosexto~~ in everyday speech.
- Mixing the historical present and the past in one paragraph. Choose one; in your own writing,
  choose the past.
- Plural *hubo*: ~~hubieron muchas batallas~~ → *hubo muchas batallas*.

## Key points

- History uses the same system as any story: imperfect for situations (*era, había, gobernaba*),
  preterite for dated events (*llegaron, cayó, se rindió, renunció*).
- A whole finished period can take the preterite: *fue parte de la Nueva España durante tres
  siglos*.
- Timelines and headlines often use the present for the past; recognize it.
- Centuries: *el siglo XVI* = *el siglo dieciséis*.
- Five moments: Tenochtitlan (traditionally 1325), the fall of the city (13 August 1521), New
  Spain (1521–1821), the War of Independence (1810–1821), the Revolution (from 1910;
  Constitution of 1917). This is one simplified telling.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: It had already happened: había + participle
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 03 you told stories with two pasts: the imperfect for the scene and the preterite for
the events. Sometimes a story needs to step one stage further back: "When I got to the movie
theater, the film had already started." The film started before the moment you are telling,
and English marks that with "had" + a past participle.

Spanish does the same with the **[[pluperfect]]** (*el pretérito pluscuamperfecto*): *había* + a
participle. *Cuando llegué al cine, la película ya había empezado.* Spanish programs that follow
the Instituto Cervantes levels usually teach the pluperfect at B1, so this lesson is a preview: learn to recognize it
in reading and to use it in simple sentences. It isn't one of the app's conjugation drills, but
you already practice both of its pieces there: *había* is the imperfect of *haber*, and the
participles are the ones from the perfect.

## The forms

The pluperfect is the present perfect (lesson 04) with *haber* moved into the imperfect:

| | *haber* (imperfect) | + participle |
|---|---|---|
| yo | había | llegado |
| tú | habías | comido |
| él, ella, usted | había | salido |
| nosotros | habíamos | visto |
| (vosotros) | (habíais) | (hecho) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | habían | dicho |

- The participle never changes: *ella había llegado, ellas habían llegado*.
- The irregular participles are the ones you know: *hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto,
  vuelto, roto, muerto*, and *descubierto* (from *descubrir*, to discover).
- Normally nothing goes between *había* and the participle. *No*, pronouns and *ya* usually go in front:
  *No había comido. Se había ido. Ya habíamos salido.* (I hadn't eaten. He had left. We had
  already gone out.)
- Here *habían* is plural when the subject is plural (*Mis amigos habían salido*). That's
  different from lesson 02's *había* meaning "there was / there were", which never changes.

## When to use it: before another past moment

![A timeline. At 8:00, la película empezó. At 8:20, llegué al cine. At the right, ahora. A curved arrow points back from 8:20 to 8:00, labeled "looking back from 8:20". At the top: Cuando llegué al cine, la película ya había empezado. At the bottom: preterite = the past moment you are telling; había + participle = before that moment.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The preterite sets a moment in the past; the pluperfect looks back from that moment:

- *Cuando llegamos a la estación, el tren ya había salido.* — When we got to the station, the
  train had already left.
- *Nunca había visto el mar antes de ese viaje.* — I had never seen the sea before that trip.
- *Me enteré de que mi prima se había casado.* — I found out that my cousin had gotten married.
- *Llegué a las diez, pero para entonces todos se habían ido.* — I arrived at ten, but by then
  everyone had left.

Compare two sentences that differ only in the tense:

- *Cuando llegué, la película empezó.* — When I arrived, the film started (it started then).
- *Cuando llegué, la película ya había empezado.* — When I arrived, the film had already started.

When the order is already clear, because you tell things in order or use *antes de* or
*después de*, Spanish speakers often don't need the pluperfect: *Perdí el autobús y llegué
tarde* is perfectly natural. Use the pluperfect when you jump back in time.

### Words that go with it

| word | example |
|---|---|
| *ya* (already) | *Ya habían cerrado la tienda.* — They had already closed the shop. |
| *todavía no, aún no* (not yet) | *Todavía no había terminado.* — I hadn't finished yet. |
| *nunca* (never before) | *Nunca había comido mole.* — I had never eaten mole. |
| *para entonces* (by then) | *Para entonces, el avión ya había despegado.* — By then the plane had already taken off. |
| *el día anterior, la noche anterior* | *La noche anterior había llovido.* — It had rained the night before. |

### After "I found out that…"

Verbs of finding out often lead into the pluperfect, because what you found out had happened
earlier: *enterarse de que* (to find out, to hear), *descubrir que* (to discover), *darse cuenta
de que* (to realize, from A1 honors), *saber* in the preterite (*supe que*).

- *Me di cuenta de que había dejado las llaves en casa.* — I realized I had left my keys at home.
  (*dejar* = to leave something)
- *Descubrí que alguien había usado mi boleto.* — I discovered that someone had used my ticket.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: building the form

Put *ver* into the pluperfect for *nosotros*.

1. *Haber* in the imperfect, *nosotros*: *habíamos*.
2. The participle of *ver* is irregular: *visto*.
3. Result: *habíamos visto*. *Nunca habíamos visto tanta gente.* (We had never seen so many
   people.)

Now *irse* for *ellos*: the pronoun goes first, then *habían*, then *ido*: *se habían ido*.

### Example 2: preterite or pluperfect?

*Cuando Ana llegó a la fiesta, Luis ya (irse).* Which happened first?

1. The moment being told is Ana's arrival (preterite *llegó*).
2. Luis left before that moment, and *ya* (already) confirms it.
3. So *irse* goes into the pluperfect: *Luis ya se había ido*.

Compare *Cuando Ana llegó a la fiesta, Luis (saludar) a todos.* Here nothing points back: Luis
greeted everyone after she arrived, so the preterite *saludó* fits. (*saludar* = to greet)

### Example 3: joining two sentences

*Llegué al aeropuerto a las diez. El avión despegó a las nueve y media.* Tell it from the moment
you arrived:

*Cuando llegué al aeropuerto, el avión ya había despegado.* The arrival stays in the preterite;
the earlier take-off moves into the pluperfect.

## Story: *Un día de mala suerte*

> El viernes pasado fue un día de mala suerte para Diego. La noche anterior se había acostado
> muy tarde, y por la mañana el despertador no sonó.
>
> Tenía un vuelo a Monterrey por trabajo, pero no llegó a tiempo. Cuando por fin llegó a la
> puerta, el avión ya había despegado. Nadie le había avisado del cambio de puerta.
>
> Diego regresó a la ciudad y llamó a su hermana Paty. Decidieron ir al cine, a la función de las
> siete, pero cuando llegaron, los boletos ya se habían agotado.
>
> Entonces buscaron un restaurante nuevo que Paty había visto en internet, pero se perdieron en
> el centro. Para entonces, Diego estaba cansado y de muy mal humor.
>
> Por la noche, cuando abrió la puerta de su casa, encontró a toda su familia y a sus amigos.
> "¡Sorpresa!", gritaron. ¡Era su cumpleaños, y con tantos problemas, Diego lo había olvidado!
>
> Más tarde se enteró de que Paty sabía todo: su mamá le había pedido tener a Diego fuera de
> casa todo el día. Y descubrió algo más: su papá había preparado su pastel favorito. Al final,
> Diego pensó: "No fue un día de mala suerte. Fue un día perfecto".

Translation:

> Last Friday was a day of bad luck for Diego. The night before he had gone to bed very late, and
> in the morning the alarm clock didn't go off.
>
> He had a flight to Monterrey for work, but he didn't get there on time. When he finally got to
> the gate, the plane had already taken off. Nobody had told him about the gate change.
>
> Diego went back to the city and called his sister Paty. They decided to go to the movies, to the
> seven o'clock showing, but when they arrived, the tickets had already sold out.
>
> Then they looked for a new restaurant that Paty had seen online, but they got lost downtown. By
> then, Diego was tired and in a very bad mood.
>
> That night, when he opened the door of his house, he found his whole family and his friends
> there. "Surprise!" they shouted. It was his birthday, and with so many problems, Diego had
> forgotten it!
>
> Later he found out that Paty knew everything: their mom had asked her to keep Diego out of the
> house all day. And he discovered something else: his dad had made his favorite cake. In the
> end, Diego thought: "It wasn't a day of bad luck. It was a perfect day."

Notes: *sonar* = to ring, to go off; *la puerta* here is the gate
at the airport; *de mal humor* = in a bad mood; *el pastel* = cake (lesson 23's word); *se
perdieron* = they got lost (*perderse*, a word from honors lesson 08h2). *Se
habían agotado*: *agotarse* = to sell out, and *agotado* is the adjective (*Los boletos están
agotados*). *Lo había olvidado*: *lo* = it (lesson 05). *Le había pedido tener a Diego fuera* =
had asked her to keep Diego out.

Every *había* + participle in the story points to something that happened before the moment
being told: the late night before the alarm, the take-off before Diego reached the gate, the
sold-out tickets before they arrived, the restaurant Paty had seen before that day, and the plan
made before the surprise.

## Common mistakes

- A regular participle for an irregular verb: ~~había hacido, habían ponido~~ → *había hecho,
  habían puesto*.
- Making the participle agree: ~~Las tiendas habían cerradas~~ → *Las tiendas habían cerrado*.
- Splitting *había* and the participle: ~~Había ya salido~~ is unusual; say *Ya había salido*.
- A plural for "there was" by analogy: in *Había muchos boletos*, *había* means "there were" and
  stays singular; in *Habían vendido los boletos* (they had sold the tickets), *habían* is the
  pluperfect and agrees with "they".
- Using the pluperfect for events told in order: ~~Me había levantado, me había bañado y había
  desayunado~~ for a simple sequence → *Me levanté, me bañé y desayuné*.

## Key points

- Pluperfect = *había, habías, había, habíamos, habían* + participle: *había llegado, habían
  visto*.
- It describes something that happened before another past moment: *Cuando llegué, la película
  ya había empezado*.
- Common partners: *ya, todavía no, nunca, para entonces, el día anterior*; and after *me
  enteré de que, descubrí que, me di cuenta de que*.
- When events are told in order, the preterite is enough.
- It's a B1 form: recognize it everywhere, use it in simple sentences. No drill of its own.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: It, him, her, them: direct object pronouns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 gave you the past tenses for telling stories. This module is about people, and about the small words that keep a conversation short: "it", "him", "her", "them". In English you don't say "I charged the phone and then I turned on the phone"; you say "I charged it and turned it on". Spanish does the same with *lo, la, los, las*, but it puts them in a different place, and that place is what this lesson is mostly about.

You already know some of these words as chunks. In A1 you bargained with *¿Me lo deja en trescientos?*, apologized with *Lo siento*, and put reflexive pronouns before the verb or on the end of an infinitive (*Me voy a bañar / Voy a bañarme*). The same two positions work for every pronoun in this module. The theme is phones, computers and the internet, where "it" comes up all the time.

## The words: phones, computers and the internet

![A smartphone and a laptop side by side, each part labeled. On the phone, the battery symbol at the top corner is labeled la batería. On the laptop, the screen is labeled la pantalla. A cable runs from the phone to a wall plug, labeled el cargador. On the laptop, the keys are labeled el teclado. A pair of headphones lies in front, labeled los audífonos.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Things | | Actions | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *la pantalla* | screen | *prender* | to turn on |
| *el teclado* | keyboard | *apagar* | to turn off |
| *la batería* | battery | *cargar* | to charge (a phone); to carry |
| *el cargador* | charger | *descargar* | to download |
| *los audífonos* | headphones, earbuds | *instalar* | to install |
| *la laptop* | laptop | *guardar* | to save (a file); to keep, put away |
| *la impresora* | printer | *borrar* | to delete |
| *la contraseña* | password | *imprimir* | to print |
| *la aplicación* | app | *grabar* | to record, film |
| *la señal* | signal (phone, Wi-Fi) | *compartir* | to share |
| *el enlace* | link | *conectarse* | to connect, go online |
| *el video* | video | | |
| *la página web* | website, web page | | |
| *la red social* | social network | | |
| *el internet* | the internet | | |

Notes on the words:

- *Prender* is the everyday Mexican verb for lights and machines: *prender la luz, prender la computadora*. *Encender* (*enciendo*) means the same and is the usual word in Spain. The opposite is *apagar*.
- In speech Mexicans often say *la app* (plural *las apps*), *el link* and *la pila* for a phone battery (*Se me acabó la pila*, my battery died; honors 08h2 explains *se me*).
