- *El internet* is usual in Mexico; *la internet* is also correct, and the word often goes without an article: *No hay internet. Lo compré por internet.* (*por internet* = online)
- *La laptop* is feminine, like *la computadora*; Spain says *el portátil*. *Los audífonos* (Spain: *los auriculares*) is normally plural.
- Verbs ending in *-gar* add a *u* before *e*: *apagué, cargué, descargué* (the preterite *yo* form).
- The participle of *imprimir* is *impreso* (*He impreso el boleto*); *imprimido* is also correct.

## What is a direct object?

The **[[direct object]]** is the thing or person the verb acts on directly. To find it, ask "what?" or "whom?" after the verb:

- *Compré el cargador.* — I bought the charger. (Bought what? The charger.)
- *Borré las fotos.* — I deleted the photos.
- *Veo a Ana.* — I see Ana. (See whom? Ana.)

When a direct object is a specific person or a pet, Spanish puts *a* before it. This is the **[[personal a]]**, and English has nothing like it: *Llamé a mi mamá* (I called my mom), *Busco a Daniel* (I'm looking for Daniel). Things don't take it: *Busco el cargador.*

## The pronouns: me, te, lo, la, nos, los, las

A **[[direct object pronoun]]** replaces the direct object, so you don't have to repeat it:

| Person | Direct object pronoun | Example |
|---|---|---|
| me | *me* | *Ana me llamó.* — Ana called me. |
| you (tú) | *te* | *Te veo mañana.* — I'll see you tomorrow. |
| him, it (masculine); you (usted, a man) | *lo* | *Lo compré ayer.* — I bought it yesterday. |
| her, it (feminine); you (usted, a woman) | *la* | *La conocí en la universidad.* — I met her at university. |
| us | *nos* | *Nos invitaron a la boda.* — They invited us to the wedding. |
| them (masculine or mixed); you (ustedes) | *los* | *Los borré.* — I deleted them. |
| them (feminine); you (ustedes, all women) | *las* | *Las imprimí.* — I printed them. |

The third-person pronouns agree with the noun they replace, in gender and number. Spanish has no word for a neutral "it": a thing is masculine or feminine, so "it" is *lo* or *la* depending on the noun.

![A chart in four rows. Each row shows a sentence with its direct object highlighted, an arrow, and the same sentence with a pronoun. Compré el cargador becomes Lo compré. Cambié la contraseña becomes La cambié. Borré los videos becomes Los borré. Imprimí las fotos becomes Las imprimí. A note says the pronoun copies the gender and number of the noun and goes before the verb.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *¿Dónde está mi cargador? — Lo tiene Pablo.* — Where's my charger? — Pablo has it.
- *¿Ya cambiaste la contraseña? — Sí, la cambié ayer.* — Did you change the password yet? — Yes, I changed it yesterday.

People work the same way, and the personal *a* disappears with the pronoun: *Veo a Ana → La veo. Llamé a mis papás → Los llamé.*

### Lo and la for usted

*Usted* is grammatically a third person, so "you" (formal) as a direct object is *lo* for a man and *la* for a woman; *ustedes* is *los* or *las*:

- *¿La ayudo, señora?* — Can I help you, ma'am?
- *Mucho gusto en conocerlo, señor Ruiz.* — Very nice to meet you, Mr. Ruiz.
- *Los espero en la entrada.* — I'll wait for you (all) at the entrance.

In shops you'll also hear *¿En qué le puedo ayudar?* (How can I help you?) with *le*. Many Latin American speakers use *le* for *usted* with a few verbs like *ayudar*; honors 08h1 explains it. In your own sentences, *lo / la* is always correct.

### Example 1: choosing the pronoun

Replace the object: *¿Tienes los audífonos?* — *Sí, ___ tengo.*

1. Find the noun: *los audífonos*.
2. Gender and number: masculine plural. So the pronoun is *los*.
3. Put it before the verb: *Sí, los tengo.*

Now *¿Viste a Marta?* — Marta is a woman, one person: *Sí, la vi en la fiesta.*

## Where the pronoun goes

English puts "it" after the verb; Spanish has three cases.

1. Before a conjugated verb. Any verb with a person ending (present, preterite, imperfect…) has the pronoun right before it. *No* comes before the pronoun, never between it and the verb.

- *Lo descargué.* — I downloaded it.
- *No lo descargué.* — I didn't download it.
- *¿La guardaste?* — Did you save it?
- In the present perfect, the pronoun goes before *haber*: *Ya lo he visto.* — I've already seen it.

2. With an infinitive: two choices. When a conjugated verb is followed by an infinitive (*ir a, tener que, querer, poder* + infinitive), the pronoun can go before the conjugated verb or on the end of the infinitive, written as one word. Both mean exactly the same, and both are common in Mexico:

- *Lo voy a descargar. = Voy a descargarlo.* — I'm going to download it.
- *La tengo que imprimir. = Tengo que imprimirla.* — I have to print it.
- *No los puedo borrar. = No puedo borrarlos.* — I can't delete them.

What you can't do is put the pronoun between the two verbs: never *Voy a lo descargar*. When the infinitive isn't joined to a helper like *ir a* or *tener que* (for example after *antes de, sin, para*), the pronoun can only go on its end: *¿La laptop? Guarda el archivo antes de apagarla* (The laptop? Save the file before you turn it off).

3. Attached to an affirmative command. With a "do it!" command, the pronoun goes on the end: *Cárgalo* (charge it), *Préndela* (turn it on), *Bórralos* (delete them). With *usted*: *Cárguelo, Préndala, Bórrelos*. Lesson 16 covers commands fully; *No* + command needs a different form, which you'll meet later as fixed phrases.

![A chart with three rows. Row 1, a conjugated verb: lo goes before it, Lo descargué, and with no in front, No lo descargué. Row 2, ir a plus infinitive: two equal choices, Lo voy a descargar or Voy a descargarlo, with lo joined to the end of the infinitive. Row 3, an affirmative command: lo is joined to the end, Descárgalo, with the accent on the a marked.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### The written accent on a command

Adding a pronoun doesn't move the stress, but it can leave the stress on the third syllable from the end, and Spanish marks every such word with a written accent. *Carga* is stressed CAR-ga; *cargalo* would still be stressed on CAR, now three syllables from the end, so it's written *cárgalo*. The same happens with *préndela, apágala, bórralo, guárdalo, descárgalo* and with *usted* commands: *guárdelo, imprímalo*. Commands of one syllable plus one pronoun don't need it: *ponlo, dilo, hazlo*. An infinitive plus one pronoun doesn't need one either, because the stress stays on the last syllable of the infinitive: *descargarlo* (des-car-GAR-lo), *imprimirla*. (Infinitives already written with *í*, such as *oír*, keep it: *oírlo*.)

### Example 2: two ways to say it

*I have to charge it* (the phone, *el celular*).

1. Pronoun: *el celular* is masculine singular, so *lo*.
2. *Tener que* + infinitive allows both positions: *Lo tengo que cargar* or *Tengo que cargarlo*.
3. And the command, to a friend: *¡Cárgalo!*; to someone you call *usted*: *¡Cárguelo!*

## Lo for an idea

*Lo* can also stand for a whole idea or situation, not a noun. Then it's always *lo*, never *la*:

- *¿Sabes que Ana tiene novio? — Sí, ya lo sé.* — Do you know Ana has a boyfriend? — Yes, I know.
- *¿Va a llover? — No lo creo.* — Is it going to rain? — I don't think so.
- *No lo puedo creer.* — I can't believe it.

English often says nothing here, but Spanish usually needs the *lo*.

## Dialogue: El celular nuevo de la abuela

Doña Carmen, who lives in Puebla, got a new phone for her birthday. Her grandson Iván comes to help.

> Doña Carmen: Iván, ¿me ayudas con el celular? Mi hija me lo regaló, pero no lo entiendo.
>
> Iván: A ver, abuela. Está apagado. ¿Lo cargaste?
>
> Doña Carmen: Sí, lo cargué anoche, pero no lo prendí. Me da miedo.
>
> Iván: No pasa nada. Préndelo con este botón, a la derecha. Ahora necesito la contraseña del wifi. ¿La tienes?
>
> Doña Carmen: La tengo en un papel, en la cocina. Ay, ¿dónde lo puse? ¡Aquí está!
>
> Iván: Gracias. Listo, ya te conecté. ¿Qué aplicación quieres?
>
> Doña Carmen: La de los videos. Tu tía me manda videos de los niños y quiero verlos.
>
> Iván: Bueno, la voy a descargar. … Ya la instalé. Mira, aquí están los videos de mi tía. Puedes guardarlos o compartirlos con tus amigas.
>
> Doña Carmen: ¿Y si los borro sin querer?
>
> Iván: Los busco en la nube. Tranquila, abuela.
>
> Doña Carmen: ¡Qué bárbaro, eres un genio! Ahora grábame un video para tu tía.
>
> Iván: Con gusto. Pero mírame a mí, no a la pantalla.

In English:

> Doña Carmen: Iván, will you help me with the phone? My daughter gave it to me, but I don't understand it.
>
> Iván: Let's see, Grandma. It's off. Did you charge it?
>
> Doña Carmen: Yes, I charged it last night, but I didn't turn it on. It scares me.
>
> Iván: It's fine. Turn it on with this button, on the right. Now I need the Wi-Fi password. Do you have it?
>
> Doña Carmen: I have it on a piece of paper, in the kitchen. Oh, where did I put it? Here it is!
>
> Iván: Thanks. Done, I've connected you. Which app do you want?
>
> Doña Carmen: The video one. Your aunt sends me videos of the kids and I want to watch them.
>
> Iván: OK, I'll download it. … I've installed it. Look, here are my aunt's videos. You can save them or share them with your friends.
>
> Doña Carmen: And what if I delete them by accident?
>
> Iván: I'll look for them in the cloud. Relax, Grandma.
>
> Doña Carmen: Wow, you're a genius! Now record me a video for your aunt.
>
> Iván: Gladly. But look at me, not at the screen.

(*me da miedo* = it scares me; *no pasa nada* = it's fine, no problem; *el botón* = button; *el wifi* = Wi-Fi; *listo* = done, ready; *¿Y si…?* = what if…?; *sin querer* = by accident, lesson 03; *la nube* = the cloud; *¡Qué bárbaro!* = wow, an informal exclamation, very common in Mexico; *el genio* = genius.) Notice *me lo regaló*: two pronouns together, which lesson 07 explains. Every other *lo, la, los* replaces a noun said just before it: *el celular, la contraseña, el papel, la aplicación, los videos*.

## Leísmo: what you'll hear in Spain

In much of Spain, people use *le* instead of *lo* for a man or boy as a direct object: *Le vi ayer* (I saw him yesterday) where Mexico says *Lo vi ayer*. This is called **[[leísmo]]**, and the Real Academia Española accepts it when it refers to one male person. You don't need to use it; just recognize it in Spanish films and in DELE exam texts that come from Spain. Honors 08h1 says more.

## Pronunciation

- Say the pronoun and the verb as one word, with no pause: *lo-com-PRÉ*, *no-lo-TEN-go*.
- Attached pronouns don't move the stress: *des-car-GAR-lo*, *CÁR-ga-lo* (stress where it was in *CAR-ga*).
- *contraseña*: con-tra-SE-ña, with *ñ* like the "ny" in "canyon".
- *audífonos*: au-DÍ-fo-nos; the *au* is one syllable, like "ow".
- *el video*: vi-DE-o in Mexico (Spain: *el vídeo*, VÍ-de-o).
- *señal* is stressed on the last syllable (se-ÑAL), *teclado* on the second-to-last (te-CLA-do).

## Common mistakes

- *Compré lo.* — English word order. The pronoun goes before a conjugated verb: *Lo compré.*
- *Voy a lo descargar.* — Before the helper or on the end of the infinitive: *Lo voy a descargar / Voy a descargarlo.*
- *Lo no tengo.* — *No* comes first: *No lo tengo.*
- *La compré* about *el cargador*. — "It" copies the noun's gender: *el cargador → lo*, *la batería → la*.
- *Descargalo* without the accent. — A command with an attached pronoun is often stressed three syllables from the end: *descárgalo*.
- *Veo Ana.* — A person as direct object takes the personal *a*: *Veo a Ana.* But the pronoun takes no *a*: *La veo.*
- *Sí, sé.* — For "I know (it)" Spanish says *Sí, lo sé.*
- *¿La ayudo?* to a man. — *Lo* for a man, *la* for a woman: *¿Lo ayudo, señor?*

## Key points

- The direct object answers "what?" or "whom?". A specific person as direct object takes *a*: *Veo a Ana.*
- Pronouns: *me, te, lo, la, nos, los, las*. *Lo / la / los / las* agree with the noun, and also mean "you" for *usted* and *ustedes*.
- Before a conjugated verb (*No lo tengo; Ya lo he visto*); with an infinitive, before the helper or attached (*Lo voy a descargar = Voy a descargarlo*); attached to an affirmative command, often with a written accent (*Cárgalo*).
- *Lo* also stands for an idea: *Lo sé. No lo creo.*
- Mexico says *prender, la laptop, los audífonos, el video*; Spain *encender, el portátil, los auriculares, el vídeo*. Spain's *le vi* (leísmo) = Mexico's *lo vi*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: To me, for her: indirect objects and verbs like gustar
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 05 you replaced "it" and "them" with *lo, la, los, las*. This lesson adds the other kind of object: the person who *receives* something or *benefits* from it. You've used these pronouns since A1 with *gustar* (*me gusta, le gusta*) and *¿Me da…?*. Now you'll use them with verbs of giving, lending and telling, and with a family of verbs that work like *gustar*: *interesar, importar, molestar, preocupar, fascinar, faltar, sobrar, parecer*. The theme is gifts, favors and borrowing, the everyday give-and-take between family and friends.

## Who receives it? The indirect object

In *I gave my mom a necklace*, the necklace is what you gave: the direct object (lesson 05). Your mom is the one who received it: the **[[indirect object]]**. Ask "to whom?" or "for whom?":

- *Le di un collar a mi mamá.* — I gave my mom a necklace. (To whom? My mom.)
- *Le compré flores a mi abuela.* — I bought my grandmother flowers. (For whom? My grandmother.)
- *¿Me prestas tu cargador?* — Can I borrow your charger? (Lend to whom? Me.)

![Two figures, Ana on the left and her mother on the right. Ana holds out a necklace. An arrow labeled ¿qué? (what?) points to the necklace: el collar, the direct object, pronoun lo. A second arrow, labeled ¿a quién? (to whom?), points to the mother: a mi mamá, the indirect object, pronoun le. Below, the full sentence: Ana le da el collar a su mamá.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The indirect object pronouns are almost the same as the direct ones. Only the third person is different:

| Person | Indirect | (Direct, lesson 05) |
|---|---|---|
| to/for me | *me* | *me* |
| to/for you (tú) | *te* | *te* |
| to/for him, her, you (usted) | *le* | *lo, la* |
| to/for us | *nos* | *nos* |
| to/for them, you (ustedes) | *les* | *los, las* |

*Le* and *les* don't show gender: *le* is "to him", "to her" or "to you (usted)". That's why Spanish often adds *a* + the person, as you'll see below.

The position rules are exactly those of lesson 05: before a conjugated verb (*No le dije nada*), before the helper or attached to an infinitive (*Le voy a regalar un perfume = Voy a regalarle un perfume*), and attached to an affirmative command (*Préstame, Pásame, Dime, Dígale*). *Préstame* has a written accent for the same reason as *cárgalo*; *dime* (two syllables) doesn't need one.

## Verbs of giving, telling and lending

Many verbs naturally have both objects: a thing (direct) and a person (indirect).

| Verb | Example |
|---|---|
| *dar* | *Le di mi número.* — I gave him my number. |
| *regalar* (to give as a gift) | *¿Qué le regalaste a tu novia?* — What did you give your girlfriend? |
| *prestar* (to lend) | *Mi vecina me prestó su escalera.* — My neighbor lent me her ladder. |
| *devolver* (to give back) | *Mañana te devuelvo el libro.* — I'll give you back the book tomorrow. |
| *mandar* | *Les mandé un paquete a mis primos.* — I sent my cousins a package. |
| *decir, contar, explicar* | *¿Le dijiste la verdad?* — Did you tell her the truth? |
| *pedir, preguntar* | *Le pedí un favor a Luis.* — I asked Luis for a favor. |
| *agradecer* (to thank for) | *Te agradezco la ayuda.* — Thank you for the help. |

Notes:

- *Regalar* is only for gifts; *dar* is the general "to give". *El regalo* (A1) is the gift itself, and *el detalle* is a small, thoughtful one: *Te traje un detalle* (I brought you a little something). *¡Qué detalle!* means "How thoughtful!"
- *Devolver* (*devuelvo, devuelves*; participle *devuelto*) means to give something back. *Volver* and *regresar* alone mean to go or come back. In Mexico you'll also hear *regresar* for giving back: *Te regreso tu pluma.*
- *Agradecer* (*agradezco*) is a warmer, slightly formal "to thank": *Le agradezco mucho, señora.* The person is the indirect object, and the thing has no preposition.

### Lending and borrowing

Spanish usually talks about borrowing from the lender's side. To ask to borrow something, you ask the other person to lend it to you:

- *¿Me prestas tu laptop?* — Can I borrow your laptop? (literally: Do you lend me your laptop?)
- *¿Me presta su pluma, por favor?* — Could I borrow your pen, please? (*usted*)

*Pedir prestado* (to ask to borrow) is for talking about borrowing, not for asking: *Le pedí prestado el carro a mi hermana* (I borrowed my sister's car), *Le voy a pedir dinero prestado a papá* (I'm going to borrow some money from Dad). The person you borrow from is the indirect object.

## Le and les with a + the person: doubling

In English you say the person once. Spanish very often says it twice: the pronoun *le / les* and then *a* + the person.

- *Le di el regalo a mi mamá.* — I gave my mom the gift.
- *Les pregunté a mis papás.* — I asked my parents.
- *A Luis le presté mi bicicleta.* — I lent Luis my bike. (person first, for emphasis)

This **[[doubling]]** isn't a mistake; it's normal Spanish. With *a mi mamá, a Luis* (a noun), the *le* is grammatically optional, but in everyday Mexican Spanish it's usually there, and leaving it out can sound stiff. With a stressed pronoun (*a él, a ella, a usted, a ellos*), the short pronoun is required: *Le di el regalo a ella*, never *Di el regalo a ella*. The *a* + person clarifies who *le* means, or adds contrast: *A ella le regalé un libro y a él una gorra.*

## Asking for favors

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| *¿Me haces un favor?* — Can you do me a favor? | *¡Claro! / Con gusto.* — Of course! / Gladly. |
| *¿Me prestas…?* — Can I borrow…? | *Sí, tómalo.* — Yes, take it. |
| *¿Me pasas la sal?* — Can you pass me the salt? | *Aquí tienes.* — Here you go. |
| *¿Me ayudas con las cajas?* — Can you help me with the boxes? | *Ahorita no puedo.* — I can't right now. |

A present-tense question with *me* is the normal friendly request in Mexico (A1's *¿Me da…?* is the *usted* version). Thank someone warmly with *¡Gracias, qué amable!* (How kind!).

### Example 1: le or lo?

Choose the pronoun for each person.

1. *Llamé a mi mamá.* *Llamar* acts directly on the person (call whom?), so it's a direct object: *La llamé.*
2. *Le dije la verdad a mi mamá.* With *decir*, the thing said is the direct object and the person is the receiver: *Le dije.*
3. *Ayudo a mis amigos.* *Ayudar* takes a direct object: *Los ayudo.* (You'll also hear *le* with *ayudar* for *usted*: honors 08h1.)
4. *Les mandé fotos a mis amigos.* The photos are sent; the friends receive them: *Les mandé fotos.*

A verb with something given, said or sent usually has the person as indirect object (*le*). A verb that acts on the person directly (*ver, llamar, conocer, ayudar, esperar, invitar*) takes *lo / la*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing lo or le for a person
  accDescr: Start with a person you want to replace with a pronoun. Ask whether the verb acts directly on the person, as with ver, llamar, conocer, ayudar, invitar or esperar. If yes, use lo or la, or los or las in the plural. If no, ask whether the person receives or benefits from something, as with dar, decir, mandar, regalar, prestar or preguntar. If yes, use le or les, usually with a plus the person as well.
  A["A person: which pronoun?"] --> B{"Does the verb act directly on the person? (ver, llamar, conocer, ayudar, invitar)"}
  B -- yes --> C["lo / la / los / las: La llamé."]
  B -- no --> D{"Does the person receive or benefit? (dar, decir, mandar, regalar, prestar)"}
  D -- yes --> E["le / les: Le dije la verdad (a mi mamá)."]
```

## Verbs like gustar

In A1 you learned that *gustar* works backwards: *Me gusta el café* means "coffee pleases me". The thing is the subject, and the person is an indirect object. Several common verbs work the same way:

| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *interesar* | to interest | *¿Te interesa la historia?* — Are you interested in history? |
| *importar* | to matter | *No me importa el precio.* — I don't care about the price. |
| *molestar* | to bother | *Me molesta el ruido.* — The noise bothers me. |
| *preocupar* | to worry | *Nos preocupa el examen.* — We're worried about the exam. |
| *fascinar* | to fascinate, to love | *Le fascinan las joyas.* — She loves jewelry. |
| *faltar* | to be missing, to need | *Me faltan diez pesos.* — I'm ten pesos short. |
| *sobrar* | to be left over | *Nos sobró comida.* — We had food left over. |
| *parecer* | to seem | *¿Qué te parece?* — What do you think? |
| *sorprender* | to surprise | *Me sorprendió la noticia.* — The news surprised me. |

The same rules as *gustar*:

- The verb agrees with the thing: *me interesa el arte* (one thing), *me interesan los museos* (several), *me interesa aprender* (an infinitive: singular).
- The pronoun shows the person: *me, te, le, nos, les*. Add *a mí, a ti, a mi papá* for emphasis or clarity: *A mi papá le preocupa todo.*
- Agree and disagree as with *gustar*: *—Me molesta el ruido. —A mí también. / A mí no.* *—No me importa. —A mí tampoco. / A mí sí.*

*Faltar* and *sobrar* turn English around completely: *Me faltan dos días* is "I have two days to go" (two days are missing to me), *Nos sobran tres boletos* is "We have three spare tickets". *Parecer* gives opinions: *¿Qué te parece el regalo? — Me parece perfecto.* (What do you think of the gift? — I think it's perfect.)

*Molestar, preocupar, parecer* and *sorprender* also take a person as subject: *Me molestas* (you're bothering me), *Pareces cansada* (you look tired), *Siempre nos sorprendes* (you always surprise us).

### Example 2: making it agree

Complete with *preocupar*: *A mis papás ___ los precios.*

1. Who is worried? *A mis papás* → the pronoun is *les*.
2. What worries them? *los precios*, plural → *preocupan*.
3. *A mis papás les preocupan los precios.* — My parents are worried about prices.

## Two useful chunks: me da igual, me da pena

- *Me da igual* — I don't mind, it's all the same to me. *—¿Pizza o tacos? —Me da igual.* Said sharply it can sound like "I don't care", so add a smile or *las dos están bien*.
- *Me da pena* — in Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, *pena* often means embarrassment or shyness: *Me da pena pedirle dinero* (I feel embarrassed asking him for money). Everywhere it can also mean sadness or pity: *Me da pena ver al perro solo* (it makes me sad to see the dog alone). Context tells you which.

Both work like *gustar*: *¿Te da pena? A mi hermano le da igual.*

## Dialogue: El cumpleaños de mamá

Sofía and her brother Mateo are planning a present for their mother.

> Sofía: Mateo, ¿me haces un favor? ¿Me prestas trescientos pesos? Me faltan para el regalo de mamá.
>
> Mateo: Está bien, pero el viernes me devuelves el dinero, ¿eh? ¿Qué le vas a regalar?
>
> Sofía: Un collar de plata. A mamá le fascinan las joyas. ¿Qué te parece?
>
> Mateo: Me parece muy bonito. ¿Y yo qué le doy? No tengo nada.
>
> Sofía: ¿Un perfume? A ella le gusta mucho el de flores.
>
> Mateo: Buena idea, pero… también me falta dinero. Le voy a pedir dinero prestado a papá.
>
> Sofía: ¡Mateo! ¿Para el regalo de su esposa? A mí me da pena.
>
> Mateo: A mí no. Además, a mamá no le importa el precio. Le importa el detalle.
>
> Sofía: Bueno, tienes razón. Mira, en el paquete del collar vienen dos cajas. Nos sobra una para tu perfume.
>
> Mateo: Perfecto. Me da igual el color de la caja.

That evening:

> Mamá: ¿Esto es para mí? ¡Un collar y un perfume! Me sorprendieron, hijos. Les agradezco mucho.
>
> Sofía: Felicidades, mamá. Y gracias a papá también…

In English:

> Sofía: Mateo, can you do me a favor? Can I borrow three hundred pesos? I'm short for Mom's present.
>
> Mateo: OK, but you give me the money back on Friday, OK? What are you going to give her?
>
> Sofía: A silver necklace. Mom loves jewelry. What do you think?
>
> Mateo: I think it's very pretty. And what do I give her? I don't have anything.
>
> Sofía: A perfume? She really likes the flowery one.
>
> Mateo: Good idea, but… I'm short of money too. I'm going to borrow some money from Dad.
>
> Sofía: Mateo! For his own wife's present? I'd be embarrassed.
>
> Mateo: Not me. Besides, Mom doesn't care about the price. What matters to her is the thought.
>
> Sofía: Well, you're right. Look, the necklace's package comes with two boxes. We have one spare for your perfume.
>
> Mateo: Perfect. I don't mind what color the box is.
>
> Mom: Is this for me? A necklace and a perfume! You surprised me, kids. Thank you so much.
>
> Sofía: Happy birthday, Mom. And thanks to Dad as well…

(*la plata* = silver; *¿eh?* = OK?, right?; *el de flores* = the one with flowers, the flowery one; *además* = besides.) In *Le voy a pedir dinero prestado a papá*, *le* and *a papá* are the same person, doubled. *Me sorprendieron* is plural because the two children surprised her.

## Pronunciation

- *collar, detalle*: *ll* sounds like *y*: co-YAR, de-TA-ye.
- *agradezco*: in Latin America the *z* is an *s*: a-gra-DES-co.
- *joya*: the *j* is the throat sound, as in *jugo*: HO-ya.
- *paquete*: *qu* is a plain *k*: pa-KE-te.
- *préstame, dígale*: the stress stays where it was (*PRES-ta, DI-ga*), so the longer word needs the accent.

## Common mistakes

- *Lo di un regalo.* — The receiver is indirect: *Le di un regalo.*
- *Di el regalo a ella.* — With *a ella*, the *le* is required: *Le di el regalo a ella.*
- *Yo intereso la historia.* — The thing is the subject: *Me interesa la historia.*
- *Me falta dos días.* — Plural thing, plural verb: *Me faltan dos días.*
- *¿Me pides prestado tu carro?* — To ask to borrow, ask the owner to lend: *¿Me prestas tu carro?*
- *Volver el libro.* — Giving something back is *devolver*: *Te devuelvo el libro.*
- *Les preocupa los precios.* — The verb agrees with *los precios*: *Les preocupan los precios.*
- *Me parece a mí que…* in every sentence. — *Me parece que…* is enough; *a mí* adds emphasis.

## Key points

- The indirect object is who receives or benefits ("to whom? for whom?"): *me, te, le, nos, les*. Only *le / les* differ from the direct *lo, la, los, las*.
- Same positions as lesson 05: *Le voy a regalar = Voy a regalarle; Préstame.*
- *Le / les* + *a* + person (doubling) is normal; with *a él, a ella, a usted* it's required.
- *¿Me prestas…?* = Can I borrow…? *Pedir prestado* talks about borrowing. *Devolver* = to give back.
- Like *gustar*: *interesar, importar, molestar, preocupar, fascinar, faltar, sobrar, parecer, sorprender*. The verb agrees with the thing: *Me faltan diez pesos.*
- *Me da igual* = I don't mind; *me da pena* = I'm embarrassed (Mexico) or it makes me sad.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Me lo, se lo: two pronouns together
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 05 gave you *lo, la, los, las* for the thing, and lesson 06 *me, te, le, nos, les* for the person who receives it. Real conversations often need both at once: "Can you wrap it for me?", "I gave it to her", "I'll lend them to you". This lesson shows the order the two pronouns go in, the one change that happens (*le* becomes *se*), and where the pair goes with infinitives and commands. You've seen the pattern already in A1's *¿Me lo deja en trescientos?* and in lesson 05's *Mi hija me lo regaló*.

The theme is clothes shopping and customer service: sizes, fitting rooms, gift-wrapping and returns. A1 taught *la ropa, la playera, el pantalón, la falda, el vestido, el zapato, los tenis, el suéter, la chamarra* and *llevar* (to wear); here you add more clothes and the language of the store.

## In the store

![A clothing store seen from inside. On the left, a large shop window facing the street with a dressed mannequin in it, marked el aparador. In the middle, a rack of shirts, one with a hanging tag that says M, marked la talla. At the back, two booths with curtains, marked el probador. On the right, a counter with a cash register and a sales assistant, marked la caja. A customer with a shopping bag stands at the counter, marked el cliente.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Word | Meaning | Word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| *el aparador* | shop window | *la marca* | brand |
| *el probador* | fitting room | *el estilo* | style |
| *la caja* | checkout, register (also "box", lesson 06) | *a la moda* | fashionable |
| *la talla* | size (clothes) | *apretado* | tight |
| *la oferta* | special offer, sale | *flojo* | loose |
| *la devolución* | return (of a purchase) | *el algodón* | cotton |
| *la garantía* | guarantee, warranty | *el cliente* | customer |
| *probarse* (*me pruebo*) | to try on | *atender* (*atiendo*) | to serve (a customer) |
| *envolver* (*envuelvo*) | to wrap | | |

![Clothes laid out on a white background, each with its name: a button-up shirt with a collar, la camisa; a woman's blouse, la blusa; a long winter coat, el abrigo; a striped scarf, la bufanda; a baseball cap, la gorra; a leather belt with a buckle, el cinturón.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

More clothes: *los jeans* (also *los pantalones de mezclilla*; Spain *los vaqueros*), *los calcetines* (socks; in Mexico also *las calcetas*), *el sombrero* (hat with a brim), *las sandalias*. *La camisa* has buttons and a collar; a T-shirt is A1's *la playera*.

### Sizes and how things fit

- *¿Qué talla usa?* — What size do you take? Mexican labels often use *CH, M, G* and *XG* (*chico* or *chica, mediano* or *mediana, grande, extra grande*).
- For shoes, the size is *el número*, and Mexican shoe sizes are usually given in centimeters: *Calzo del 26* (I take a 26). (*calzar* = to take a shoe size)
- A1's *quedar* also means "to fit, to look on someone". It works like *gustar*: the clothes are the subject. *Me queda grande* (it's too big for me), *Te quedan apretados* (they're tight on you), *¿Cómo me queda?* (How does it look on me?), *Le queda muy bien* (It really suits her).
- *Atender* is the shop assistant's verb: *¿Ya lo atienden?* (Is someone helping you, sir?) is what a Mexican sales assistant says when you walk in. A polite answer: *No, gracias, solo estoy viendo* (I'm just looking; *estoy viendo* is *estar* + the *-ndo* form, lesson 09).

## Two pronouns: the person first

When a sentence has both an indirect object (the person) and a direct object (the thing), the indirect comes first, and both go before a conjugated verb:

| Without pronouns | With two pronouns |
|---|---|
| *Mi mamá me regaló la bufanda.* | *Mi mamá me la regaló.* — My mom gave it to me. |
| *¿Te presto mis audífonos?* | *¿Te los presto?* — Shall I lend them to you? |
| *Nos envolvieron los regalos.* | *Nos los envolvieron.* — They wrapped them for us. |

A memory hook: the person comes before the thing, the opposite of English "give *it* to *me*". In this lesson the first pronoun is always *me, te, nos* (or *se*, below) and the second is always *lo, la, los, las*.

### Example 1: building a pair

*¿Me prestas tu gorra?* — *Sí, ___ presto.*

1. The thing: *tu gorra*, feminine singular → *la*.
2. The person: you are lending it to the speaker, so to "you" → *te*.
3. Person first: *te la*. → *Sí, te la presto.* — Yes, I'll lend it to you.

## Le and les become se

When *le* or *les* comes right before *lo, la, los, las*, it changes to *se*. Spanish never says *le lo* or *les la*:

- *Le di el regalo.* → *Se lo di.* — I gave it to him / her / you.
- *Les mandé las fotos.* → *Se las mandé.* — I sent them to them / to you (all).
- *¿Le envuelvo la camisa?* → *¿Se la envuelvo?* — Shall I wrap it for you?

![A chart. At the top, le plus lo, with an arrow to se lo, and next to it the word never above le lo crossed out in red. Below, four rows: le plus lo gives se lo, le plus la gives se la, les plus los gives se los, les plus las gives se las. A note says: se can mean to him, to her, to you (usted), to them, to you all; add a él, a ella, a usted, a ellos to make it clear.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This *se* is not the reflexive *se* of *levantarse*; it's just *le* or *les* in disguise. (Medieval Spanish said *gelo* here, a sound that later became *se lo*.) Because *se* can mean "to him, to her, to you, to them", add *a* + the person when it isn't clear:

- *Se lo di a ella, no a él.* — I gave it to her, not to him.
- *¿Se lo envuelvo a usted?* — Shall I wrap it for you?

### Example 2: two steps

*Le devolví los jeans a la tienda.* Replace both objects.

1. The thing: *los jeans* → *los*.
2. The receiver: *a la tienda* → *le*.
3. Person first: *le los* → *le* becomes *se*: *Se los devolví.* — I returned them (to the store).

## Where the pair goes

The two pronouns always travel together, in the same positions as one pronoun:

1. Before a conjugated verb, with *no* in front: *Se lo dije. No me lo dijo. Ya te lo he dicho.*
2. With an infinitive, before the helper or attached to the infinitive. Both are correct and both are common:
   - *Te lo voy a envolver.* = *Voy a envolvértelo.* — I'm going to wrap it for you.
   - *Se la quiero regalar.* = *Quiero regalársela.* — I want to give it to her.
   - Never split the pair: not *Te voy a envolverlo*.
3. Attached to an affirmative command: *Dámelo* (give it to me), *Préstamela* (lend it to me), *Envuélvamelo* (*usted*: wrap it for me).

When two pronouns are attached, the stress is always three or four syllables from the end, so the written accent is always needed: *envolvér-te-lo, regalár-se-la, dá-me-lo, envuélva-me-lo*.

### Shopping chunks

Learn these as they are; lesson 16 explains command forms fully.

| Chunk | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *¿Me lo envuelve para regalo?* | Could you gift-wrap it for me? |
| *Envuélvamelo, por favor.* | Wrap it for me, please. |
| *¿Me lo puedo probar? / ¿Puedo probármelo?* | Can I try it on? |
| *Démelo en talla mediana.* | Give it to me in a medium. |
| *¿Me la cambia por una talla más grande?* | Could you exchange it for a bigger size? |
| *Me lo llevo.* | I'll take it. |

In *¿Me lo puedo probar?* the *me* is the reflexive pronoun of *probarse* (to try on oneself), but it follows the same order: *me* before *lo*. *Me lo llevo* uses *llevarse* (to take away with you). Notice that a polite request in Mexico is often a simple present question with *usted*, like A1's *¿Me da…?*: *¿Me lo envuelve?*

## Dialogue: En la tienda de ropa

Lucía is shopping at a department store in Guadalajara.

> Vendedor: Buenas tardes. ¿Ya la atienden?
>
> Lucía: No. Busco un regalo para mi papá: la bufanda gris del aparador.
>
> Vendedor: Es una bufanda muy buena, de algodón, y hoy está en oferta. ¿Se la envuelvo para regalo?
>
> Lucía: Sí, envuélvamela, por favor. Y también quiero ver esos jeans. ¿Me los puedo probar?
>
> Vendedor: Claro. ¿Qué talla usa?
>
> Lucía: Mediana, creo. ¿Dónde están los probadores?
>
> Vendedor: Al fondo, a la izquierda.
>
> Vendedor: ¿Cómo le quedan?
>
> Lucía: Me quedan un poco apretados. ¿Me los da en talla grande?
>
> Vendedor: Aquí los tiene. Son de la misma marca.
>
> Lucía: Estos me quedan perfectos. Me los llevo. Oiga, ¿y si a mi papá no le gusta la bufanda?
>
> Vendedor: Tiene treinta días para cambiarla. Pídale el ticket a la cajera y guárdelo.
>
> Lucía: Perfecto. ¿Me la da con el ticket de regalo?
>
> Vendedor: Sí, ya se la doy. Pase a la caja, por favor.

In English:

> Assistant: Good afternoon. Is someone helping you?
>
> Lucía: No. I'm looking for a present for my dad: the gray scarf in the window.
>
> Assistant: It's a very good scarf, cotton, and it's on sale today. Shall I gift-wrap it for you?
>
> Lucía: Yes, wrap it for me, please. And I also want to look at those jeans. Can I try them on?
>
> Assistant: Of course. What size do you take?
>
> Lucía: Medium, I think. Where are the fitting rooms?
>
> Assistant: At the back, on the left.
>
> Assistant: How do they fit?
>
> Lucía: They're a bit tight on me. Could you give them to me in a large?
>
> Assistant: Here you are. They're the same brand.
>
> Lucía: These fit perfectly. I'll take them. Excuse me, and what if my dad doesn't like the scarf?
>
> Assistant: You have thirty days to exchange it. Ask the cashier for the receipt and keep it.
>
> Lucía: Perfect. Can you give it to me with the gift receipt?
>
> Assistant: Yes, I'll give it to you right away. Go to the register, please.

(*el vendedor* = sales assistant, A1; *la cajera* = cashier; *el ticket de regalo* = gift receipt; *al fondo* = at the back; *misma* = same; *ya se la doy* = I'll give it to you right now.) Count the pairs: *se la envuelvo, envuélvamela, me los puedo probar, me los da, me los llevo, me la da, se la doy*. In *Pídale el ticket a la cajera*, *le* and *a la cajera* are the same person.

## Pronunciation

- Say the pair and the verb as one word: *se-lo-DI*, *te-la-PRES-to*.
- Long attached forms keep the verb's stress: *en-vol-VÉR-te-lo*, *en-VUÉL-va-me-lo*, *DÁ-me-lo*.
- *cinturón, algodón, devolución*: stressed on the last syllable, so they carry an accent, which goes away in the plural: *cinturones, devoluciones*.
- *bufanda*: bu-FAN-da; *calcetines*: cal-se-TI-nes (with seseo, *ce* = *se*).
- *jeans* is said much as in English, often closer to "yeens".

## Common mistakes

- *Le lo di.* — *Le / les* become *se* before *lo, la, los, las*: *Se lo di.*
- *Lo me das.* — Person first: *Me lo das.*
- *Te voy a envolverlo.* — Keep the pair together: *Te lo voy a envolver* or *Voy a envolvértelo.*
- *Dame lo / Damelo.* — One word, with an accent: *Dámelo.*
- *Se lo di a él* when you mean a woman. — *Se* hides the gender; the *a* phrase must match: *Se lo di a ella.*
- *La camisa me queda chico.* — The adjective agrees with the clothes: *me queda chica*; *los jeans me quedan grandes*.
- *¿Qué talla son tus zapatos?* — Shoes have a *número*: *¿Qué número calzas?*

## Key points

- Two pronouns: indirect (person) before direct (thing): *me lo, te la, nos los*.
- *Le / les* + *lo, la, los, las* → *se lo, se la, se los, se las*. Add *a él, a ella, a usted, a ellos* to make *se* clear.
- The pair stays together: before a conjugated verb (*Se lo di*), before the helper or attached to the infinitive (*Te lo voy a dar = Voy a dártelo*), attached to an affirmative command (*Dámelo*). Two attached pronouns always mean a written accent.
- Shopping: *¿Ya lo / la atienden?, ¿Me lo puedo probar?, ¿Me lo envuelve?, Me lo llevo*. *Quedar* = to fit: *Me queda grande.* Clothes have a *talla*, shoes a *número*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Love and friendship: reflexive and reciprocal verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A1 you learned reflexive verbs for your daily routine: *me levanto, me baño, me visto*. The pronoun showed that you do the action to yourself. This lesson goes further in three directions. First, many verbs exist both with and without *se*, and the *se* changes the meaning (*ir* = to go, *irse* = to leave). Second, some verbs almost always come with *se*, even though nobody does anything "to themselves" (*quejarse*, to complain). Third, the plural pronouns *nos* and *se* can mean "each other": *Nos conocimos en 2019* (We met each other in 2019).

The theme is relationships: love, friendship, quarrels and making up. Everything from lessons 05–07 about where pronouns go still applies.

## Reflexive verbs: a quick review

A **[[reflexive verb]]** carries a pronoun that refers back to the subject: *me, te, se, nos, (os), se*. The pronoun goes in the same places as the object pronouns of lessons 05–07:

- before a conjugated verb: *Me acuerdo. No me acuerdo. Se enojó.*
- before the helper or on the end of an infinitive: *Nos vamos a casar. = Vamos a casarnos.*
- on the end of an affirmative command: *Acuérdate. Siéntate.*

With body parts and clothes, Spanish uses *el, la, los, las*, not "my": *Me lavo las manos* (I wash my hands), *Se puso la chamarra* (he put on his jacket). The reflexive pronoun already says whose.

## The same verb with and without se

Many verbs change meaning when they take *se*. Without *se*, the action goes to someone or something else; with *se*, it stays with the subject, or the meaning shifts.

| Without *se* | With *se* |
|---|---|
| *lavar el carro* — to wash the car | *lavarse* — to wash (oneself) |
| *llamar a alguien* — to call someone | *llamarse* — to be called |
| *dormir* — to sleep | *dormirse* — to fall asleep |
| *ir* — to go | *irse* — to leave, go away |
| *poner* — to put | *ponerse* — to put on (clothes); to become, get (*ponerse nervioso*) |
| *acordar* — to agree on | *acordarse de* — to remember |
| *llevar* — to carry, wear | *llevarse bien / mal con* — to get along well / badly with |
| *sentir* + noun — to feel (*Siento frío*), to be sorry (*Lo siento*) | *sentirse* + adjective — to feel (*Me siento cansado*) |
| *despedir* — to fire (lesson 17) | *despedirse de* — to say goodbye to |

- *Dormí ocho horas.* — I slept eight hours. / *Me dormí en el cine.* — I fell asleep at the movies.
- *Voy al centro.* — I'm going downtown. / *Ya me voy.* — I'm leaving now.
- *Pon el regalo en la mesa.* — Put the present on the table. / *Me puse muy nerviosa.* — I got very nervous. (*ponerse* + an adjective = to become, for a change of feeling or color: *ponerse rojo*, to blush)
- *Acordamos una fecha.* — We agreed on a date. / *¿Te acuerdas de mí?* — Do you remember me? (A1's *recordar* means the same: *¿Me recuerdas?*)
- *Me llevo muy bien con mi suegra.* — I get along really well with my mother-in-law.

*Sentirse* changes its stem like *pedir* in the third-person preterite: *me sentí, te sentiste, se sintió, se sintieron*. So does *despedirse*: *me despido, se despidió, se despidieron*. And careful: *me siento* is both "I feel" (*sentirse*) and "I sit down" (*sentarse*, lesson 09); the rest of the sentence tells you which.

### Example 1: with or without se?

Choose: *Ana (puso / se puso) el abrigo en la silla* and *Ana (puso / se puso) el abrigo porque hacía frío.*

1. In the first, the coat goes onto a chair: the action goes to something else. *Ana puso el abrigo en la silla.*
2. In the second, the coat goes onto Ana herself. *Ana se puso el abrigo porque hacía frío.*
3. Test: if you can add "on herself", "herself" or "each other" in English, or the meaning is a change of state ("got nervous", "fell asleep"), you probably need *se*.

## Verbs that almost always take se

In the meanings below, these common verbs are used with *se*. Grammars call them **[[pronominal verbs]]**: the *se* is part of the verb, and there's no "oneself" in the meaning. Some are almost never used without *se* (*quejarse, darse cuenta*); others have a plain form with another meaning (*acordar* = to agree on, *comprometer* = to compromise, to commit someone). Learn each with its preposition:

| Verb | Preposition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *quejarse* — to complain | *de* (about) | *Se queja de todo.* — He complains about everything. |
| *enojarse* — to get angry | *con* (with) | *Mi mamá se enojó conmigo.* — My mom got angry with me. |
| *enamorarse* — to fall in love (A1) | *de* (with) | *Me enamoré de ella.* — I fell in love with her. |
| *comprometerse* — to get engaged | *con* (to) | *Se comprometió con su novio.* — She got engaged to her boyfriend. |
| *darse cuenta* — to realize (A1) | *de* | *No me di cuenta de la hora.* — I didn't notice the time. |
| *pelearse* — to fight, quarrel | *con* (with) | *Me peleé con mi hermano.* — I had a fight with my brother. |
| *acordarse* — to remember | *de* | *No me acuerdo de su nombre.* — I don't remember her name. |

*Enojarse* is the Mexican word; Spain usually says *enfadarse*. *Comprometerse* also means "to commit to": *Me comprometo a llegar temprano* (I promise to arrive early).

## Each other: reciprocal nos and se

With plural subjects, *nos* and *se* can mean "each other". This is the **[[reciprocal]]** use:

- *Nos conocimos en una fiesta.* — We met (each other) at a party.
- *Se escriben todos los días.* — They write to each other every day.
- *Se besaron y se abrazaron.* — They kissed and hugged.
- *¿Ustedes se llevan bien?* — Do you get along?
- *Nos vemos mañana.* — See you tomorrow. (literally "we see each other")

![Two scenes side by side. On the left, one man stands in front of a mirror and looks at his reflection; the caption says Se mira: he looks at himself. On the right, a man and a woman face each other with arrows going from each to the other; the caption says Se miran: they look at each other.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Se miran* can mean "they look at each other" or "they each look at themselves" (in a mirror, say). Context usually decides. To make "each other" clear, add *el uno al otro* (two men, or a man and a woman), *la una a la otra* (two women) or *los unos a los otros* (a group): *Se ayudan el uno al otro.* — They help each other.

### Example 2: reflexive or reciprocal?

*Paola y Andrés se escribieron.* Does it mean they wrote to themselves, or to each other?

1. The verb is plural, and people don't usually write to themselves, so: each other.
2. *Paola y Andrés se escribieron cartas.* — Paola and Andrés wrote each other letters. (*la carta* = letter)
3. Compare *Paola se escribió una nota en la mano* — Paola wrote a note on her hand: one person, reflexive.

## Love and friendship: the words

| Spanish | English | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *la pareja* | couple; partner | *besar, el beso* | to kiss, kiss |
| *el amor* | love | *abrazar* (*abracé*) | to hug |
| *la amistad* | friendship | *pelearse, la pelea* | to fight, fight |
| *la relación* | relationship | *hacer las paces* | to make up |
| *el sentimiento* | feeling | *perdonar* | to forgive |
| *salir con* | to go out with, date | *confiar en* (*confío*) | to trust |
| *celoso* | jealous | *la confianza* | trust |
| *cariñoso* | affectionate | *odiar* | to hate |

- *La pareja* is always feminine, whether your partner is a man or a woman: *Mi pareja se llama Raúl.* It also means "a couple": *una pareja de recién casados* (a newly married couple).
- *Salir con* is "to date": *Salgo con Andrés desde marzo.* In much of Mexico young people also say *andar con* (*Ando con Andrés*). A date is *una cita*, the same word as A1's "appointment": *Tenemos una cita el viernes.*
- *Confiar* stresses the *í*: *confío, confías, confía, confían* (*confiamos* has no accent). Use *en*: *Confío en ti.*
- *Hacer las paces* (literally "make the peaces") is always plural: *Ya hicimos las paces.*

![A timeline of a couple's story with a small picture above each year. 2019, a speech bubble saying Mucho gusto: se conocieron (they met). 2020, two cups of coffee: salieron por primera vez (they went out for the first time). 2021, a heart: se enamoraron (they fell in love). 2023, a ring with a stone: se comprometieron (they got engaged). 2024, two linked rings: se casaron (they got married). Below: Nos conocimos en 2019 y nos casamos en 2024.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Story verbs like these are usually in the preterite (lesson 01), and most of them are reciprocal or pronominal: *se conocieron, se enamoraron, se comprometieron, se casaron* (*casarse*, lesson 01).

## Dialogue: ¿Ya hicieron las paces?

Diana meets her friend Paola for coffee in Monterrey.

> Diana: ¿Qué te pasa, Paola? Te ves triste.
>
> Paola: Ayer me peleé con Andrés. Se enojó porque no me acordé de nuestro aniversario.
>
> Diana: ¡Ay, no! ¿Y qué pasó?
>
> Paola: Me fui a mi casa y ni siquiera nos despedimos. Me sentí muy mal toda la noche.
>
> Diana: Pero ustedes se llevan muy bien. Se conocieron en la universidad, ¿no?
>
> Paola: Sí, en 2021. Salimos un año y nos enamoramos. Él es muy cariñoso, pero un poco celoso.
>
> Diana: ¿Celoso? ¿Confías en él?
>
> Paola: Sí, confío en él, y él en mí. La confianza no es el problema. El problema es que siempre se queja de mi trabajo.
>
> Diana: ¿Y ya hicieron las paces?
>
> Paola: Hoy en la mañana me llamó y me pidió perdón, y yo lo perdoné. Nos vamos a ver esta noche.
>
> Diana: ¡Qué bueno! Oye, ¿y es cierto que se van a comprometer?
>
> Paola: ¡Shhh! Es un secreto… pero creo que sí.

In English:

> Diana: What's the matter, Paola? You look sad.
>
> Paola: Yesterday I had a fight with Andrés. He got angry because I didn't remember our anniversary.
>
> Diana: Oh, no! And what happened?
>
> Paola: I went home and we didn't even say goodbye. I felt really bad all night.
>
> Diana: But you two get along really well. You met at university, didn't you?
>
> Paola: Yes, in 2021. We went out for a year and fell in love. He's very affectionate, but a bit jealous.
>
> Diana: Jealous? Do you trust him?
>
> Paola: Yes, I trust him, and he trusts me. Trust isn't the problem. The problem is that he always complains about my job.
>
> Diana: And have you made up yet?
>
> Paola: This morning he called me and said he was sorry, and I forgave him. We're going to see each other tonight.
>
> Diana: Great! Hey, and is it true you're going to get engaged?
>
> Paola: Shhh! It's a secret… but I think so.

(*¿Qué te pasa?* = what's wrong?; *te ves* = you look, from *verse*; *el aniversario* = anniversary, lesson 23; *ni siquiera* = not even; *pedir perdón* = to apologize; *hoy en la mañana* = this morning, the usual Mexican way; *es cierto* = it's true; *el secreto* = secret.) Notice the three kinds of *se*: reflexive or pronominal (*me peleé, se enojó, me acordé, me sentí, se queja*), reciprocal (*nos despedimos, se conocieron, nos enamoramos, nos vamos a ver*), and the verbs used without *se* (*me llamó, lo perdoné*), where *me* and *lo* are object pronouns from lessons 05 and 06.

## Pronunciation

- *abrazar, abracé*: with seseo both *z* and *c* are *s*: a-bra-SAR, a-bra-SÉ.
- *confío*: three syllables, con-FÍ-o; the accent keeps *í* and *o* apart.
- *pareja*: pa-RE-ha, with the throat *j*.
- *cariñoso*: ca-ri-ÑO-so. *Celoso*: se-LO-so.
- *hacer las paces*: a-SER-las-PA-ses; link the words.

## Common mistakes

- *Me enamoré con ella.* — *Enamorarse de*: *Me enamoré de ella.*
- *No me acuerdo su nombre.* — *Acordarse de*: *No me acuerdo de su nombre.* (Or *No recuerdo su nombre*, with no *de*.)
- *Andrés enojó.* — It needs *se*: *Andrés se enojó.*
- *Me lavo mis manos.* — Use the article: *Me lavo las manos.*
- *Se pelió con su novio.* — *Pelear* is regular: *se peleó* (pe-le-Ó).
- *Dormí en el cine* for "I fell asleep". — *Dormirse*: *Me dormí en el cine.*
- *Siento triste.* — With an adjective use *sentirse*: *Me siento triste.* (*Lo siento* = I'm sorry.)
- *Confio en ti.* — Write the accent: *confío*.

## Key points

- Reflexive pronouns *me, te, se, nos, se* go where object pronouns go: *Nos vamos a casar = Vamos a casarnos; Acuérdate.*
- *Se* changes the meaning of many verbs: *ir / irse, dormir / dormirse, poner / ponerse, acordar / acordarse de, llevar / llevarse bien, despedir / despedirse.*
- Pronominal verbs take *se*, and often a fixed preposition: *quejarse de, enojarse con, enamorarse de, comprometerse con, pelearse con, darse cuenta de.*
- Plural *nos / se* can mean "each other": *Nos conocimos en 2019; Se escriben.* Add *el uno al otro* for clarity.
- *Salir con* = to date; *hacer las paces* = to make up; *confiar en* (*confío*) = to trust.

lessons.title: Honors: Pronouns across the Spanish-speaking world
lessons.body:
## Why this lesson

Lessons 05–08 taught one system of object pronouns, the one most Mexicans use: *lo / la* for "him, her, it", *le / les* for "to him, to them", and *se lo* when the two meet. It's a complete, correct system, and it's the one to use yourself. But Spanish has more than 500 million native speakers (Instituto Cervantes, 2025) in about twenty countries, and pronouns are one of the places where they differ. You'll meet the differences in films, songs, the DELE exam (whose texts often come from Spain) and conversations with people from other countries.

This lesson describes five variants, as variants, not as mistakes: **[[leísmo]]** in Spain, *le* for *usted*, the Latin American *se los*, *le* for "to them", and the object forms that go with **[[voseo]]**. It ends with how people ask for things politely in three countries. The descriptions follow the Real Academia Española's grammar (the *Nueva gramática*, 2009) and its *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (DPD); see the notes for sources. The goal is recognition: understand them when you hear them.

## 1. Leísmo: le for "him" in Spain

In Mexico, a man as direct object is *lo*: *A Juan lo vi ayer.* In much of Spain, especially the center and north, many speakers say *le* instead: *A Juan le vi ayer.* Both mean "I saw Juan yesterday". This use of *le* is called **[[leísmo]]**.

| Meaning | Mexico (and most of Latin America) | Many speakers in Spain |
|---|---|---|
| I saw him. | *Lo vi.* | *Le vi.* |
| I'll call him tomorrow. | *Lo llamo mañana.* | *Le llamo mañana.* |
| Do you know my brother? | *¿Conoces a mi hermano? — Sí, lo conozco.* | *Sí, le conozco.* |

The RAE accepts this *le* when it means one male person, so *Le vi* is standard Spanish in Spain. It does not accept *le* for a thing (*El libro le compré*, heard in some areas) or *la* for an indirect object (*La dije la verdad* for *Le dije la verdad*, called *laísmo*). For you: understand *le vi*, but keep saying *lo vi*; it's correct everywhere.

### Example 1: reading Spain's Spanish

A Spanish friend writes: *Ayer vi a tu primo en el metro. Le saludé, pero no me reconoció.*

1. *Le saludé* has *le*, but *saludar* (to greet) acts directly on the person: you greet someone, you don't give them something. So *le* here is a direct object, a man: leísmo.
2. In Mexican Spanish: *Lo saludé, pero no me reconoció.* — I said hello to him, but he didn't recognize me.
3. Nothing is wrong; it's simply Spain's usual form. (*reconocer* = to recognize)

## 2. Le for usted: the courtesy le

Mexico normally uses *lo / la* for *usted* as a direct object: *Mucho gusto en conocerla, señora. Lo espero en la entrada.* But in much of Latin America (and in Spain), people in shops, offices and call centers also say *le* to the person they call *usted*, even with verbs that would take *lo / la*:

- *¿En qué le puedo ayudar?* — How can I help you?
- *Le espero mañana a las diez.* — I'll expect you tomorrow at ten.
- *Gracias por su paciencia, le atendemos en un momento.* — Thank you for your patience, we'll be with you in a moment.

The RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* describes this courtesy *le* as very widespread and accepts it. It sounds polite and a little formal. In your own speech *¿La ayudo?* and *¿Le ayudo?* are both fine; *lo / la* is never wrong.

## 3. Se los: "I told them"

Lesson 07 taught that *le* and *les* both turn into *se* before *lo, la, los, las*. That creates a problem: *se* doesn't show singular or plural. *Se lo dije* can mean "I told him", "I told her", "I told you" or "I told them".

In much of Latin America, speakers solve it by moving the plural onto the next pronoun. If "them" are the people, they say *los*, even though the thing told is singular:

| What happened | Careful standard | Common Latin American speech |
|---|---|---|
| I told *them* (it, the news). | *Se lo dije (a ellos).* | *Se los dije.* |
| I gave it to *you all* (the present). | *Se lo di (a ustedes).* | *Se los di.* |
| I told *him* (it). | *Se lo dije.* | *Se lo dije.* |

The *Nueva gramática* describes *se los* for "to them … it" as very frequent in the spoken language of much of America (and the Canary Islands), and says it is spreading into educated use in Mexico, the Caribbean coast and parts of Central America, the Río de la Plata and the Andes. The DPD still recommends *se lo* in careful speech and writing. So: in a formal e-mail write *se lo*; in a conversation in Mexico you'll hear *se los* all the time.

### Example 2: decoding se los

You hear: *—¿Ya saben lo de la fiesta? —Sí, ya se los dije.*

1. *Lo de la fiesta* (the thing about the party) is one piece of news, singular. So *los* can't be the news.
2. The question was about "they" (*saben*), several people. So *los* carries their plural: "I've already told them."
3. Careful standard: *Sí, ya se lo dije (a ellos).* Both are understood instantly by Mexicans.

But *se los* can also be the plain lesson-07 meaning, with a plural thing: *—¿Y los boletos? —Se los di a Marta.* (I gave them to Marta.) Ask what the thing is. If the thing is plural, *los* is the thing; if the thing is singular and the people are plural, *los* is the people.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to read se los
  accDescr: When you hear se los, first ask whether the thing given or told is plural. If yes, los is the thing, as in Se los di a Marta, I gave them to Marta. If the thing is singular, ask whether the receivers are several people. If yes, los shows that plural: Se los dije means I told them, which careful standard Spanish writes Se lo dije.
  A["You hear: se los"] --> B{"Is the thing plural? (los boletos)"}
  B -- yes --> C["los = the things: Se los di a Marta = I gave them to Marta."]
  B -- no --> D{"Are the receivers several people?"}
  D -- yes --> E["los = the people: Se los dije = I told them (careful: Se lo dije)."]
```

A related habit: with a plural person after the verb, many speakers everywhere use singular *le*: *Le dije a mis papás* instead of *Les dije a mis papás*. The grammar calls it widespread in speech; in writing, match the number: *Les dije la verdad a mis papás.*

## 4. Voseo: vos and its pronouns

In Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, eastern Bolivia, much of Central America and parts of Colombia (and in rural Chiapas in Mexico), many people say *vos* instead of *tú*, with its own verb forms (*vos tenés, vos sos*; A1 honors 04h1 introduced them). This is **[[voseo]]**. What matters for this lesson: the object pronoun doesn't change. *Vos* uses *te* as object and *tu* as possessive, exactly like *tú*:

| *tú* | *vos* |
|---|---|
| *Te llamo mañana.* | *Te llamo mañana.* |
| *¿Te gusta?* | *¿Te gusta?* |
| *Es para ti. Voy contigo.* | *Es para vos. Voy con vos.* |
| *Tu celular.* | *Tu celular.* |

Only after a preposition does *vos* replace *ti* and *contigo*. *Vos* commands have the stress on the last syllable (*contá, pasá, decí*), so with one attached pronoun they need no accent, and with two they do: *contame* (tell me), *pasámelo* (pass it to me), *decímelo* (tell it to me).

### Example 3: an Argentine message

*Che, ¿me prestás tu cargador? El mío no anda. Pasámelo hoy, porfa. Te lo devuelvo mañana. ¡Gracias, sos un genio!*

1. *Me prestás*: *vos* form of *prestar* (= *me prestas*). The pronoun *me* is the same.
2. *Pasámelo*: *vos* command + *me* + *lo* = *pásamelo* in Mexico. Both need a written accent, but on different syllables: pa-SÁ-me-lo (*vos*), PÁ-sa-me-lo (*tú*).
3. *Te lo devuelvo*: identical in both systems. *Sos* = *eres*.
4. In Mexican Spanish: *Oye, ¿me prestas tu cargador? El mío no sirve. Pásamelo hoy, porfa. Te lo devuelvo mañana. ¡Gracias, eres un genio!* (*che* = hey, Argentina; *el mío* = mine; *andar* = to work, of machines, and in Mexico *servir*; *porfa* = please, informal.)

## 5. Asking politely: ¿Me da…?, ¿Me regala…?, ¿Me pone…?

The verb you use to ask for something in a shop or café also varies:

- Mexico: *¿Me da un café, por favor?* (A1) or *¿Me trae…?* in a restaurant.
- Colombia: *¿Me regala un tinto, por favor?* — literally "will you give me a black coffee as a present?" — but you pay for it. It's simply the polite way to ask there. (*un tinto* = a small black coffee in Colombia.) A Spanish tourist quoted by *Infobae* in 2025 said he was puzzled at first, because people said it while paying.
- Spain: bar orders often use *poner*: *¿Me pone un café?, ¿Me pones una caña?* (*una caña* = a small beer)

All three put the indirect pronoun *me* before the verb, exactly as in lesson 06.

## Text: En el foro

On a language forum, a learner asks a question and four people answer. (*el foro* = forum)

> Emma (Canadá): Hola. En mi libro dice «Lo vi», pero mi amiga de Madrid dice «Le vi». ¿Cuál es correcto? ¿Y qué es «se los dije»? Me suena raro.
>
> Javier (Madrid): Las dos formas son correctas. En mi zona casi todos decimos «le vi» para un hombre. Para una cosa, nunca: «el libro lo compré».
>
> Lupita (Ciudad de México): En México siempre decimos «lo vi». Y «se los dije» es muy común aquí: significa «les dije eso a ellos». En un correo formal yo escribo «se lo dije».
>
> Camilo (Medellín): Depende del país, Emma. Aquí también usamos «vos» y no cambia nada: «te llamo», «te quiero». Y en la panadería decimos «¿me regala un pan?», pero claro que lo pagamos.
>
> Emma: ¡Gracias a todos! Entonces uso «lo vi» y entiendo las otras variantes.

In English:

> Emma (Canada): Hi. My book says "Lo vi", but my friend from Madrid says "Le vi". Which is correct? And what is "se los dije"? It sounds strange to me.
>
> Javier (Madrid): Both forms are correct. In my area nearly everyone says "le vi" for a man. For a thing, never: "el libro lo compré".
>
> Lupita (Mexico City): In Mexico we always say "lo vi". And "se los dije" is very common here: it means "I told them that". In a formal e-mail I write "se lo dije".
>
> Camilo (Medellín): It depends on the country, Emma. Here we also use "vos", and nothing changes: "te llamo", "te quiero". And at the bakery we say "¿me regala un pan?", but of course we pay for it.
>
> Emma: Thanks, everyone! So I'll use "lo vi" and understand the other variants.

(*la panadería* = bakery; *claro que* = of course.) Notice the vocabulary of language itself: *la variante, el uso, la zona, común, raro, sonar* (*me suena raro* = it sounds strange to me), *depender de*. A Spanish speaker from Argentina or Spain may also call the language *el castellano*; most Mexicans say *el español*.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking *le vi* is wrong. In Spain it's accepted for one man. Just don't use *le* for a thing.
- Using *se los* in formal writing. For "I told them (it)", write *Se lo dije (a ellos)*.
- Reading *se los* as always "them (the things)". If the thing is singular, *los* points to the people.
- Changing *te* for *vos*. *Vos* takes *te*: *Te quiero*, never *Vos quiero*.
- Assuming *¿Me regala…?* is the usual request everywhere. In a Mexican shop or café, the everyday form is *¿Me da…?*
- Calling one variant "the correct Spanish". The RAE's grammar describes all these uses; it marks some as less suited to careful writing.

## Key points

- Spain's **[[leísmo]]**: *Le vi* (a man) = *Lo vi*. Accepted for one male person; *le* for a thing and *la dije* are not standard.
- Courtesy *le* for *usted* is common across Latin America: *¿En qué le puedo ayudar?*
- Latin American *se los* = "to them … it": *Se los dije* = I told them. Careful writing: *Se lo dije (a ellos)*.
- *Le* for a plural person (*Le dije a mis papás*) is common in speech; write *les*.
- **[[Voseo]]** keeps *te* and *tu*; only *ti / contigo* become *vos / con vos*. *Vos* commands: *contame, pasámelo*.
- Polite requests: Mexico *¿Me da…?*, Colombia *¿Me regala…?*, Spain *¿Me pone…?*

lessons.title: Honors: It got away from me: se me olvidó, se me cayó
lessons.body:
## Why this lesson

You've now met *se* in three jobs: reflexive (*se lava*), reciprocal (*se escriben*) and *le / les* in disguise (*se lo di*). This honors lesson adds one more, one of the most typical patterns of everyday Spanish: *se me olvidó* (I forgot), *se me cayó* (I dropped it), *se me rompió* (it broke on me). Grammars call it the **[[accidental se]]** or "no-fault *se*", because it presents a mishap as something that happened *to* you rather than something you did.

It combines two things you already know: a verb with *se* (lesson 08) and an indirect object pronoun for the person affected (lesson 06). Once you see how the pieces fit, you'll hear it everywhere, especially in apologies.

## The pattern

Start with a verb that has a *se* form for things that happen by themselves: *caerse* (to fall, lesson 03), *romperse* (to break, lesson 20), *olvidarse* (to be forgotten), *perderse* (to get lost), *acabarse* (to run out). Then put the person who suffers the accident in the middle, as an indirect pronoun:

| se | person (indirect) | verb | thing (subject) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *se* | *me* | *cayó* | *el celular* |
| *se* | *te* | *olvidaron* | *las llaves* |
| *se* | *le* | *rompió* | *la pantalla* |
| *se* | *nos* | *acabó* | *la leche* |
| *se* | *les* | *perdió* | *el perro* |

- *Se me cayó el celular.* — I dropped my phone. (literally "the phone fell on me")
- *¿Se te olvidaron las llaves?* — Did you forget your keys?
- *Se le rompió la pantalla.* — His screen broke.
- *Se nos acabó la leche.* — We ran out of milk.
- *Se les perdió el perro.* — Their dog got lost.

![A chart showing the parts of Se me cayeron las llaves in four colored boxes: se (always first), me (the person it happened to: me, te, le, nos, les), cayeron (the verb, third person, agreeing with the thing), las llaves (the thing, which is the grammatical subject). An arrow links cayeron to las llaves with the note plural thing, plural verb. Below: Se me cayó el celular, singular thing, singular verb.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Three rules make it work:

1. The thing is the subject, so the verb agrees with the thing, not with the person: *se me cayó el vaso* (one glass), *se me cayeron los vasos* (glasses). The verb is always third person, singular or plural. (*el vaso* = glass, lesson 16)
2. The order is fixed: *se* first, then the person: *se me, se te, se le, se nos, se les*. Never *me se*.
3. The person is an indirect object, so it can be doubled with *a* + person, as in lesson 06: *A mi hermano se le descompuso el carro. A ustedes se les olvidó la tarea.*

### Example 1: building the sentence

"I left my umbrella" (I forgot it), with *olvidarse* and *el paraguas*.

1. The thing: *el paraguas* (umbrella), singular. So the verb is *olvidó*.
2. The person it happened to: me → *se me*.
3. *Se me olvidó el paraguas.* — I forgot my umbrella.
4. Now "we forgot the tickets": the thing is plural (*los boletos*), the person is "us": *Se nos olvidaron los boletos.*

Notice that you don't need *mi* (my): *Se me olvidó el paraguas*. The *me* already says whose, as with body parts in lesson 08. With belongings, though, a possessive is also common and correct: *Se me olvidó mi paraguas*, *Se me perdió tu libro*.

## Why use it? Fault and politeness

Compare two ways to give the same news:

| Active: I did it | No-fault: it happened to me |
|---|---|
| *Rompí el plato.* — I broke the plate. | *Se me rompió el plato.* — The plate broke (on me). |
| *Olvidé tu cumpleaños.* — I forgot your birthday. | *Se me olvidó tu cumpleaños.* — Your birthday slipped my mind. |
| *Perdí tu libro.* — I lost your book. | *Se me perdió tu libro.* — Your book got lost (on me). |

Both are correct. The active sentence sounds like you're stating what you did, and can even sound deliberate. The *se me* version presents it as an accident, so it's the natural choice for owning up to a small mishap without sounding as if you meant it. Speakers use it all the time in apologies, and you'll often hear the two together: *Perdón, se me rompió tu taza. Fue sin querer.* (Sorry, your mug broke. I didn't mean it.)

This is a tendency in how people talk, not a rule: Spanish speakers take responsibility like anyone else, and *Lo rompí yo* (I broke it myself) is a perfectly good confession. If you broke something on purpose, say so with the active verb and *a propósito* (on purpose): *Lo rompí a propósito.*

## Common verbs

| Verb | Example | English |
|---|---|---|
| *olvidarse* | *Se me olvidó tu nombre.* | I forgot your name. |
| *caerse* (lesson 03) | *Se me cayeron las llaves.* | I dropped my keys. |
| *romperse* (lesson 20) | *Se le rompió la pantalla.* | Her screen broke. |
| *perderse* | *Se nos perdió la cartera.* | We lost the wallet. |
| *acabarse* | *Se me acabó la batería.* | My battery ran out. |
| *descomponerse* (Mexico) | *Se me descompuso el carro.* | My car broke down. |
| *derramarse* | *Se me derramó el café.* | I spilled the coffee. |
| *ocurrirse* (lesson 03's *ocurrir*) | *Se me ocurrió una idea.* | I had an idea. |
| *hacerse tarde* | *Se me hizo tarde.* | I'm running late / I lost track of time. |

Notes:

- *Descomponerse* is the everyday Mexican verb for machines that stop working (A1's *descompuesto* = out of order). It's conjugated like *poner*: *se descompuso, se descompusieron*.
- *Se me ocurrió* isn't a mishap at all: an idea "occurred to me". It uses the same pattern because the idea arrives on its own.
- *Se me hizo tarde* is a very common Mexican excuse for being late; *¡Perdón, se me hizo tarde!*
- *¡Ah, se me olvidaba!* (in the imperfect) means "Oh, I almost forgot!", said just before you mention something.
- Without the person, the same verbs describe events: *Se acabó la fiesta* (the party's over), *Se descompuso el elevador* (the elevator broke down; *el elevador*, lesson 12).
- *Olvidarse* and *perderse* can also take a person as subject: *Me olvidé de tu cumpleaños* (with *de*), *Nos perdimos en el centro* (we got lost).

## Where the pronouns go

With one conjugated verb, *se* + person go right before it, and *no* goes before *se*: *No se me olvidó.* With an infinitive, they go before the helper: *Se me va a acabar la batería* (my battery's going to run out). Attached forms such as *va a acabárseme* exist but are rare in speech; use the first position.

### Example 2: making an excuse

Your boss asks why the report is late (*el informe*). You meant to bring it, but your printer broke down and then you were late.

1. The printer: *la impresora*, singular → *se me descompuso la impresora.*
2. Being late: *se me hizo tarde.*
3. Joined: *Perdón, se me descompuso la impresora y se me hizo tarde. Se lo mando por correo en una hora.* — Sorry, my printer broke down and I lost track of time. I'll send it to you by e-mail in an hour.

*Se lo mando* is lesson 07's *se* (*le* + *lo*: to you, *usted*, it). Two different *se* in one message, each doing its own job.

### Example 3: which person, which verb?

Complete: *A los niños ___ ___ (perder) los guantes.*

1. Person: *a los niños* → *les*, so *se les*.
2. Thing: *los guantes* (gloves), plural → *perdieron*.
3. *A los niños se les perdieron los guantes.* — The kids lost their gloves.

## Text: Un lunes terrible

![A comic strip in four numbered panels, each with a caption. Panel 1: a cup tipping over and coffee spilling onto a laptop keyboard. Panel 2: a bus-stop sign that says PARADA, and a phone on the ground with a cracked screen. Panel 3: a man outside a closed door, with a thought bubble showing a key on a table. Panel 4: a small car stopped on the road, with a fuel gauge pointing to empty above it. The captions read: Se me derramó el café. Se me cayó el celular. Se me olvidaron las llaves. Se nos acabó la gasolina.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> El lunes pasado fue el peor día de mi vida. Primero, en el desayuno, se me derramó el café en el teclado de la laptop. La limpié rápido, pero ya no prendió.
>
> Salí tarde de la casa y, en la parada del camión, se me cayó el celular. Se le rompió la pantalla, y con la pantalla rota no podía llamar a nadie.
>
> Regresé a la casa por mi celular viejo y… ¡se me olvidaron las llaves adentro! Tuve que esperar a mi vecina, que tiene una copia.
>
> Por fin le pedí prestado el carro a mi hermano. Pero en la carretera se nos acabó la gasolina, porque a él se le olvidó llenar el tanque. ¿El final? Llegué a la oficina a las doce. Mi jefa me miró y yo solo le dije: «Perdón, se me hizo tarde».

In English:

> Last Monday was the worst day of my life. First, at breakfast, I spilled coffee on my laptop's keyboard. I cleaned it up fast, but it wouldn't turn on anymore.
>
> I left the house late, and at the bus stop I dropped my phone. Its screen broke, and with a broken screen I couldn't call anyone.
>
> I went back home for my old phone and… I'd left the keys inside! I had to wait for my neighbor, who has a copy.
>
> Finally I borrowed my brother's car. But on the highway we ran out of gas, because he forgot to fill the tank. The end? I got to the office at twelve. My boss looked at me and all I said was: "Sorry, I'm running late."

(*el peor* = the worst; *ya no* = no longer, lesson 02; *rota* = broken, from *romper*; *adentro* = inside; *la copia* = copy; *la carretera* = highway; *la gasolina* = gasoline; *llenar el tanque* = to fill the tank.) The narrator uses the active voice for deliberate actions (*la limpié, salí, regresé, le pedí*) and the no-fault *se* for every accident. *Se nos acabó* includes the brother: "we" ran out.

### An apology message

> *Hola, Carla. Te pido una disculpa: se me olvidó por completo nuestra cita de ayer. Se me descompuso el celular y no vi tu mensaje. Fue un descuido, no lo hice a propósito. ¿Te invito un café el sábado para compensarte?*

> Hi, Carla. I owe you an apology: I completely forgot our meeting yesterday. My phone broke down and I didn't see your message. It was a slip; I didn't do it on purpose. Can I buy you a coffee on Saturday to make up for it?

(*te pido una disculpa* = I apologize, a common Mexican formula; *la disculpa* is lesson 23's word; *por completo* = completely; *compensar* = to make up for; *¿Te invito un café?* = Can I buy you a coffee?, A1.)

## Common mistakes

- *Me se cayó.* — You'll hear it in casual speech, but standard Spanish always puts *se* first: *Se me cayó.*
- *Se me cayó las llaves.* — The verb agrees with the thing: *Se me cayeron las llaves.*
- *Se me olvidé.* — The verb is third person, for the thing: *Se me olvidó.*
- *Se cayó el celular a mí.* — The person needs the pronoun: *Se me cayó el celular (a mí).*
- Using it for something you did on purpose. *Se me rompió* means it was an accident; for a deliberate act use *Lo rompí*.

## Key points

- The **[[accidental se]]**: *se* + indirect pronoun (*me, te, le, nos, les*) + third-person verb + the thing: *Se me cayó el celular.*
- The thing is the subject: *se me cayó el vaso / se me cayeron los vasos.*
- *Se* always comes first: *se me*, never *me se*. Add *a* + person to say who: *A Pedro se le olvidó.*
- It presents a mishap as an accident, so it's the usual way to admit small mistakes: *Perdón, se me olvidó.*
- Verbs: *olvidarse, caerse, romperse, perderse, acabarse, descomponerse* (Mexico), *derramarse*; chunks *se me ocurrió, se me hizo tarde, ¡se me olvidaba!*
