lessons.title: What's happening? Estar + gerund and describing a photo
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 told stories in the past, and module 2 gave you the object pronouns. This lesson adds the form that English expresses with "-ing": *Estoy platicando con mi hermana* (I'm chatting with my sister). You'll learn to make the **[[gerund]]** (*platicando, comiendo, leyendo, durmiendo*), to use it with *estar* for what's going on now and what was going on in the past, to say "still doing" with *seguir*, and where pronouns go.

Then you'll put it to work. One of the DELE A2 speaking tasks asks you to describe a photo of an everyday scene, which is exactly what estar + gerund is for: *Un niño está lanzando una pelota.* You'll learn the position words for a picture (*al fondo, en primer plano*) and the difference between *está sentado* (is sitting) and *se está sentando* (is sitting down). When you finish, the gerund joins your conjugation drills.

## Making the gerund

The gerund is one form that never changes: not for the person, not for gender, not for number. *Ella está comiendo, ellos están comiendo.* You make it from the stem of the infinitive (the infinitive without *-ar, -er, -ir*):

| Verb type | Ending | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -ar | *-ando* | *hablar → hablando, platicar → platicando, saludar → saludando* |
| -er, -ir | *-iendo* | *comer → comiendo, recoger → recogiendo, escribir → escribiendo* |
| stem ends in a vowel | *-yendo* | *leer → leyendo, oír → oyendo, traer → trayendo, caer → cayendo* |
| -ir verbs that change their stem | *e → i, o → u* | *pedir → pidiendo, decir → diciendo, venir → viniendo, dormir → durmiendo, morir → muriendo* |
| irregular | | *ir → yendo, poder → pudiendo* |

![A chart of the five ways to make the gerund: -ar verbs add -ando (hablar, hablando); -er and -ir verbs add -iendo (comer, comiendo); after a vowel -iendo is spelled -yendo (leer, leyendo; oír, oyendo); -ir verbs with a stem change turn e into i and o into u (pedir, pidiendo; dormir, durmiendo); and two irregulars, ir, yendo and poder, pudiendo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Why -yendo? Spanish doesn't let an unstressed *i* sit between two vowels, so *le-iendo* becomes *leyendo*; the same happens in *construir* (to build): *construyendo*.

The -ir stem changers. If an -ir verb changes its stem in the present (*pido, duermo, siento*), its gerund usually changes too, to *i* or *u*. A handy check: the gerund has the same vowel as the *él* form of the preterite you learned in lesson 1. *Pidió → pidiendo, durmió → durmiendo, sintió → sintiendo* (from *sentir*, to feel), *repitió → repitiendo, se vistió → vistiendo*. The two verbs of this lesson that laugh and smile belong here as well: *reír → riendo, sonreír → sonriendo*. Notice there's only one *i*: *ri-endo*, not *rii-endo*.

-ar and -er stem changers don't change. *Pensar → pensando, volver → volviendo, querer → queriendo, mostrar → mostrando.* Apart from *poder* (*pudiendo*, in the table above), only -ir verbs change their stem in the gerund.

## Estar + gerund: what's happening right now

Put the present of *estar* before the gerund and you have the Spanish for "am / are / is doing":

| | estar | + gerund |
|---|---|---|
| yo | estoy | *platicando* |
| tú | estás | *comiendo* |
| él, ella, usted | está | *leyendo* |
| nosotros | estamos | *esperando* |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | están | *durmiendo* |

- *¿Qué estás haciendo?* — *Estoy viendo una serie.* — What are you doing? — I'm watching a series.
- *Los niños están jugando en el parque.* — The children are playing in the park.
- *No puedo hablar ahora, estamos comiendo.* — I can't talk now, we're eating.

Spanish uses this form less than English uses "-ing". The simple present covers habits and facts (*Trabajo en un banco*) and often the present moment too: *¿Qué haces? — Leo.* Estar + gerund stresses that an action is in progress, often in contrast with what's normal: *Normalmente trabajo en la oficina, pero hoy estoy trabajando en casa.*

There are three places where English uses "-ing" and Spanish doesn't use estar + gerund:

- Plans for the future. *Mañana salgo a las ocho* or *Mañana voy a salir* (I'm leaving tomorrow), not *estoy saliendo*.
- States, not actions. *Tengo dos hermanos* (not *estoy teniendo*); *Llevo una chamarra azul* (I'm wearing a blue jacket); *Me gusta* (I like it).
- The "-ing" noun. "Swimming is good for you" is *Nadar es bueno*, with the infinitive. *Me gusta caminar* — I like walking.

## In the past: estaba + gerund

Lesson 3 showed you the scene and the event: the imperfect for what was going on, the preterite for what happened. With *estaba* + gerund you stress that the background action was in progress at that moment:

- *Estaba lloviendo cuando salí.* — It was raining when I left.
- *¿Qué estabas haciendo cuando te llamé?* — What were you doing when I called you?
- *Estábamos platicando cuando de repente se fue la luz.* — We were chatting when suddenly the power went out.

*Llovía cuando salí* means nearly the same; the gerund version paints the action as happening right then. (You'll also hear *estuve* + gerund for a finished stretch of time: *Ayer estuve trabajando hasta las diez*.)

## Seguir + gerund: still doing

*Seguir* (A1: to continue, to follow) + gerund means "to still be doing" or "to keep doing". It changes like *pedir* in the present: *sigo, sigues, sigue, seguimos, siguen*.

- *¿Sigues viviendo en Puebla?* — Are you still living in Puebla?
- *Sigue lloviendo.* — It's still raining.
- *Mi abuelo sigue trabajando a los ochenta años.* — My grandfather is still working at eighty.

The opposite is *ya no* (lesson 2): *Ya no vivo en Puebla* — I don't live in Puebla anymore. (*Todavía está lloviendo* is also correct.)

## Pronouns with the gerund

Object and reflexive pronouns (lessons 5–8) have two places, exactly as with an infinitive: before *estar*, or attached to the end of the gerund.

- *Lo estoy leyendo.* = *Estoy leyéndolo.* — I'm reading it.
- *Me estoy riendo.* = *Estoy riéndome.* — I'm laughing.
- *Te lo estoy diciendo.* = *Estoy diciéndotelo.* — I'm telling you (it).

An attached pronoun leaves the stress where it was, now three or more syllables from the end, so the gerund needs a written accent: *le-YEN-do → le-YÉN-do-lo*. Both positions are correct and common, and this course's typed answers accept both.

## Sitting or sitting down? Positions and actions

This is one of the biggest traps for English speakers. "She's sitting on the bench" describes a position, not an action, and Spanish says it with *estar* + the participle-like adjective *sentado*:

| Position (estar + adjective) | Action in progress (gerund) |
|---|---|
| *Está sentada en la banca.* — She's sitting on the bench. | *Se está sentando.* — She's sitting down (right now). |
| *Está acostado en el pasto.* — He's lying on the grass. | *Se está acostando.* — He's lying down. |
| *Están de pie.* — They're standing. | *Se están levantando.* — They're getting up. |

*Sentado* and *acostado* agree like any adjective (*sentada, sentados*); *de pie* never changes. In Mexico, as in much of Latin America, *parado* (standing) is very common: *Está parado junto a la puerta*. (*Parado* can also mean "stopped", and in Spain "unemployed", so *de pie* is safer in writing.) *Sentarse* changes like *pensar*: *me siento, te sientas*; command *¡Siéntate!* / *Siéntese*.

## Describing a photo

Go from the whole scene to the details: what it is (*En la foto hay una plaza*), where things are, what people are doing, and a guess at the end (*Creo que…*, *Parece que…*). The position words:

![A picture frame divided into zones. The top band is labeled al fondo, the bottom band en primer plano. Left, middle and right columns are labeled a la izquierda, en medio and a la derecha. A small tree in the middle of the frame has arrows labeled junto a, pointing to a bench beside it, and alrededor de, curving around it.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *al fondo* | in the background, at the back |
| *en primer plano* | in the foreground |
| *a la izquierda / a la derecha* (A1) | on the left / on the right |
| *en medio de, en el centro de* | in the middle of |
| *junto a* | beside, right next to |
| *alrededor de* | around |
| *detrás de, enfrente de, entre* (A1) | behind, in front of, between |

*Junto a* and *al lado de* (A1) are close; *junto a* suggests "right beside". Two chunks help a lot: *hay* and *se ve / se ven* (you can see; the impersonal *se* of lesson 17, learned here as a phrase): *Al fondo se ve una iglesia.*

## The plaza on Sunday

![A town plaza on a sunny Sunday. In the background is a church with two towers between trees. In the middle is a round fountain with three children running around it. In the foreground on the left, under a big tree, an older man and a woman are sitting on a bench; he is reading a book and she is laughing. In front of them a young man is lying on the grass. On the right, a girl is holding a red balloon and her father is pointing at the fountain. Behind them, two women are standing and chatting; one is waving. Near the center, a boy is throwing a ball and a dog is running after it.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A model description

A description of the picture, as a learner might give it in the exam:

> En la imagen hay una plaza, y creo que es domingo porque hay mucha gente. Al fondo se ve una iglesia con dos torres y unos árboles. En medio de la plaza hay una fuente, y alrededor de la fuente tres niños están corriendo. En primer plano, a la izquierda, hay una banca debajo de un árbol grande. Un señor mayor está sentado en la banca y está leyendo un libro. Junto a él, una señora se está riendo. Enfrente de ellos, un joven está acostado en el pasto. A la derecha hay una niña con un globo rojo, y su papá está señalando la fuente. Detrás de ellos, dos mujeres están de pie y están platicando; una está saludando a alguien. En el centro, un niño está lanzando una pelota y un perro está corriendo detrás de ella. Me parece que es una tarde muy tranquila.

In English: In the picture there's a plaza, and I think it's Sunday because there are a lot of people. In the background you can see a church with two towers and some trees. In the middle of the plaza there's a fountain, and three children are running around the fountain. In the foreground, on the left, there's a bench under a big tree. An older man is sitting on the bench and reading a book. Beside him, a woman is laughing. In front of them, a young man is lying on the grass. On the right there's a girl with a red balloon, and her dad is pointing at the fountain. Behind them, two women are standing and chatting; one is waving at someone. In the middle, a boy is throwing a ball and a dog is running after it. It seems to me it's a very quiet afternoon.

(*el pasto* = grass, lawn, in Mexico; *mayor* = older, lesson 11; *la torre* = tower.) Notice the order: the whole scene, the background, the middle, the foreground, then an opinion. *Saludar* is "to greet" in any way: waving, saying hello, shaking hands.

## Dialogue: ¿Dónde estás?

Andrés calls his sister Valeria, who is late for Sunday lunch.

> Andrés: ¿Bueno? Vale, ¿dónde estás? Te estamos esperando para comer.
>
> Valeria: Perdón, sigo en la plaza. Estoy sentada en una banca, junto a la fuente.
>
> Andrés: ¿Y qué estás haciendo ahí?
>
> Valeria: Nada, estoy viendo a la gente. Hay un grupo de niños corriendo alrededor de la fuente, y un señor está vendiendo globos.
>
> Andrés: Oye, ¿está ahí Mariana? Siempre va a la plaza los domingos.
>
> Valeria: ¡Sí! La estoy viendo ahora mismo. Está al fondo, platicando con unas amigas… Ahora me está saludando.
>
> Andrés: Salúdala de mi parte. ¿Vienes o no?
>
> Valeria: Sí, ya me estoy levantando. Llego en veinte minutos.

In English:

> Andrés: Hello? Vale, where are you? We're waiting for you to eat.
>
> Valeria: Sorry, I'm still at the plaza. I'm sitting on a bench, right by the fountain.
>
> Andrés: And what are you doing there?
>
> Valeria: Nothing, I'm watching the people. There's a group of children running around the fountain, and a man is selling balloons.
>
> Andrés: Hey, is Mariana there? She always goes to the plaza on Sundays.
>
> Valeria: Yes! I'm looking at her right now. She's at the back, chatting with some friends… Now she's waving at me.
>
> Andrés: Say hi to her from me. Are you coming or not?
>
> Valeria: Yes, I'm getting up now. I'll be there in twenty minutes.

(*vender* = to sell; *de mi parte* = from me.) In *un grupo de niños corriendo*, the gerund follows the noun without *estar*, as in English "children running".

## Pronunciation

- *-ando, -iendo*: the stress falls on the ending: *ha-BLAN-do*, *co-MIEN-do* (*ie* is one syllable).
- *leyendo, oyendo, cayendo*: the *y* is the same sound as *ll* in Mexico (*le-YEN-do*).
- *sonreír*: three syllables, *son-re-ÍR*. After *n*, a single *r* is trilled, as in *Enrique*. The written accent on *í* keeps *e* and *i* in separate syllables.
- *reírse*: *re-ÍR-se*, with a trilled *r*; *se ríe*: *RÍ-e*. The preterite *se rio* counts as one syllable and has no accent (RAE 2010 spelling), but two-syllable *sonrió* keeps it.
- *alrededor*: *al-re-de-DOR*; the *r* after *l* is trilled.

## Common mistakes

- *Está sentando en la banca* for "he's sitting on the bench". A position takes the adjective: *Está sentado en la banca.* (*Se está sentando* = he's sitting down.)
- *Estoy saliendo mañana.* Spanish doesn't use estar + gerund for plans: *Salgo mañana* or *Voy a salir mañana*.
- *Estoy teniendo un carro nuevo.* States take the simple present: *Tengo un carro nuevo.*
- *Me gusta nadando.* After *gustar* and as a subject, use the infinitive: *Me gusta nadar.*
- *Pediendo, dormiendo, deciendo.* -ir stem changers take *i* or *u*: *pidiendo, durmiendo, diciendo*.
- *Estoy leyendolo* without the accent. With an attached pronoun: *leyéndolo*.
- *Estoy lo leyendo.* The pronoun goes before *estar* or at the end of the gerund, never between them.

## Key points

- The gerund: *-ando* (-ar), *-iendo* (-er, -ir), *-yendo* after a vowel (*leyendo, oyendo*); -ir stem changers take *i* or *u* like the *él* preterite (*pidiendo, durmiendo, sonriendo*); *yendo, pudiendo*. It never changes its ending.
- *estar* + gerund: an action in progress now (*Estoy platicando*); *estaba* + gerund: in progress in the past (*Estaba lloviendo cuando salí*); *seguir* + gerund: still doing (*Sigue lloviendo*).
- Not for plans (*Salgo mañana*), states (*Tengo*) or "-ing" nouns (*Nadar es bueno*).
- Pronouns before *estar* or attached with an accent: *Lo estoy leyendo / Estoy leyéndolo*.
- Positions: *está sentado / acostado / de pie* (Mexico also *parado*); actions: *se está sentando*.
- A picture: *En la foto hay…, al fondo se ve…, en primer plano…, en medio de…, junto a…, alrededor de…*, then *Creo que…*

lessons.title: What's she like? Appearance and character
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Spanish A1 you described people with a handful of adjectives (*alto, bajo, joven, simpático*) and learned that *ser* says what something is like while *estar* says how it is right now. Lesson 9 added estar + gerund for what people are doing. This lesson fills in the rest of a description: hair, eyes, beard and build; height with *medir*; character words such as *amable, tímido, trabajador*; the difference between *parecerse a* (to look like) and *parecer* (to seem, lesson 6); and how to describe people kindly, because some words that are fine in a dictionary are not fine to someone's face.

By the end you can describe a friend so that someone else can find her at an airport, and talk about a family member's personality. Comparisons (*más alto que, el más alto*) come in lesson 11.

## Hair, eyes and face

For hair and eyes, Spanish uses *tener* + the definite article + the noun + the adjective. English says "she has straight hair"; Spanish says "she has the hair straight":

- *Tiene el pelo lacio y largo.* — She has long, straight hair.
- *Tiene los ojos cafés.* — He has brown eyes.
- *Tiene la cara redonda.* — She has a round face (*redondo* = round).

| Spanish | English | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| *el pelo* | hair | also *el cabello*, a bit more formal |
| *lacio* | straight (hair) | Spain usually says *liso* |
| *rizado* | curly | in Mexico usually *chino*: *Tiene el pelo chino* |
| *negro, castaño, rubio* | black, brown, blond (hair) | Mexico: *güero* for blond |
| *moreno* | dark (hair or skin) | see "Describing people kindly" below |
| *calvo* | bald | Mexico also *pelón*, informal |
| *la barba, el bigote* | beard, mustache | |
| *la cara* | face | |

*Castaño* is the usual word for brown hair; for eyes Mexico usually says *cafés* (*ojos cafés*), and you'll also hear *castaños*. With *el pelo*, the adjectives agree with *pelo*, so they stay masculine even for a woman: *Ella tiene el pelo rizado*.

### Llevar and tener

Lesson 7 used *llevar* for clothes. It also works for glasses and for a beard or a hairstyle that someone has chosen:

- *Lleva lentes.* — He wears glasses. In Mexico *usa lentes* is just as common.
- *Lleva barba* or *Tiene barba.* — He has a beard. No article here: *barba, bigote, lentes* follow the verb directly.
- *Lleva el pelo corto.* — She wears her hair short.

With *ser*, a few features describe the whole person: *Es calvo. Es rubia. Es moreno.* *Es calvo* and *Está calvo* are both heard; *está* suggests he has become bald.

![Four faces in a row, each with a name below. Raúl has short black hair and a black beard. Don Ernesto is bald on top and has a gray mustache. Lucía has curly brown hair. Sofía has long, straight blond hair.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Raúl tiene barba y el pelo corto y negro. Don Ernesto es calvo y tiene bigote. Lucía tiene el pelo rizado (chino) y castaño. Sofía tiene el pelo lacio, largo y rubio.*

## Build and height

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *alto / bajo* (A1) | tall / short |
| *delgado* | thin, slim |
| *gordo* | fat (careful: see below) |
| *fuerte* | strong |
| *guapo* | good-looking, handsome, pretty |

*Guapo* works for men and women: *Tu hermana es muy guapa.* *Fuerte* has other everyday meanings too: *música fuerte* (loud music), *un café fuerte* (strong coffee).

To give a height, use *medir* (to measure), an -ir verb that changes *e → i*: *mido, mides, mide, medimos, miden*; preterite *midió, midieron*. Heights are in meters and centimeters, and the word *metro* is said only once:

- *¿Cuánto mides?* — *Mido un metro setenta.* — How tall are you? — I'm 1.70 m (about 5 ft 7 in).
- *Mi papá mide un metro ochenta y dos.* — My dad is 1.82 m.
- *La mesa mide dos metros.* — The table is two meters long.

For weight, *pesar* (to weigh) is a regular -ar verb: *Peso setenta kilos.*

### Example 1: a full description

Describe Lucía from the picture as if to a friend.

1. Start with *ser* and what she's like in general: *Lucía es joven, delgada y no muy alta.*
2. Add height with *medir*: *Mide como un metro sesenta.* (*como* = about.)
3. Hair and eyes with *tener* + article: *Tiene el pelo chino y castaño, y los ojos cafés.*
4. Glasses or clothes with *llevar*: *Hoy lleva una blusa rosa.*
5. Character with *ser*: *Es muy alegre y muy amable.*

Together: *Lucía es joven, delgada y no muy alta: mide como un metro sesenta. Tiene el pelo chino y castaño y los ojos cafés. Hoy lleva una blusa rosa. Es muy alegre y muy amable.*

## Character: what someone is like

| Spanish | English | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| *el carácter* | character, personality | plural *los caracteres* (stress moves: *ca-rac-TE-res*) |
| *amable* | kind, friendly | same form for both genders |
| *tímido* | shy | |
| *alegre* | cheerful | same form for both genders |
| *serio* | serious, quiet, reserved | |
| *trabajador* | hard-working | feminine *trabajadora* |
| *perezoso* | lazy | Mexico also *flojo* (lesson 7's "loose") |
| *egoísta* | selfish | same form for both genders: *un niño egoísta, una niña egoísta* |
| *educado* | polite, well-mannered | false friend: not "educated" |
| *grosero* | rude | *una grosería* = a rude remark, also a swear word |

Two of these trip up English speakers. *Educado* is about manners: *un niño muy educado* is a polite child, not one with a degree. "Educated" is *culto* (cultured) or *con estudios*: *Es una persona con estudios universitarios.* And *flojo*, which lesson 7 taught as "loose" for clothes, is the everyday Mexican word for "lazy": *¡Qué flojo eres!* — You're so lazy!

To ask about character, use *¿Cómo es?*: *¿Cómo es tu jefe? — Es muy trabajador, pero un poco serio.* To ask about looks specifically: *¿Cómo es físicamente?* (physically).

## Ser or estar for people

A1 taught the basic rule. With people it works like this: *ser* for what someone is like (character, lasting looks); *estar* for how someone is or looks now, especially after a change.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Ser, estar, tener or llevar for describing people
  accDescr: To describe a person, first ask what you are describing. For what the person is like in general, character or lasting looks, use ser, as in Es alto, Es tímida. For a state now or a change, use estar, as in Está cansado, Está más delgada. For hair, eyes or a beard, use tener, as in Tiene el pelo lacio. For clothes or glasses, use llevar, as in Lleva lentes.
  A["What are you describing?"] --> B["What the person is like in general"]
  A --> C["A state now, or a change"]
  A --> D["Hair, eyes, beard"]
  A --> E["Clothes, glasses"]
  B --> F["ser: Es alto. Es tímida."]
  C --> G["estar: Está cansado. Está más delgada."]
  D --> H["tener: Tiene el pelo lacio."]
  E --> I["llevar: Lleva lentes."]
```

The same adjective can change meaning with the verb:

| ser | estar |
|---|---|
| *Es delgado.* — He's slim (that's how he is). | *Está más delgado.* — He's thinner (than before). |
| *Es guapa.* — She's pretty. | *¡Qué guapa estás!* — You look great (today)! |
| *Es serio.* — He's a serious, quiet person. | *Está serio.* — He's quiet today (something's wrong?). |
| *Es alegre.* — She's a cheerful person. | *Está alegre.* — She's in a good mood. |

In everyday Mexican speech you'll hear *estar* with body words quite often (*Está muy delgada*), meaning "she looks very thin". Both are correct; the difference is the speaker's point of view.

### Example 2: choosing the verb

Choose *ser* or *estar*.

1. *Mi abuela ___ muy trabajadora.* Character, in general: *es*.
2. *Después de las vacaciones, mi hermano ___ más fuerte.* A change: *está*.
3. *Tu prima ___ muy guapa hoy con ese vestido.* How she looks today: *está*.
4. *El maestro nuevo ___ un poco tímido.* Character: *es*.

## Parecerse a and parecer

Lesson 6 taught *parecer* for "to seem": *Pareces cansado* (You seem tired), *¿Qué te parece?* The reflexive *parecerse a* means "to look like, to resemble". It changes like *conocer*: *me parezco, te pareces, se parece, nos parecemos, se parecen*.

- *Te pareces mucho a tu mamá.* — You look a lot like your mom.
- *Mi hermano y yo nos parecemos en la cara, pero no en el carácter.* — My brother and I look alike in the face, but not in personality.
- *Lucía parece muy alegre.* — Lucía seems very cheerful (no *se*, no *a*).

So: *parecer* + adjective = to seem; *parecerse a* + person = to look like.

## Describing people kindly

Every language has words that are accurate but unkind. A few guidelines for Spanish:

- Soften negative adjectives with *un poco* or *algo* (somewhat): *Es un poco tímido. Es algo serio.* Or use *no muy* + the positive word: *No es muy alto* sounds kinder than *Es bajo*.
- Diminutives (Spanish A1, honors 8h2) soften a lot in Mexico: *Es gordito* (a bit chubby), *chaparrito* (shortish; *chaparro* = short, informal Mexico), *morenito*.
- *Gordo* said directly about someone can be rude, as in English. At the same time, in many Mexican families *gordo* or *gordita* is an affectionate nickname. As a learner, avoid it about people and say *llenito* (a bit plump) or nothing.
- Age: for an older person, say *una señora mayor* (*mayor* = older, lesson 11) rather than *vieja*, which can sound rude.
- *Güero, moreno*: everyday Mexican descriptions of hair and skin tone (*güero* = blond or fair; *moreno* = dark-haired or brown-skinned). Vendors call customers *güero* or *güerita* in a friendly way, whatever their coloring. But comments on skin color can be sensitive, and in some situations they touch on discrimination, so when in doubt, describe hair, height and clothes instead.

## Dialogue: ¿Cómo es tu prima?

Tomás is going to pick up Ana's cousin at the airport, but he has never met her.

> Tomás: Oye, Ana, voy a recoger a tu prima al aeropuerto, pero no la conozco. ¿Cómo es?
>
> Ana: Se llama Daniela. Es alta, mide como un metro setenta y cinco, y es delgada.
>
> Tomás: ¿Y el pelo?
>
> Ana: Antes lo tenía castaño y chino… pero ahora creo que lo tiene lacio y más corto. Ah, y usa lentes.
>
> Tomás: ¿Se parece a ti?
>
> Ana: Un poco. Todos dicen que nos parecemos en la cara, pero ella es más seria que yo. Bueno, seria no; es un poco tímida con la gente que no conoce.
>
> Tomás: Tranquila, yo hablo mucho.
>
> Ana: Ya lo sé. Y cuando te conoce es muy alegre y muy amable. Creo que se van a llevar bien.
>
> Tomás: ¿Y qué ropa va a llevar?
>
> Ana: Una chamarra roja. Me lo dijo por mensaje.
>
> Tomás: Perfecto: una muchacha alta, delgada, con lentes y chamarra roja. La voy a encontrar fácilmente.

In English:

> Tomás: Hey, Ana, I'm going to pick up your cousin at the airport, but I don't know her. What does she look like?
>
> Ana: Her name is Daniela. She's tall, she's about 1.75, and she's slim.
>
> Tomás: And her hair?
>
> Ana: She used to have it brown and curly… but now I think it's straight and shorter. Oh, and she wears glasses.
>
> Tomás: Does she look like you?
>
> Ana: A bit. Everyone says we look alike in the face, but she's more serious than me. Well, not serious; she's a bit shy with people she doesn't know.
>
> Tomás: Relax, I talk a lot.
>
> Ana: I know. And once she knows you she's very cheerful and very kind. I think you're going to get along.
>
> Tomás: And what is she going to be wearing?
>
> Ana: A red jacket. She told me by text.
>
> Tomás: Perfect: a tall, slim young woman with glasses and a red jacket. I'll find her easily.

(*la muchacha* = young woman, girl; *fácilmente* = easily.) *¿Cómo es?* here means "What does she look like / what's she like?"; it covers both looks and character. *Antes lo tenía* uses the imperfect of lesson 2 for how her hair used to be, and *la gente que no conoce* uses *que* as "who", which lesson 18 explains.

## Pronunciation

- *güero*: the two dots (*diéresis*) mean the *u* is pronounced: *GWE-ro*. Without them, *guerra* has a silent *u*.
- *egoísta*: four syllables, *e-go-ÍS-ta*; the accent keeps *o* and *i* apart.
- *carácter*: *ca-RÁC-ter*; plural *caracteres*, *ca-rac-TE-res*, with no written accent.
- *lacio*: two syllables, *LA-cio* (LA-syo); *rizado*: *ri-SA-do*, with the Latin American *z* = *s*.
- *la barba, el bigote*: inside a phrase (after a vowel, *l* or *r*) the *b* is soft, with the lips barely touching; it is a hard *b* only at the start of a phrase or after *m, n*.
- *guapo*: *GUA-po*, one syllable for *gua*.

## Common mistakes

- *Tiene su pelo lacio.* With hair, eyes and other parts of the body, Spanish uses the article, not the possessive: *Tiene el pelo lacio. Tiene los ojos azules.*
- *Ella tiene el pelo rizada.* The adjective agrees with *pelo*: *rizado*.
- *Es muy educado* for "he's well educated". *Educado* = polite. Say *Tiene estudios* or *Es muy culto*.
- *Mido 1.70 metros* read as *uno punto setenta metros*. Say *un metro setenta*.
- *Parezco a mi papá.* "To look like" is reflexive with *a*: *Me parezco a mi papá.*
- *Ella es egoísta* is right; *egoísto* doesn't exist. *Egoísta, amable, alegre* don't change for gender.
- *Está tímido* for a shy person. Shyness as character takes *ser*: *Es tímido.* (*Está tímido* = he's being shy right now, which is possible but less common.)

## Key points

- *tener* + article + noun + adjective: *Tiene el pelo chino / los ojos cafés.* *llevar* (or *usar*) for glasses and clothes; *Lleva / Tiene barba* without an article.
- Mexican hair words: *lacio, chino* (curly; also *rizado*), *güero* (blond; also *rubio*), *pelón* (bald; also *calvo*).
- *medir* (e → i): *Mido un metro setenta.*
- *ser* for character and lasting looks; *estar* for states and changes: *es delgado / está más delgado*.
- Character: *amable, tímido, alegre, serio, trabajador(a), perezoso / flojo, egoísta, educado* (polite!), *grosero*.
- *parecer* = to seem; *parecerse a* = to look like.
- Be kind: *un poco / algo* + negative adjective, *no muy* + positive, diminutives, *mayor* rather than *viejo*; avoid *gordo* and skin-color comments when in doubt.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: City or country? Comparatives and superlatives
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 10 described people. Now you describe and compare places: regions, landscapes and the choice between city and country. In Spanish A1 you learned the basic **[[comparative]]** (*más barato que, menos caro que, tan caro como*) and the two irregular forms *mejor* and *peor*. This lesson completes the picture:

- *más de / menos de* before a number (*más de un millón*);
- *tanto* with nouns and verbs (*tantos carros como, tanto como tú*);
- *igual de* + adjective;
- *mayor* and *menor*;
- the **[[superlative]]** (*la ciudad más grande del país*);
- the ending *-ísimo* (*riquísimo, larguísimo*);
- *lo mejor, lo peor, lo más* + adjective.

Along the way you'll learn the words for Mexico's landscapes and some real facts about the country, each with its date and source.

## Landscapes and regions

![A simple map of Mexico with a compass rose showing N, S, E and O. The north has a large desert area; the mountains of the two Sierras Madre run down the country; Lake Chapala is marked west of Mexico City; the island of Cozumel lies off the Yucatán Peninsula in the Caribbean; a rainforest area covers Chiapas in the south; the Pacific coast is labeled in the west, and Mexico City sits in a valley in the center. The Pico de Orizaba is marked east of Mexico City.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English | In Mexico |
|---|---|---|
| *el campo* | the countryside; a field | *Vivo en el campo* — I live in the country. |
| *la naturaleza* | nature | |
| *el paisaje* | landscape, scenery | |
| *el desierto* | desert | the north: Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila |
| *la selva* | rainforest, jungle | the south: Chiapas, the Yucatán Peninsula |
| *la costa* | coast | the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean |
| *el lago* | lake | Lake Chapala, between Jalisco and Michoacán |
| *la isla* | island | Cozumel, in the Caribbean |
| *el valle* | valley | Mexico City lies in the Valley of Mexico |
| *el cerro* | hill | almost every city has one; Monterrey's *Cerro de la Silla* is famous |
| *la región* | region | |
| *el estado* | state (of a country) | 31 states plus Mexico City |

*El cerro* is the everyday Latin American word for a hill, even a big one; *la colina* (also correct) sounds more like a textbook. *La montaña* (A1) is a mountain, and *la sierra* a mountain range: *la Sierra Madre Occidental*.

A few facts to compare with later. Mexico is divided into 32 *entidades federativas*: 31 *estados* and Mexico City, which is not a state. In the 2020 census (INEGI) the country had 126,014,024 inhabitants. The biggest state by area is Chihuahua, and the smallest is Tlaxcala. The largest lake is Lake Chapala, about 1,100 km² (Conagua). The highest mountain is the Pico de Orizaba, a volcano on the border of Puebla and Veracruz, more than 5,600 meters high.

### The points of the compass

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| *el norte* — north | *el sur* — south | |
| *el este* — east | *el oeste* — west | Mexico also *el oriente* (east), *el poniente* (west) |

*Monterrey está en el norte de México.* — Monterrey is in the north of Mexico. *Puebla está al este de la Ciudad de México.* — Puebla is east of Mexico City. Use *en el norte* for a place inside the area and *al norte de* for a direction from somewhere else. You'll see *oriente* and *poniente* on Mexican street names and signs (*Avenida 5 Poniente*, *Ote.*, *Pte.*). *Este* is also "this" (A1: *este libro*); with the article, *el este* is the noun "east".

## Comparing: the full set

Here is the A1 set again, with what's new.

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| *más / menos* + adjective + *que* (A1) | *El campo es más tranquilo que la ciudad.* |
| *tan* + adjective + *como* (A1) | *El lago no es tan grande como el mar.* |
| *mejor / peor que* (A1) | *El clima de Cuernavaca es mejor que el de aquí.* |
| *más / menos de* + number | *La ciudad tiene más de un millón de habitantes.* |
| *tanto, tanta, tantos, tantas* + noun + *como* | *Aquí no hay tantos carros como en el centro.* |
| verb + *tanto como* | *No viajo tanto como tú.* |
| *igual de* + adjective + *que* | *Puebla es igual de bonita que Querétaro.* |

### Más de with numbers

Before a number, "more than" and "less than" are *más de* and *menos de*:

- *Guadalajara tiene más de un millón de habitantes.* — Guadalajara has more than a million inhabitants.
- *El viaje dura menos de dos horas.* — The trip takes less than two hours.

Compare *Jalisco tiene más habitantes que Veracruz*, where *que* introduces the second thing compared, not a number. (In a negative sentence, *No tengo más que cien pesos* means "I only have a hundred pesos": a different meaning to recognize.)

### Tanto … como

For "as much / as many … as" with a noun, *tanto* agrees with the noun like an adjective:

- *No hay tanto tráfico como ayer.* — There isn't as much traffic as yesterday. (*el tráfico*)
- *No tengo tanta paciencia como tú.* — I don't have as much patience as you. (*la paciencia*)
- *Allá no hay tantas tiendas como aquí.* — There aren't as many shops there as here. (*las tiendas*)
- *En el norte no hay tantas selvas como en el sur.* — In the north there aren't as many rainforests as in the south.

After a verb, *tanto como* doesn't change: *Aquí no llueve tanto como en Chiapas* (It doesn't rain as much here as in Chiapas). With an adjective or adverb, it's *tan*: *tan grande, tan lejos*. Never *tan mucho*: "so much" is *tanto*.

### Igual de and igual

*Igual de* + adjective + *que* means the same as *tan … como*, and it's very common in everyday speech: *Mi hermana es igual de alta que yo* = *Mi hermana es tan alta como yo*. On its own, *igual* means "the same, equal": *Las dos casas son iguales.* *Es igual* means "it's all the same, it doesn't matter" (like lesson 6's *me da igual*). And *igual que* is "the same as, like": *Hablas igual que tu papá.*

## Mayor and menor

*Mayor* (older, bigger) and *menor* (younger, smaller) are mainly for age and for importance or amount:

- *Mi hermano mayor vive en Tijuana.* — My older brother lives in Tijuana.
- *Soy menor que mi esposa.* — I'm younger than my wife.
- *El mayor problema de la ciudad es el tráfico.* — The city's biggest problem is traffic.
- *Los menores de 18 años no pueden entrar.* — Under-18s can't go in.

For physical size, everyday Spanish uses *más grande* and *más pequeño* (Mexico often says *más chico*): *Mi casa es más grande que la tuya*. (*Mayor que* for size isn't wrong, but it sounds formal or technical: *un número mayor*.) In Mexico you'll also hear *mi hermano más grande* for "my older brother", especially when talking about children. *Mayor* and *menor* have the same form for both genders: *mi hermana mayor*.

![A bar chart titled Población 2020, in millions of inhabitants, from the INEGI census. Estado de México 17.0, Ciudad de México 9.2, Jalisco 8.3, Veracruz 8.1, Colima 0.7. A note says that Mexico City is not a state but the capital, a federal entity, and an example under the chart reads: Jalisco tiene casi tantos habitantes como Veracruz.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The superlative: the biggest, the most beautiful

To say "the most … in", Spanish puts *el, la, los, las* (and usually the noun) before *más* or *menos*, and uses *de* for "in" or "of":

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| article + noun + *más / menos* + adjective + *de* | *la ciudad más grande del país* — the biggest city in the country |
| article + *más / menos* + adjective + *de* (no noun) | *Este cerro es el más alto de la región.* — This hill is the highest in the region. |
| article + *mejor / peor* + noun + *de* | *el mejor restaurante de la colonia* — the best restaurant in the neighborhood |

- *El Estado de México es el estado más poblado del país.* — The State of Mexico is the most populous state in the country. (*poblado* = populated)
- *Colima es el estado menos poblado de México.* — Colima is the least populous state in Mexico.
- *Chihuahua es el estado más grande, y Tlaxcala el más pequeño.* — Chihuahua is the largest state, and Tlaxcala the smallest.

Two things to watch: no *más* before *mejor* or *peor* (*el mejor*, never *el más mejor*), and "in" is *de*, not *en*: *el más alto de la clase*.

![A three-step podium titled Los estados más poblados de México, 2020 (INEGI). First place, Estado de México, 17.0 million; second, Jalisco, 8.3 million; third, Veracruz, 8.1 million. A note says Mexico City, with 9.2 million, is not a state.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: reading the chart

Use the bar chart and the podium to make five true sentences.

1. A number: *El Estado de México tiene casi diecisiete millones de habitantes* (16,992,418), so *más de dieciséis millones*.
2. Two things, more: *La Ciudad de México tiene más habitantes que Jalisco* (9.2 vs 8.3 million).
3. Two things, nearly equal: *Jalisco tiene casi tantos habitantes como Veracruz* (8.3 vs 8.1 million). *Habitantes* is masculine plural, so *tantos*.
4. The top of the list: *El Estado de México es el estado más poblado del país.*
5. The bottom: *Colima es el estado menos poblado: tiene menos de un millón de habitantes* (731,391).

## Very, very: -ísimo

To say "extremely" with a single word, add *-ísimo* to an adjective. It's stronger than *muy*, so never use both (*muy riquísimo* is wrong). Drop a final vowel and add the ending; it agrees like any adjective:

| Rule | Examples |
|---|---|
| ends in a vowel: drop it | *caro → carísimo, grande → grandísimo, bonita → bonitísima* |
| ends in a consonant: add | *fácil → facilísimo, difícil → dificilísimo* |
| *-co → -quísimo* | *rico → riquísimo, poco → poquísimo* |
| *-go → -guísimo* | *largo → larguísimo* |
| *-z → -císimo* | *feliz → felicísimo* |

The spelling changes keep the sound: *rico* has a *k* sound, and *-cí* would change it to *s*, so it becomes *-quí-*. The stress always moves to the *í*, and the written accent on the original word disappears: *fácil → facilísimo*. Some adjectives have special forms; honors lesson 12h2 covers them.

- *Los tacos de aquí están riquísimos.* — The tacos here are delicious.
- *El paisaje es bonitísimo.* — The scenery is really beautiful.
- *Fue un viaje larguísimo.* — It was an extremely long trip.

## Lo mejor, lo peor, lo más…

*Lo* + *mejor*, *peor* or *más* + adjective means "the best thing", "the worst thing", "the most … thing":

- *Lo mejor del campo es la tranquilidad.* — The best thing about the countryside is the peace.
- *Lo peor de la ciudad es el tráfico.* — The worst thing about the city is the traffic.
- *Lo más difícil es encontrar trabajo.* — The hardest thing is finding a job.

*Lo* is not *el* here: it refers to an idea, not a noun (lesson 5's neuter *lo*).

## Safe, noisy, dangerous

Three adjectives help with comparing places: *ruidoso* (noisy), *peligroso* (dangerous) and *seguro*. *Seguro* has two meanings, and the verb tells them apart: *Es un barrio seguro* (It's a safe neighborhood, *ser*: a quality), but *Estoy seguro* (I'm sure, *estar*: a state of mind). *¿Estás seguro de que es aquí?* — Are you sure it's here?

## Dialogue: ¿Ciudad o campo?

Martín is leaving Mexico City for a small town in Veracruz. His friend Paola isn't convinced.

> Paola: ¿Es cierto que te vas a vivir a un pueblo?
>
> Martín: Sí, a un pueblo cerca de Xalapa, en Veracruz. Estoy cansado de la ciudad: hay muchísimo tráfico y es ruidosísima.
>
> Paola: Pero el pueblo es mucho más pequeño que la Ciudad de México. ¿No vas a estar aburrido?
>
> Martín: No creo. Allá no hay tantas cosas que hacer como aquí, pero el paisaje es bonitísimo: hay cerros, ríos y mucha naturaleza.
>
> Paola: ¿Y es más seguro que aquí?
>
> Martín: Mis primos viven allá. Para ellos, es menos peligroso. Y lo mejor es que la renta cuesta menos de la mitad.
>
> Paola: Para mí, el campo es igual de aburrido que una película de tres horas.
>
> Martín: ¡Exagerada! Bueno, tú eres menor que yo; a tu edad yo pensaba igual.
>
> Paola: ¿Y qué es lo peor?
>
> Martín: Que voy a extrañar a mis amigos. Ustedes son lo mejor de la ciudad.

In English:

> Paola: Is it true you're going to live in a small town?
>
> Martín: Yes, a town near Xalapa, in Veracruz. I'm tired of the city: there's so much traffic and it's extremely noisy.
>
> Paola: But the town is much smaller than Mexico City. Aren't you going to be bored?
>
> Martín: I don't think so. There aren't as many things to do there as here, but the scenery is really beautiful: there are hills, rivers and lots of nature.
>
> Paola: And is it safer than here?
>
> Martín: My cousins live there. For them, it's less dangerous. And the best thing is that the rent is less than half.
>
> Paola: For me, the country is as boring as a three-hour movie.
>
> Martín: You exaggerate! Well, you're younger than me; at your age I thought the same.
>
> Paola: And what's the worst thing?
>
> Martín: That I'm going to miss my friends. You guys are the best thing about the city.

(*es cierto* = it's true; *la mitad* = half; *¡Exagerada!* = what an exaggeration, said to a woman; *pensaba igual* = I thought the same.) Find each pattern: *más pequeño que*, *tantas cosas como*, *menos de la mitad* (*de* before an amount), *igual de aburrido que*, *menor que*, *lo mejor, lo peor*, and *-ísimo* with *muchísimo, bonitísimo, ruidosísima*.

## Pronunciation

- *habitante*: the *h* is silent: *a-bi-TAN-te*. *Región*: *re-HIÓN*, with *g* before *e* or *i* sounding like *j*.
- *valle* and *selva*: *VA-ye* (*ll* = *y* in Mexico); *SEL-va* with a soft *v* like *b*.
- *oeste*: three syllables, *o-ES-te*. *Desierto*: *de-SIER-to*.
- *-ísimo* always takes the stress: *ri-QUÍ-si-mo, ca-RÍ-si-mo, fa-ci-LÍ-si-mo*.
- *paisaje*: three syllables, *pai-SA-je*, with *ai* as in "eye".
- *peligroso*: *pe-li-GRO-so*; *ruidoso*: *rui-DO-so*, with a trilled *r* at the start.

## Common mistakes

- *Tiene más que un millón de habitantes.* Before a number: *más de un millón*.
- *La ciudad más grande en México.* After a superlative, "in" is *de*: *la ciudad más grande de México*.
- *Muy riquísimo, muy carísimo.* *-ísimo* already means "very": *riquísimo*.
- *Ricísimo, largísimo.* Keep the sound: *riquísimo, larguísimo*.
- *Más mejor, el más mejor.* *Mejor* is already a comparative: *mejor que, el mejor de*.
- *No hay tan muchos carros.* With nouns, *tanto* agrees: *No hay tantos carros como antes.*
- *Mi casa es mayor que la tuya* in conversation. It's correct but sounds stiff; for size, say *más grande que*.

## Key points

- Landscape words: *el campo, la naturaleza, el paisaje, el desierto, la selva, la costa, el lago, la isla, el valle, el cerro, la región, el estado*; *norte, sur, este / oriente, oeste / poniente*.
- *más / menos de* + number; *más / menos que* to compare two things.
- *tanto, tanta, tantos, tantas* + noun + *como*; verb + *tanto como*; *tan* + adjective + *como*; *igual de* + adjective + *que*.
- *mayor / menor* for age and importance; *más grande / más pequeño (chico)* for size.
- Superlative: *el / la / los / las* (+ noun) + *más / menos* + adjective + *de*; *el mejor, el peor* + noun + *de*.
- *-ísimo* = very: *carísimo, facilísimo, riquísimo, larguísimo, felicísimo*; never with *muy*.
- *lo mejor, lo peor, lo más difícil* + *es…*
- *Es seguro* (safe) vs *Estoy seguro* (sure).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Is there any…? None at all: indefinites and negatives; finding a place to live
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 11 compared places; now you find one to live in. Looking for an apartment means asking questions like "Is there any washing machine?", "Do you have any other apartment?" and understanding answers like "No, there isn't any" or "Nobody lives upstairs". The words for these are the **[[indefinites]]** (*algún, alguno, cualquier, varios*) and the negatives (*ningún, nada, nadie, nunca*).

Spanish A1 gave you *algo, alguien, nada, nadie, nunca, tampoco* and *otro*, and the honors lessons added *cada*. Here you use them all together, learn the rule of the **[[double negative]]** (*No vino nadie*), and add *algún / ningún, cualquier, varios, demasiado* and *todo el / toda la*. The theme is renting a *departamento* in Mexico: reading an ad, visiting the place and the contract.

## Housing words

![A cutaway drawing of a four-story apartment building. At the top is the flat roof with a water tank, a washing machine and a clothesline. Below are three floors of apartments; one has a balcony with a plant. An elevator shaft with its cabin runs up the middle. At the bottom is the ground floor with the entrance door.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| *la planta baja* | ground floor | the floor above is *el primer piso* |
| *el elevador* | elevator | Spain *el ascensor* |
| *el balcón* | balcony | plural *los balcones* |
| *la azotea* | flat roof, roof terrace | |
| *el techo* | roof; ceiling | |
| *el suelo* | floor (the surface); the ground | Mexico also *el piso* |
| *la lavadora* | washing machine | |
| *el microondas* | microwave | same in the plural: *los microondas* |
| *la luz* | light; electricity | *pagar la luz* = to pay the electric bill |
| *el mueble* | piece of furniture | *los muebles* = furniture |
| *la lámpara, el espejo* | lamp, mirror | |
| *la vista* | view | *una vista al parque* |
| *el espacio* | space, room | *No hay espacio* — There's no room. |
| *el vecino, la vecina* | neighbor | |

Mexican buildings count floors from *la planta baja* (PB on the elevator buttons): the next one up is *el primer piso*, then *el segundo piso*. In many Mexican buildings and houses, *la azotea* is a flat roof you can walk on, often with the water tank (*el tinaco*) and a place to wash and hang clothes. *El techo* is both the roof seen from outside and the ceiling seen from inside.

*El suelo* and *el piso* overlap. *El piso* (A1) is a floor or story of a building; in Mexico it's also the everyday word for the floor you walk on (*El piso es de madera*, the floor is wooden), while *el suelo* is more common for the ground outdoors (*Se cayó al suelo*, he fell to the ground).

## Renting in Mexico

To rent a place, you start with *un anuncio* (an ad), often online or on a sign on the building: *Se renta departamento* (Apartment for rent; *se renta* is the impersonal *se* of lesson 17). Typical words in an ad and a contract:

- *amueblado* (furnished), *semiamueblado* (part-furnished);
- *la renta* (A1: the rent), *mantenimiento incluido* (building maintenance fee included);
- *el depósito*: a deposit, very often one month's rent, returned when you leave if there are no debts or damage;
- *el aval*: a guarantor, a person who signs the contract with you and promises to pay if you don't. Landlords in Mexico often ask for an *aval* who owns property in the same city, which is hard for newcomers;
- *la póliza jurídica*: a common alternative to an *aval*, a service you pay for in which a legal firm checks your income and references;
- *el contrato*: the lease, which you sign (*firmar*, A1);
- *la mudanza*: the move, moving house; also the moving company. *El día de la mudanza* — moving day.

These are typical practices described by Mexican and expat guides (2022–2023), not rules: every landlord sets their own conditions.

![A rental ad on a sheet of paper headed SE RENTA DEPARTAMENTO, Colonia Jardines. It lists: 2 recámaras, 1 baño; tercer piso con elevador; balcón con vista al parque; amueblado: cocina con estufa, refrigerador y microondas; área de lavado en la azotea; renta 9,500 MXN al mes, mantenimiento incluido; depósito: un mes; aval o póliza jurídica; sin mascotas.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: reading the ad

1. How many bedrooms? *2 recámaras* (*la recámara* = bedroom, Mexico; A1's *el cuarto* also works).
2. Is there an elevator? *Tercer piso con elevador*: yes, it's on the third floor and there's an elevator.
3. Where do you wash clothes? *Área de lavado en la azotea*: on the roof.
4. What do you pay before you move in? The first month's rent and *depósito: un mes*, so 9,500 + 9,500 = 19,000 pesos, plus the cost of a *póliza jurídica* if you have no *aval*.
5. Can you bring your cat? *Sin mascotas* (no pets; *la mascota*, lesson 22): no.

## Algún, alguno: some, any

*Alguno* means "some" or "any" (one or more of a kind). It agrees like an adjective, and it drops the *-o* before a masculine singular noun, like *uno → un* (A1):

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| singular, before a noun | *algún* | *alguna* |
| singular, alone | *alguno* | *alguna* |
| plural | *algunos* | *algunas* |

- *¿Hay algún elevador?* — Is there an elevator? (any elevator at all)
- *¿Tienes alguna pregunta?* — Do you have any questions?
- *Algunos vecinos son muy amables.* — Some neighbors are very nice.
- *Necesito una lámpara. ¿Tienes alguna?* — I need a lamp. Do you have one?

Notice that English "any questions" is plural but Spanish asks in the singular: *¿alguna pregunta?* In the plural, *algunos* is close to A1's *unos* (some): *unos* is just "some", *algunos* suggests "some but not all".

## Ningún, ninguno: no, not any, none

*Ninguno* is the negative of *alguno*. It also drops the *-o* before a masculine singular noun, and it's almost never plural: you deny one at a time.

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| before a noun | *ningún* | *ninguna* |
| alone | *ninguno* | *ninguna* |

- *No hay ningún problema.* — There's no problem at all.
- *No tengo ninguna duda.* — I have no doubt.
- *¿Hay balcón? — No, no hay ninguno.* — Is there a balcony? — No, there isn't one.

For a simple "no", Mexicans more often just say *No hay elevador* (There's no elevator). *No hay ningún elevador* stresses "not a single one".

## The double negative

In standard English "I don't know nobody" is wrong. In Spanish it's the rule. When a negative word (*nada, nadie, nunca, jamás, tampoco, ningún*) comes after the verb, you must also put *no* before the verb. When it comes first, there's no *no*:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Where does no go with negative words?
  accDescr: Ask whether the negative word, such as nada, nadie, nunca, tampoco or ningún, comes before the verb. If yes, don't add no, as in Nadie vino or Nunca voy. If it comes after the verb, put no before the verb, as in No vino nadie, No voy nunca, No hay nada.
  A["A negative word: nada, nadie, nunca, tampoco, ningún"] --> B{"Does it come before the verb?"}
  B -- yes --> C["No extra no: Nadie vino. Nunca voy."]
  B -- no --> D["Put no before the verb: No vino nadie. No voy nunca. No hay nada."]
```

| Negative word after the verb | Negative word first |
|---|---|
| *No vino nadie.* | *Nadie vino.* — Nobody came. |
| *No voy nunca.* | *Nunca voy.* — I never go. |
| *No me gusta tampoco.* | *Tampoco me gusta.* — I don't like it either. |
| *No hay nada en el refri.* | — There's nothing in the fridge (*el refri* = *el refrigerador*). |

You can stack them: *No hay nadie en ninguna parte* (There's nobody anywhere); *Nunca le digo nada a nadie* (I never tell anybody anything).

Two more details:

- People take *a*. *Alguien, nadie* and *alguno, ninguno* referring to people take the personal *a* as objects (lesson 5): *¿Conoces a alguien en Monterrey? — No, no conozco a nadie.*
- *Nada de* + noun means "no … at all": *No hay nada de ruido* — There's no noise at all.

### Example 2: making a sentence negative

Turn *Alguien vive en la planta baja y siempre hay algo en el buzón* (*el buzón* = mailbox) into the negative.

1. *alguien → nadie*. It's first, so no *no*: *Nadie vive en la planta baja.*
2. *siempre → nunca*, *algo → nada*. *Nunca* comes before the verb, so it already makes the sentence negative and there's no *no*; *nada* follows *hay*: *nunca hay nada en el buzón*.
3. Together: *Nadie vive en la planta baja y nunca hay nada en el buzón.*

## Cualquier and cualquiera: any at all

*Cualquier* goes before a singular noun of either gender and means "any, whichever, no matter which":

- *Puedes llamarme a cualquier hora.* — You can call me at any time.
- *Cualquier persona puede venir.* — Anyone can come.
- *Cualquier día de la semana está bien.* — Any day of the week is fine.

Alone, or after the noun, it's *cualquiera*: *¿Qué lámpara quieres? — Cualquiera.* (Any one.) *Un día cualquiera* (an ordinary day).

So there are two "any"s. In a question about whether something exists, use *algún*: *¿Tienes alguna pregunta?* When it means "it doesn't matter which", use *cualquier*: *Haz cualquier pregunta* (Ask any question you like).

## Varios, demasiado, todo, cada, otro

| Word | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *varios, varias* | several (agrees) | *Vi varios departamentos y varias casas.* |
| *demasiado* + adjective | too (never changes) | *Es demasiado caro. Las rentas son demasiado caras.* |
| *demasiado, -a, -os, -as* + noun | too much, too many (agrees) | *Hay demasiado ruido y demasiadas escaleras.* |
| *todo el, toda la* + noun | all the, the whole | *todo el edificio, toda la noche* |
| *todos los, todas las* + noun | all the, every | *todos los vecinos, todas las semanas* |
| *cada* + singular noun | each, every (never changes) | *cada mes, cada departamento* |
| *otro, otra* | another, other (never *un otro*) | *¿Tiene otro departamento?* |

*Demasiado* is "too", not "very": *Es muy caro* (it's very expensive) can still be possible for you, but *Es demasiado caro* means you won't take it. *Todo el día* is "all day", *todos los días* "every day" (A1); *cada día* also means "every day", looking at each one separately.

## Dialogue: Visiting the apartment

Elena is visiting the apartment from the ad. Mrs. Ríos, the owner, shows her around.

> Sra. Ríos: Pase, pase. Este es el departamento. Como ve, está amueblado.
>
> Elena: ¡Qué bonito! ¿Todos los muebles se quedan?
>
> Sra. Ríos: Sí, todos: la cama, el sofá, la mesa y varias lámparas. Y en la recámara hay un espejo grande.
>
> Elena: ¿Hay alguna lavadora?
>
> Sra. Ríos: En el departamento no hay ninguna, pero en la azotea hay dos lavadoras para todos los vecinos.
>
> Elena: Perfecto. ¡Y qué vista tan bonita desde el balcón!
>
> Sra. Ríos: Sí, se ve todo el parque. Y en la noche no hay nada de ruido.
>
> Elena: ¿Y los vecinos?
>
> Sra. Ríos: Muy tranquilos. Nunca he tenido ningún problema con nadie.
>
> Elena: ¿Qué necesito para rentarlo?
>
> Sra. Ríos: Un mes de depósito y un aval, o si no, una póliza jurídica. Puede venir a firmar el contrato cualquier día.
>
> Elena: Nueve mil quinientos es un poco caro para mí, pero no es demasiado. ¿Lo puedo pensar hasta mañana?

In English:

> Mrs. Ríos: Come in, come in. This is the apartment. As you can see, it's furnished.
>
> Elena: How nice! Does all the furniture stay?
>
> Mrs. Ríos: Yes, all of it: the bed, the sofa, the table and several lamps. And in the bedroom there's a big mirror.
>
> Elena: Is there a washing machine?
>
> Mrs. Ríos: There isn't one in the apartment, but on the roof there are two washing machines for all the neighbors.
>
> Elena: Perfect. And what a lovely view from the balcony!
>
> Mrs. Ríos: Yes, you can see the whole park. And at night there's no noise at all.
>
> Elena: And the neighbors?
>
> Mrs. Ríos: Very quiet. I've never had any problem with anyone.
>
> Elena: What do I need to rent it?
>
> Mrs. Ríos: A month's deposit and a guarantor, or if not, a *póliza jurídica*. You can come and sign the contract any day.
>
> Elena: Nine thousand five hundred is a bit expensive for me, but it's not too much. Can I think about it until tomorrow?

(*Pase* = come in, an *usted* command; *como ve* = as you see; *quedarse* = to stay, A1.) Find the three negatives in *Nunca he tenido ningún problema con nadie*: Spanish is happy to stack them, while English allows only one ("never … any … anyone").

## Pronunciation

- *azotea*: four syllables, *a-so-TE-a*, with *z* = *s*.
- *microondas*: *mi-cro-ON-das*; the two *o*'s are separate syllables.
- *algún, ningún*: stressed on the last syllable, hence the accent; *alguno, ninguno* on the middle: *al-GU-no*.
- *cualquier*: two syllables, *cual-QUIER* (kwal-KYER); *cualquiera*: *cual-QUIE-ra*.
- *espejo*: *es-PE-jo*, with the throat sound of *j*. *Mueble*: *MUE-ble*, two syllables.
- *lámpara*: stress on the first syllable, *LÁM-pa-ra*, hence the accent.

## Common mistakes

- *Nadie no vino.* When the negative word comes first, no *no*: *Nadie vino* (or *No vino nadie*).
- *Hay nada.* After the verb, *no* is required: *No hay nada.*
- *¿Hay alguno elevador?* Before a masculine singular noun: *algún elevador*.
- *No hay ninguno problema.* Same rule: *ningún problema*.
- *No tengo algún libro.* The negative is *ningún*: *No tengo ningún libro.*
- *Conozco alguien.* People take *a*: *Conozco a alguien.*
- *Cualquiera día.* Before a noun: *cualquier día*.
- *Son demasiadas caras.* Before an adjective *demasiado* doesn't change: *Son demasiado caras.*
- *Es demasiado bonito* for "it's very pretty". *Demasiado* means "too": *Es muy bonito.*
- *Un otro departamento.* Just *otro departamento*.

## Key points

- Housing: *el anuncio, amueblado, el contrato, el depósito, la mudanza, la planta baja, el elevador, el balcón, la azotea, el techo, el suelo, la lavadora, el microondas, la luz, el mueble, la lámpara, el espejo, la vista, el espacio, el vecino*.
- Renting in Mexico often needs a *depósito* (often one month), an *aval* or a *póliza jurídica*, and a *contrato*.
- *algún / alguno / alguna / algunos / algunas*; *ningún / ninguno / ninguna* (almost never plural); short forms before a masculine singular noun.
- Double negative: *no* + verb + negative word (*No vino nadie*), or the negative word first without *no* (*Nadie vino*).
- *a alguien, a nadie* for people as objects.
- *cualquier* + noun, *cualquiera* alone; *varios*; *demasiado* (too); *todo el / toda la*; *cada*; *otro* without *un*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Describing a painting: murals and portraits
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 9 you described a photo with estar + gerund and position words, in lesson 10 you described people, and in lesson 11 you compared things. A painting puts all three together. Mexico is a very good place to practice, because some of its most famous art is public: huge murals on the walls of government buildings, schools and markets, painted so that people who couldn't read could still see the country's history. And Frida Kahlo, probably the best-known Mexican painter of the 20th century around the world, painted herself again and again.

This lesson gives you a short, simplified history of Mexican muralism and portraiture, the words to talk about a painting (*el cuadro, el retrato, el autorretrato, los colores vivos*), and a method for describing any picture in about two minutes. The two pictures in this lesson are original sketches "in the style of" Mexican murals and portraits, drawn for this course; they are not copies of real works. To see the real ones, the museum and building names below are a good start.

## Murals for everyone: a short history

After the Mexican Revolution, which began in 1910, the new government wanted art that ordinary people could see and understand. In 1921 José Vasconcelos became Secretary of Public Education, and the government began asking artists to paint murals on public buildings in Mexico City, such as the Secretariat of Public Education (*la SEP*) and the National Preparatory School (*la Escuela Nacional Preparatoria*). The murals showed Mexico's history, its indigenous past, its workers and farmers, and the ideas of the Revolution. Most were painted in *fresco*: the paint goes onto fresh, wet plaster, so it becomes part of the wall.

Three painters became known as *los tres grandes* (the big three):

- Diego Rivera (1886–1957), born in Guanajuato. He painted his first mural in Mexico City in 1922 and then covered the walls of the SEP's courtyards (finished in 1928). In 1929 he started his best-known work, the history of Mexico on the great staircase of the National Palace (*el Palacio Nacional*) in Mexico City, and he kept adding to the palace's murals until 1951. He also painted *Detroit Industry* (1932–1933) at the Detroit Institute of Arts.
- José Clemente Orozco (1883–1949), from Jalisco. His murals are darker and more dramatic. His most famous work is in Guadalajara, at the Hospicio Cabañas, a former orphanage (now a museum and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997), where he painted 57 frescoes in the late 1930s, including *El hombre de fuego* (The Man of Fire) in the dome.
- David Alfaro Siqueiros (1896–1974), born in Chihuahua, who experimented with new paints and techniques.

Rivera's murals are full of people, color and detail; Orozco's are full of movement, fire and suffering. That's a simplification, of course, but it's a good first comparison.

## Frida Kahlo and the self-portrait

Frida Kahlo (1907–1954) was born in Coyoacán, in Mexico City, in the house now called *la Casa Azul* (the Blue House), today the Museo Frida Kahlo, and she died in Coyoacán. After a serious bus accident at eighteen, she began to paint while she was recovering, and many of her paintings are self-portraits. She married Diego Rivera in 1929. Her portraits often show her with flowers in her hair, traditional clothes, plants and animals, and a direct, serious gaze. One of her best-known paintings, *Las dos Fridas* (1939), shows two Fridas sitting side by side holding hands; it hangs in the Museo de Arte Moderno in Mexico City.

Murals and self-portraits look very different, a huge public wall and a small private canvas, but both tell stories about Mexico and about identity.

## Words for talking about a painting

| Spanish | English | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| *pintar* | to paint | regular -ar |
| *la pintura* | painting (the art); paint | *la pintura mexicana*; *pintura roja* |
| *el cuadro* | painting, picture (one work) | *un cuadro de Kahlo* |
| *el retrato* | portrait | |
| *el autorretrato* | self-portrait | *auto-* = self, with *rr* |
| *el mural* (A1) | mural | *el muralista, la muralista* = muralist |
| *el artista, la artista* | artist | same form, the article shows the gender |
| *representar* | to show, to depict, to represent | *El mural representa la historia de México.* |
| *el boceto* | sketch | a first drawing before the real work |
| *el personaje* | figure, character | a person in a painting or a story (also in honors lesson 90) |
| *el símbolo* | symbol | |
| *colorido* | colorful | |
| *vivo* | bright (color); alive | *colores vivos* |
| *la mirada* | gaze, look (in someone's eyes) | *una mirada seria* |

*Un cuadro de Rivera* means "a painting by Rivera": *de* gives the artist. *Pintado* (painted) works as an adjective: *un mural pintado en 1929*. And *en el cuadro aparece…* (*aparecer* = to appear) is a useful way to start: *En el cuadro aparecen dos mujeres.*

## How to describe a painting

The method is the photo description from lesson 9, with two extra steps at the beginning and the end:

1. The facts: what it is, who painted it, when, where it is. *Es un mural de Diego Rivera. Está en el Palacio Nacional.*
2. The scene: what it represents. *Representa la historia de México.*
3. Where things are: *al fondo, en primer plano, en el centro, a la izquierda, a la derecha, arriba* (at the top), *abajo* (at the bottom).
4. The people: who they are and what they're doing, with estar + gerund or a position: *Un hombre está cargando maíz. Una mujer está sentada.* In a painting, these actions are frozen, but Spanish still uses the present: the painting shows them doing it now.
5. Colors and style: *Los colores son vivos / oscuros. Es un cuadro muy colorido.*
6. Your opinion and a comparison: *Me parece que… Para mí, lo más interesante es… Es más colorido que…*

### Example 1: the mural sketch

![An original sketch in the style of a Mexican mural. In the background is a snow-capped volcano under a big yellow sun. In the middle is a field of tall corn plants. In the foreground on the left, a teacher holding an open book stands next to two children. In the center, two farmers in white clothes and straw hats carry a basket of corn between them. On the right, a woman holds a bunch of big white flowers.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Describe the sketch, step by step.

1. Facts: *Es un boceto al estilo del muralismo mexicano. No es un mural real.*
2. Scene: *Representa el trabajo en el campo y la educación.*
3. Background and middle: *Al fondo hay un volcán con nieve y un sol muy grande, arriba, a la derecha. En el centro de la imagen hay una milpa* (a cornfield).
4. People: *En primer plano, a la izquierda, una maestra está leyendo un libro y dos niños están escuchando. En el centro, dos campesinos* (farmworkers) *están cargando una canasta de maíz. A la derecha, una mujer tiene muchas flores blancas; creo que las está vendiendo.*
5. Colors: *Los colores son vivos: amarillo, verde, blanco y café.*
6. Opinion: *Me parece que el mural quiere mostrar que el trabajo y la escuela son igual de importantes. Lo que más me gusta es el volcán.* (*lo que* = what, lesson 18.)

Notice *las está vendiendo*: the pronoun *las* (the flowers) goes before *estar*, or attached: *está vendiéndolas*.

### Example 2: the portrait sketch

![An original portrait sketch in the style of Mexican portraiture: a woman seen from the shoulders up, against a background of green leaves. Her dark hair is braided on top of her head, with three flowers in it, red, orange and yellow. She has strong dark eyebrows that almost meet, a serious mouth, round yellow earrings and a white blouse with a red embroidered neckline.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. Facts: *Es un retrato. También puede ser un autorretrato, como muchos cuadros de Frida Kahlo, pero es un boceto original.*
2. Scene: *Representa a una mujer joven.* The personal *a* goes before people, even in a painting.
3. Where things are: *La mujer está en el centro, y al fondo hay hojas verdes* (*la hoja* = leaf).
4. The person (lesson 10): *Tiene el pelo negro, con trenzas* (braids) *y tres flores. Tiene las cejas* (eyebrows) *muy oscuras. Lleva aretes amarillos* (earrings) *y una blusa blanca.*
5. Her expression: *No está sonriendo; su mirada es seria y directa. Parece tranquila, pero un poco triste.*
6. Comparison: *Este cuadro es más pequeño y más personal que el mural. El mural tiene muchos personajes; el retrato solo tiene uno, pero su mirada es lo más fuerte del cuadro.*

## A visit to the museum

Lucía and her friend Sam visit an exhibition of Mexican art. Sam is learning Spanish.

> Sam: Mira este cuadro. ¿Es un autorretrato?
>
> Lucía: Sí, es de una pintora de los años cuarenta. Fíjate en la mirada: está mirando directamente al público.
>
> Sam: Es muy seria. ¿Y qué representan los animales del fondo?
>
> Lucía: Dicen que son símbolos, pero cada persona los interpreta de una forma diferente.
>
> Sam: Me gustan los colores. Son mucho más vivos que en los cuadros europeos de esta sala.
>
> Lucía: ¿Y el mural de la otra sala? Es enorme. Tiene más de cien personajes.
>
> Sam: Sí, pero para mí es demasiado grande. No sé dónde mirar.
>
> Lucía: Por eso los muralistas pintaban para todos: cada persona encuentra su historia.

In English:

> Sam: Look at this painting. Is it a self-portrait?
>
> Lucía: Yes, it's by a woman painter from the forties. Look at the gaze: she's looking straight at the viewer.
>
> Sam: She's very serious. And what do the animals in the background represent?
>
> Lucía: People say they're symbols, but each person interprets them in a different way.
>
> Sam: I like the colors. They're much brighter than in the European paintings in this room.
>
> Lucía: And the mural in the other room? It's huge. It has more than a hundred figures.
>
> Sam: Yes, but for me it's too big. I don't know where to look.
>
> Lucía: That's why the muralists painted for everyone: each person finds their own story.

(*Fíjate en* = look at, notice; *el público* = the audience, the viewers; *interpretar* = to interpret; *la sala* = room, gallery; *por eso* = that's why, lesson 22.) The painter and the paintings in this dialogue are imaginary.

## Common mistakes

- *Un cuadro por Rivera.* The artist takes *de*: *un cuadro de Rivera*. (*Pintado por Rivera* is fine with the participle.)
- *El artista* for a woman. Use *la artista*: *Frida Kahlo es una artista mexicana.*
- *Representa dos mujeres.* People take the personal *a*: *Representa a dos mujeres.*
- *Colores vivientes* for "bright colors". The phrase is *colores vivos*.
- *En el fondo* on its own for "in the background". *Al fondo* is the usual phrase; on its own, *en el fondo* usually means "deep down" (*En el fondo es buena persona*). (*En el fondo del cuadro*, with the noun, is fine.)
- *Autoretrato.* After a prefix, *r* is doubled to keep the trilled sound: *autorretrato*.
- Forgetting that *la pintura* has two meanings. *Una pintura* (a painting) is correct, but *pintura* is also "paint"; *el cuadro* is only the painting.

## Key points

- Mexican muralism began in 1921, under José Vasconcelos at the Secretariat of Public Education, to bring art to everyone; *los tres grandes* are Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros.
- Rivera: the National Palace staircase (from 1929); Orozco: the Hospicio Cabañas in Guadalajara (late 1930s); Kahlo: self-portraits, the Casa Azul in Coyoacán, *Las dos Fridas* (1939).
- Words: *pintar, la pintura, el cuadro, el retrato, el autorretrato, el artista, el muralista, representar, el boceto, el símbolo, colorido, vivo, la mirada*.
- *un cuadro de* + artist; *representa a* + person; *al fondo* for "in the background".
- Method: facts → scene → positions → people (estar + gerund) → colors → opinion and comparison.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Super, bien and -ísimo: making it stronger or softer
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 11 gave you *-ísimo* for "extremely" (*riquísimo, carísimo*), and lesson 10 showed you how to soften a description with *un poco* and *algo*. Textbook Spanish mostly stops at *muy*. Real Spanish, and Mexican Spanish in particular, has many more ways to turn the volume up or down, and you'll hear them in every conversation, every series and every chat: *Está bien bonito. Fue súper divertido. Estoy medio cansada. Espérame tantito.*

This lesson collects them on one scale, says which ones are informal or typical of Mexico, and adds the irregular *-ísimo* forms, the **[[extreme adjectives]]** that don't take *muy*, and *lo* + adjective (*lo bueno es que…*). Most of it is for understanding; the informal forms are worth using only with friends.

![A scale titled ¿Qué tan cansado estás? (How tired are you?), from weakest to strongest: nada cansado (not tired at all); un poco or algo cansado (a bit, somewhat); medio cansado (kind of, informal); bastante cansado (quite, rather); muy or bien cansado (very; bien is informal); súper cansado (really, informal); cansadísimo (extremely). An arrow points down to más fuerte (stronger).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The order on the scale is a rough guide: tone of voice matters as much as the word.

## Stronger: bien, súper and friends

### Bien + adjective = very

In Mexico and much of Latin America, *bien* before an adjective or an adverb means "very", and in everyday speech it's often more common than *muy*:

- *La película estuvo bien buena.* — The movie was really good.
- *Tu casa está bien bonita.* — Your house is really nice.
- *Llegaste bien tarde.* — You got here really late.

The *Diccionario de la lengua española* lists this use of *bien*, so it isn't a mistake, but it sounds informal; in writing for work or the exam, use *muy*. Watch the difference: *Estoy bien* (I'm fine) vs *Estoy bien cansado* (I'm very tired). After the verb on its own, *bien* still means "well, fine".

### Súper

*Súper* in front of an adjective means "really, super": *súper fácil, súper rico*. You'll hear it in Spanish everywhere, and very often in Mexico. Two notes:

- Spelling. Spanish spelling rules treat *super-* as a prefix and join it to the word: *superbonito, superfácil*. In chats and informal writing you'll very often see it apart, *súper bonito*, and many speakers stress it as a separate word. In this course both are accepted.
- Alone, *súper* is an adverb or adjective with an accent: *¿Cómo te fue? — ¡Súper!* (How did it go? — Great!) *Nos la pasamos súper* (We had a great time; *pasarla bien*, A1).

### Re-, requete- (recognition)

In very informal speech, *re-* and *requete-* also mean "very": *requetebién* (really well), *rebueno* (really good). *Requete-* is the one you're most likely to hear in Mexico, usually in fixed phrases like *requetebién*; *re-* as a free intensifier (*re lindo*) is typical of Argentina and Uruguay. Recognize them; you don't need to use them.

### Mexican informal favorites

| Spanish | English | Register |
|---|---|---|
| *padre* | cool, great | informal, Mexico: *¡Qué padre!*, *una fiesta muy padre* |
| *chido* | cool, nice | very informal, Mexico: *¡Qué chido!* |
| *un montón* | a lot, loads | informal, everywhere: *un montón de gente, me gustó un montón* |
| *tantito* | a little, a bit | Mexico: *Espérame tantito. Tantito más, por favor.* |

*Padre* as an adjective doesn't change for gender: *una película muy padre*; the plural is *padres*: *unos tenis muy padres*. *Padrísimo* is its *-ísimo* form. *Tantito*, from *tanto*, means "a little" in Mexican Spanish (*tantito ruido*, a bit of noise); the Mexican linguist José G. Moreno de Alba called it a clear Mexicanism.

## Extreme adjectives: no muy

Some adjectives already mean "very good" or "very bad". In careful Spanish they don't take *muy*, just as English doesn't say "very excellent":

| Neutral | Extreme | English |
|---|---|---|
| *bueno* | *excelente, fantástico, maravilloso* | excellent, fantastic, wonderful |
| *malo* | *pésimo, horrible* | terrible, awful |
| *bonito* | *precioso* | beautiful, lovely |
| *rico* | *delicioso* | delicious |
| *grande* | *enorme* (A1) | huge |

- *El servicio fue pésimo.* — The service was terrible.
- *¡Qué vista tan preciosa!* — What a beautiful view!

To make them even stronger, use *realmente* (really) or *absolutamente*, or just your voice: *Fue realmente horrible.* In relaxed Mexican speech you'll also hear *muy delicioso* or *súper precioso*; they aren't wrong in conversation, but in writing the extreme word alone is better. In everyday speech *precioso* means "beautiful" or "lovely". It keeps the sense "precious, of great value" in set phrases such as *piedras preciosas* (precious stones) and *metales preciosos*, but for "valuable" in general say *valioso*.

## More -ísimo

Lesson 11 gave the regular pattern. A few adjectives are special:

| Adjective | -ísimo form | Why |
|---|---|---|
| *amable* | *amabilísimo* | *-ble → -bilísimo* |
| *antiguo* | *antiquísimo* | *-guo → -quísimo* |
| *bueno* | *buenísimo* | the usual form (*bonísimo* is literary) |
| *joven* | *jovencísimo* | a *c* is added |
| *fuerte* | *fuertísimo* | the usual form (*fortísimo* is formal) |

*-Ísimo* also goes on some adverbs: *muchísimo* (a huge amount), *poquísimo*, *tardísimo* (very late), *lejísimos* (very far; note the *s*, from *lejos*), *cerquísima* (very close).

Diminutives (Spanish A1 honors) sometimes intensify instead of shrinking: *Está cerquita* (it's really close), *ahorita* (right now… or in a while), *solito* (all alone). Context tells you which.

### Example 1: building the forms

Give the strongest single word for *muy amable, muy antiguo, muy joven, muy lejos* and *muy rico*.

1. *amable* ends in *-ble*: *amabilísimo* (*amabilísima* for a woman).
2. *antiguo*: *-guo → -quísimo* keeps the sound: *antiquísimo*.
3. *joven* adds a *c*: *jovencísimo*.
4. *lejos* is an adverb ending in *-s*: *lejísimos*.
5. *rico* (lesson 11): *-co → -quísimo*: *riquísimo*.

## Softer: medio, algo, tantito

- *un poco*, *algo* + adjective: *un poco caro, algo raro* (somewhat strange). Neither changes for gender.
- *medio* + adjective = "kind of, half": *Estoy medio cansada. La película estuvo medio aburrida.* Here *medio* is an adverb and, in standard Spanish, it doesn't change: *medio cansada*, not *media cansada* (you'll hear the second, but it's considered incorrect).
- *no muy* or *no tan* + a positive word: *No está tan lejos* (It isn't that far).
- *tantito* (Mexico) for quantities and time: *Súbele tantito* (Turn it up a little), *Espérame tantito* (Wait a moment for me).

## Lo + adjective: the good thing is…

Lesson 11 gave you *lo mejor, lo peor, lo más difícil*. Any adjective works with *lo*, which turns it into "the … thing" or "the … part":

- *Lo bueno es que el hotel está cerquita del mar.* — The good thing is that the hotel is really close to the sea.
- *Lo malo es que llovió todo el fin de semana.* — The bad thing is that it rained all weekend.
- *Lo importante es que estás bien.* — The important thing is that you're OK.
- *Lo raro es que nadie contestó.* — The strange thing is that nobody answered.

*Lo* never changes: *lo bueno*, never *la buena*, even when you're talking about a feminine noun.

### Example 2: changing the register

Rewrite this neutral review twice, for a friend and for a formal note: *La comida fue muy buena, el restaurante es muy bonito, pero el servicio fue muy malo y la cuenta fue muy cara.*

1. To a friend in Mexico (informal): *La comida estuvo buenísima y el restaurante está bien bonito, pero el servicio, pésimo… y la cuenta, carísima. ¡Uf!* Notice *estuvo* (Mexican speakers often use *estar* for how an experience turned out), *bien* for "very", and dropped verbs for effect.
2. Formal (an e-mail to the restaurant): *La comida fue excelente y el restaurante es precioso. Sin embargo* (however), *el servicio fue muy lento y la cuenta nos pareció demasiado alta.* No *bien*, no *súper*; extreme adjectives for praise, softer *muy lento* and *demasiado alta* for the complaint.

## A chat after a concert

Two friends message each other the morning after a concert.

> Majo: ¿Qué tal el concierto?
>
> Iván: ¡Súper padre! Estuvo buenísimo, cantaron todas las canciones.
>
> Majo: ¡Qué envidia! ¿Había mucha gente?
>
> Iván: Un montón. Y el estadio está lejísimos de mi casa, regresé bien tarde.
>
> Majo: ¿Y estás cansado?
>
> Iván: Medio cansado, pero feliz. Lo malo es que hoy tengo examen.
>
> Majo: Jajaja. Lo bueno es que el examen es en la tarde, ¿no?
>
> Iván: Sí, a las cuatro. Oye, espérame tantito, me está llamando mi mamá.

In English:

> Majo: How was the concert?
>
