> Iván: So cool! It was really good, they sang all the songs.
>
> Majo: I'm so jealous! Were there a lot of people?
>
> Iván: Loads. And the stadium is miles from my house, I got back really late.
>
> Majo: And are you tired?
>
> Iván: Kind of tired, but happy. The bad thing is I have an exam today.
>
> Majo: Hahaha. The good thing is the exam is in the afternoon, right?
>
> Iván: Yes, at four. Hey, hang on a sec, my mom's calling me.

(*¡Qué envidia!* = I'm so jealous, literally "what envy"; *Majo* is a common nickname for María José.) Count the intensifiers: *súper padre, buenísimo, un montón, lejísimos, bien tarde, medio cansado, tantito*. In a formal message you'd find almost none of them.

## Common mistakes

- *Muy riquísimo, muy excelente.* *-ísimo* and extreme adjectives already mean "very": *riquísimo, excelente*.
- *Estoy media cansada.* *Medio* + adjective doesn't change in standard Spanish: *medio cansada*.
- *Amablísimo, antigüísimo.* The forms are *amabilísimo, antiquísimo*.
- *Lejísimo.* With the *s* of *lejos*: *lejísimos*.
- *La buena es que…* for "the good thing is". Use neuter *lo*: *Lo bueno es que…*
- Using *bien*, *súper*, *chido* or *un montón* in a formal e-mail or an exam essay. Save them for friends; write *muy*, *mucho*, *excelente*.
- Using *precioso* for "valuable" (*un reloj precioso* is a beautiful watch). In everyday speech it means "beautiful, lovely"; "valuable" is *valioso*. (Only set phrases such as *piedras preciosas* keep the old sense.)
- *Una película muy padra.* *Padre* (cool) doesn't change for gender: *muy padre*.

## Key points

- Stronger: *muy* (neutral), *bien* + adjective (informal, very common in Mexico), *súper* (informal; standard spelling joins it: *superfácil*), *-ísimo*; *re-, requete-* for recognition.
- Extreme adjectives (*excelente, fantástico, maravilloso, pésimo, horrible, precioso, delicioso, enorme*) don't take *muy* in careful Spanish.
- Irregular *-ísimo*: *amabilísimo, antiquísimo, jovencísimo*; adverbs *muchísimo, tardísimo, lejísimos*.
- Softer: *un poco, algo, medio* (invariable: *medio cansada*), *no muy, no tan*; Mexican *tantito* (a little).
- Mexican informal: *padre, chido, un montón*.
- *lo* + adjective: *lo bueno, lo malo, lo importante, lo raro es que…*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: What will happen? The future tense
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 is about plans, trips and free time, and plans need the future. In Spanish A1 you learned the everyday way to talk about plans, *ir a* + infinitive: *Voy a viajar en diciembre* (I'm going to travel in December). This lesson adds the **[[future tense]]** (*el futuro simple*): one word that means "will …", as in *Viajaré en diciembre* (I will travel in December).

You'll learn the forms (some of the most regular in Spanish), the twelve verbs with a special stem, and *when* people actually use the future: in everyday Mexican conversation *ir a* is still the normal way to talk about plans, while the simple future belongs to forecasts, predictions, promises and more formal language.

When you complete this lesson, the future opens in your conjugation drills for every verb you know.

## The forms: the whole infinitive + one set of endings

Most tenses start from the stem (*habl-*). The future starts from the whole infinitive and adds endings, the same endings for -ar, -er and -ir verbs:

| | *hablar* | *comer* | *vivir* |
|---|---|---|---|
| yo | *hablaré* | *comeré* | *viviré* |
| tú | *hablarás* | *comerás* | *vivirás* |
| él, ella, usted | *hablará* | *comerá* | *vivirá* |
| nosotros, nosotras | *hablaremos* | *comeremos* | *viviremos* |
| (vosotros, Spain) | (*hablaréis*) | (*comeréis*) | (*viviréis*) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | *hablarán* | *comerán* | *vivirán* |

- The stress falls on the ending, so every form has a written accent except *nosotros* (*ha-bla-RE-mos*, stressed where a word ending in *-s* normally is).
- Stem changes and spelling changes don't matter, because you start from the infinitive: *volver → volveré* (not ~~vuelveré~~), *pedir → pediré*, *llegar → llegaré*.
- Reflexive verbs keep the pronoun in front: *me levantaré, te quedarás, se bañará*.
- *Ir* is completely regular in the future: *iré, irás, irá, iremos, irán*. So are *ser* (*seré*) and *estar* (*estaré*).

Example: *¿Estarás en casa a las ocho?* — Will you be home at eight?

## Twelve verbs with a special stem

A short list of very common verbs change the infinitive before the ending. The endings stay exactly the same. They fall into three groups, which makes them easier to learn:

![A wheel chart of the twelve irregular future stems in three colored groups. Group 1, the vowel drops: poder podr-, saber sabr-, haber habr-, querer querr-, caber cabr-. Group 2, a d replaces the vowel: tener tendr-, poner pondr-, salir saldr-, venir vendr-, valer valdr-. Group 3, shortened: hacer har-, decir dir-. In the middle: the same endings -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Group | Infinitive | Stem | yo | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. The *e* of *-er* drops | *poder* | *podr-* | *podré* | *¿Podrás venir?* — Will you be able to come? |
| | *saber* | *sabr-* | *sabré* | *Mañana sabremos el resultado.* — We'll know the result tomorrow. |
| | *haber* | *habr-* | *habrá* | *Habrá una fiesta.* — There will be a party. |
| | *querer* | *querr-* | *querré* | *No querrán salir con esta lluvia.* — They won't want to go out in this rain. |
| | *caber* | *cabr-* | *cabré* | *No cabrá en la maleta.* — It won't fit in the suitcase. |
| 2. A *d* takes the vowel's place | *tener* | *tendr-* | *tendré* | *Tendré tiempo el sábado.* — I'll have time on Saturday. |
| | *poner* | *pondr-* | *pondré* | *¿Dónde pondrás el sillón?* — Where will you put the armchair? |
| | *salir* | *saldr-* | *saldré* | *El vuelo saldrá a tiempo.* — The flight will leave on time. |
| | *venir* | *vendr-* | *vendré* | *¿Vendrán tus papás?* — Will your parents come? |
| | *valer* | *valdr-* | *valdrá* | *Valdrá la pena.* — It will be worth it. |
| 3. Shortened | *hacer* | *har-* | *haré* | *¿Qué harás en vacaciones?* — What will you do on vacation? |
| | *decir* | *dir-* | *diré* | *No le diré nada.* — I won't tell him anything. |

- *Habrá* is the future of *hay*, and like *hay* it stays singular: *Habrá nubes* — There will be clouds (not ~~habrán nubes~~ in standard Spanish).
- *Caber* (to fit) and *valer* (to be worth) are less common: *No cabe* (It doesn't fit), *Vale la pena* (It's worth it).
- Verbs built on *tener, poner, venir, salir* and *hacer* keep the change: *mantener → mantendré* (maintain), *proponer → propondré* (suggest; lesson 15), *deshacer → desharé* (undo, unpack).

## Which future? How Mexicans talk about what's ahead

Spanish has three common ways to talk about the future, and they don't sound the same.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a way to talk about the future
  accDescr: Start by asking what you are talking about. If it is a fixed arrangement or a timetable, use the present with a time word, for example Mañana salgo a las ocho. If it is a plan or intention, use ir a plus infinitive, for example Voy a estudiar medicina; this is the most common choice in conversation. If it is a prediction, a forecast, a promise or formal or written plans, use the simple future, for example Mañana lloverá en el norte or Te llamaré.
  A{"What are you talking about?"} -- "a fixed arrangement, a timetable" --> B["present + time word: Mañana salgo a las ocho."]
  A -- "a plan, an intention" --> C["ir a + infinitive: Voy a estudiar medicina."]
  A -- "a prediction, forecast, promise, formal plan" --> D["simple future: Mañana lloverá. Te llamaré."]
  C --> E["The usual choice in conversation"]
```

- The present for arrangements: *El camión sale a las 6:40.* — The bus leaves at 6:40.
- *Ir a* for plans: *Este verano vamos a pintar la casa.* — This summer we're going to paint the house.
- The simple future for predictions and promises, and in news and official plans: *En el futuro todos los carros serán eléctricos* (In the future all cars will be electric); *La tecnología cambiará nuestra forma de trabajar* (Technology will change the way we work); *La nueva línea del metro abrirá en marzo* (The new metro line will open in March).

How strong is the preference? In recorded conversations from Mexico City, Lastra and Martín Butragueño (2008) found that about 84 % of some 1,500 future expressions used *ir a* and only about 16 % the simple future. And the authors classed more than half of those simple futures as expressing doubts, guesses or estimates rather than plain future time, for example guesses about the present (*¿Dónde estará?* — Where can she be?), which you can study in honors lesson 16h2. So: learn the future well, because you'll read and hear it, but don't replace every *voy a* with it in conversation.

## Promises, predictions and the weather

The simple future sounds firm, which suits a promise: *Te prometo que llegaré a tiempo* (I promise I'll be on time); *Algún día iremos a Japón* (One day we'll go to Japan).

For predictions about the world, add a word for how sure you are. From most to least sure:

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *seguro que* | for sure | *Seguro que ganarán.* — They'll win for sure. |
| *seguramente* | very probably | *Seguramente lloverá.* — It will very probably rain. |
| *probablemente* | probably | *Probablemente llegaremos tarde.* — We'll probably be late. |
| *quizás* (also *quizá, tal vez*) | maybe, perhaps | *Quizás cambiaré de trabajo.* — Maybe I'll change jobs. |

*Seguramente* is a trap for English speakers: it looks like "surely" but usually means "very probably". At this level use *quizás* with the forms you know (*quizás iré*); later you'll learn another verb form that often follows it.

## If it rains, we won't go: si + present, future

To say what will happen *if* something happens, use the present after *si* and the future (or *ir a*, or the present) in the other half:

- *Si llueve, no iremos a la playa.* — If it rains, we won't go to the beach.
- *Si ahorras, podrás comprar la laptop.* — If you save, you'll be able to buy the laptop.
- *Te llamo si salgo temprano.* — I'll call you if I leave early.

Never put the future right after *si* in these sentences: ~~Si lloverá~~ is wrong. English works the same way ("if it rains", not "if it will rain"), so trust your instinct.

## Time words for the future

| | |
|---|---|
| *pronto* | soon |
| *pasado mañana* | the day after tomorrow |
| *dentro de dos días / tres años* | in two days / three years (from now) |
| *el año que viene* (also *el próximo año*) | next year |
| *el mes que viene, la semana que viene* | next month, next week |
| *algún día* | someday, one day |
| *en el futuro* | in the future |

*Dentro de* + a period counts from now: *Dentro de cinco años tendré mi propio negocio* — Five years from now I'll have my own business. A classic exercise: *Imagina tu vida dentro de diez años. ¿Dónde vivirás? ¿Qué harás?* — Imagine your life ten years from now. Where will you live? What will you do?

## The weather forecast: el pronóstico del tiempo

Forecasts are full of the future. Here is the map from an imaginary evening news program in Mexico (the cities are real, the weather is invented):

![A map of Mexico with weather icons for tomorrow. Tijuana in the northwest: a sun with 24 degrees. Chihuahua: a sun with 31 degrees. Monterrey in the northeast: a sun with 36 degrees. Guadalajara: a sun partly behind a cloud, 27 degrees. Mexico City: a cloud with rain, 21 degrees. Acapulco on the Pacific coast: a dark cloud with lightning, 30 degrees. Off the coast of Quintana Roo, in the Caribbean, a red hurricane symbol. Mérida: a gray cloud, 33 degrees. The title says Pronóstico para mañana.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> Buenas noches. Este es el pronóstico del tiempo para mañana, jueves. En el norte del país, el cielo estará despejado y el ambiente será seco y caluroso: en Monterrey la temperatura máxima llegará a 36 grados. En Guadalajara habrá algunas nubes, pero estará soleado casi todo el día. En la Ciudad de México lloverá por la tarde, como es normal en la temporada de lluvias; les recomendamos salir con paraguas. En la costa de Guerrero habrá tormentas eléctricas, y en Acapulco el ambiente será muy húmedo. Atención en el Caribe: el huracán Rosa se acercará a la costa de Quintana Roo y probablemente tocará tierra pasado mañana. Las autoridades darán más información pronto. ¡Buenas noches!

*Good evening. This is the weather forecast for tomorrow, Thursday. In the north of the country the sky will be clear and the air dry and hot: in Monterrey the high will reach 36 degrees. In Guadalajara there will be some clouds, but it will be sunny almost all day. In Mexico City it will rain in the afternoon, as is normal in the rainy season; we recommend going out with an umbrella. On the coast of Guerrero there will be thunderstorms, and in Acapulco the air will be very humid. Attention in the Caribbean: Hurricane Rosa will approach the coast of Quintana Roo and will probably make landfall the day after tomorrow. The authorities will give more information soon. Good night!*

(*El ambiente* — the air, the atmosphere; *caluroso* — hot; *la tormenta eléctrica* — thunderstorm; *tocar tierra* — to make landfall; *las autoridades* — the authorities. Hurricane Rosa is invented.)

Notice the forecast's patterns: *estará* + adjective (*soleado, despejado, nublado*), *habrá* + noun, *lloverá*, *la temperatura máxima será de … grados*. In conversation you'll still hear A1's *Mañana va a hacer mucho calor*.

Mexico has two coasts and two hurricane seasons. The national weather service (the SMN) gives the official start as 15 May in the eastern Pacific and 1 June in the Atlantic, and both seasons end on 30 November (dates from SMN announcements reported in 2024 and 2026).

## Dialogue: Propósitos de Año Nuevo

On 31 December, Mariana and her brother Iván talk about their New Year's resolutions (*los propósitos de Año Nuevo*).

> Mariana: Bueno, Iván, ¿cuáles son tus propósitos para el año que viene?
>
> Iván: Esta vez sí voy a cumplirlos. Primero, ahorraré dinero. Quiero comprar una laptop.
>
> Mariana: ¿Otra vez? El año pasado dijiste lo mismo.
>
> Iván: Ya sé, pero ahora tengo un plan. Te prometo que no gastaré en tonterías.
>
> Mariana: Mmm… Si ahorras quinientos pesos al mes, en diciembre tendrás seis mil.
>
> Iván: ¡Exacto! ¿Y tú? ¿Qué harás?
>
> Mariana: Yo empiezo un curso de inglés el 8 de enero. Y quizás buscaré otro trabajo.
>
> Iván: ¿De verdad? ¿Y si no encuentras nada?
>
> Mariana: Pues me quedo donde estoy. Pero algún día tendré mi propio proyecto, ya verás.

*Mariana: So, Iván, what are your resolutions for next year? — Iván: This time I really am going to keep them. First, I'll save money. I want to buy a laptop. — Mariana: Again? Last year you said the same thing. — Iván: I know, but now I have a plan. I promise you I won't spend money on silly things. — Mariana: Hmm… If you save five hundred pesos a month, in December you'll have six thousand. — Iván: Exactly! And you? What will you do? — Mariana: I'm starting an English course on 8 January. And maybe I'll look for another job. — Iván: Really? And if you don't find anything? — Mariana: Well, I'll stay where I am. But one day I'll have my own project, you'll see.*

(*cumplir* — to keep, to fulfill (a resolution, a promise); *gastar* — to spend; *la tontería* — a silly thing; *ya verás* — you'll see.) Notice the mix: Mariana uses the present for her fixed course (*empiezo*), Iván uses the future for promises, and both use *si* + present.

## Pronunciation

- Stress the ending: *ha-bla-RÉ, co-me-RÁS, vi-vi-RÁN*. Saying *HA-bla-re* or *co-ME-ras* makes the word hard to understand.
- The *h* of *habrá* is silent, so it sounds like a-BRÁ. Compare *abra* (open!, from *abrir*), stressed A-bra: only the stress tells them apart, so stress the ending.
- *huracán*: the *h* is silent, u-ra-KÁN. *húmedo*: Ú-me-do, stress on the first syllable. *pronóstico*: pro-NÓS-ti-co.

## Common mistakes

- Adding the regular ending to an irregular verb: ~~teneré, poneré, haceré, deciré~~ → *tendré, pondré, haré, diré*.
- Dropping the accent: ~~hablare, comeran~~ → *hablaré, comerán*.
- The future after *si*: ~~Si tendré tiempo, te ayudaré~~ → *Si tengo tiempo, te ayudaré*.
- Mixing *ir a* and the future: ~~Voy a iré~~ → *Voy a ir* or *Iré*.
- A plural *habrá*: ~~Habrán muchas personas~~ → *Habrá muchas personas*.
- Using the simple future for every plan: *¿Qué harás el sábado?* is correct but sounds a little formal between friends; *¿Qué vas a hacer?* is more usual.

## Key points

- Future = whole infinitive + *-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án*, the same for all verbs; accents on every form except *nosotros*.
- Twelve verbs change the stem: *podr-, sabr-, habr-, querr-, cabr-; tendr-, pondr-, saldr-, vendr-, valdr-; har-, dir-*. Their compounds do too (*propondré*).
- *Habrá* = there will be, always singular.
- In conversation, Mexicans mostly use *ir a* for plans and the present for arrangements; the simple future is for forecasts, predictions, promises and formal plans.
- *si* + present, then the future: *Si llueve, no iremos*.
- *seguramente* = very probably; *quizás* + the indicative at this level.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Planning a trip: por and para
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 gave you the future for plans and forecasts. Now you'll plan a real trip: flights, airports, hotels and tours. And every trip is full of two small words that English speakers find hard: *por* and *para*. Both often translate as "for", but Spanish uses them for different ideas, and choosing the wrong one can change the meaning.

In A1 you met *para* with destinations and with an infinitive (*Voy al mercado para comprar fruta*) and *por* in *por la mañana*. This lesson gives you the main uses of each, a chart for deciding, and the fixed phrases you'll hear every day.

## Para: looking ahead to a goal

Think of *para* as an arrow pointing forward, toward a goal, a destination, a person who receives something, or a deadline.

| Use | Example |
|---|---|
| purpose: *para* + infinitive | *Ahorro para viajar a Perú.* — I'm saving (in order) to travel to Peru. |
| purpose of a thing: *para qué* | *¿Para qué es esta tarjeta? — Para abrir la puerta.* — What's this card for? — To open the door. |
| destination | *El vuelo para Monterrey sale a las seis.* — The flight to Monterrey leaves at six. |
| recipient | *Estos dulces son para ti.* — These sweets are for you. |
| deadline | *Necesito los boletos para el viernes.* — I need the tickets by Friday. |
| opinion | *Para mí, el mejor destino es Oaxaca.* — For me (in my opinion), the best destination is Oaxaca. |
| employer | *Trabaja para una aerolínea.* — She works for an airline. |

Notice that English often uses "to" or "in order to" where Spanish needs *para*: *Fui a la agencia de viajes para comprar el paquete* — I went to the travel agency to buy the package. Spanish can't simply leave the *para* out (after a verb of motion such as *ir*, *a* also works: *Fui a la agencia a comprar el paquete*).

## Por: the cause, the route and the exchange

*Por* looks back to a cause, or describes the way something happens: the route, the means, the exchange, the rate.

| Use | Example |
|---|---|
| cause, reason | *Cancelaron el vuelo por la tormenta.* — They canceled the flight because of the storm. |
| thanks for | *Gracias por tu ayuda.* — Thanks for your help. |
| through, along, around | *Dimos un recorrido por el centro.* — We took a tour around downtown. *Pasamos por Puebla.* — We went through Puebla. |
| means | *Hice la reservación por internet.* — I made the reservation online. *Me avisaron por teléfono.* — They told me by phone. |
| exchange, price | *Compré el boleto por 2,300 pesos.* — I bought the ticket for 2,300 pesos. |
| rate: "per" | *La habitación cuesta 900 pesos por noche.* — The room costs 900 pesos a night. *dos veces por semana, 100 kilómetros por hora* |
| vague place or time | *¿Hay una gasolinera por aquí?* — Is there a gas station around here? *por la tarde* — in the afternoon |
| duration | *Me quedé en Mérida por dos semanas.* — I stayed in Mérida for two weeks. |

Two notes on duration. Mexicans very often use no preposition at all (*Me quedé dos semanas en Mérida*), and *durante* is also common (*durante el vuelo* — during the flight). And when a period is what a booking is *for*, *para* is fine: *una reservación para tres noches* (a reservation for three nights).

## Choosing: a quick chart

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing por or para
  accDescr: Ask what the "for" means. If it points forward to a purpose, a goal or in order to, use para. If it names a destination, a person who receives something, a deadline or an opinion, also use para. If it gives a cause or reason, or follows gracias, use por. If it describes a route through or around a place, a means such as phone or internet, a price or exchange, a rate such as per night, or a vague time or place, use por.
  A{"What does the 'for' or 'to' mean?"} --> B["purpose, in order to"]
  A --> C["destination, receiver, deadline, opinion"]
  A --> D["cause, reason, thanks"]
  A --> E["route, means, price, per, around"]
  B --> P["para"]
  C --> P
  D --> Q["por"]
  E --> Q
```

The same sentence can change meaning with the preposition:

| *para* | *por* |
|---|---|
| *Trabajo para mi papá.* — I work for my dad (he's my boss). | *Trabajo por mi papá.* — I work for my dad's sake (or in his place). |
| *Salimos para Cancún.* — We're leaving for Cancún (that's where we're going). | *Pasamos por Cancún.* — We're going through Cancún. |
| *Lo hice para ti.* — I made it for you (it's yours). | *Lo hice por ti.* — I did it for you (because of you). |

## Fixed phrases

Learn these as whole chunks:

| With *por* | With *para* |
|---|---|
| *por favor* — please | *para siempre* — forever |
| *por fin* — at last, finally | *para llevar* — to go (food) |
| *por suerte* — luckily | *para nada* — not at all |
| *por ejemplo* — for example | |
| *por supuesto* — of course | |
| *por cierto* — by the way | |

*Por cierto, ¿ya documentaste las maletas?* — By the way, have you checked the suitcases yet?

## At the airport

Air travel in Mexico has its own words, some different from Spain's. This chart follows a trip from booking to the hotel:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A trip from booking to the hotel
  accDescr: First you make a reservation, online or at a travel agency. At the airport you check your suitcase at the airline counter and get your boarding pass. You go through security to the gate. You board the plane; the flight may have a stopover. On an international trip you go through immigration and customs when you arrive. Finally you check in at the hotel reception.
  A["la reservación (por internet o en una agencia de viajes)"] --> B["documentar la maleta en el mostrador de la aerolínea"]
  B --> C["el pase de abordar"]
  C --> D["la puerta de salida"]
  D --> E["abordar el avión; el vuelo, a veces con escala"]
  E --> F["migración y la aduana (viajes internacionales)"]
  F --> G["la recepción del hotel"]
```

- *Documentar* (Mexico; Spain says *facturar*) is to check a bag in: *Voy a documentar una maleta.* What you carry onto the plane is *el equipaje de mano*.
- *El pase de abordar* (Spain: *la tarjeta de embarque*) shows your *vuelo, asiento* and *puerta*. At the airport *la puerta* is the gate, and *la salida* (A1's "exit") is the departure: *Salidas nacionales* — Domestic departures.
- *¿Ventanilla o pasillo?* — Window or aisle? (*La ventanilla* is the window of a plane, bus or car; a window in a house is *la ventana*.)
- *Abordar* is to board: *Los pasajeros del vuelo 584 ya pueden abordar.*
- *Un vuelo directo* has no stops; *un vuelo con escala* stops on the way.
- Crossing a border (*la frontera*) means *migración* (immigration, where they check your passport and, if you need one, your *visa*) and *la aduana* (customs).

Here is a boarding pass. The airline and the people are invented:

![An invented boarding pass from the airline Aerolíneas Colibrí. Passenger: Ortiz Ramos / Lucía. Flight CB 584 from Ciudad de México (MEX) to Mérida (MID), date 12 DIC, departure 07:45. Gate 23, seat 14A (ventanilla), group 3. On the right a stub with a barcode repeats the flight, the seat and the gate. At the top: PASE DE ABORDAR.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In July 2026 Mexico's consumer agency, Profeco, reminded travelers that under Mexican law each passenger may carry two pieces of hand luggage weighing up to 10 kilos together, within set sizes, without an extra charge. Airlines may still sell cheaper fares without hand luggage if they say so clearly, and some low-cost fares do. Rules and fees change, so check your fare and your airline before you fly.

## At the hotel and on tour

- *Tengo una reservación a nombre de Ortiz.* — I have a reservation in the name of Ortiz. (*La reservación* is usual in Mexico; Spain says *la reserva*.)
- *una habitación sencilla / doble* — a single / double room. *Sencillo* also means "simple", and in Mexico *un boleto sencillo* is a one-way ticket (A1's *de ida y vuelta* is the round trip).
- *¿El desayuno está incluido?* — Is breakfast included? Ask at *la recepción* (the front desk), where you also leave the key: *Deje la llave en la recepción.*
- *El guía* (or *la guía*, for a woman) leads *el recorrido*, the tour: *El recorrido por las ruinas dura tres horas.* *La guía* can also be a guidebook.

## Dialogue: En el mostrador de la aerolínea

Lucía is checking in for her flight to Mérida (the boarding pass above). *El mostrador* is the counter.

> Empleado: Buenos días. ¿Para dónde viaja?
>
> Lucía: Para Mérida, en el vuelo de las siete cuarenta y cinco. Aquí está mi identificación.
>
> Empleado: Gracias. ¿Va a documentar equipaje?
>
> Lucía: Sí, esta maleta. Y llevo una mochila como equipaje de mano.
>
> Empleado: Muy bien. ¿Prefiere ventanilla o pasillo?
>
> Lucía: Ventanilla, por favor. Es mi primera vez en Yucatán y quiero ver el mar.
>
> Empleado: Listo: asiento 14A. El vuelo es directo; aborde por la puerta 23 a las siete y cuarto.
>
> Lucía: Perfecto. Por cierto, ¿hay retraso por la lluvia?
>
> Empleado: Por ahora no. Aquí tiene su pase de abordar. ¡Buen viaje!
>
> Lucía: Muchas gracias por todo.

*Employee: Good morning. Where are you traveling to? — Lucía: To Mérida, on the 7:45 flight. Here's my ID. — Employee: Thank you. Are you checking any luggage? — Lucía: Yes, this suitcase. And I'm taking a backpack as carry-on. — Employee: Very good. Would you prefer a window or an aisle seat? — Lucía: Window, please. It's my first time in Yucatán and I want to see the sea. — Employee: Done: seat 14A. The flight is direct; board at gate 23 at a quarter past seven. — Lucía: Perfect. By the way, is there a delay because of the rain? — Employee: Not for now. Here's your boarding pass. Have a good trip! — Lucía: Thanks very much for everything.*

(*la identificación* — ID; *listo* — done, ready; *el retraso* — delay, A1 honors; *por ahora* — for now.) Count the prepositions: *para* for her destination; *por* in *por favor, por cierto, por la puerta 23* (through), *por la lluvia* (cause), *por ahora* and *gracias por*.

## Pronunciation

- *aerolínea* has six syllables: a-e-ro-LÍ-ne-a. Each vowel is pronounced; don't run *ea* together into "nya".
- *equipaje*: e-ki-PA-je, with the *j* as a breathy "h". *aduana*: a-DWA-na (*ua* is one syllable).
- *por* and *para*: in fast, informal speech *para* often shrinks to *pa'* (*pa' la playa*), in Mexico and in many other countries. Recognize it; write *para*.

## Common mistakes

- *para* for a cause: ~~Gracias para la invitación~~ → *Gracias por la invitación*. ~~Cancelaron el vuelo para la lluvia~~ → *por la lluvia*.
- *por* for a purpose: ~~Estudio español por viajar~~ → *Estudio español para viajar*.
- Leaving out *para* before an infinitive of purpose: ~~Fui al aeropuerto recoger a mi hermana~~ → *Fui al aeropuerto para recoger a mi hermana* (or *a recoger*, after a verb of motion).
- Prices with *para*: ~~Lo compré para 500 pesos~~ → *Lo compré por 500 pesos*.
- "Per" with *a*: ~~900 pesos a noche~~ → *900 pesos por noche*. (With units of time you'll also hear *al* or *a la*: *dos veces a la semana, 500 pesos al mes*; both are correct.)
- Spain's travel words in Mexico: *facturar, la tarjeta de embarque, el visado* are understood, but Mexicans say *documentar, el pase de abordar, la visa*.

## Key points

- *para* points forward: purpose (+ infinitive), destination, recipient, deadline, opinion, employer.
- *por* explains or describes: cause, *gracias por*, route (through, along, around), means, price and exchange, "per", vague place and time, duration.
- When in doubt, ask "in order to / heading to / meant for?" (*para*) or "because of / through / in exchange for / per?" (*por*).
- Airport words in Mexico: *documentar, el pase de abordar, abordar, la puerta, la escala, la aduana*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Making plans: invitations, excuses and verb + infinitive phrases
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now talk about the future (lesson 13) and organize a trip (lesson 14). This lesson is about the weekend: inviting friends, suggesting a plan, saying yes, saying no without hurting anyone, and agreeing on a time and place. Along the way you'll learn a family of very useful **[[verbal periphrases]]**: a conjugated verb, often a small linking word, and an infinitive, which together add an idea such as "start", "stop", "again" or "just". You already know several from A1: *ir a* + infinitive (*Voy a salir*), *tener que* (*Tengo que trabajar*), *poder* and *querer* (*¿Puedes venir?*).

## Six phrases with an infinitive

Only the first verb changes; the infinitive stays the same.

| Phrase | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *empezar a* + inf. | to start (doing) | *Empecé a jugar ajedrez el año pasado.* — I started playing chess last year. |
| *volver a* + inf. | to do again | *Volví a ver la película.* — I watched the film again. |
| *dejar de* + inf. | to stop (doing) | *Dejé de ir al gimnasio en marzo.* — I stopped going to the gym in March. |
| *acabar de* + inf. | to have just (done) | *Acabo de comprar los boletos.* — I've just bought the tickets. |
| *tener ganas de* + inf. | to feel like (doing) | *Tengo ganas de salir a bailar.* — I feel like going out dancing. |
| *pensar* + inf. | to plan to, intend to | *Pienso acampar en Semana Santa.* — I'm planning to go camping at Easter. |

Two more for trying: *tratar de* + infinitive and *intentar* + infinitive (lesson 4) both mean "to try to": *Traté de llamarte* / *Intenté llamarte* — I tried to call you.

![A timeline of an activity, playing chess. Before the activity: tener ganas de jugar (feel like playing). The activity bar starts at a point labeled empezar a jugar (start playing). The bar ends at a point labeled dejar de jugar (stop playing). Right after the end, a small flag says acabar de jugar (have just played). Later, a second bar starts with volver a jugar (play again).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Some details that make these phrases sound natural:

- *Acabar de* is used in the present for something that has just happened. *Acabamos de llegar* means "We've just arrived", even though the verb is present. (On its own, *acabar* means "to finish, to end": *La película acaba a las diez*.) In a story you'll also meet *acababa de* + infinitive, "had just": *Acababa de salir cuando empezó a llover* — I had just gone out when it started to rain. Recognize it for now.
- *Volver a* replaces "again". *Vuelve a llamar* (He's calling again) is more natural than adding *otra vez*, though *otra vez* is fine too.
- *Dejar de* needs the *de*. Without it, *dejar* means "to leave (something)" or "to let": *Dejé el libro en tu casa* (I left the book at your place), *Mis papás no me dejan salir* (My parents don't let me go out).
- *Pensar* + infinitive has no preposition: ~~Pienso a ir~~ → *Pienso ir*. (*Pensar en* = to think about.)
- You'll also hear *ponerse a* + infinitive for starting something suddenly: *Se puso a llorar* — She burst into tears. Just recognize it.

Any tense works with the first verb: *Mañana volveré a llamar* (future), *De niña empezaba a leer antes de dormir* (imperfect), *He dejado de tomar refresco* (perfect).

## Inviting and suggesting

A1 taught *¿Quieres* + infinitive? and *Te invito*. Here are four more ways to suggest a plan, from neutral to very informal:

| Phrase | Example |
|---|---|
| *¿Qué tal si* + present? | *¿Qué tal si vamos a la feria el sábado?* — How about going to the fair on Saturday? |
| *¿Por qué no* + present? | *¿Por qué no hacemos un día de campo?* — Why don't we have a picnic? |
| *¿Te parece si* + present? | *¿Te parece si nos vemos a las cinco?* — Is it OK with you if we meet at five? |
| *¿Te late* + infinitive or noun? | *¿Te late ir al cine?* — Do you feel like going to the movies? (Mexico, informal) |

To suggest something more formally, use *proponer* (to suggest, to propose; like *poner*: *propongo, propuse*, future *propondré*): *Te propongo un plan: cenamos y luego vamos al teatro.* — Here's my suggestion: we have dinner and then go to the theater.

After *¿Qué tal si…?* and *¿Te parece si…?* use the present, not the infinitive: *¿Qué tal si cenamos?* *Me late* (it appeals to me, sounds good) is everyday Mexican slang among friends; don't use it with your boss.

## Saying yes, saying no

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Answering an invitation
  accDescr: Someone invites you. If you say yes, use phrases such as Claro, Perfecto or Me late, then agree on a time and place with quedar. If you say no, first apologize with Lo siento or Qué lástima, then give a reason with Es que or Tengo un compromiso, and then suggest another time with Qué tal otro día or A lo mejor el sábado.
  A["An invitation: ¿Qué tal si vamos al festival?"] --> B{"Yes or no?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["¡Claro! ¡Perfecto! ¡Me late!"]
  C --> D["Agree on time and place: ¿Dónde quedamos?"]
  B -- "no" --> E["Apologize: Lo siento. ¡Qué lástima!"]
  E --> F["Give a reason: Es que… Tengo un compromiso."]
  F --> G["Offer another time: ¿Qué tal otro día? A lo mejor el sábado."]
```

In Mexico, as in many places, people usually say no to a friend gently, with an apology and a reason, often introduced by *es que* (the thing is…): *Lo siento, es que tengo que trabajar.* A flat *No, gracias* to a friend's invitation can sound cold. Useful pieces:

- *Ya tengo un compromiso.* — I already have something on (a prior engagement). *El compromiso* is usually a commitment or obligation; it rarely means a "compromise" (an agreement where both sides give up something is usually *un acuerdo*).
- *No estoy libre el viernes, pero el sábado sí.* — I'm not free on Friday, but on Saturday I am.
- *A lo mejor el domingo.* — Maybe on Sunday. (*A lo mejor* = maybe, very common in conversation.)
- *¿Qué tal otro día?* — How about another day?

A real reason is better than *una excusa* (an excuse) that nobody believes: *Siempre tiene una excusa para no venir.*

Accepting and declining are *aceptar* and *rechazar*: *Aceptó la invitación*, *Rechazó la invitación* — though in conversation people rarely use *rechazar* about friends; they just say *No pudo venir*.

## Making arrangements: quedar

In A1 honors you met *quedar* as "to be located" (*¿Dónde queda el museo?*). With people, *quedar* also means "to arrange to meet, to agree":

- *¿Dónde quedamos?* — Where shall we meet? *Quedamos en el café a las seis.* — We'll meet at the café at six.
- *quedar en* + infinitive or *que*: to agree to. *Quedamos en ir juntos.* — We agreed to go together.
- *quedar de* + infinitive: the same meaning, still very common in Mexico (and Colombia), as the Spanish Academy's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* notes. *Quedamos de vernos a las seis en la taquilla.* — We agreed to meet at six at the box office.
- *quedar con* + person: to arrange to see someone. *Ya quedé con Laura.* — I've already arranged to see Laura.

## Things to do

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *la exposición* (*la expo*) | exhibition |
| *el espectáculo* | show, performance |
| *el festival, la feria* | festival, fair |
| *la taquilla* | box office, ticket office: *No hay boletos disponibles* (no tickets available) |
| *el juego de mesa, el ajedrez* | board game, chess |
| *acampar, la casa de campaña* | to camp, tent (Spain: *la tienda de campaña*) |
| *el día de campo* | picnic (Mexico: *hacer un día de campo*) |
| *pescar* | to fish, to go fishing |

Mexico has big festivals all year. Two examples, with dates that change every year: the Festival Internacional Cervantino in Guanajuato, an international arts festival, held its 54th edition from 3 to 18 October 2026; and the Feria Nacional de San Marcos in Aguascalientes, a huge traditional fair, ran from 18 April to 10 May 2026.

Two reflexive verbs describe how it went: *divertirse* (to have fun, e → ie like *preferir*: *me divierto*; preterite *se divirtió, se divirtieron*) and *aburrirse* (to get bored, regular): *¡Nos divertimos muchísimo!* — We had a great time! *Me aburrí en la exposición.* — I got bored at the exhibition.

Here is a poster for an invented festival:

![A poster for the invented Festival de Jazz Los Fresnos. Text: Sábado 14 y domingo 15 de marzo. Foro del Lago, Parque Los Fresnos. Sábado 19:00: Trío Luna. Domingo 13:00: Big Band Universitaria (para toda la familia). Boletos: 250 pesos en taquilla o por internet. Niños menores de 12: gratis. Habrá comida y juegos de mesa. Drawings of a saxophone and musical notes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: ¿Qué tal si vamos al festival?

Sofía calls her friend Tomás.

> Sofía: Oye, Tomás, acabo de ver un cartel del Festival de Jazz Los Fresnos. ¿Qué tal si vamos el sábado en la noche?
>
> Tomás: ¡Qué lástima! Es que el sábado tengo un compromiso: es el cumpleaños de mi abuela.
>
> Sofía: ¿Y el domingo? Hay un concierto a la una, para toda la familia.
>
> Tomás: El domingo sí estoy libre. ¡Me late! ¿Cuánto cuestan los boletos?
>
> Sofía: Doscientos cincuenta pesos. Pienso comprarlos por internet hoy, porque a lo mejor se acaban.
>
> Tomás: Perfecto. Oye, ¿por qué no llevamos algo de comer y hacemos un día de campo después?
>
> Sofía: ¡Buena idea! Hace mucho que no hago un día de campo.
>
> Tomás: Y si nos aburrimos del jazz, jugamos ajedrez en el pasto.
>
> Sofía: ¡No te vas a aburrir, ya verás! Entonces, ¿dónde quedamos?
>
> Tomás: Quedamos de vernos a las doce y media en la entrada del parque, ¿va?
>
> Sofía: ¡Va! Nos vemos el domingo.

*Sofía: Hey, Tomás, I've just seen a poster for the Los Fresnos Jazz Festival. How about going on Saturday night? — Tomás: What a shame! The thing is, on Saturday I have something on: it's my grandmother's birthday. — Sofía: And Sunday? There's a concert at one, for the whole family. — Tomás: On Sunday I am free. Sounds great! How much are the tickets? — Sofía: Two hundred and fifty pesos. I'm planning to buy them online today, because maybe they'll sell out. — Tomás: Perfect. Hey, why don't we take something to eat and have a picnic afterwards? — Sofía: Good idea! I haven't had a picnic in ages. — Tomás: And if we get bored with the jazz, we'll play chess on the grass. — Sofía: You won't get bored, you'll see! So, where shall we meet? — Tomás: Let's meet at half past twelve at the entrance to the park, OK? — Sofía: OK! See you on Sunday.*

(*el cartel* — poster; *en la noche* — at night, common in Mexico for *por la noche*; *se acaban* — they run out (*acabarse*); *hace mucho que no* … — I haven't … for a long time, lesson 4; *el pasto* — grass, lawn (Mexico); *¿va?* and *¡va!* — OK? OK!, informal Mexican.)

## Pronunciation

- *ajedrez*: a-he-DRES, stress on the last syllable; the final *z* sounds like *s*.
- *divertirse*: di-ber-TIR-se; *v* and *b* sound the same.
- *¿Qué tal si…?* is said as one unit, with the voice rising at the end like any yes/no question.

## Common mistakes

- Dropping the linking word: ~~Empecé estudiar~~ → *Empecé a estudiar*; ~~Dejé fumar~~ → *Dejé de fumar*.
- Adding one where there is none: ~~Pienso de viajar~~ → *Pienso viajar*.
- *Acabar de* in the preterite for "have just": in Mexico you'll hear *Acabo de comer* (present) for "I've just eaten". *Acabé de comer* means "I finished eating".
- The infinitive after *¿Qué tal si…?*: ~~¿Qué tal si ir al cine?~~ → *¿Qué tal si vamos al cine?*
- *libre* for "free of charge": ~~La entrada es libre~~ is understood (*entrada libre* appears on signs), but in conversation say *Es gratis*. *Libre* is about time: *¿Estás libre?*
- *el compromiso* as "compromise": in everyday use it means a commitment or engagement; for a compromise say *un acuerdo*.

## Key points

- Verb + (linking word) + infinitive: *empezar a, volver a* (again), *dejar de* (stop), *acabar de* (have just), *tener ganas de* (feel like), *pensar* (plan to), *tratar de* (try to).
- Suggest with *¿Qué tal si / ¿Por qué no / ¿Te parece si* + present; *¿Te late…?* is informal Mexican.
- Decline gently: apology + *es que* + reason + another option.
- *quedar* (en, de, con) for arranging to meet; *quedar de* + infinitive is very Mexican.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: In the kitchen: commands with pronouns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The kitchen is full of instructions: cut it, add it, stir it, pass it to me. In A1 you learned the affirmative **[[imperative]]** for *tú* and *usted* (*corta, corte; pon, ponga*), and in module 2 you learned the object pronouns *lo, la, los, las, me, te, le, nos, les* and the pair *se lo*. This lesson puts them together, *córtala, póngalo, dámelo*, and shows why many of these commands need a written accent. You'll also meet commands for a group (*ustedes*), a handful of negative commands to learn as phrases, and the way written recipes give instructions. The theme is cooking, with a Mexican recipe to finish.

## Pronouns go on the end of affirmative commands

With an affirmative command, the pronoun is attached to the end of the verb, written as one word:

| Without a pronoun | With a pronoun | |
|---|---|---|
| *Pica la cebolla.* | *Pícala.* | Chop it. |
| *Pela las papas.* | *Pélalas.* | Peel them. |
| *Ponga el arroz.* | *Póngalo.* | Put it in. |
| *Pasa la sal a tu papá.* | *Pásale la sal.* | Pass him the salt. |
| *Siéntate.* | | Sit down. (A1: reflexive commands) |

Remember from module 2 that a pronoun can never go in front of an affirmative command: ~~Lo pica~~ is not a command (it means "He chops it").

### Two pronouns

When there are two, the indirect (who gets it) comes before the direct (what), exactly as in *Me lo das*, and *le* or *les* turns into *se* before *lo, la, los, las*:

- *Dame la cuchara → Dámela.* — Give it to me.
- *Sírvele la sopa a tu abuela → Sírvesela.* — Serve it to her.
- *Tráiganos la cuenta → Tráiganosla.* — Bring it to us. (usted)
- *Dígaselo.* — Tell him / her / them. (usted)

Order to remember: (reflexive) → indirect → direct: *Lávatelas* (wash them, your hands: *te* + *las*).

## Why the accent? Keeping the stress where it was

Adding syllables to the end of a word doesn't move its stress: *corta* is stressed on *cor-*, and so is *córtala*. But Spanish spelling rules say that a word stressed three syllables from the end (or earlier) always carries a written accent. So the accent appears on the same vowel that was stressed before:

![A chart showing how a command keeps its stress. corta has two syllables, COR-ta, and no written accent. Add la: cór-ta-la, three syllables with the stress on the first, so it needs an accent. Add me and la: cór-ta-me-la, four syllables, accent on the same vowel. Below, the short command pon: pon-lo has two syllables and no accent, but pón-me-lo has three and needs one.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Command | + 1 pronoun | + 2 pronouns |
|---|---|---|
| *corta* | *córtala* | *córtamela* |
| *mezcla* | *mézclalo* | *mézclamelo* |
| *sirve* | *sírvelo* | *sírveselo* |
| *calienta* | *caliéntala* | *caliéntamela* |
| *corte* (usted) | *córtelo* | *córtemelo* |
| *pon* | *ponlo* | *pónmelo* |
| *di* | *dilo* | *dímelo* |
| *haz* | *hazlo* | *házmelo* |
| *da* | *dame* | *dámelo* |

The rule in one sentence: count back from the end; if the stressed vowel is now the third syllable or earlier, write the accent on it.

- One-syllable commands (*pon, di, haz, da, ten, ven, sal*) plus one pronoun make a two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable, which is normal, so no accent: *ponlo, dilo, hazlo, dame, tenlo*. With two pronouns they need one: *pónmelo, dímelo, házmelo, dámelo*.
- Commands with an accent already keep it: *fríe → fríelo* (fry it).
- With *usted*, the same rule: *traiga → tráigamelo* (bring it to me), *sirva → sírvaselo*.

## Commands for a group: ustedes

For two or more people, use the *ustedes* form: the *usted* command + *-n* (A1). Pronouns attach the same way, and the accent stays on the same syllable:

- *Corten la cebolla.* — Cut the onion. → *Córtenla.*
- *Pongan la mesa, por favor.* — Set the table, please.
- *Lávense las manos.* — Wash your hands. (reflexive: *se*)
- *Vayan a la tienda y compren tortillas.* — Go to the store and buy tortillas.

You'll hear these from a cook teaching a class or a parent talking to two children. Recognize them and use the common ones; the drills practice *tú* and *usted* only.

## Negative commands: learn a few as phrases

"Don't cut it" is not ~~No córtalo~~. A **[[negative command]]** uses a different verb form, the present subjunctive, which you will learn at B1. Its pronouns also move in front of the verb. For now, learn these as fixed phrases:

| tú | usted | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *No te preocupes.* | *No se preocupe.* | Don't worry. |
| *No lo toques.* | *No lo toque.* | Don't touch it. (*tocar* = to touch, also to play an instrument) |
| *No te olvides.* | *No se olvide.* | Don't forget. (*No te olvides de la sal.*) |

### No + infinitive on signs and in instructions

Signs, recipes and printed instructions often avoid commands altogether and use *No* + infinitive: *No fumar* (No smoking), *No tocar* (Do not touch), *No dejar hervir* (Do not let it boil). This form is easy: just *no* and the infinitive.

## Reading a recipe

Spanish recipes give instructions in three ways. Mexican cookbooks and websites use all three, so learn to read them all:

| Infinitive (very common in written recipes) | tú | usted |
|---|---|---|
| *Pelar las papas.* | *Pela las papas.* | *Pele las papas.* |
| *Picar la cebolla.* | *Pica la cebolla.* | *Pique la cebolla.* |
| *Agregar la sal.* | *Agrega la sal.* | *Agregue la sal.* |

Recipes start with a list of *ingredientes*. Besides the ones in this lesson's recipe, you'll often see *el azúcar* (sugar; *la azúcar* is also heard), *la harina* (flour, as in *tortillas de harina*) and *el limón* (in Mexico usually the small green lime: *Sírvelo con limón*).

Quantity words you'll find:

- *una cucharada* — a tablespoon (a spoonful); *una cucharadita* — a teaspoon
- *una taza* — a cup (as a measure too); *medio kilo* — half a kilo
- *un diente de ajo* — a clove of garlic
- *una pizca de sal* — a pinch of salt; *sal al gusto* — salt to taste

### Arroz rojo

*Arroz rojo* (red rice, also called *arroz a la mexicana*) is one of the most common side dishes in Mexican home cooking. This version follows the usual method: fry the rice, add a blended tomato sauce, then cook it slowly in broth.

![A recipe card titled Arroz rojo, 4 porciones. Ingredientes: 1 taza de arroz, 2 jitomates, un cuarto de cebolla, 1 diente de ajo, 2 tazas de caldo de pollo, 2 cucharadas de aceite, sal al gusto, 1 zanahoria (opcional). Preparación: 1. Lavar el arroz y escurrirlo. 2. Licuar los jitomates, la cebolla y el ajo con media taza de caldo. 3. Calentar el aceite y freír el arroz hasta dorarlo (unos 5 minutos). 4. Agregar la salsa y mezclar. 5. Agregar el resto del caldo y la sal. Hervir. 6. Tapar y cocinar a fuego bajo unos 15 minutos. 7. Dejar reposar 10 minutos y servir. A small drawing of a pot.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

New words on the card: *escurrir* (to drain), *licuar* (to blend, with *la licuadora*, the blender), *el caldo* (broth, stock), *dorar* (to brown, to turn golden), *tapar* (to cover, put the lid on), *a fuego bajo* (on low heat), *reposar* (to rest), *la zanahoria* (carrot), *la porción* (serving). *Freír hasta dorar* (fry until golden) is a common recipe phrase.

## The utensils

![A kitchen counter with seven utensils, each labeled: la olla (a large pot with two handles and a lid), el sartén (a frying pan with a long handle), el cuchillo (a knife), la cuchara (a spoon), el tenedor (a fork), el vaso (a drinking glass), la taza (a mug with a handle).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*El sartén* is masculine in most of Mexico; Spain and the dictionary standard say *la sartén*, and both are correct. *La olla* is a deep pot for soups, beans and rice. *El horno* is the oven. Setting the table: *Pon los tenedores a la izquierda y los vasos a la derecha. — ¿Y los cuchillos? — Ponlos junto a los platos.* (Put the forks on the left and the glasses on the right. — And the knives? — Put them next to the plates.)

## Dialogue: Cocinando con la abuela

Diego is learning to make arroz rojo with his grandmother, doña Rosa.

> Abuela: Primero lávate las manos, Diego. Y ponte el delantal.
>
> Diego: Ya. ¿Qué hago con el arroz?
>
> Abuela: Lávalo bien y escúrrelo. Luego pícame esta cebolla, pero no toda: solo un cuarto.
>
> Diego: ¿Así? ¿Te la pongo en la licuadora?
>
> Abuela: Sí, pónmela ahí con los jitomates y el ajo. Agrega media taza de caldo y prende la licuadora.
>
> Diego: Abuela, el aceite está muy caliente.
>
> Abuela: No te preocupes. Echa el arroz y muévelo unos cinco minutos; tiene que quedar dorado. ¡Ay, no lo toques con la mano!
>
> Diego: Perdón. ¿Ahora la salsa?
>
> Abuela: Sí, agrégala y mézclala. Después el resto del caldo. Ahora tápalo y déjalo así, sin moverlo.
>
> Diego: ¿Y la sal?
>
> Abuela: ¡Ay, la sal! Dámela… listo. Dentro de quince minutos se lo servimos a tu abuelo.

*Grandmother: First wash your hands, Diego. And put on the apron. — Diego: Done. What do I do with the rice? — Grandmother: Wash it well and drain it. Then chop this onion for me, but not all of it: just a quarter. — Diego: Like this? Shall I put it in the blender for you? — Grandmother: Yes, put it in there for me with the tomatoes and the garlic. Add half a cup of broth and turn on the blender. — Diego: Grandma, the oil is very hot. — Grandmother: Don't worry. Put the rice in and stir it for about five minutes; it has to turn golden. Oh, don't touch it with your hand! — Diego: Sorry. The sauce now? — Grandmother: Yes, add it and mix it. Then the rest of the broth. Now put the lid on and leave it like that, without stirring it. — Diego: And the salt? — Grandmother: Oh, the salt! Give it to me… done. In fifteen minutes we'll serve it to your grandfather.*

(*el delantal* — apron; *echar* — to put in, to throw in; *mover* — to stir, to move; *quedar* — here, to turn out, to end up.) Count the attached pronouns: *lávate, ponte, lávalo, escúrrelo, pícame, pónmela, muévelo, agrégala, mézclala, tápalo, déjalo, dámela*.

## Pronunciation

- Keep the stress on the verb, not on the pronoun: *CÓR-ta-la*, not cor-ta-LA; *DÁ-me-lo*.
- *fríe*: two syllables, FRÍ-e; the accent on *í* separates the vowels. *hierve*: two syllables, HYER-be.
- *cebolla, olla*: *ll* sounds like *y* in most of Latin America: se-BO-ya, O-ya.

## Common mistakes

- Missing accent: ~~cortala, damelo, sirvelo~~ → *córtala, dámelo, sírvelo*.
- An accent where none is needed: ~~pónlo, dílo~~ → *ponlo, dilo*.
- Wrong order: ~~Lame da~~ or ~~Dalame~~ → *Dámela* (indirect before direct).
- *le lo*: ~~Dale lo~~ → *Dáselo*.
- Making a negative command from the affirmative: ~~No córtalo~~, ~~No toca~~ → learn *No lo toques*; for other negatives, use *No* + infinitive in instructions or rephrase (*Hay que esperar*).

## Key points

- Affirmative command + pronoun(s), one word: *pícala, póngalo, dámelo, sírvanselo*; indirect before direct; *le/les* → *se* before *lo, la, los, las*.
- Add a written accent when the stress ends up three syllables from the end or earlier: *córtala, caliéntalo, tráigamelo*; *ponlo, dilo, hazlo, dame* need none, *pónmelo, dímelo* do.
- *ustedes* = *usted* command + *-n*: *corten, pongan, lávense*.
- Negative commands use a new form (B1): for now *No te preocupes, No lo toques, No te olvides*, and *No* + infinitive on signs.
- Recipes often use the infinitive: *Picar la cebolla. Agregar la sal.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: A road trip through Mexico
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 13 to 16 gave you the future, *por* and *para*, plans and commands. This honors lesson puts them to work on a classic trip: driving from Mexico City to Oaxaca. You'll plan a route, rent a car, fill the tank, read road signs and a toll receipt, know whom to call if something goes wrong, and finally read a travel blog that tells the trip in the past tenses. Distances, times and prices here are approximate and dated: tolls and fuel prices change every year, so always check before you travel.

## Planning the route

![A simplified route map. Ciudad de México is at the top left. A thick blue line, the toll road (autopista de cuota), runs east to Puebla, about 130 km, with two toll booth symbols marked caseta. From Puebla the blue line continues south-east to a junction, then turns south through the mountains to Oaxaca, about 300 km from Puebla, with more toll booths. A thin dashed line marked carretera libre runs further west from Mexico City to Oaxaca, longer and slower. A small legend explains the line styles and the caseta symbol.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Mexico has two kinds of highway. *La carretera de cuota* (or *la autopista*, or just *la cuota*) is a toll road: you pay at *la caseta* (the toll booth, in full *la caseta de cobro*), and in return the road is usually faster and better kept. *La carretera libre* (*la libre*) is free, but it usually goes through towns, with traffic and *topes*, so it's slower. *Libre* here is the same word as lesson 15's "free (not busy)": free of charge, in this case.

Approximate figures for this trip (checked in 2026):

| Stretch | Distance | Time by toll road |
|---|---|---|
| Ciudad de México → Puebla | about 130 km | about 2 hours |
| Puebla → Oaxaca | about 300 km | about 4 hours |

In June 2026 a news site added up the two toll booths between Mexico City and Puebla for a car: 173 and 53 pesos, 226 pesos in all. The toll road from the Puebla area to Oaxaca, through the mountains, opened in 1994.

### Example 1: Talking about the plan

Here is how three different speakers might describe the same plan, each choosing the form that suits them (lesson 13):

1. A friend on the phone, using *ir a* for plans: *Vamos a salir el viernes temprano y vamos a tomar la cuota para llegar más rápido.* — We're going to leave early on Friday and take the toll road to get there faster.
2. A fixed arrangement, in the present: *Salimos el viernes a las seis.* — We're leaving on Friday at six.
3. A written itinerary, in the future, with *por* and *para*: *El viernes saldremos para Oaxaca a las seis. Pasaremos por Puebla y pararemos para desayunar.* — On Friday we will leave for Oaxaca at six. We will go through Puebla and stop to have breakfast.

Notice the prepositions in 3: *para Oaxaca* (destination), *por Puebla* (route, through), *para desayunar* (purpose).

## Renting a car

You already know *rentar* from A1 (rent). At the counter (*el mostrador*) you'll hear and need:

- *Quisiera rentar un carro por cuatro días.* — I'd like to rent a car for four days.
- *¿Me permite su licencia de manejo y una tarjeta de crédito?* — May I have your driver's license and a credit card?
- *¿El seguro está incluido?* — Is insurance included? (*el seguro* — insurance)
- *Lo entregamos con el tanque lleno; devuélvalo lleno, por favor.* — We give it to you with a full tank; please return it full. (*el tanque* — tank; *devolver*, lesson 6)
- *¿Tiene kilometraje libre?* — Does it have unlimited mileage? (*el kilometraje* — mileage, in kilometers)

Ask exactly what the insurance covers before you sign: rental prices in ads often don't include all of it.

## At the gas station

Mexican gas stations (*las gasolineras*) are usually full-service: an attendant fills the tank for you. You say how much you want:

- *Lleno, por favor.* — Fill it up, please.
- *Póngale quinientos pesos de Magna, por favor.* — Put in five hundred pesos of regular, please. (*Magna* is the name you'll usually hear for regular gasoline in Mexico; *Premium* is the higher grade.)
- *¿Me revisa las llantas?* — Could you check the tires? (*revisar* — to check)

Before they start, check that the pump shows zero (attendants often say *en ceros*, "at zero"). A small tip is customary, especially if they clean the windshield or check the tires.

## Reading road signs

![Six road signs as seen in Mexico, each with a number: 1, a yellow diamond with a bump drawn on it and the word TOPE; 2, a white sign with VELOCIDAD MÁXIMA 110 km/h; 3, a white sign with PROHIBIDO REBASAR; 4, a white sign with NO ESTACIONARSE; 5, an orange sign with DESVIACIÓN and an arrow; 6, a green sign with CASETA DE COBRO 2 km.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: What does each sign tell you to do?

Signs often use the *usted* command, *No* + infinitive (lesson 16) or *Prohibido* + infinitive:

1. *TOPE* — a speed bump ahead. *El tope* (Mexico) is a raised bump across the road, very common at the entrance to towns and near schools. Slow down a lot: some are high.
2. *VELOCIDAD MÁXIMA 110 km/h* — maximum speed: *ciento diez kilómetros por hora*. (*por* = per, lesson 14.)
3. *PROHIBIDO REBASAR* — no passing (*prohibido* — forbidden, A1; *rebasar*, Mexico; Spain *adelantar*). Painted signs sometimes say *NO REBASE* instead: that is a negative *usted* command, a form you'll learn at B1 (like the chunk *No se preocupe*). Just recognize it.
4. *NO ESTACIONARSE* — no parking: *No* + infinitive. (*estacionarse* — to park; Spain *aparcar*.)
5. *DESVIACIÓN* — detour. Follow the arrow, perhaps because of roadwork (*obras*).
6. *CASETA DE COBRO 2 km* — toll booth in two kilometers: have your money or card ready.

You'll also see *Disminuya su velocidad* (reduce your speed) and *Maneje con precaución* (drive carefully), both *usted* commands.

## Reading a toll receipt

![An invented toll receipt. Heading: AUTOPISTA DEL VALLE, Caseta Los Pinos (the names are invented). Fecha 08/05, hora 07:12. Clase: Automóvil. Forma de pago: Efectivo. Tarifa: 173.00 pesos. At the bottom: ¡Buen viaje! Conserve su comprobante.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 3: Finding the information

Read the receipt and answer in Spanish.

- *¿Cuánto pagaron?* — *Pagaron ciento setenta y tres pesos.* (*la tarifa* — the rate, the fare)
- *¿Cómo pagaron?* — *En efectivo* (in cash). The other common option is *con tarjeta* or with a toll tag (*un tag*, as it's often called in Mexico).
- *¿Qué tipo de vehículo era?* — *Un automóvil.* Trucks and buses pay more.
- *¿Qué les pide la caseta?* — *Conservar el comprobante* (keep the receipt): *conserve* is an *usted* command of *conservar*.

The date is written day/month: *08/05* is 8 May.

## If something goes wrong

Mexico's federal highways have free roadside help:

- *Los Ángeles Verdes* (the Green Angels), the tourism ministry's roadside assistance on federal highways and tourist routes: dial **078**.
- On toll roads run by the federal operator CAPUFE: dial **074**.
- For emergencies: **911**.

(Numbers as given in an Excélsior article of March 2026; both services are free.) Useful sentences: *Se ponchó una llanta* (We have a flat tire), *Nos quedamos sin gasolina* (We ran out of gas), *Estamos en el kilómetro 85 de la autopista a Oaxaca* (We're at kilometer 85 of the Oaxaca highway). Mexican highways have kilometer markers, so the number tells the helpers exactly where you are.

## A travel blog: De la Ciudad de México a Oaxaca

Valeria writes a travel blog. This entry tells her trip in the past: the preterite for events that move the story, the imperfect for the background (module 1).

> El viernes pasado mi hermano y yo rentamos un carro y salimos para Oaxaca a las seis de la mañana. Todavía estaba oscuro y no había mucho tráfico. Tomamos la autopista de cuota porque queríamos llegar temprano. Hasta Puebla pagamos dos casetas, casi doscientos treinta pesos en total.
>
> En Puebla paramos en una gasolinera. El despachador nos llenó el tanque y nos revisó las llantas. Luego desayunamos chilaquiles en una fonda junto a la carretera.
>
> Después, la autopista empezó a subir por las montañas. El paisaje era increíble: había cactus enormes y cerros de color café. Mi hermano manejaba muy despacio en las curvas, porque llovía un poco. Un camión nos rebasó a toda velocidad y nos asustamos.
>
> Cerca de Oaxaca encontramos una desviación por obras y tardamos media hora más. Por fin, a las dos de la tarde, llegamos al centro. Nos estacionamos frente al hotel, cansados pero muy contentos. ¿El próximo viaje? ¡Chiapas!

*Last Friday my brother and I rented a car and left for Oaxaca at six in the morning. It was still dark and there wasn't much traffic. We took the toll road because we wanted to arrive early. As far as Puebla we paid at two toll booths, almost two hundred and thirty pesos in all. — In Puebla we stopped at a gas station. The attendant filled the tank and checked the tires for us. Then we had chilaquiles for breakfast at a small restaurant by the highway. — Afterwards, the freeway started to climb through the mountains. The landscape was incredible: there were enormous cacti and brown hills. My brother drove very slowly on the curves, because it was raining a little. A truck passed us at full speed and we got scared. — Near Oaxaca we came across a detour because of roadwork and it took us half an hour longer. Finally, at two in the afternoon, we arrived downtown. We parked in front of the hotel, tired but very happy. The next trip? Chiapas!*

(*el despachador* — gas station attendant; *los chilaquiles* — fried tortilla pieces in salsa, a classic breakfast; *la fonda* — small, simple restaurant (A1 honors); *subir* — to climb; *el cactus* — cactus (plural *los cactus*); *el cerro* — hill (lesson 11); *la curva* — curve, bend; *el camión* — truck (in Mexico also a bus); *a toda velocidad* — at full speed; *asustarse* — to get scared (lesson 3); *tardar* — to take (time).)

Look at the tenses: *estaba oscuro, no había tráfico, queríamos, era increíble, había cactus, manejaba, llovía* set the scene (imperfect); *rentamos, salimos, tomamos, pagamos, paramos, rebasó, llegamos* are the events (preterite).

## Common mistakes

- *libre* as "free of charge" in other contexts: on the road *la libre* is the free highway, but a free ticket is *un boleto gratis*.
- *peaje* on the road: Spain's usual word (*la autopista de peaje*) appears in official Mexican texts too, but drivers in Mexico say *la cuota* and *la caseta*.
- ~~Llena, por favor~~ → *Lleno, por favor* (the tank, *el tanque*, is masculine).
- *por* for a destination: ~~Manejamos por Oaxaca~~ when you mean "to Oaxaca" → *Manejamos a Oaxaca* (or *Salimos para Oaxaca*). *Por Oaxaca* means around or through Oaxaca.

## Key points

- *la cuota* (toll road, pay at *la caseta*) vs *la libre* (free road, slower, with *topes*).
- At the gas station: *Lleno, por favor* or *Póngale … pesos*; check the pump starts at zero.
- Signs use *usted* commands (*Disminuya su velocidad*) and *No* or *Prohibido* + infinitive (*No estacionarse, Prohibido rebasar*); *No rebase*, on some painted signs, is a negative command to recognize.
- Roadside help in Mexico (2026): Ángeles Verdes 078, CAPUFE 074, emergencies 911.
- Tell a trip with the preterite for events and the imperfect for the scene.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: I wonder where she is: the future of probability
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 13 you learned the future tense for things that *will* happen. You also read that in conversations recorded in Mexico City, most simple futures were not about the future at all. This honors lesson explains what they were doing: guessing about the present. *¿Dónde estará Ana?* doesn't mean "Where will Ana be?" but "Where can Ana be? I wonder where Ana is." This use is called the **[[future of probability]]**, and once you know it you'll hear it everywhere: *¿Qué hora será?*, *Tendrá unos treinta años*, *¿Será?* You'll also learn other ways to guess and to say how sure you are. The forms are the ones from lesson 13; only the meaning is new.

## The future for guesses about now

When you're sure, use the present. When you're guessing about the present, Spanish can use the future:

| Sure (present) | A guess (future) | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Son las tres.* | *Serán las tres.* | It's three. / It must be about three. |
| *Ana está en el tráfico.* | *Ana estará en el tráfico.* | Ana is stuck in traffic. / Ana is probably stuck in traffic. |
| *Tiene treinta años.* | *Tendrá unos treinta años.* | He's thirty. / He must be about thirty. |
| *Hay cien personas.* | *Habrá unas cien personas.* | There are a hundred people. / There must be about a hundred people. |

In questions, the future turns a plain question into wondering aloud, often to yourself:

- *¿Qué hora será?* — I wonder what time it is.
- *¿Quién será?* — Who can that be? (someone knocks at the door)
- *¿Dónde estarán mis llaves?* — Where can my keys be?
- *¿Será verdad?* — I wonder if it's true. Could it be true?

On its own, *¿Será?* is a common skeptical reaction, a bit like "Really? I'm not so sure": *—Dicen que mañana no habrá clases. —Mmm… ¿será?*

### Example 1: From fact to guess

Change each sentence into a guess with the future. Keep the person; only the verb changes.

1. *El jefe está en una junta.* → *El jefe estará en una junta.* (The boss is probably in a meeting.)
2. *Tienen hambre.* → *Tendrán hambre.* (They must be hungry.)
3. *Sabe la respuesta.* → *Sabrá la respuesta.* (She probably knows the answer.)
4. *Es el cartero.* → *Será el cartero.* (It must be the mail carrier.)
5. *Hace frío en Toluca.* → *Hará frío en Toluca.* (It's probably cold in Toluca.)

The irregular stems are the same as always: *tendr-, sabr-, har-* (lesson 13).

## Future or guess? Let the context decide

The same form can point to the future or to a guess about now. Time words and the situation make it clear:

- *Mañana Ana estará en Puebla.* — Tomorrow Ana will be in Puebla. (future: *mañana*)
- *Ana no contesta. Estará en el metro.* — Ana isn't answering. She's probably on the metro. (now: she isn't answering now)

A good test: if you can add *ahora* or *ahorita* without changing the meaning, it's a guess about the present.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Present, future or future of probability
  accDescr: Ask whether you are talking about now or later. If later, the future means will: Mañana estará en Puebla. If now, ask whether you are sure. If you are sure, use the present: Está en el metro. If you are guessing, use the future of probability, Estará en el metro, or another guessing phrase such as Debe de estar en el metro or A lo mejor está en el metro.
  A{"Now or later?"} -- "later" --> B["future = will: Mañana estará en Puebla."]
  A -- "now" --> C{"Are you sure?"}
  C -- "yes" --> D["present: Está en el metro."]
  C -- "no, it's a guess" --> E["future of probability: Estará en el metro."]
  C -- "no, it's a guess" --> F["other phrases: Debe de estar… A lo mejor está…"]
```

### Example 2: Fact or guess?

Mónica and Raúl are waiting for their friend Pepe outside a cinema. Decide which sentences are facts and which are guesses.

> Mónica: Ya son las siete y diez y Pepe no llega.
>
> Raúl: Estará estacionándose. Siempre tarda mucho en encontrar lugar.
>
> Mónica: ¿Y si se le olvidó? Le mandé un mensaje y no contesta.
>
> Raúl: Tendrá el celular apagado. Mañana tiene examen; a lo mejor está estudiando.
>
> Mónica: Mmm… o estará dormido.

- *Ya son las siete y diez* — a fact (present: Mónica can see the time).
- *Estará estacionándose* — a guess (He's probably parking). Notice that *estar* + gerund (lesson 9) works in the future too.
- *Le mandé un mensaje y no contesta* — facts.
- *Tendrá el celular apagado* — a guess. *Mañana tiene examen* — a fact (a fixed arrangement, in the present). *A lo mejor está estudiando* — a guess with *a lo mejor* + present.
- *Estará dormido* — a guess.

(*se le olvidó* — he forgot, a form you can study in honors lesson 8h2; *el lugar* — here, a parking space.)

## Other ways to guess

The future of probability is common, but it isn't the only way. Here are the main alternatives, from most to least sure:

![A horizontal scale from completely sure on the left to no idea on the right. Left end: Está en casa (present) and Seguro que está en casa. Next: Debe de estar en casa, Estará en casa (future of probability), Seguramente está en casa. Next: Supongo que está en casa, Probablemente está en casa. Next: A lo mejor está en casa, Quizás está en casa. Right end: No sé dónde está.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Pattern | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *deber de* + infinitive | *Debe de estar en casa.* — She must be at home. | a confident guess |
| future of probability | *Estará en casa.* | a confident guess |
| *seguramente / probablemente* + present | *Seguramente está en casa.* | lesson 13's words, now with the present |
| *supongo que / me imagino que* + present | *Supongo que está en casa.* — I suppose she's at home. | *suponer* (like *poner*: *supongo*) |
| *a lo mejor* + present | *A lo mejor está en casa.* — Maybe she's at home. | very common in conversation |
| *quizás / tal vez* + present | *Quizás está en casa.* | lesson 13 |

A note on *deber* and *deber de*. Traditional grammar, including the Spanish Academy's guides, keeps them apart: *deber* + infinitive for obligation (*Debes estudiar* — You must / should study) and *deber de* + infinitive for a guess (*Debe de tener frío* — He must be cold). In everyday speech many people use *deber* without *de* for guesses as well (*Debe tener frío*), and that is generally accepted; what careful speakers avoid is *deber de* for obligation (~~Debes de estudiar~~ in formal writing). If you use *deber de* only for guesses, you'll always be right.

As short answers, use *Es posible* (It's possible) and *Es probable* (It's likely): *—¿Vendrá Luis? —Es probable.* And to say you're wondering, *preguntarse*: *Me pregunto dónde estará* (I wonder where she is).

*A lo mejor* takes the present indicative: *A lo mejor viene* (maybe he's coming). It sounds informal and very natural in Mexico.

## How common is it?

In the study of Mexico City speech mentioned in lesson 13 (Lastra and Martín Butragueño, 2008), the researchers found 243 simple futures; they classed about 150 of them, roughly six in ten, as modal: expressing doubts, guesses and estimates, like the examples in this lesson, rather than plain future time. So when you hear a simple future in a Mexican conversation, there's a good chance it's a guess. In writing, the news and formal speech, the future for "will" is more common.

## A mini mystery: ¿Quién se comió el pastel?

Read this short story. The guesses use the future, *deber de* and *a lo mejor*.

> Es domingo por la tarde. En la cocina de la familia Herrera hay un misterio: el pastel de chocolate de la abuela ya no está en el refrigerador.
>
> —¿Dónde estará el pastel? —pregunta papá.
>
> Mamá busca pistas. En la mesa hay una cuchara con chocolate y, en el suelo, unas migas que van hacia el patio.
>
> —Será el perro —dice Luisito—. A lo mejor tiene hambre.
>
> —El perro no usa cuchara —contesta mamá—. Sospecho de alguien más alto.
>
> En el patio, la tía Carmen está sentada en una banca con un plato vacío. Tiene chocolate en la cara.
>
> —Tía, ¿tú sabrás algo del pastel? —pregunta Luisito, sonriendo.
>
> —¿Yo? Ni idea… Debe de estar en el refrigerador, ¿no?
>
> Todos se ríen. El misterio está resuelto.

*It's Sunday afternoon. In the Herrera family's kitchen there's a mystery: Grandma's chocolate cake isn't in the fridge any more. — "Where can the cake be?" asks Dad. — Mom looks for clues. On the table there's a spoon with chocolate on it and, on the floor, some crumbs leading to the patio. — "It must be the dog," says Luisito. "Maybe he's hungry." — "The dog doesn't use a spoon," Mom answers. "I suspect someone taller." — In the patio, Aunt Carmen is sitting on a bench with an empty plate. She has chocolate on her face. — "Auntie, would you happen to know anything about the cake?" asks Luisito, smiling. — "Me? No idea… It must be in the fridge, right?" — Everyone laughs. The mystery is solved.*

(*la miga* — crumb; *ni idea* — no idea; *resuelto* — solved; *la banca* — bench, lesson 9.)

### Example 3: Solving the mystery with guesses

Answer each question with a guess, as a detective would. Several answers are possible; here are good ones.

1. *¿Quién tendrá el pastel?* → *Lo tendrá la tía Carmen.* / *Debe de tenerlo la tía Carmen.*
2. *¿Por qué hay migas en el suelo?* → *A lo mejor la tía comió en el camino al patio.* (A guess about the past: at A2, *a lo mejor* + preterite.)
3. *¿Qué piensa la tía?* → *Pensará que nadie la vio.* (She probably thinks nobody saw her.)
4. *¿Cómo se siente ahora?* → *Estará un poco avergonzada.* (She's probably a bit embarrassed; *avergonzado* — embarrassed.)

## Guessing about the past: a preview

To guess about the past, Spanish uses two other forms: the conditional (*Serían las diez* — It was probably about ten), whose forms you'll learn in lesson 19 but whose guessing use is B1, and the future perfect (*¿Qué habrá pasado?* — I wonder what has happened), also B1. For now, recognize them, and at A2 use *a lo mejor* or *probablemente* + preterite: *A lo mejor se quedó dormido* — Maybe he overslept.

## Pronunciation

- *¿Será?* rises at the end, with a slight drawl when it's skeptical: se-RÁ↗.
- *¿Qué hora será?* sounds like one breath: ke-O-ra-se-RÁ. The *h* is silent.
- In *debe de estar*, the two *e*s often run together in fast speech: DE-be-des-TAR.

## Common mistakes

- Translating every future as "will": *¿Dónde estará?* is "Where can she be?", not "Where will she be?" (unless a future time word says so).
- Using the future of probability when you know the fact: if you can see the clock, say *Son las tres*, not *Serán las tres*.
- *deber de* for obligation in careful Spanish: ~~Debes de pagar la renta~~ → *Debes pagar la renta*.
- *a lo mejor* with the future of probability: ~~A lo mejor estará en casa~~ is heard, but the two guesses overlap; say *A lo mejor está en casa* or *Estará en casa*.

## Key points

- The future can guess about the present: *Serán las tres*, *Tendrá treinta años*, *¿Dónde estará?* (I wonder where she is).
- *¿Será?* = Could it be? Really?
- Other ways to guess: *deber de* + infinitive, *seguramente / probablemente* + present, *supongo que* + present, *a lo mejor / quizás* + present.
- *deber* (obligation) vs *deber de* (guess); many people use *deber* for both.
- In Mexican conversation, many simple futures are guesses, not plans.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Looking for work: job ads, interviews and impersonal se
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Spanish A1 you said what you do (*Soy enfermera*). This module moves into work, studies
and services: a job, school, the bank, the doctor's. This first lesson is about finding work:
reading a job ad, talking about your experience and getting through an interview.

The new grammar is a small word you have used since A1 without thinking about it: the *se* in
*¿Cómo se dice…?* (How do you say…?). Here it becomes a tool. With the **[[impersonal se]]** you
can say what people in general do, or what a sign offers, without saying who does it: *Se
busca mesero* (Waiter wanted), *Aquí se come muy bien* (You eat very well here). You also put
module 1's past tenses to work, because an interview is mostly about your past.

## Jobs and the people who do them

You know *el maestro, el doctor, el ingeniero, el mesero, el vendedor, el policía* and *el
cocinero* from A1. Here are more, with their feminine forms. As in A1, no article after
*ser* unless you add an adjective: *Soy contadora*, but *Es una contadora excelente*.

| Masculine | Feminine | English |
|---|---|---|
| *el empleado* | *la empleada* | employee |
| *el abogado* | *la abogada* | lawyer |
| *el contador* | *la contadora* | accountant (Spain: *el contable*) |
| *el enfermero* | *la enfermera* | nurse |
| *el mecánico* | *la mecánica* | mechanic |
| *el programador* | *la programadora* | programmer |
| *el compañero de trabajo* | *la compañera de trabajo* | coworker |

Mostly *-o* becomes *-a*, and a consonant adds *-a* (*contador → contadora*); some words in
*-ista* or *-e* have one form (*el / la dentista*). People work in *la empresa* (a company),
*la fábrica* (a factory) or their own *negocio* (a business). Without a job, you are
*desempleado*. *El empleo* (employment, a job) is the word of ads and official texts; in
conversation most people say *el trabajo*.

## The impersonal se

English often uses "you", "people", "they" or a passive ("is spoken") when nobody in
particular does something. Spanish uses *se* + a verb in the third person.

### Se + verb on its own: what people do

- *Aquí se come muy bien.* — You eat very well here. / The food is very good here.
- *En esta oficina se trabaja de nueve a seis.* — In this office people work from nine to six.
- *¿Por dónde se entra?* — Which way do you go in?
- *No se puede fumar aquí.* — You can't smoke here.

The verb is always singular here, because there is no noun for it to agree with. This is the
*se* of the A1 chunks: *¿Cómo se dice "job" en español?* is literally "How is 'job' said in
Spanish?", and *¿Cómo se escribe?* is "How is it written?"

### Se + verb + noun: signs and ads

When the sentence has a thing (or a group of people) after the verb, the verb agrees with it:
singular for one, plural for more than one.

| One | More than one |
|---|---|
| *Se vende casa.* (House for sale.) | *Se venden casas.* |
| *Se renta departamento.* (Apartment for rent, Mexico) | *Se rentan departamentos.* |
| *Se busca mesero.* (Waiter wanted.) | *Se buscan meseros.* |
| *Se necesita programador.* | *Se necesitan programadores.* |
| *Se solicita personal.* (Staff wanted.) | *Se solicitan empleados.* |
| *Se habla inglés.* (English spoken.) | *Se hablan varios idiomas.* |

Grammars call this agreeing kind the "passive *se*" (*Se venden casas* = Houses are sold).
This course calls both kinds the impersonal se: look at the noun after the verb, and make
the verb plural if the noun is plural.
