![Four signs. SE SOLICITA PERSONAL, with the lines Turno de la tarde and Informes aquí. SE RENTA DEPARTAMENTO, with a phone number. AQUÍ SE HABLA INGLÉS, Escuela de idiomas. SE VENDEN TAMALES, Hoy: 20 pesos cada uno.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Se solicita* (*solicitar* = to request, to apply for) and *Se busca* are typical of Mexican
job signs. With a plural noun you'll sometimes see a singular verb (*Se solicita meseros*),
especially on handwritten signs, but the plural (*Se solicitan meseros*) is the standard form to
write: the Real Academia's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* advises making the verb agree with
a plural noun of things, or of people when there is no *a* before them.

### Se in questions

The same pattern asks how things are done:

- *¿Dónde se compran los boletos?* — Where do you buy the tickets?
- *¿Cómo se llena esta solicitud?* — How do you fill in this application form?
- *¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta?* — Can you pay by card?

With *se puede* + infinitive, *puede* stays singular: *¿Se puede entrar?* (Can we come in?)

## Reading a job ad

Job ads usually say who is wanted, the requirements (*los requisitos*), what is offered and
how to apply. This ad is invented.

![An invented job ad from Clínica Santa Fe, a clinic in Puebla. Headline: SE SOLICITA ENFERMERO O ENFERMERA. Requisitos: licenciatura en Enfermería, dos años de experiencia, disponibilidad para turno de noche. Ofrecemos: empleo de tiempo completo, sueldo de 14,000 pesos al mes, prestaciones de ley, capacitación. Interesados: enviar currículum a empleo.clinica@correo.mx o presentarse de lunes a viernes de 9 a 14 h.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Words to notice:

- *de tiempo completo* (full-time), *de medio tiempo* (part-time).
- *el turno* (shift): *el turno de la mañana, de la tarde, de noche*.
- *el sueldo* (salary, pay), also *el salario*.
- *prestaciones de ley*: the benefits the law requires (honors lesson 20h1).
- *Interesados* (those interested): the masculine plural covers men and women.
- *licenciatura en Enfermería* = a nursing degree (lesson 18); *la disponibilidad* =
  availability; *la capacitación* = training at work.

To apply, send *el currículum* (also *el CV*; plural *los currículums*) or fill in *una
solicitud* (an application form): *Solicité el puesto* (I applied for the job). *El puesto*, a
market stall in A1, also means "position, job".

### Work in Mexico in 2026: three facts

- The general minimum wage for 2026 is 315.04 pesos a day (440.87 pesos in the northern
  border zone), in force since 1 January 2026.
- The legal working week is 48 hours in 2026. A constitutional reform published on 3 March
  2026 lowers it by two hours each January, from 46 hours in 2027 to 40 hours in 2030.
- An employer must register each worker with the IMSS (*Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social*,
  the public social security and health system) within five working days of hiring them.

These numbers change: check them when you need them.

## In the interview

An interview mixes the tenses you already know:

| You want to say | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| your job now, how long | present + *desde hace* / *hace … que* | *Trabajo en una empresa de software desde hace tres años.* |
| experience up to now | perfect | *He trabajado tres años como programador.* |
| a finished job | preterite | *Trabajé dos años en una fábrica.* |
| what it was like | imperfect | *Era un trabajo interesante, pero el sueldo era bajo.* |
| what you must do | *tener que, hay que* | *En este puesto hay que viajar mucho.* |

Typical questions (with *usted*): *¿Dónde trabaja actualmente?* (Where do you work at the
moment? *actualmente* = currently, lesson 04), *¿Qué experiencia tiene?*, *¿Por qué quiere
trabajar aquí?*, *¿Por qué dejó su último empleo?*

Three verbs are about getting and leaving a job:

- *contratar* = to hire: *La empresa contrató a cinco personas* (with the personal *a* before
  people).
- *despedir* = to fire: *Lo despidieron en marzo* (They fired him in March). It changes like
  *pedir*: *despido, despidió, despidieron, despidiendo*. Don't confuse it with *despedirse*
  (lesson 08), "to say goodbye".
- *renunciar* = to resign, to quit: *Renuncié en mayo*; with a noun, *renunciar a*: *Renunció a
  su trabajo*.

At work, a meeting is usually *una junta* in Mexico: *Tengo una junta a las once*. *La
reunión* (A1) is the general word and is understood everywhere.

## Dialogue: an interview in Guadalajara

Andrés Díaz has an interview for a job at a software company. The interviewer is Licenciada
Ortega, from human resources (*recursos humanos*).

> Lic. Ortega: Buenos días, señor Díaz. Siéntese, por favor. Leí su currículum con mucho interés.
>
> Andrés: Buenos días, licenciada. Muchas gracias por la entrevista.
>
> Lic. Ortega: Para empezar, ¿dónde trabaja actualmente?
>
> Andrés: Soy programador en una empresa pequeña aquí en Guadalajara. He trabajado allí tres años.
>
> Lic. Ortega: ¿Y antes?
>
> Andrés: Antes trabajé dos años de medio tiempo en una fábrica de muebles, en el turno de la tarde. En las mañanas estudiaba la carrera.
>
> Lic. Ortega: Muy bien. El puesto es de tiempo completo. Hay que venir a la oficina tres días por semana; los otros dos se trabaja desde casa.
>
> Andrés: Perfecto. ¿Hay muchas juntas?
>
> Lic. Ortega: Una a la semana, los lunes. ¿Por qué quiere dejar su empleo actual?
>
> Andrés: Me gusta mucho, pero la empresa es muy pequeña y quiero aprender más.
>
> Lic. Ortega: Entiendo. El último requisito es un examen de inglés. Le vamos a mandar la información por correo esta semana.
>
> Andrés: Muchas gracias. Quedo atento.

Translation:

> Lic. Ortega: Good morning, Mr. Díaz. Have a seat, please. I read your CV with great interest.
>
> Andrés: Good morning. Thank you very much for the interview.
>
> Lic. Ortega: To start with, where do you work at the moment?
>
> Andrés: I'm a programmer at a small company here in Guadalajara. I've worked there for three years.
>
> Lic. Ortega: And before that?
>
> Andrés: Before that I worked part-time for two years in a furniture factory, on the afternoon shift. In the mornings I was studying for my degree.
>
> Lic. Ortega: Very good. The position is full-time. You have to come into the office three days a week; on the other two, people work from home.
>
> Andrés: Perfect. Are there a lot of meetings?
>
> Lic. Ortega: One a week, on Mondays. Why do you want to leave your current job?
>
> Andrés: I like it a lot, but the company is very small and I want to learn more.
>
> Lic. Ortega: I understand. The last requirement is an English test. We'll send you the information by e-mail this week.
>
> Andrés: Thank you very much. I'll look out for it.

Notes: *Lic.* (*licenciada*) is the title for a graduate (A1 honors 04h2). *He trabajado allí
tres años* is experience up to now; *trabajé dos años*, a finished job; *estudiaba*, the
background. *Quedo atento* (from *Quedo atento a su respuesta*, A1) closes politely.

## Pronunciation

- *Currículum* is *ku-RRI-ku-lum*, with a trilled *rr*; *fábrica* and *mecánico* are
  *FA-bri-ka, me-KA-ni-ko*.
- *Empleo* has three syllables, *em-PLE-o*: *e* and *o* don't join. *Requisito* is
  *re-ki-SI-to*: the *u* after *q* is silent.
- *Junta* begins with the Spanish *j* (like a strong English *h*): *HOON-ta*.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the plural: ~~*Se vende casas*~~ → *Se venden casas*. The verb agrees with the
  noun after it.
- Adding a subject: ~~*Ellos se habla inglés*~~ → *Se habla inglés*. The point of *se* is that
  nobody is named.
- *Aplicar* for "apply": *aplicar a un trabajo* (from English "apply") is common in Mexico, and
  the DLE now lists it as a Latin American use, but many people still find it too informal or
  too English for a formal letter. *Solicitar un trabajo* is the safe choice in writing.
- *Renunciar* without *a* before a noun: ~~*Renuncié mi trabajo*~~ → *Renuncié a mi trabajo*.
  Alone it needs nothing: *Renuncié*.
- *Despedir* and *despedirse*: *Me despidieron* = I was fired; *Me despedí* = I said goodbye.

## Key points

- Impersonal *se* + third person: *Aquí se come bien* (people in general), *¿Cómo se dice…?*
- With a noun after the verb, agree with it: *Se vende casa / Se venden casas; Se busca
  mesero / Se buscan meseros*.
- Job ads: *Se solicita…, requisitos, de tiempo completo / de medio tiempo, el turno, el sueldo,
  enviar currículum*.
- Interview tenses: present for now, perfect for experience up to now, preterite for a
  finished job, imperfect for what it was like.
- *contratar* (hire), *despedir* (fire: *despidió*), *renunciar (a)* (quit); *la junta* =
  meeting at work in Mexico.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: School and university: describing with que, donde and lo que
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 was about work; this one is about studying: the Mexican school system, subjects
and grades, and learning a language. The grammar lets you build longer, more natural
sentences. Instead of two short ones (*Tengo una profesora. La profesora es de Oaxaca.*) you
join them: *Tengo una profesora que es de Oaxaca.* The joined part, *que es de Oaxaca*, is a
**[[relative clause]]**: a clause that describes a noun, as "who is from Oaxaca" does in English.

You'll use four words to make them: *que*, *donde*, *quien* and *lo que*. In lesson 02 you
met *la primaria* and *la secundaria*; here the ladder goes all the way up.

## The Mexican education ladder

![A ladder of the Mexican education system from bottom to top: preescolar (ages 3 to 5), primaria (six years, about 6 to 12), secundaria (three years, about 12 to 15), preparatoria or bachillerato (usually three years, about 15 to 18), licenciatura (usually four or five years) and maestría (usually two years). A bracket marks preescolar, primaria and secundaria as educación básica, and an arrow says más años de estudio.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Level | Usual length | English |
|---|---|---|
| *la primaria* (lesson 02) | 6 years, about ages 6–12 | primary / elementary school |
| *la secundaria* (lesson 02) | 3 years, about 12–15 | lower secondary, middle school |
| *la preparatoria* (*la prepa*) | usually 3 years, about 15–18 | high school; also called *el bachillerato* |
| *la licenciatura* | usually 4–5 years | bachelor's degree |
| *la maestría* | usually 2 years | master's degree |

- Mexico's constitution (article 3) makes basic education (which includes *preescolar,
  primaria* and *secundaria*) and upper secondary (*la prepa*) compulsory, and says the state
  must provide higher education on the terms the article sets.
- *La carrera* (lesson 01) is the degree course you study at university: *Estudio la carrera de
  Derecho* (I'm studying law). The degree itself is *la licenciatura*, and a graduate is *un
  licenciado / una licenciada* (*Lic.*, A1 honors 04h2).
- *La UNAM* (*Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México*) in Mexico City is the country's best-known
  public university. The law that created it as the *Universidad Nacional de México* was
  issued on 26 May 1910, it opened that September, and it became autonomous in 1929.

Lengths vary: some *prepas* last two years, and medicine takes longer than most degrees.

## Subjects and grades

*La materia* is a school subject (Spain: *la asignatura*): *las matemáticas* (usually plural:
*Las matemáticas son difíciles*), *la química, la geografía, la ciencia* (often *Ciencias* as a
school subject), *el arte* (usually masculine in the singular, feminine in the plural: *las
bellas artes*). The school year in prepa and university is often divided into *semestres*.

Mexican grades (*las calificaciones*) usually go up to 10. You *sacas* a grade (*sacar*, lesson
19: to get, to take out): *Saqué 9 en química* (I got a 9 in chemistry). In *secundaria*, the
rules the SEP (the federal education ministry) published in September 2023 grade from 5 to
10, and 6 is the lowest pass. Universities set their own rules, and some ask for 7.

- *aprobar* (A1) = to pass; *reprobar* (*repruebo*) = to fail: *Reprobé geografía*. Spain says
  *suspender*.
- *una beca* = a scholarship: *Tengo una beca del 50 %.*
- *inscribirse en* = to enroll in, sign up for: *Me inscribí en un curso de inglés*.
- *el profesor / la profesora* is usual in *secundaria*, *prepa* and university; *el maestro / la
  maestra* (A1) is the everyday word in *primaria*, though both are heard everywhere. *El alumno
  / la alumna* = pupil, student; *el director / la directora* = the principal.

Ways to study: *repasar* (to review, go over), *memorizar* (*memoricé*), *tomar apuntes* (to
take notes), *buscar en el diccionario*, *tener una duda* (to have a question about something
you don't understand: *¿Alguien tiene dudas?*), *subir de nivel* (to go up a level).

## Relative clauses with que

*Que* joins a clause to a noun. It works for people and for things, and it can be the subject
or the object of the new clause:

- *La maestra que me enseñó a leer se jubiló.* — The teacher who taught me to read retired.
- *Es una materia que me encanta.* — It's a subject (that) I love.
- *El libro que leí para la clase era muy largo.* — The book (that) I read for the class was
  very long.
- *Tengo un compañero que habla cuatro idiomas.* — I have a classmate who speaks four
  languages.

The noun the clause describes (*la maestra, el libro*) is the **[[antecedent]]**. Two things are
different from English:

1. Spanish never drops *que*. English says "the book I read"; Spanish must say *el libro
   que leí*.
2. Use *que* for people too, not *quien*, when nothing comes before it: *la profesora que
   tengo*, not ~~*la profesora quien tengo*~~.

*Que* here has no accent. *¿Qué?* with an accent is the question word.

## Donde for places

*Donde* (no accent) describes a place: "where".

- *Es la escuela donde estudié la primaria.* — It's the school where I went to primary
  school.
- *Hay una biblioteca donde puedes estudiar en silencio.* — There's a library where you can
  study in silence.
- *Puebla es la ciudad donde conocí a mi esposa.* — Puebla is the city where I met my wife.

*¿Dónde?* (accent) is the question word: *¿Dónde estudias?*

## Quien after a preposition

After a preposition (*con, de, para, a*), use *quien* for one person and *quienes* for more:

- *La amiga con quien estudio vive cerca.* — The friend I study with lives nearby.
- *Los alumnos para quienes es la beca…* — The students the scholarship is for…
- *Es el profesor de quien te hablé.* — He's the teacher I told you about.

English puts the preposition at the end ("the friend I study *with*"); Spanish puts it
first, before *quien*. You'll also hear and read *el que, la que, los que, las que* after a
preposition, for people and things: *la casa en la que vivo* (the house I live in), *la
profesora con la que hice mi tesis*. Recognize them now; *que* and *quien* are enough to speak.

## Lo que: "what", "the thing that"

*Lo que* means "what" when it isn't a question, "the thing(s) that":

- *No entiendo lo que dices.* — I don't understand what you're saying.
- *Lo que más me gusta es la química.* — What I like most is chemistry.
- *Eso es lo que dijo la directora.* — That's what the principal said.
- *Repasa todo lo que vimos en clase.* — Review everything we saw in class.

English speakers often write ~~*Eso es qué dijo*~~: in a statement like this, "what" is *lo
que*. (*¿Qué dijo?*, with the accent, is the question.)

This chart sums up the choice:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which relative word?
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question: does the clause describe a place? If yes, use donde, for example la escuela donde estudié. If no, is there a noun before it? If there is no noun and you mean "the thing that" or "what", use lo que, for example No entiendo lo que dices. If there is a noun, is there a preposition such as con, de or para before the relative word and is the noun a person? If yes, use quien or quienes, for example la amiga con quien estudio, or el que or la que. Otherwise use que, for people and things, for example el libro que leí or la maestra que me enseñó.
  A["Does it describe a place?"] -- yes --> D["donde: la escuela donde estudié"]
  A -- no --> B["Is there a noun before it?"]
  B -- "no: 'what, the thing that'" --> L["lo que: No entiendo lo que dices."]
  B -- yes --> C["A person after con, de, para...?"]
  C -- yes --> Q["quien / quienes: la amiga con quien estudio (or con la que)"]
  C -- no --> R["que: el libro que leí, la maestra que me enseñó"]
```

## A text: learning Spanish at the university

Megan, from Ohio, writes in a forum for students who are learning Spanish in Mexico.

> Hola a todos. Soy Megan y estoy en Puebla con una beca de la universidad donde estudio en Estados Unidos.
>
> Me inscribí en un curso de español de nivel A2. La profesora que nos da la clase se llama Rocío y es muy paciente: nunca se enoja cuando cometemos errores.
>
> Este semestre tengo cuatro materias: español, historia de México, arte y una de geografía que es en inglés.
>
> Lo que más me cuesta es entender a la gente cuando habla rápido. Lo que más me gusta es practicar con mi compañera de cuarto, con quien platico todas las noches.
>
> Mi consejo: tomen apuntes en español, repasen los apuntes cada día y practiquen con frases completas, no solo con listas de palabras. Si tienen una duda, pregúntenle a la profesora.
>
> Ah, y el primer examen salió bien: ¡saqué 9! Una compañera reprobó, pero la profesora le va a dar otra oportunidad.

Translation:

> Hi, everyone. I'm Megan and I'm in Puebla on a scholarship from the university where I study in the United States.
>
> I signed up for a level A2 Spanish course. The teacher who gives us the class is called Rocío and she's very patient: she never gets angry when we make mistakes.
>
> This semester I have four subjects: Spanish, Mexican history, art and a geography one that's in English.
>
> What I find hardest is understanding people when they speak fast. What I like most is practicing with my roommate, who I chat with every night.
>
> My advice: take notes in Spanish, go over your notes every day and practice with whole sentences, not just lists of words. If you have a question, ask the teacher.
>
> Oh, and the first exam went well: I got a 9! A classmate failed, but the teacher is going to give her another chance.

Notes: *cometer errores* = to make mistakes; *me cuesta* (from *costar*) = I find it hard;
*la compañera de cuarto* = roommate; *salir bien* = to go well; *el error* = mistake (lesson
24). *Tomen, repasen, practiquen, pregúntenle* are *ustedes* commands (lesson 16). *El
consejo* (advice) is lesson 20's word.

## Pronunciation

- *Química* is *KI-mi-ka*: *qu* = k. *Matemáticas* is *ma-te-MA-ti-kas*, and *geografía* has
  five syllables, *he-o-gra-FI-a*, with *g* before *e* like a strong English *h*.
- With seseo, *licenciatura* is *li-sen-sia-TU-ra* and *calificación* is
  *ka-li-fi-ka-SION*.
- *Que* and *donde* in relative clauses are unstressed and run into the next word: *la
  escuela donde-estudié*. The question words *qué, dónde* are stressed.

## Common mistakes

- Dropping *que*: ~~*El libro leí es largo*~~ → *El libro que leí es largo*.
- *Quien* with no preposition: ~~*la maestra quien me enseñó*~~ → *la maestra que me enseñó*.
  (After a comma, in careful writing, *quien* is possible: you'll meet it in texts.)
- Ending with the preposition: ~~*la amiga quien estudio con*~~ → *la amiga con quien
  estudio*.
- *Qué* at the start of a statement: ~~*Qué más me gusta es…*~~ → *Lo que más me gusta es…*
  (After *no sé* or *no entiendo*, both are fine: *No sé qué quiere / No sé lo que quiere*.)
- Accents: relative *que, donde* have none; question words *qué, dónde* do.
- *Colegio* in Mexico is a school (often a private one), not a college; "college" is *la
  universidad*.

## Key points

- A relative clause describes a noun (the antecedent): *la maestra que me enseñó*.
- *que* for people and things; never dropped.
- *donde* for places: *la escuela donde estudié*.
- After a preposition, *quien / quienes* for people: *la amiga con quien estudio* (also *con
  la que*).
- *lo que* = what, the thing that: *No entiendo lo que dices; Lo que más me gusta es…*
- School: *primaria, secundaria, prepa, licenciatura, maestría*; grades out of 10: *Saqué 9*;
  *aprobar / reprobar*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Could you…? Polite requests at the bank, the post office and the repair shop: the conditional
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 13 you learned the future: *Te llamaré* (I'll call you). This lesson adds its close
relative, the **[[conditional]]**: *¿Me llamaría mañana?* (Would you call me tomorrow?). It's the
"would" form of Spanish, and at A2 you use it above all to be polite: to ask for things, to
say what you'd like and to complain without sounding rude. That makes it the verb form of
banks, post offices, repair people and customer service, which are this lesson's theme.

Good news first: if you know the future, you already know the hard part. The conditional
uses the same stems, including the twelve irregular ones. Completing this lesson also adds
the conditional to your verb drills.

## How the conditional is built

Take the whole infinitive and add one set of endings, the same for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.

| | hablar | comer | vivir |
|---|---|---|---|
| yo | hablaría | comería | viviría |
| tú | hablarías | comerías | vivirías |
| él, ella, usted | hablaría | comería | viviría |
| nosotros | hablaríamos | comeríamos | viviríamos |
| (vosotros) | (hablaríais) | (comeríais) | (viviríais) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | hablarían | comerían | vivirían |

![A chart: the infinitive hablar, comer or vivir, a plus sign, and the endings -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían. Below, a second row shows the same endings added to irregular stems: podr-, tendr-, har-, dir-, querr-, sabr-, saldr-, pondr-, vendr-. A note says every form has an accent on the í, and yo and él are the same form.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Three things to notice:

1. Every form has a written accent on the *í*: *hablaría, comeríamos*.
2. The endings are the imperfect endings of *comer* (*comía, comías…*, lesson 02), but added to
   the whole infinitive: *comía* (I used to eat) vs *comería* (I would eat).
3. *yo* and *él / ella / usted* have the same form (*hablaría*), as in the imperfect. Add the
   pronoun if it isn't clear who: *Yo hablaría con el gerente* (I'd speak to the manager).

### The irregular stems: the same as the future

| Infinitive | Stem | Conditional | Future (lesson 13) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *poder* | podr- | *podría* | *podré* |
| *tener* | tendr- | *tendría* | *tendré* |
| *hacer* | har- | *haría* | *haré* |
| *decir* | dir- | *diría* | *diré* |
| *querer* | querr- | *querría* | *querré* |
| *saber* | sabr- | *sabría* | *sabré* |
| *salir* | saldr- | *saldría* | *saldré* |
| *poner* | pondr- | *pondría* | *pondré* |
| *venir* | vendr- | *vendría* | *vendré* |
| *haber* | habr- | *habría* (there would be) | *habrá* |

*Caber* (*cabría*) and *valer* (*valdría*) follow the same pattern, and so do compounds:
*proponer → propondría* (lesson 15), *mantener → mantendría*. Every other verb is regular,
including stem-changers: *dormiría, pediría, volvería*.

## Polite requests

Spanish has several levels of politeness for the same request. The further down this ladder,
the softer and more formal it sounds.

![A ladder with five steps, from direct at the top to most polite at the bottom: Dame el recibo. ¿Me das el recibo? ¿Me puedes dar el recibo? ¿Me podrías dar el recibo? ¿Me podría dar el recibo, por favor? (usted). An arrow beside it says más directo at the top and más cortés at the bottom.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- Command (lesson 16): *Dame el recibo.* Fine with family and friends, often with *por
  favor*.
- Present question: *¿Me das…? ¿Me puedes dar…?* Everyday and friendly.
- Conditional question: *¿Me podrías dar…?* (tú) / *¿Me podría dar…?* (usted). The normal
  choice with strangers, staff, offices and on the phone.

The phrases you'll use most:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *¿Podría ayudarme? / ¿Me podría ayudar?* | Could you help me? |
| *¿Le importaría esperar un momento?* | Would you mind waiting a moment? |
| *¿Sería posible cambiar la cita?* | Would it be possible to change the appointment? |
| *Me gustaría abrir una cuenta.* | I'd like to open an account. |
| *Me encantaría.* | I'd love to. |
| *¿Te gustaría venir?* | Would you like to come? |
| *Preferiría pagar en efectivo.* | I'd prefer to pay in cash. |

With *¿Podría…?* the pronoun can go before *podría* or on the end of the infinitive, as with
any helper verb: *¿Me podría ayudar? = ¿Podría ayudarme?*

*¿Le importaría…?* ("Would it bother you to…?") works like *gustar*: *le* (to you, usted) or
*te* (to you, tú) + *importaría* + infinitive. To say "sure, I don't mind", the clearest
answers are *No, para nada* (No, not at all) and *Claro que no* (Of course not): it doesn't
bother you.

*Me gustaría* also follows *gustar*: with a plural thing, *Me gustarían dos boletos*. With an
infinitive it stays singular: *Me gustaría ver los precios*.

### Quería and quisiera

Two more polite forms are very common in shops and offices:

- The imperfect *quería* (literally "I wanted"): *Quería información sobre los préstamos* (I'd
  like some information about loans). The past tense makes the request softer.
- *Quisiera* (A1): *Quisiera depositar este cheque.* It's a form you'll study at B1; for now,
  learn it as a set phrase meaning "I would like".

*Querría* exists, but in Mexico you'll usually hear *quisiera* or *me gustaría* instead.

## At the bank and the post office

![A counter scene in two halves, labeled in Spanish. BANCO: el cajero automático (an ATM) and la fila (a line of three people waiting). OFICINA DE CORREOS: la ventanilla (a service window with a clerk, number 2), el paquete (a package on the counter), el sobre (an envelope) and el timbre (the stamp in its corner).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At the bank (*el banco*, A1):

- *el cajero automático* (often just *el cajero*) = ATM: *sacar dinero* (to withdraw money;
  *saqué*), *depositar* (to deposit), *consultar el saldo* (to check your balance).
- *transferir* (*transfiero, transfirió*) = to transfer; *una transferencia*. In Mexico, a
  transfer between banks usually goes to the account's *CLABE*, an 18-digit number.
- *el préstamo* = loan; *la comisión* = fee; *cobrar* = to charge: *¿Cobran comisión?* (Do you
  charge a fee?) *Este cajero me cobró treinta pesos.*
- *hacer fila* = to stand in line: *Hay mucha fila* (There's a long line). Spain: *hacer cola*.

At the post office (*el correo*): *el sobre* (envelope), *el timbre* (postage stamp in
Mexico; *la estampilla* in much of Latin America, *el sello* in Spain), *el paquete* (lesson
06), *la ventanilla* (the service window; in lesson 14, a plane or bus window), *entregar* (to deliver, to hand in;
*entregué*): *¿Cuándo entregan el paquete?*

Paperwork: *un trámite* is any official procedure (getting a passport, opening an
account). Almost every one asks for *una identificación oficial*. For Mexican citizens that
is usually *la INE*, the voter card issued by the *Instituto Nacional Electoral*, which is
valid for ten years from the date it is issued and is accepted as official ID; visitors
generally use their passport.

## Repairs and complaints

When something breaks, you call *el técnico* (technician), *el plomero* (plumber; Spain *el
fontanero*) or *el electricista* (electrician; *la electricista* for a woman). *Arreglar* =
to fix (also *reparar*, more formal): *¿Me podría arreglar la regadera?* *Una fuga* is a leak:
*Hay una fuga de agua en la cocina*.

After the work, ask for *la factura* if you need an official receipt for taxes (in Mexico, a
*factura* is a tax document linked to your tax number); a simple shop receipt is *el ticket*
(A1).

To complain politely (*poner una queja*, to make a complaint), start softly and use the
conditional for what you want:

1. *Disculpe, tengo un problema con…* (Excuse me, I have a problem with…)
2. Explain in the past: *Ayer saqué dinero y el cajero me cobró dos veces.*
3. Ask: *¿Me podría ayudar? / ¿Sería posible…?*
4. If it doesn't work: *Quería poner una queja. ¿Me podría dar el número de atención al
   cliente?*

## Dialogue: a fee that shouldn't be there

Laura goes to her bank in Mérida. She was charged a fee she didn't expect.

> Ejecutivo: Buenas tardes. Siguiente, por favor. ¿En qué le puedo ayudar?
>
> Laura: Buenas tardes. Disculpe, tengo un problema con mi cuenta. El sábado saqué dinero en un cajero de este banco y me cobraron una comisión de treinta pesos.
>
> Ejecutivo: ¿Me podría dar su número de cuenta y una identificación, por favor?
>
> Laura: Sí, aquí tiene mi INE.
>
> Ejecutivo: Gracias. Mmm… Sí, aquí está. Fue un cajero de otro banco, por eso se cobró la comisión.
>
> Laura: Pero el cajero estaba en la sucursal de ustedes, en la calle 60.
>
> Ejecutivo: Ah, entonces es un error. ¿Le importaría esperar unos minutos? Voy a revisarlo con mi supervisora.
>
> Laura: No, para nada. Y otra cosa: me gustaría hacer una transferencia a la cuenta de mi hermana. ¿Sería posible hacerla aquí?
>
> Ejecutivo: Claro. Solo necesito la CLABE de la cuenta de su hermana. Y la comisión se la devolvemos hoy mismo.
>
> Laura: Muchas gracias. Es usted muy amable.

Translation:

> Bank officer: Good afternoon. Next, please. How can I help you?
>
> Laura: Good afternoon. Excuse me, I have a problem with my account. On Saturday I took money out of one of this bank's ATMs and they charged me a thirty-peso fee.
>
> Bank officer: Could you give me your account number and some ID, please?
>
> Laura: Yes, here's my INE card.
>
> Bank officer: Thank you. Hmm… Yes, here it is. It was another bank's ATM; that's why the fee was charged.
>
> Laura: But the ATM was in your branch, on 60th Street.
>
> Bank officer: Ah, then it's an error. Would you mind waiting a few minutes? I'm going to check it with my supervisor.
>
> Laura: No, not at all. And one more thing: I'd like to make a transfer to my sister's account. Would it be possible to do it here?
>
> Bank officer: Of course. I just need the CLABE of your sister's account. And we'll give you back the fee today.
>
> Laura: Thank you very much. You're very kind.

Notes: *el ejecutivo / la ejecutiva* = the bank officer at a desk; *la sucursal* = branch;
*Siguiente* = Next; *¿En qué le puedo ayudar?* = How can I help you? *Se cobró la comisión*
is the impersonal *se* of lesson 17. In *La comisión se la devolvemos*, *se* is *le* (to you)
before *la* (it), lesson 07; the noun comes first for emphasis. Many streets in Mérida have
numbers (*la calle 60*).

## Hypothetical "if" sentences: not yet

English uses "would" in sentences like "If I had money, I would buy a house". Spanish uses the
conditional there too, but the *si* part needs a new form (B1). At A2, use the conditional on
its own, for politeness and wishes. With a real condition, *si* + present + future or present
(lesson 13) still works: *Si tengo tiempo, te ayudo.*

## Pronunciation

- The stress always falls on the *í*: *po-DRÍ-a, gus-ta-RÍ-a, im-por-ta-RÍ-a*. Don't swallow the
  *a* after it: *í-a* is two syllables.
- *Podría* (could, would be able) and *podía* (could, used to be able) differ by one *r*: say
  it clearly, *po-DRI-a* vs *po-DI-a*.
- *Cajero* has the strong Spanish *j*: *ka-HE-ro*. *Plomero* is *plo-ME-ro*; *electricista*
  is *e-lek-tri-SIS-ta*.

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out the accent: ~~*podria, gustaria*~~ → *podría, gustaría*.
- Regular stems for irregular verbs: ~~*podería, hacería, tenería, decería*~~ → *podría,
  haría, tendría, diría*.
- Confusing *podía* (imperfect: I could, used to be able) with *podría* (conditional: I could,
  would be able). *¿Podría ayudarme?* is the polite request.
- *Me gusta* when you mean "I'd like": *Me gusta el café* (I like coffee) vs *Me gustaría un
  café* (I'd like a coffee).
- Answering *¿Le importaría…?* with a bare *Sí* when you mean "sure": strictly it means "yes, I
  would mind". People often say *Sí, claro* and the tone makes it clear, but *No, para nada* is
  safest.

## Key points

- Conditional = infinitive (or the future's irregular stem) + *-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían*:
  *hablaría, comería, podría, tendría, haría, diría*.
- Polite requests: *¿Podría…? ¿Me podría…? ¿Le importaría + infinitive? ¿Sería posible…?*
- Wishes: *Me gustaría…, Me encantaría, Preferiría…*; also *quería* and *quisiera* as polite
  "I'd like".
- Politeness ladder: command → present question → conditional question.
- Services: *sacar, depositar, transferir, cobrar, la comisión, hacer fila, el sobre, el timbre,
  entregar, arreglar, la fuga, la factura, la queja, el trámite, la identificación*.

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: At the doctor's: accidents, symptoms and advice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Spanish A1 you said what hurts (*Me duele la cabeza*), talked about flu and a temperature,
and in honors 20h2 went to the pharmacy. This lesson adds three things you need when
something has actually happened: telling an accident (*Me caí y me rompí el brazo*), answering
the doctor's "since when?" questions, and giving and understanding advice (*Deberías
descansar; Yo que tú, iría al dentista*). The advice uses the conditional from lesson 19.

The dialogues and advice here are for practicing the language, not medical advice.

## The body: more parts

![A simple front view of a person, labeled in Spanish: la herida (a small bandaged wound on the forehead), el cuello (the neck), el hombro (a shoulder), el dedo (a finger), la rodilla (a knee) and el yeso (a cast on one forearm).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *el cuello* | neck | *el dedo* | finger; toe (*el dedo del pie*) |
| *el hombro* | shoulder | *la rodilla* | knee |
| *el hueso* | bone | *la sangre* | blood |
| *la muela* | molar, back tooth | *la herida* | wound, cut |

A1 gave you *la cabeza, el brazo, la mano, la pierna, el pie, la espalda, el estómago, la
garganta* and *el diente* (any tooth). *La muela* is a back tooth, and it's the word in the
most common dental complaint: *Me duele una muela* (I have a toothache).

## Accidents: reflexive verbs and the body

To say what happened to your own body, Spanish uses a verb with *me, te, se…* and the
article, not a possessive:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *Me rompí el brazo.* | I broke my arm. |
| *Se quemó la mano con el sartén.* | She burned her hand on the frying pan. |
| *Me lastimé la rodilla.* | I hurt my knee. |
| *Te cortaste el dedo.* | You cut your finger. |
| *Nos lastimamos jugando futbol.* | We got hurt playing soccer. |

The pronoun already says whose arm it is, so *mi* would say it twice: ~~*Me rompí mi
brazo*~~. The same holds for *doler* (A1: *Me duele la rodilla*) and for clothes: *Me puse la
chamarra*.

- *romperse* (to break a bone): its participle is *roto*, as for *romper* (A1): *Se ha roto
  el dedo* (He has broken his finger).
- *lastimarse* (to hurt oneself) is the usual Mexican word; Spain says *hacerse daño*.
- *quemarse* (to burn oneself), *cortarse* (to cut oneself, from *cortar*, lesson 16), and
  *caerse* (lesson 03: *Me caí de la bicicleta*).

Without a body part, the verb still takes *se*: *Me lastimé* (I hurt myself). For an
accident with an action in progress, use the imperfect or a gerund for the background
(module 1, lesson 09): *Me lastimé cuando jugaba futbol; Me quemé cocinando.*

After an accident: *la herida* (wound) may need *una inyección* (an injection, a shot); a broken
bone (*el hueso roto*) needs *un yeso* (a cast): *Voy a llevar el yeso seis semanas*.

## The doctor's questions: since when?

Lesson 04 taught *desde, desde hace* and *hace … que*. They are exactly what a doctor asks:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| *¿Qué le pasó?* (What happened to you?) | *Me caí en la escalera.* (I fell on the stairs.) |
| *¿Cómo se lastimó?* (How did you hurt yourself?) | *Jugando basquetbol.* (Playing basketball.) |
| *¿Desde cuándo le duele?* (Since when has it hurt?) | *Desde el sábado.* / *Desde hace tres días.* (Since Saturday. / For three days.) |
| *¿Cuánto tiempo hace que le duele?* (How long has it hurt?) | *Hace una semana (que me duele).* (For a week.) |
| *¿Le duele aquí?* (Does it hurt here?) | *Sí, ahí me duele mucho.* (Yes, it hurts a lot there.) |
| *¿Toma algún medicamento?* (Are you taking any medication?) | *No, ninguno.* (No, none.) |

Remember the present: *Me duele desde hace tres días* (it has hurt for three days and still
does). English uses "has hurt"; Spanish uses the present, as in lesson 04. At the doctor's,
both sides normally use *usted*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A visit to the clinic after an accident
  accDescr: At reception you are asked for your health insurance and an ID. A nurse asks what happened, and you answer with a reflexive verb, for example Me caí y me lastimé la rodilla. The doctor asks since when it has hurt, and you answer Desde el sábado or Desde hace dos días. The doctor examines you and may order an X-ray. Then comes the result: either No es grave, it's nothing serious, or Está roto, it's broken, and you need a cast. Last, the advice: Debe descansar, Debería volver en una semana, Es importante no caminar mucho.
  A["Recepción: ¿Tiene seguro médico? ¿Me permite una identificación?"] --> B["Enfermera: ¿Qué le pasó? — Me caí y me lastimé la rodilla."]
  B --> C["Doctor: ¿Desde cuándo le duele? — Desde hace dos días."]
  C --> D["Doctor: Vamos a sacar una radiografía."]
  D --> E{"¿Es grave?"}
  E -- no --> F["No es grave: es solo un golpe."]
  E -- sí --> G["Está roto: necesita un yeso."]
  F --> H["Consejos: Debe descansar. Debería volver en una semana."]
  G --> H
```

(*la radiografía* = X-ray; *sacar una radiografía* = to take an X-ray; *el golpe* = a knock, a bruise.)

## Giving advice

Here are the ways to say what someone should do, from the strongest to the softest:

| Spanish | Strength | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *tener que* + infinitive (A1) | you must | *Tiene que tomar la medicina cada ocho horas.* |
| *hay que* + infinitive (A1) | general rule | *Hay que lavar la herida.* |
| *deber* + infinitive | you should, you must | *Debes descansar.* |
| *debería* + infinitive | you should (softer) | *Deberías dormir más.* |
| *es importante / necesario / mejor* + infinitive | general advice | *Es mejor no fumar.* |
| *yo que tú* / *yo en tu lugar* + conditional | if I were you | *Yo que tú, iría al dentista hoy.* |

- *Deber* is a regular verb: *debo, debes, debe, debemos, deben*. Followed directly by the
  infinitive, with no word in between: *Debes ir*, not ~~*Debes a ir*~~.
- *Debería* (conditional) is the polite way, the one to use with friends and with *usted*:
  *Debería ir al médico* (You should go to the doctor). It also gives advice to yourself: *Debería
  hacer más ejercicio.*
- *Yo que tú* (literally "I, that you") means "if I were you", followed by the conditional:
  *Yo que tú, no fumaría.* With *usted*: *Yo que usted, descansaría unos días*. *Yo en tu lugar*
  (in your place) means the same.
- *Deber* also means "to owe": *Te debo cien pesos.* *El consejo* is one piece of advice: *Te
  doy un consejo* (Let me give you some advice); *consejos* is advice in general.

You'll also hear *deber de* + infinitive in speech with the same meaning; grammars prefer *deber
de* for guesses (honors 16h2) and plain *deber* for obligation. Use plain *deber* for advice.

## Healthy habits

*La salud* (health) is general: *Fumar es malo para la salud.* Two adjectives:

- *sano* = healthy, in good health (people), and good for you (food, habits): *Mi abuela está
  muy sana. Una comida sana.*
- *saludable* = good for your health (things, habits): *una vida saludable, un desayuno
  saludable.*

*Hacer ejercicio* = to exercise; *fumar* = to smoke; *una enfermedad* = an illness, a disease;
*grave* = serious: *No es nada grave* (It's nothing serious).

*El seguro médico* is health insurance. In Mexico, employers must register their workers with
the IMSS (*Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social*), the public social security system, which
people often call *el Seguro*: *Voy a ir al Seguro*. Some people also have a private policy,
often called *el seguro de gastos médicos*. At *el dentista* (the same form for a woman: *la
dentista*) and in a clinic, you are *el paciente* or *la paciente*.

## Dialogue: after the soccer game

Diego hurt his knee playing soccer on Saturday. On Monday he goes to a clinic in Querétaro.

> Doctora: Buenos días. Pase, siéntese. ¿Qué le pasó?
>
> Diego: Buenos días, doctora. El sábado estaba jugando futbol, me caí y me lastimé la rodilla.
>
> Doctora: ¿Desde cuándo le duele así?
>
> Diego: Desde el sábado. Ayer me dolía menos, pero hoy me duele más.
>
> Doctora: A ver… ¿Le duele aquí?
>
> Diego: ¡Sí, ahí! Y también el hombro: me caí sobre el brazo.
>
> Doctora: Bueno, vamos a sacar una radiografía. … Mire: el hueso no está roto. Es un golpe fuerte, no es nada grave.
>
> Diego: ¡Qué bueno! ¿Puedo jugar el sábado?
>
> Doctora: No, este sábado no. Debe descansar una semana. Y yo que usted, iría a terapia unas semanas.
>
> Diego: ¿Y para el dolor?
>
> Doctora: Le voy a dar una receta. Si no mejora en cinco días, debería volver.
>
> Diego: Muchas gracias, doctora.

Translation:

> Doctor: Good morning. Come in, sit down. What happened to you?
>
> Diego: Good morning, doctor. On Saturday I was playing soccer, I fell and I hurt my knee.
>
> Doctor: Since when has it been hurting like this?
>
> Diego: Since Saturday. Yesterday it hurt less, but today it hurts more.
>
> Doctor: Let's see… Does it hurt here?
>
> Diego: Yes, there! And my shoulder too: I fell on my arm.
>
> Doctor: OK, we're going to take an X-ray. … Look: the bone isn't broken. It's a bad knock, nothing serious.
>
> Diego: Great! Can I play on Saturday?
>
> Doctor: No, not this Saturday. You must rest for a week. And if I were you, I'd go to physical therapy for a few weeks.
>
> Diego: And for the pain?
>
> Doctor: I'll give you a prescription. If it doesn't get better in five days, you should come back.
>
> Diego: Thank you very much, doctor.

Notes: *estaba jugando* (lesson 09) sets the scene, and *me caí, me lastimé* are the events
(lesson 03). *La terapia* = physical therapy. *La receta* (A1) = prescription. *Si no mejora*
= if it doesn't get better. *Debe* is firm; *debería* and *yo que usted, iría* are softer.

## Pronunciation

- *Rodilla* and *cuello* have *ll*, which in most of Mexico sounds like the English *y* in
  "yes": *ro-DI-ya, KUE-yo*.
- *Hueso* starts with a *w* sound: *WE-so* (the *h* is silent and *ue* glides).
- *Inyección* is *in-yek-SION*: the *cc* is a *k* then an *s* sound (seseo).
- *Muela* is two syllables, *MUE-la*; *saludable* is *sa-lu-DA-ble*.

## Common mistakes

- The possessive with body parts: ~~*Me rompí mi brazo*~~ → *Me rompí el brazo*.
- Forgetting *me*: ~~*Lastimé la rodilla*~~ (whose knee?) → *Me lastimé la rodilla*.
- *a* or *de* after *deber* for advice: ~~*Debes a descansar*~~ → *Debes descansar*.
- The tense after *yo que tú*: ~~*Yo que tú, voy al médico*~~ is heard in casual speech, but the
  standard pattern is the conditional: *Yo que tú, iría al médico*.
- *Desde* and *desde hace*: *desde el sábado* (from a point in time), *desde hace tres días*
  (for a period up to now), not ~~*desde tres días*~~.
- *Sano* and *saludable* are close; for a person who is well, use *sano*: *Estoy sano*.

## Key points

- Accidents: reflexive verb + article + body part: *Me rompí el brazo; Se quemó la mano; Me
  lastimé la rodilla.*
- Doctor's questions: *¿Qué le pasó? ¿Desde cuándo le duele? — Desde el sábado / Desde hace
  dos días; Hace una semana que me duele.*
- Advice, strongest to softest: *tener que, hay que, debes, deberías, es mejor + infinitive,
  yo que tú + conditional.*
- *sano* (healthy, in good health), *saludable* (good for you); *el seguro médico*; *el Seguro*
  = the IMSS.

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Applying for a job in Mexico
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 taught you to read a job ad and survive an interview. This honors lesson goes
through a whole application, step by step, as you might do it in Mexico: a CV in the usual
Mexican layout, a formal e-mail to send with it, a mock interview with model answers, and
what the law says about the questions and requests an employer may not make. It brings
together the past tenses (module 1), the conditional of politeness (lesson 19) and the
formal letter phrases from A1 (*Estimada…, Quedo atento a su respuesta, Atentamente*).

## The CV: the Mexican layout

A Mexican *currículum* is usually one or two pages, in this order:

![An invented one-page Mexican CV for Ana Sofía Ruiz Castro. At the top, her name and the word Contadora. Then five sections with headings: Datos personales (phone, e-mail, city), Objetivo profesional (one sentence), Experiencia laboral (two jobs, most recent first), Formación académica (a bachelor's degree and a diploma course) and Idiomas y habilidades (Spanish, English, software skills).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. *Datos personales*: name (both surnames, A1 honors 04h2), phone, e-mail, city. Many
   templates also have spaces for a photo, the date of birth or marital status; none of
   these is required, and the law forbids turning someone down because of age or marital
   status (see below).
2. *Objetivo profesional* (optional): one sentence on what you're looking for.
3. *Experiencia laboral*: your jobs, the most recent first, with dates, the company, the
   position (*el puesto*) and what you did.
4. *Formación académica*: your degrees and courses: *licenciatura, maestría, diplomado* (a
   diploma course).
5. *Idiomas y habilidades*: languages with a level (*inglés: avanzado; francés: básico*) and
   skills (*las habilidades*): software, driver's license, teamwork.

Under each job, describe what you did in one of two styles, and keep one style throughout:

- Preterite verbs in the first person (with no *yo*): *Coordiné un equipo de cinco
  personas. Aumenté las ventas un 15 %.*
- Nouns: *Coordinación de un equipo de cinco personas. Atención a clientes.*

For your current job use the present (*Coordino…*) or the noun style; *Actualmente* (lesson 04)
introduces it. Put your best result as a *logro* (achievement): *Logro: abrí una nueva
sucursal en Toluca* (*la sucursal* = branch).

### Example 1: turning notes into a CV section

Tom, from Toronto, has these notes about his last job: "Hotel Real, Cancún, 2021–2024,
receptionist. Answered guests in English and Spanish. Trained new staff. Best review score
of the team in 2023."

Step 1: the heading line, with dates and the position (*Recepcionista* = receptionist).
> *Hotel Real, Cancún — Recepcionista (2021–2024)*

Step 2: the tasks, as preterite verbs, because the job is finished.
> *Atendí a huéspedes en inglés y español. Capacité a empleados nuevos.*

Step 3: the achievement, with a number if possible.
> *Logro: la mejor calificación de los huéspedes de todo el equipo en 2023.*

(I served guests in English and Spanish. I trained new employees. Achievement: the best guest
rating on the whole team in 2023.) *Capacitar* = to train staff (*la capacitación* =
training); *el huésped* = hotel guest;
*atender* (lesson 07) = to serve, to attend to. Notice that *calificación* (lesson 18) is used
here for a guest rating, a grade given by the guests.

## The cover e-mail

You usually send the CV attached to a short formal e-mail, which works as *la carta de
presentación* (the cover letter). It uses *usted*, a title if you know it (*Lic.*, *Ing.*), and
the A1 formulas.

### Example 2: an e-mail for a vacancy

> Asunto: Solicitud para la vacante de recepcionista
>
> Estimada Lic. Pérez:
>
> Le escribo para solicitar la vacante de recepcionista que su hotel publicó en su página web.
>
> Tengo tres años de experiencia en hoteles de Cancún, donde atendí a huéspedes en inglés y en español. Actualmente estudio un diplomado en turismo y me gustaría seguir creciendo en un hotel como el suyo.
>
> Le adjunto mi currículum. Me encantaría tener la oportunidad de una entrevista. Tengo disponibilidad inmediata.
>
> Quedo a sus órdenes y atento a su respuesta.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Thomas Wilson
> Tel. 998 123 45 67

Translation: *Subject: Application for the receptionist vacancy. Dear Ms. Pérez: I am writing
to apply for the receptionist vacancy that your hotel posted on its website. I have three
years' experience in hotels in Cancún, where I served guests in English and Spanish. I am
currently taking a diploma course in tourism and I would like to keep growing in a hotel like
yours. I attach my CV. I would love to have the opportunity of an interview. I can start right
away. I remain at your service and look forward to your reply. Sincerely, Thomas Wilson.*

What each part does:

1. *Asunto* (A1): the subject line says what you are applying for: *Solicitud para la
   vacante de…* (*la vacante* = vacancy, opening).
2. *Estimada Lic. Pérez:* with a colon, the Spanish convention after the greeting.
3. Why you write: *Le escribo para solicitar…*
4. Your experience in one or two sentences, using the preterite (*atendí*) for the finished
   job, a relative clause (*donde atendí…*, lesson 18) and the present for now (*Actualmente
   estudio*).
5. The polite wish, in the conditional: *me gustaría, me encantaría* (lesson 19).
6. The attachment: *Le adjunto mi currículum* (*adjuntar*, A1). *Tengo disponibilidad
   inmediata* = I can start right away.
7. The close: *Quedo a sus órdenes* (I remain at your service: very common in Mexican formal
   writing and on the phone) and *atento a su respuesta*; a woman writes *atenta*. Then
   *Atentamente* and your name.

The whole e-mail is about 90 words. A short, clear e-mail is normal; the CV carries the detail.

## The interview: model answers

Interviewers use *usted* with you unless they suggest *tú*. Here are common questions with
model answers you can adapt. Notice which tense each answer uses.

### Example 3: a mock interview

> *Hábleme de usted.* (Tell me about yourself.)
>
> Me llamo Thomas Wilson. Soy canadiense y vivo en Cancún desde hace cinco años. Estudié Turismo en Toronto y he trabajado tres años en recepción de hoteles.
>
> *¿Por qué le interesa este puesto?*
>
> Porque su hotel es conocido por su servicio, y me gustaría trabajar en un equipo grande, donde voy a aprender mucho.
>
> *¿Cuáles son sus fortalezas?* (What are your strengths?)
>
> Soy muy organizado, hablo tres idiomas y me gusta resolver problemas. Por ejemplo, el año pasado un grupo llegó sin reservación y conseguí habitaciones para todos en menos de una hora.
>
> *¿Por qué dejó su último empleo?*
>
> Terminó mi contrato y quería un puesto con más responsabilidad.
>
> *¿Qué sueldo espera?*
>
> Según el mercado, entre 13,000 y 15,000 pesos al mes, pero me gustaría conocer también las prestaciones.
>
> *¿Tiene alguna pregunta?*
>
> Sí: ¿cómo sería la capacitación en las primeras semanas?

Translation of the answers: *My name is Thomas Wilson. I'm Canadian and I've lived in Cancún
for five years. I studied Tourism in Toronto and I've worked in hotel reception for three
years. — Because your hotel is known for its service, and I'd like to work in a big team,
where I'm going to learn a lot. — I'm very organized, I speak three languages and I like
solving problems. For example, last year a group arrived without a reservation and I got
rooms for all of them in less than an hour. — My contract ended and I wanted a position with
more responsibility. — Based on the market, between 13,000 and 15,000 pesos a month, but I'd
also like to know about the benefits. — Yes: what would the training be like in the first
weeks?*

How the answers work:

- *Vivo en Cancún desde hace cinco años* (lesson 04): present + *desde hace* for something that
  continues.
- *Estudié* (finished), *he trabajado tres años* (experience up to now): the two pasts as
  lesson 17 used them.
- The story about the group is a mini-anecdote: every verb is an event, so both are preterite
  (*llegó, conseguí*). Give one short example like this for each strength you claim.
- *En un equipo grande, donde voy a aprender mucho* adds a relative clause (lesson 18) to a
  wish in the conditional (*me gustaría*).
- *¿Cómo sería la capacitación?* uses the conditional to ask politely about something
  hypothetical.

*Las prestaciones* are the employment benefits. *Prestaciones de ley* are the ones the law
requires, and an ad may promise *prestaciones superiores a las de ley* (better than the
legal minimum). Under the *Ley Federal del Trabajo* (the federal labor law), these include:

| Benefit | What the law says (checked November 2026) |
|---|---|
| *el aguinaldo* (year-end bonus) | at least 15 days' pay, paid before December 20 (article 87); a proportional part if you worked less than a year |
| *las vacaciones* | at least 12 working days of paid vacation after the first year, rising by two days a year up to 20, then two more for every five years (article 76) |
| *la prima vacacional* | an extra payment of at least 25 % of your pay for the vacation days (article 80) |
| *el Seguro Social* | the employer registers you with the IMSS within five working days (*Ley del Seguro Social*, article 15) |

Laws change; check the current text before relying on any number.

## What an employer may not ask or demand

Mexican law doesn't give a list of forbidden interview questions. What it does, in article
133 of the *Ley Federal del Trabajo*, is forbid employers and their representatives to:

- refuse to hire someone because of ethnic or national origin, gender, age, disability,
  social condition, health conditions, religion, opinions, sexual preferences, marital
  status or any other ground that leads to discrimination (fraction I);
- demand a medical certificate showing that a woman is not pregnant (*un certificado de no
  embarazo*) to hire, keep or promote her (fraction XIV);
- fire a worker, or pressure her to resign, because she is pregnant, has changed her marital
  status or looks after young children (fraction XV).

The article is about what an employer does, not about which questions are asked. If you hear
*¿Está casada? ¿Piensa tener hijos?*, the answer may not be used to turn you down, and you
can answer politely without details: *Prefiero hablar de mi experiencia para el puesto*. This
summary is for language learning, not legal advice.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing styles in the CV: ~~*Coordiné el equipo. Atención a clientes.*~~ → all verbs or all
  nouns.
- Using *tú* with the interviewer or in the e-mail: stay with *usted* (*Le escribo, Le
  adjunto*) unless they switch.
- *Aplicar a la vacante*: common, and listed in the DLE for Latin America, but *solicitar la
  vacante* is the safer choice in a formal e-mail (lesson 17).
- Forgetting the colon after *Estimada Lic. Pérez*: Spanish uses a colon, not a comma.
- *Actualmente* is "currently", not "actually" (lesson 04): *Actualmente trabajo en…*
- Translating "I'm available" as ~~*Estoy disponible inmediata*~~: say *Tengo disponibilidad
  inmediata* or *Puedo empezar de inmediato*.

## Key points

- The CV: *datos personales, experiencia laboral* (most recent first), *formación académica,
  idiomas y habilidades*; tasks as preterite verbs or as nouns, one style throughout.
- The cover e-mail: *Asunto: Solicitud para la vacante de…; Estimada…: Le escribo para…; Le
  adjunto mi currículum; Me gustaría…; Quedo a sus órdenes; Atentamente.*
- In the interview: present + *desde hace* for now, the perfect for experience, the preterite
  for finished jobs and anecdotes, the conditional for wishes and polite questions.
- *Prestaciones de ley*: aguinaldo, vacations, the vacation bonus and the IMSS.
- The law forbids turning someone down for, among other things, age, gender, marital status or
  pregnancy, and forbids demanding a no-pregnancy certificate (LFT article 133).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: On the phone: appointments, voicemail and spelling
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 19 gave you the polite conditional (*¿Podría…? ¿Sería posible…?*). On the phone you
need it more than anywhere else, because you can't point, smile or show a piece of paper:
everything depends on words, numbers and names said clearly. This honors lesson covers
calling an office and being put through, making and changing an appointment, leaving a
voicemail and understanding one, and reading phone numbers and e-mail addresses aloud.

Short recorded messages (on an answering machine, in a shop, at a station) are also one of
the kinds of text in the DELE A2 listening test. The strategies at the end of this lesson
help with them; the scripts here are original and are not exam tasks.

## Calling an office

You know from A1 that Mexicans answer the phone with *¿Bueno?* and ask *¿De parte de quién?*
(Who's calling?). An office or a business usually answers with its name and a greeting:
*Consultorio Dental Sonrisa, buenas tardes.* Here are the phrases you'll hear and use:

| Caller | Office |
|---|---|
| *¿Me comunica con la licenciada Ríos, por favor?* (Could you put me through to Ms. Ríos?) | *¿De parte de quién?* |
| *Habla Paul Smith.* (Paul Smith speaking.) | *Permítame un momento.* (One moment, please.) |
| *¿Con quién hablo?* (Who am I speaking to?) | *Le comunico.* (I'll put you through.) |
| *¿Cuál es la extensión de ventas?* (What's the sales extension?) | *La licenciada está en una junta.* |
| *¿Podría decirle que me marque?* (Could you ask her to call me?) | *¿Quiere dejarle un recado?* (Would you like to leave her a message?) |
| *Le marco más tarde.* (I'll call back later.) | *Con gusto.* (Gladly. / You're welcome.) |

- *El conmutador* is the main number of a company, the switchboard; from there you are put
  through (*comunicar*) to *una extensión*.
- *Marcar* (A1) is "to dial" and, in Mexico, "to call": *Le marco mañana*.
- *Un recado* is a message left for someone; *el mensaje* (A1) is the general word (texts too).
- When the line is bad: *No se oye bien* (I can't hear well), *Se oye cortado* (You're
  breaking up), and when it drops: *Se cortó la llamada* (The call got cut off). *No se oye
  bien* and *Se oye cortado* use the impersonal *se* of lesson 17; in *Se cortó la llamada*,
  *cortarse* simply means "to get cut off", with the call as its subject.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A call to an office
  accDescr: The office answers with its name and Buenas tardes. The caller greets and asks Me comunica con la licenciada Ríos. The office asks De parte de quién and the caller says Habla Paul Smith. The office says Permítame un momento. If Ms. Ríos is available, the office says Le comunico and puts the call through. If she isn't, the office says Está en una junta, Quiere dejarle un recado? The caller either leaves a message with name, number and reason, or says Le marco más tarde.
  A["Oficina: Consultorio Sonrisa, buenas tardes."] --> B["Usted: Buenas tardes. ¿Me comunica con la licenciada Ríos?"]
  B --> C["Oficina: ¿De parte de quién? — Habla Paul Smith."]
  C --> D["Oficina: Permítame un momento."]
  D --> E{"¿Está disponible?"}
  E -- sí --> F["Le comunico."]
  E -- no --> G["Está en una junta. ¿Quiere dejarle un recado?"]
  G --> H["Sí: nombre, número y motivo"]
  G --> I["No, gracias. Le marco más tarde."]
```

## Making and changing an appointment

### Example 1: booking a dental appointment

> Recepcionista: Consultorio Dental Sonrisa, buenas tardes.
>
> Paul: Buenas tardes. Quería hacer una cita con la doctora Méndez, por favor. Me duele una muela desde el sábado.
>
> Recepcionista: ¿Es usted paciente de la doctora?
>
> Paul: No, es la primera vez.
>
> Recepcionista: Muy bien. Tengo un espacio mañana a las cuatro y media o el viernes a las diez.
>
> Paul: Mañana, por favor. Lo antes posible.
>
> Recepcionista: Perfecto. ¿Me da su nombre completo y un teléfono?
>
> Paul: Paul Smith, ese, eme, i, te, hache. El celular es cincuenta y cinco, cuarenta y siete, doce, treinta, ochenta y nueve.
>
> Recepcionista: Le repito: cincuenta y cinco, cuarenta y siete, doce, treinta, ochenta y nueve. Lo esperamos mañana a las cuatro y media.

*Receptionist: Sonrisa Dental Office, good afternoon. — Paul: Good afternoon. I'd like to make
an appointment with Dr. Méndez, please. I've had a toothache since Saturday. — Receptionist:
Are you one of the doctor's patients? — Paul: No, it's the first time. — Receptionist: Very
well. I have a slot tomorrow at four thirty or on Friday at ten. — Paul: Tomorrow, please. As
soon as possible. — Receptionist: Perfect. Could you give me your full name and a phone
number? — Paul: Paul Smith, S, M, I, T, H. My cell phone is 55 47 12 30 89. — Receptionist:
Let me repeat it: 55 47 12 30 89. We'll expect you tomorrow at four thirty.*

Step by step:

1. Paul asks with the polite imperfect *Quería* (lesson 19) and gives a reason in the present
   + *desde* (lesson 20).
2. *Un espacio* (a slot) and *lo antes posible* (as soon as possible) are typical of booking.
3. He spells his surname letter by letter and reads his number in pairs, the way Mexicans
   usually say phone numbers (A1 lesson 03).
4. The receptionist reads the number back (*Le repito*): do the same when you take a number.

### Example 2: changing the appointment

The next morning Paul has a problem at work and calls again.

> Paul: Buenos días. Habla Paul Smith. Tengo cita hoy a las cuatro y media con la doctora Méndez, pero tengo una junta a esa hora. ¿Sería posible cambiarla?
>
> Recepcionista: Permítame un momento… Le podría dar el viernes a las diez o el lunes a las cinco.
>
> Paul: El viernes a las diez me queda perfecto. ¿Y le importaría mandarme la dirección por mensaje?
>
> Recepcionista: Claro, se la mando ahorita. ¿Algo más?
>
> Paul: No, eso es todo. Muchas gracias.
>
> Recepcionista: A sus órdenes. Hasta el viernes.

*Paul: Good morning. This is Paul Smith. I have an appointment today at four thirty with Dr.
Méndez, but I have a meeting at that time. Would it be possible to change it? —
Receptionist: One moment… I could give you Friday at ten or Monday at five. — Paul: Friday at
ten suits me perfectly. And would you mind sending me the address by text? — Receptionist: Of
course, I'll send it to you right now. Anything else? — Paul: No, that's all. Thank you very
much. — Receptionist: You're welcome. See you on Friday.*

Notice:

- Three conditionals in a row: *¿Sería posible…?*, *Le podría dar…*, *¿le importaría…?*
- *Me queda perfecto* (it suits me perfectly) uses A1's *quedar* in the sense "to suit, to fit
  (a time)".
- *Se la mando* = *le* + *la* (the address) → *se la* (lesson 07).
- *A sus órdenes* (at your service) is a common Mexican reply to *gracias* in offices and
  shops.

## Voicemail

When nobody answers, you hear a recording: *Deje su mensaje después del tono* (Leave your
message after the tone), or the phone company's *El número que usted marcó no está
disponible*. A good message has five parts, in this order:

1. greeting and name: *Hola, buenas tardes, habla Paul Smith.*
2. who it's for, if needed: *Este mensaje es para la licenciada Ríos.*
3. the reason: *Le llamo por la cita del viernes.*
4. what you want, politely: *¿Me podría marcar al cincuenta y cinco…?*
5. the number again, slowly, and goodbye: *Mi número otra vez: … Muchas gracias, hasta luego.*

### Example 3: from voicemail to a written message

Daniela works at an office in Monterrey. She listens to this message on her boss's *buzón de
voz* (voicemail):

> "Buenas tardes, este mensaje es para el ingeniero Garza. Habla Sofía Treviño, de Transportes del Norte. Le llamo porque el camión con su pedido va a llegar el jueves, no el miércoles, por la lluvia. ¿Me podría marcar para confirmar la hora? Mi número es ochenta y uno, veintitrés, cuarenta y cinco, cero seis, setenta y ocho, extensión ciento doce. Le repito: ochenta y uno, veintitrés, cuarenta y cinco, cero seis, setenta y ocho. Muchas gracias, hasta luego."

*Good afternoon, this message is for Mr. Garza (an engineer). This is Sofía Treviño, from
Transportes del Norte. I'm calling because the truck with your order is going to arrive on
Thursday, not Wednesday, because of the rain. Could you call me to confirm the time? My
number is 81 23 45 06 78, extension 112. I'll repeat: 81 23 45 06 78. Thank you very
much, goodbye.*

(*el pedido* = the order; *el camión* = here a truck.) Daniela writes it on a message slip:

![An invented paper message slip titled RECADO. Para: Ing. Garza. De: Sofía Treviño, Transportes del Norte. Teléfono: 81 2345 0678, ext. 112. Mensaje: El pedido llega el jueves, no el miércoles (lluvia). Llamar para confirmar la hora. Recibió: Daniela, martes 4:15 p. m.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

How she got it right:

- She listened first for the four facts a *recado* needs: who it's for, who called, the number
  and the message.
- She wrote the number while it was read and checked it on the repeat.
- She wrote only the key words of the message, not every word.

### Listening to recorded messages: strategies

- Predict. Before the message starts, think what it could contain: a name, a number, a
  day, a time, a change of plan.
- Listen for the change. Messages often correct something: *el jueves, no el miércoles*;
  *ya no a las cinco, sino a las seis*. The word after *no* or *sino* (but rather) is the
  new information.
- Numbers in pairs. Mexican phone numbers come in pairs (*ochenta y uno, veintitrés…*);
  extensions are often read as one number (*ciento doce*).
- Don't stop at a word you don't know. Keep going; the repeat usually comes.

## Spelling names and e-mail addresses

To spell, say the letters (A1 lesson 01): *Smith: ese, eme, i, te, hache.* Two tricks avoid
confusion:

- *b* and *v* sound the same, so Mexicans often say *be grande* and *ve chica*, or add a word:
  *be de burro, ve de vaca*.
- For any letter that could be misheard, add a word: *eme de mamá, ene de Nicolás*.

E-mail addresses use these words:

| Sign | Spanish |
|---|---|
| @ | *arroba* |
| . | *punto* |
| _ | *guion bajo* |
| - | *guion* (*guion medio* to be clear) |
| all one word | *todo junto* |
| lower-case letters | *minúsculas* |

*paul_smith88@correo.mx* → *paul, guion bajo, smith, ochenta y ocho, arroba, correo, punto,
eme, equis*. If a part is unusual, spell it: *smith se escribe ese, eme, i, te, hache*.

## Common mistakes

- Answering an office call with just *¿Bueno?*: that's fine at home, but an office says its
  name.
- *Marcar* in Spain: in Mexico *Le marco* means "I'll call you", but in Spain *marcar* is
  normally just "to dial"; *llamar* works everywhere.
- Reading a phone number digit by digit too fast. In pairs and slowly is clearer, and you can
  ask *¿Me lo repite, por favor?*
- *Guión* with an accent: since 2010 the RAE writes *guion* (one syllable) without it.
- Confusing *el recado* (a message taken for someone) and *la receta* (prescription, recipe).
- Leaving out the reason in a voicemail: always say why you called, so the person can call
  back ready.

## Key points

- Office calls: *¿Me comunica con…? ¿De parte de quién? Permítame un momento. Le comunico.
  ¿Quiere dejarle un recado? Le marco más tarde.*
- Appointments: *Quería hacer una cita…; ¿Sería posible cambiarla?; Le podría dar el viernes;
  Me queda perfecto.*
- Problems on the line: *No se oye bien; Se cortó la llamada.*
- A voicemail: name, who it's for, reason, polite request, number twice, goodbye.
- Spelling: *be grande / ve chica*; *arroba, punto, guion, guion bajo, todo junto*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: In the news: reporting what people say
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

News is mostly people telling you what other people said: *El gobierno dijo que…, Según la
policía…, Una vecina contó que…* This lesson teaches you to do the same thing: to pass on what
someone says or said, and to ask what someone asked. It also gives you the words of newspapers,
TV, radio and social media, and shows how news reports use the two past tenses you learned in
module 1 (the **[[preterite]]** for events, the **[[imperfect]]** for the scene and for states). Finally,
it shows how Spanish writes and reads big numbers and percentages, which fill every news story
and every survey.

You already know *decir*, *preguntar* and *contar* (to tell) from A1; now they frame a new kind of
sentence.

## Reporting what someone says now: *dice que*

When you pass on someone's words, you are using **[[reported speech]]** (also called indirect
speech). If the person is speaking now, or what they said is still fresh, use *dice que* and keep
the same tense the person used:

| What Ana says | What you tell someone else |
|---|---|
| *"Estoy en el tráfico."* | *Ana dice que está en el tráfico.* — Ana says she's in traffic. |
| *"Llego en diez minutos."* | *Dice que llega en diez minutos.* — She says she'll be here in ten minutes. |
| *"Ya compré los boletos."* | *Dice que ya compró los boletos.* — She says she already bought the tickets. |
| *"Voy a llamar a mi mamá."* | *Dice que va a llamar a su mamá.* — She says she's going to call her mom. |

Two things change, and one never does:

- The person changes. Ana's *yo* becomes *ella*, so *estoy* becomes *está*, and *mi mamá*
  becomes *su mamá*. If Ana talks to you about you, her *tú* becomes your *yo*: *"Te llamo mañana."* →
  *Dice que me llama mañana.* (She says she'll call me tomorrow.)
- The tense stays the same with *dice que*: present stays present, preterite stays
  preterite, *ir a* stays *ir a*.
- *Que* is never left out. English can drop "that" (*she says she's in traffic*); Spanish can't:
  *Dice que está en el tráfico*, never ~~*Dice está en el tráfico*~~.

![Two speech bubbles turned into reported sentences. "Estoy cansada" becomes "Dice que está cansada" (now) and "Dijo que estaba cansada" (later). "Perdí el vuelo" becomes "Dice que perdió el vuelo" and "Dijo que perdió el vuelo".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Other verbs work the same way and make your reports less repetitive: *contar que* (to tell, to
recount), *explicar que* (to explain), *comentar que* (to remark, to comment), *informar que* (to
report, to announce officially, a news word), *escribir que*. *Según* (according to) introduces a
source without a verb at all: *Según Ana, el tráfico está horrible.*

## Reporting questions: *pregunta si*, *pregunta dónde*

A reported question is an **[[indirect question]]**. There are two kinds:

1. Yes/no questions take *si*, which here means "whether" or "if". It has no accent (*sí*
   with an accent is "yes"):
   - *"¿Vienes a la junta?"* → *Mi jefe pregunta si vienes a la junta.* — My boss is asking if
     you're coming to the meeting.
   - *"¿Ya publicaron el artículo?"* → *La periodista pregunta si ya publicaron el artículo.* — The
     journalist is asking if they've published the article yet.
2. Questions with a question word keep the word, and it keeps its accent: *qué, quién, dónde,
   cuándo, cómo, cuánto, por qué*:
   - *"¿Cuándo es la elección?"* → *Pregunta cuándo es la elección.* — She's asking when the
     election is.
   - *"¿Qué canal es?"* → *Mi abuelo pregunta qué canal es.* — My grandfather is asking what
     channel it is.
   - *"¿Por qué no votaste?"* → *Me pregunta por qué no voté.* — He's asking me why I didn't
     vote.

The reported version needs no question marks: it's a statement about a question. *Quiere saber*
(wants to know) works the same way: *Quiere saber dónde vives* (She wants to know where you live).

In relaxed speech, in Mexico and elsewhere, you'll often hear an extra *que* before *si* or the
question word: *Me preguntó que si iba a venir* (He asked me if I was going to come). It's very
common in conversation; in writing, leave it out.

## Reporting the past: *dijo que*

Most news is reported after the fact, with *dijo que, contó que, explicó que*. Then you choose
between the two pasts by the same logic as in module 1:

- A finished event that the person told about stays in the preterite:
  *"Perdí el vuelo."* → *Dijo que perdió el vuelo.* (She said she missed the flight.)
- A state or description at the time of speaking goes into the imperfect:
  *"Estoy cansada."* → *Dijo que estaba cansada.* (She said she was tired.)
  *"Hay mucha gente."* → *Dijo que había mucha gente.* (She said there were a lot of people.)
  *"Tengo hambre."* → *Contó que tenía hambre.* (He said he was hungry.)

English does the same thing (*is* → *was*), so the imperfect will feel natural. If the state is
obviously still true now, the present is also correct: *Dijo que está enferma* (and she still
is). The imperfect is the safe choice when you're not sure.

Questions in the past follow the same pattern: *"¿Tienes tiempo?"* → *Me preguntó si tenía
tiempo.* (He asked me if I had time.)

There are more changes in careful reported speech, for example a future becoming *vendría*
("would come"). They're in honors lesson 24h1; for now, the preterite and the imperfect are all
you need.

### Words for time and place

When you report later, "today" is no longer today. In writing you'll see these shifts; recognize
them:

| In the original | In a later report |
|---|---|
| *hoy* (today) | *ese día* (that day) |
| *mañana* (tomorrow) | *al día siguiente* (the next day) |
| *ayer* (yesterday) | *el día anterior* (the day before) |
| *aquí* (here) | *allí, ahí* (there) |

In speech, people keep the original words if the time is still the same: *Hace un rato me dijo
que hoy no viene* (a little while ago he told me he isn't coming today).

## The words of the news

| Media | Words |
|---|---|
| print and online | *el periódico* (newspaper), *la revista* (magazine), *el artículo*, *el titular* (headline), *el periodista, la periodista* |
| TV | *la televisión* (*la tele*), *el canal*, *el programa*, *la serie* (TV series) |
| sound | *la radio* (radio as a medium); in Mexico the set itself is usually *el radio* |
| online | *la red social, el video, el enlace, compartir* (lesson 05), *el comentario* |

The TV news in Mexico is usually *el noticiero*. *El programa* is masculine although it ends in
*-a*, like *el día*.

Reporters *entrevistan* (interview) people and *publican* (publish) or *informan* (report).
*Publicar* changes *c* to *qu* before *e*: *publiqué, publicaste, publicó*.

News about politics uses *el gobierno* (government), *el presidente, la presidenta* (president),
*la elección* (election; often plural, *las elecciones*), *votar* (to vote) and *el tema*
(topic, issue). *La presidenta* is the standard feminine, and you'll hear it constantly in Mexican
news: Claudia Sheinbaum took office on 1 October 2024 as Mexico's first woman president.

### Headlines

Headlines (*los titulares*) are short. They often drop the article and use the present for an
event that has just happened:

- *Bomberos apagan incendio en panadería del centro* — Firefighters put out fire in downtown
  bakery
- *Publican encuesta sobre jóvenes y redes sociales* — Survey on young people and social media
  published

The article below the headline then tells the story in the past, with the preterite for what
happened and the imperfect for the scene. *Sobre* here means "about".

![The front page of an invented newspaper, El Diario del Valle. Labels point to its parts: la fecha (the date under the paper's name), el titular (the large headline), la foto (a fire truck and firefighters), el artículo (the text in columns) and la encuesta (a small bar chart).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## A radio report

Raúl Méndez reports for an invented local radio station, *Radio Centro*, after a fire.

> Raúl: Buenos días. Estamos en la calle Reforma, donde anoche ocurrió un incendio. Señora, ¿usted vio lo que pasó?
>
> Vecina: Sí. Eran como las once. Estaba viendo una serie en la tele cuando escuché un ruido muy fuerte.
>
> Raúl: ¿Y qué hizo?
>
> Vecina: Salí al balcón y vi humo en la panadería. Mi esposo llamó a los bomberos.
>
> Raúl: ¿Cuándo llegaron?
>
> Vecina: En unos diez minutos. Afortunadamente, la panadería estaba cerrada y no había nadie adentro.
>
> Raúl: Según los bomberos, el fuego empezó en la cocina. ¿Los vecinos están preocupados?
>
> Vecina: Un poco. Pero el dueño dice que va a abrir otra vez el mes que viene.
>
> Raúl: Muchas gracias, señora. Desde la calle Reforma, informó Raúl Méndez para Radio Centro.

> Raúl: Good morning. We're on Reforma Street, where a fire broke out last night. Ma'am, did you see what happened?
>
> Neighbor: Yes. It was about eleven. I was watching a series on TV when I heard a very loud noise.
>
> Raúl: And what did you do?
>
> Neighbor: I went out onto the balcony and saw smoke at the bakery. My husband called the fire department.
>
> Raúl: When did they arrive?
>
> Neighbor: In about ten minutes. Fortunately, the bakery was closed and there was nobody inside.
>
> Raúl: According to the firefighters, the fire started in the kitchen. Are the neighbors worried?
>
> Neighbor: A little. But the owner says he's going to open again next month.
>
> Raúl: Thank you very much, ma'am. From Reforma Street, this was Raúl Méndez for Radio Centro.

New words in passing: *el humo* (smoke), *la panadería* (bakery), *adentro* (inside), *el fuego*
(fire, flames). *Informó* at the end is a common sign-off in Mexican news reports: literally
"reported".

The next morning, the newspaper turns the interview into reported speech:

> Incendio en una panadería del centro; no hay heridos
>
> Anoche hubo un incendio en una panadería de la calle Reforma. Según los bomberos, el fuego
> empezó en la cocina. Una vecina contó a Radio Centro que estaba viendo la tele cuando escuchó
> un ruido. Dijo que su esposo llamó a los bomberos y que llegaron en diez minutos. Explicó que
> la panadería estaba cerrada y que no había nadie adentro. El dueño comentó que va a abrir otra
> vez el mes que viene.

Events (*llamó, llegaron*) stay preterite; the scene (*estaba viendo, estaba cerrada, no había
nadie*) is imperfect; the owner's plan *va a abrir* stays, as it's still in the future. *Los
heridos* are injured people.

## Numbers in the news: millions and percentages

### Millions

*Mil* (A1) doesn't change in numbers (*dos mil, diez mil*), but *el millón* is a noun with a plural, *los millones*, and it takes
*de* when the thing counted comes right after it:

- *un millón de personas* — a million people
- *veinte millones de habitantes* — twenty million inhabitants
- *dos millones quinientos mil pesos* — 2,500,000 pesos (no *de*: more numbers come before the noun)

Mexico usually writes decimals with a point, as in the US: *2.3 millones*, read *dos punto tres
millones*, which people also say as *dos millones trescientos mil*. Spain and many other
countries use a comma (*2,3 millones*, read *dos coma tres*), so you'll see both in Spanish news.

### Percentages

*Por ciento* (percent) is written *40 %* or *40 por ciento*, and the number usually takes the
article *el*: *el 40 por ciento de los jóvenes* (40 percent of young people). Other useful words:
*la mitad* (half), *más de la mitad* (more than half), *la mayoría* (most, the majority).

When a percentage of a plural group is the subject, you'll hear the verb in the singular and in
