In short: Mateo and Sofía climb the tower, put the part back, and the bell rings again.

![The bell tower of San Jacinto's church, drawn in cross-section, with its parts labeled in Spanish. At the top, under a pointed roof, hangs la campana (the bell). Below it, el reloj (the clock face) shows ten past four, with las manecillas (the hands). Inside the lower part of the tower are las ruedas (gear wheels) and la manivela (the crank handle), la escalera (a narrow staircase) on the left and la puerta (a wooden door) on the right at the bottom.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5. Las cuatro y diez

> Dos meses después, don Ernesto vino de visita con Laura. Se sentó en una banca de la plaza y miró la torre durante mucho tiempo. Yo me senté junto a él.
>
> —Usted tenía la pieza —le dije—. Usted paró el reloj, ¿verdad?
>
> Don Ernesto no contestó enseguida. Luego dijo:
>
> —Mi esposa, Rosario, murió un martes, a las cuatro y diez de la tarde. Ese día subí a la torre y quité la pieza. No quería oír las horas sin ella. Durante treinta años guardé el secreto.
>
> —¿Y por qué me la dio a mí?
>
> Sonrió como siempre.
>
> —Porque el pueblo necesitaba sus horas. Y porque tú fuiste el único que me lo preguntó.
>
> Laura no vendió el taller. Hoy tengo veinticinco años y soy relojero. Los sábados, un niño de la casa de enfrente me ayuda a limpiar las piezas. Y todas las tardes, a las cuatro y diez, miro la torre y me acuerdo de don Ernesto.

Words: *de visita* (on a visit), *enseguida* (straight away), *parar* (to stop), *quitar* (to
take out, to remove), *el único* (the only one).

In short: don Ernesto stopped the clock when his wife died; today Mateo is the clockmaker.

![A storyboard in five panels. 1: an old man with glasses on the tip of his nose works at a bench of tools while a boy cleans small parts. 2: a closed shop door, and a woman with a broom talking to the boy. 3: an open wooden box with a key, a blue notebook and a small round metal part. 4: the boy and a girl with a flashlight at the top of the tower, the bell ringing. 5: the old man and the boy on a bench in the plaza, looking up at the tower. Captions in Spanish: Los sábados en el taller. El taller cerrado. La caja de madera. ¡La campana suena! En la banca de la plaza.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Working with the story

### Example 1: Guessing *las manecillas* from context

Part 1 says: *En la torre había un reloj enorme… Sus manecillas marcaban siempre las cuatro y
diez.*

1. What kind of word? *Sus manecillas* (its ___): a plural thing that belongs to the clock.
2. What does it do? It *marcaba* (showed) a time. Guess: the hands.
3. Check: in part 4 *las manecillas se movieron* and *las pusimos en las doce*. Hands move and
   can be set to twelve, so the guess holds.

(*Manecilla* comes from *mano*, hand. In Spain the hands of a clock are usually *las agujas*.)

### Example 2: An inference: what does *Ya es hora* mean?

The note says *Ya es hora*, the everyday phrase for "it's time". The story never explains it:

1. Facts: the note comes with the missing part; don Ernesto stopped the clock when his wife
   died (part 5); *Algunas cosas no se arreglan con herramientas* (part 1).
2. Connect them: for thirty years he didn't want the clock to run. Now, old and ill, he gives
   the part to the boy who asked about it.
3. Inference: it's time to fix the clock, and time for don Ernesto to let the town have its
   hours again.

An inference must rest on the text: "Don Ernesto hated the church" has no support, so it isn't a
reading of this story.

### Example 3: Story order and telling order

The story is told mostly in order, but part 5 jumps back thirty years: *Mi esposa murió un
martes… Ese día subí a la torre y quité la pieza.* A jump back like this is a **[[flashback]]**.
Rebuild the real order from the time clues:

| When | Event (part) |
|---|---|
| thirty years earlier | Rosario dies; don Ernesto takes out the part (5) |
| Mateo's childhood | Saturdays in the shop (1); the hospital (2); the box (2, 3); the bell (4) |
| two months later | Don Ernesto tells his secret (5) |
| today | Mateo is the clockmaker (5) |

In the last paragraph the present (*tengo, soy, miro*) shows the narrator has been looking back
at his childhood all along.

## Pronunciation

- The dash (—) starts a speaker's words; in *—¿Cómo está su papá? —le pregunté*, the second
  dash brings back the narrator. Drop your voice a little for the narrator.
- *reloj*: re-LOH; in casual speech the final *j* is often very soft or silent (*reló*).
- *oscuridad*: os-ku-ree-DAD (ends in a consonant other than *n, s*: last-syllable stress).

## Common mistakes

- Reading every word with a dictionary: you lose the story. Read a whole part first.
- Mixing up the tenses' jobs when retelling: *Nadie abrió* (one event: nobody opened), not
  ~~Nadie abría~~ for this one moment; *yo miraba la puerta* (every afternoon: a repeated
  action).
- Treating *decía* as "was saying" for a note. With written texts, *dice / decía* means "it
  says / it said": *El cuaderno decía: «aquí».*
- Losing track of pronouns. Find what each one replaces: *La buscamos* = *buscamos la llave*;
  *me la dio* = *me dio la pieza*.

## Key points

- Three strategies for a long text: use **[[cognates]]** (*mecanismo, perfecta, exactamente*), guess
  from context, and skip words the sentence doesn't need.
- The imperfect sets the scene (*había, era, tenía*); the preterite moves the story (*abrí,
  subimos, sonó*). Follow the preterites to find the plot.
- An **[[inference]]** is a conclusion the text supports but doesn't state: *Ya es hora* = it's time
  to let the clock, and don Ernesto, move on.
- A **[[flashback]]** tells an earlier event later; rebuild the real order from time clues (*treinta
  años, ese día, dos meses después, hoy*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Crónica de viaje: Bogotá, Lima y Buenos Aires
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A *crónica de viaje* is a travel chronicle: a personal account of a trip, today usually a blog.
It's a favorite kind of text for A2 reading because it mixes everything you've learned: the
preterite for what the traveler did, the imperfect for what places were like, comparisons
(module 3) and the impersonal *se* (*se ve toda la ciudad*).

Here you'll read three entries from the blog of Valeria, an invented traveler from Monterrey,
on a trip through three South American capitals in July. You'll practice two ways of reading
for information, **[[skimming]]** and **[[scanning]]**; meet the **[[regionalisms]]** she hears; and
recognize *vos* in Buenos Aires, which you first met in the A1 honors lesson on sounds
(04h1). Keep using *tú* yourself: *vos* is for recognition only.

## Two ways to read for information

- **[[Skimming]]** means reading fast for the general idea: the title, the first line of each
  paragraph, the words that repeat. Skim first to answer "what is this entry about?"
- **[[Scanning]]** means hunting for one detail: a number, a name, a date. You don't read every
  line; your eyes look for digits or capital letters. Scan to answer "how high is Bogotá?"

Try it: skim each entry below in about a minute and give it a title in English. Then read it
properly with the glosses.

## *Diario de una viajera*: three entries

![A map of South America. Three cities are marked with red dots: Bogotá in the Andes in the northwest, in Colombia; Lima on the Pacific coast, in Peru; and Buenos Aires on the Río de la Plata, in Argentina, by the Atlantic. A brown line of small peaks marks the Andes running down the west of the continent. The two oceans are labeled: Océano Pacífico to the west, Océano Atlántico to the east.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Bogotá, 6 de julio

> ¡Hola desde Bogotá! Llegué el martes en la noche y lo primero que noté fue el frío. Bogotá está a unos 2,600 metros de altura, más alta que la Ciudad de México, y la temperatura media es de 14 grados. Yo traje una chamarra ligera… y el miércoles me compré otra más gruesa.
>
> El primer día me mareé un poco al subir las escaleras del hotel. La señora de la recepción me dijo: «Es normal, es la altura. Tómese un tinto y camine despacio.» Aquí un tinto no es vino: es un café negro, pequeño y muy rico. Lo tomé en La Candelaria, el barrio colonial, con sus casas de colores, sus calles de piedra y muchísimos murales.
>
> El sábado subí en teleférico al cerro de Monserrate. Desde el mirador se ve toda la ciudad: es enorme, y está en un valle verde rodeado de montañas. Arriba hacía todavía más frío, pero la vista era increíble.
>
> Lo mejor fue ayer, domingo. Los domingos y los días festivos cierran más de cien kilómetros de calles a los carros, y la gente sale a andar en bicicleta, a correr o a caminar. Se llama la Ciclovía. Renté una bici y di un paseo larguísimo. Un señor que iba a mi lado me preguntó de dónde era. «¡Mexicana! ¡Qué chévere!», me dijo. Aquí todo es chévere.

Words: *notar* (to notice), *ligero* (light), *grueso* (thick, warm), *la piedra* (stone), *el
teleférico* (cable car), *rodeado de* (surrounded by), *el día festivo* (public holiday), *dar
un paseo* (to go for a walk or ride).

### Lima, 12 de julio

> De la montaña al mar: Lima está en la costa del océano Pacífico. Pero en julio no es un lugar de sol y playa: aquí es invierno, y el cielo de Lima casi siempre está gris. Hay una neblina fina que los limeños llaman garúa, y la ropa tarda mucho en secarse. Lo curioso es que casi nunca llueve de verdad: Lima es una de las ciudades más secas que conozco.
>
> Lima es enorme: tiene más de diez millones de habitantes, más que Bogotá. Su centro histórico también es colonial, como La Candelaria, y tiene unos balcones de madera preciosos.
>
> Mi lugar favorito es el malecón de Miraflores, un paseo muy largo arriba de los acantilados, junto al mar. Caminé por ahí al atardecer y vi a varias personas volando en parapente sobre el océano.
>
> ¿Y la comida? ¡Qué comida! Probé el ceviche: pescado crudo con limón, cebolla y chile, que aquí se llama ají. También pedí una ensalada con palta. «¿Palta?», le pregunté al mesero. Era aguacate, claro: en Perú se dice palta. Ya llevo dos palabras nuevas en mi libreta.

Words: *fino* (fine, thin), *el limeño* (person from Lima), *tardar en* (to take a long time to), *secarse* (to dry),
*lo curioso* (the strange thing), *seco* (dry), *el balcón* (balcony), *el malecón* (seafront
promenade), *el acantilado* (cliff), *al atardecer* (at sunset), *el parapente* (paragliding),
*crudo* (raw), *ya llevo* (here: I've already collected, so far I have), *la libreta* (little notebook).

### Buenos Aires, 22 de julio

> Llegué a Buenos Aires y… ¡hace frío otra vez! Claro: Argentina está en el hemisferio sur, y en julio es pleno invierno. Mientras mis amigos en Monterrey sufren con el calor del verano, yo ando con bufanda y guantes.
>
> La ciudad está a orillas del Río de la Plata, que es tan ancho que parece el mar. En la ciudad viven unos tres millones de personas, pero con los municipios de alrededor son casi catorce millones. Avenidas anchas, edificios antiguos y cafés por todos lados: es elegantísima.
>
> Me quedo en el departamento de Martín, un argentino muy amable. El primer día me dijo: «¿Vos sos mexicana? ¡Qué bueno! ¿Querés un mate?» El mate es una bebida de hierbas que se toma con una bombilla de metal y que se comparte con los amigos. Después me explicó cómo moverme: «Mirá, para el centro tomá el subte, y para La Boca, el colectivo. ¿Tenés tarjeta?» El colectivo es el autobús, y el subte es el metro, que aquí funciona desde 1913: fue el primero de América Latina.
>
> El domingo fuimos a la feria de San Telmo. Había antigüedades, música y, en una esquina, una pareja bailando tango. Martín me dijo: «Che, ¿bailamos?» Yo le contesté: «¡Ni loca!» Pero bailé. Mal, pero bailé.
>
> Tres ciudades, tres maneras de hablar. Y en las tres me entendieron perfectamente con mi español de Monterrey.

Words: *pleno invierno* (the middle of winter), *sufrir con* (to suffer in), *los guantes*
(gloves), *ancho* (wide), *el municipio* (municipality), *la hierba* (herb), *la bombilla*
(here: metal straw), *la antigüedad* (antique), *la manera* (way), *¡Ni loca!* (no way!, said by a woman).

## Regional words

A **[[regionalism]]** is a word or use typical of one region. Valeria's Mexican Spanish works
everywhere, but each city has its own words. These are the ones in her blog:

| In the blog | Meaning | Where (usually) | In Mexico |
|---|---|---|---|
| *el tinto* | small black coffee | Colombia, Ecuador | *un café americano, un café negro* |
| *¡Qué chévere!* | great!, cool! | Venezuela, Colombia, much of the Caribbean, parts of Peru and Ecuador | *¡Qué padre!* |
| *el ají* | chili pepper | Peru and much of South America | *el chile* |
| *la palta* | avocado | Peru, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay | *el aguacate* |
| *el colectivo* | city bus | Argentina | *el camión, el autobús* |
| *el subte* | subway | Buenos Aires | *el metro* |
| *che* | hey (to a friend) | Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia | *oye* |

*Chévere* is heard in parts of Mexico too, and none of these lists is complete: words travel,
and inside each country usage varies. *Palta* comes from Quechua and *aguacate* from Nahuatl.

## *Vos* in Buenos Aires

Martín uses *vos* instead of *tú*. You saw the present forms at A1 (*vos sos, vos hablás*).
In the blog there are two more patterns:

| Martín says | You say (*tú*) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *¿Vos sos mexicana?* | *¿Tú eres mexicana?* | Are you Mexican? |
| *¿Querés un mate?* | *¿Quieres un mate?* | Do you want a mate? |
| *¿Tenés tarjeta?* | *¿Tienes tarjeta?* | Do you have a card? |
| *Mirá* | *Mira* | Look |
| *Tomá el subte* | *Toma el subte* | Take the subway |

- Present: the stress moves to the ending and there's no stem change: *querés* (not
  *quieres*), *tenés*, *podés*. The accent shows the stress.
- Commands: the infinitive without its *-r*, stressed on the last vowel: *mirar → mirá, tomar
  → tomá, venir → vení, decir → decí* (*ir* is the exception: *andá*). For regular verbs
  that's the *tú* command plus an accent, but not for irregular or stem-changing ones: the *tú*
  forms of *vení, decí, cerrá* are *ven, di, cierra*. With a pronoun attached, the stress stays
  put and the accent goes: *mirame, contame*.
- The object pronoun *te* and the possessive *tu* stay the same: *Vos te llamás Martín; tu casa*.

## Comparing the three cities

| | Bogotá | Lima | Buenos Aires |
|---|---|---|---|
| Height above the sea | about 2,600 m | on the coast | on the Río de la Plata |
| People | about 8.0 million (city, 2024) | about 10.4 million (metropolitan Lima, 2025) | about 3.1 million (city, 2022); almost 14 million with the 24 surrounding districts |
| Weather | cool all year, average 14 °C | gray in winter, very little rain | four seasons; winter is June to August |

Sources and dates are in this module's notes: the figures are official estimates and change
every year. When you compare, compare like with like: the city of Buenos Aires is the smallest
of the three, but Greater Buenos Aires is the largest area.

### Example 1: Scanning for a number

Question: *¿A qué altura está Bogotá?*

1. Look for digits in the Bogotá entry: *6 de julio, 2,600, 14*.
2. Choose the one with a unit of height: *2,600 metros de altura*.
3. Answer in a full sentence: *Bogotá está a unos 2,600 metros de altura.* (*unos* = about.)

Note the number: Mexico writes *2,600* with a comma, like the US; Colombia and Argentina
usually write *2.600*, with a period. Both mean two thousand six hundred.

### Example 2: From *vos* to *tú*

Martín says: *Mirá, para el centro tomá el subte. ¿Tenés tarjeta?*

1. Find the *vos* forms: *mirá, tomá* (commands), *tenés* (present).
2. Commands: for these regular verbs, drop the accent: *mira, toma*.
3. Present: *tener* is *tienes* for *tú* (with its stem change).
4. Result: *Mira, para el centro toma el subte. ¿Tienes tarjeta?*

### Example 3: Writing comparisons from the table

1. Height: Bogotá is the only high city. *Bogotá es la más alta de las tres.*
2. People: 10.4 million against 8.0 million. *Lima tiene más habitantes que Bogotá.*
3. Rain: Valeria says it almost never rains in Lima. *Lima es más seca que Bogotá.*
4. Like with like: *La ciudad de Buenos Aires es más pequeña que Lima, pero el Gran Buenos
   Aires es más grande.*

Each sentence uses module 3: *más … que*, the superlative *la más … de*.

## Pronunciation

- In Buenos Aires *ll* and *y* sound like "sh" or "zh": *calle* (CA-she), *yo* (sho). You met
  this at A1; listen for it, but keep your own *y*.
- *Bogotá* and *Perú* stress the last syllable; *Lima* the first.
- *¡Qué chévere!*: CHE-be-re, stress on the first syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Answering a scanning question with the wrong number: in *6 de julio, 2,600 metros, 14 grados*
  only one is a height. Check the unit.
- Thinking *tinto* means red wine in Bogotá. In a Colombian café it's coffee; *vino tinto* is
  red wine.
- Copying *vos* forms. Martín understands *tú* perfectly; mixing *vos* and *tú* sounds odd.
- Forgetting the seasons: south of the equator, July is winter.
- Comparing a city with a metropolitan area: say which one you mean.

## Key points

- A *crónica de viaje* mixes the preterite (what I did), the imperfect (what it was like) and
  comparisons.
- **[[Skimming]]** = fast reading for the main idea; **[[scanning]]** = hunting for one detail.
- **[[Regionalisms]]** in the blog: *tinto* (Colombia), *chévere* (Venezuela, Colombia, the
  Caribbean), *ají* and *palta* (Peru and further south), *colectivo, subte, che* (Argentina).
- *Vos*: *sos, querés, tenés; mirá, tomá*. Recognize it; use *tú*.
- New words: *el viajero, la altura, el mirador, la neblina, el océano, la orilla, marearse,
  colonial, el paseo, el hemisferio, chévere, el tinto, la palta, el colectivo*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Vidas: three Latin American biographies
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 gave you the language of a life story: *nació en, a los 18 años, se graduó, se
casó, murió*. This lesson uses it to read three short biographies of real people from three
different places and fields: a Mexican chemist, a Chilean poet and teacher, and a baseball
player from Puerto Rico. All three texts were written for this course from the sources listed
in the module notes, and every date was checked.

A short biography is a typical text in A2 reading, and the DELE A2 writing test can ask you to
write a short life story from dates or pictures. So you'll also see how a biography is built,
meet the **[[historical present]]** that many biographies use, and write one of your own.

## How a biography is built

Most short biographies follow the same order: birth and childhood, studies, work and main
achievement, later life, death, and why the person matters today. Dates carry the text, so the
preterite does most of the work (*nació, estudió, ganó*), with the imperfect for background
(*le fascinaba la ciencia*).

![A timeline of Mario Molina's life from 1943 to 2020, drawn as a vertical line with seven dated points. 1943: nace en la Ciudad de México. 1965: se gradúa en la UNAM. 1972: doctorado en Berkeley. 1974: artículo sobre los CFC y el ozono. 1987: Protocolo de Montreal. 1995: Premio Nobel de Química. 2020: muere en la Ciudad de México.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Vida 1: Mario Molina, el químico del ozono (México, 1943–2020)

> Mario Molina nació en la Ciudad de México el 19 de marzo de 1943. De niño le fascinaba la ciencia: convirtió un baño de su casa en un pequeño laboratorio, con microscopios de juguete y un juego de química.
>
> Estudió Ingeniería Química en la UNAM y se graduó en 1965. Después estudió en Alemania y en Estados Unidos, y en 1972 terminó el doctorado en la Universidad de California en Berkeley.
>
> En 1973 empezó a trabajar con el químico F. Sherwood Rowland en la Universidad de California en Irvine. Juntos investigaron los CFC, unos gases que se usaban en los aerosoles y los refrigeradores. En 1974 publicaron un artículo muy importante: según su investigación, los CFC subían a la atmósfera y destruían la capa de ozono, que nos protege de la luz ultravioleta del sol.
>
> Al principio, muchas empresas no aceptaron sus conclusiones. Pero otros investigadores confirmaron el problema, y en 1987 muchos países firmaron el Protocolo de Montreal para reducir los CFC. En 1995 Molina recibió el Premio Nobel de Química con Rowland y con el holandés Paul Crutzen. Fue el primer mexicano que ganó el Nobel de Química.
>
> Durante muchos años se dedicó a la investigación y a la enseñanza en universidades de Estados Unidos, como el MIT. En 2005 fundó en la Ciudad de México el Centro Mario Molina, dedicado a la energía y el medio ambiente, y en 2013 recibió la Medalla Presidencial de la Libertad de Estados Unidos. Murió en la Ciudad de México el 7 de octubre de 2020, a los 77 años.

Words: *el laboratorio* (laboratory), *de juguete* (toy), *el juego de química* (chemistry set),
*el doctorado* (doctorate, PhD), *subir* (here: to rise), *la luz ultravioleta* (ultraviolet
light), *al principio* (at first), *la conclusión* (conclusion), *firmar* (to sign), *reducir*
(to reduce), *la enseñanza* (teaching), *la libertad* (freedom).

Notice *convirtió un baño en un laboratorio*: *convertir* A *en* B = to turn A into B. With
*se* it means "to become": *se convirtió en un científico famoso*.

## Vida 2: Gabriela Mistral, maestra y poeta (Chile, 1889–1957)

This biography is told in the present, although everything in it is past.

> Lucila Godoy Alcayaga nace el 7 de abril de 1889 en Vicuña, en el valle de Elqui, en Chile. A los quince años ya trabaja como ayudante en una escuela rural, y durante muchos años es maestra en distintas partes del país.
>
> Desde joven escribe poesía con un nombre nuevo: Gabriela Mistral. En 1914 gana un concurso de poesía en Santiago con sus «Sonetos de la muerte», y poco a poco se convierte en una poeta muy conocida.
>
> En 1922 el gobierno de México la invita a colaborar en la reforma de la educación, y allí trabaja con José Vasconcelos, el secretario de Educación, en proyectos de escuelas y bibliotecas. Ese mismo año publica en Nueva York su primer libro, *Desolación*.
>
> A partir de 1932 trabaja como cónsul de Chile en varias ciudades de Europa y América. En 1945 recibe el Premio Nobel de Literatura: es la primera persona de América Latina que gana ese premio.
>
> Muere el 10 de enero de 1957 en Hempstead, cerca de Nueva York. Hoy su cara aparece en el billete de cinco mil pesos chilenos, un homenaje a la maestra y a la poeta.

Words: *el ayudante* (assistant), *rural* (rural, in the country), *distinto* (different), *el
concurso* (competition), *el soneto* (sonnet), *poco a poco* (little by little), *colaborar* (to work together, to contribute), *la reforma* (reform), *a
partir de* (from, starting in), *el cónsul* (consul), *el billete* (banknote).

### The historical present

The **[[historical present]]** tells past events in the present tense: *nace en 1889, gana un
concurso, recibe el Premio Nobel*. Encyclopedias, museum labels, timelines and the Spanish
press use it often for lives and history. It makes the text feel immediate, and the dates
leave no doubt that it's the past. Read it as the past: most verbs are events (*nace, gana*
= *nació, ganó*), a few are background (*ya trabaja* = *ya trabajaba*), and a sentence with *hoy*
is a real present (*Hoy su cara aparece en el billete*). When you write, choose one tense and
keep it.

## Vida 3: Roberto Clemente, beisbolista y héroe (Puerto Rico, 1934–1972)

> Roberto Clemente nació el 18 de agosto de 1934 en Carolina, Puerto Rico. En 1955 empezó a jugar con los Piratas de Pittsburgh, en las Grandes Ligas de Estados Unidos, y jugó con ese equipo toda su carrera.
>
> Fue uno de los mejores jugadores de su época: ganó dos Series Mundiales, en 1960 y en 1971, cuatro títulos de bateo de la Liga Nacional, y fue el Jugador Más Valioso de la liga en 1966. En su última temporada, la de 1972, llegó a los 3,000 hits.
>
> En diciembre de 1972 hubo un terremoto terrible en Nicaragua. Clemente organizó la ayuda para las víctimas desde Puerto Rico, y el 31 de diciembre decidió viajar en uno de los aviones con comida y medicinas. El avión cayó al mar poco después de salir de San Juan. Nunca encontraron su cuerpo.
>
> Normalmente un jugador tiene que esperar cinco años después de su último partido para entrar al Salón de la Fama del Beisbol, pero para Clemente hicieron una excepción: entró en 1973, y fue el primer jugador nacido en América Latina en el Salón de la Fama. Para muchos puertorriqueños, se convirtió en un héroe. Desde 1973, el premio Roberto Clemente reconoce cada año a un jugador de las Grandes Ligas por su trabajo en la comunidad.

Words: *las Grandes Ligas* (the major leagues), *la época* (era, time), *la Serie Mundial*
(World Series), *el título de bateo* (batting title), *valioso* (valuable), *el hit* (hit, in
baseball), *la víctima* (victim), *la medicina* (medicine), *el Salón de la Fama* (Hall of
Fame), *la excepción* (exception), *nacido en* (born in), *la comunidad* (community).

Puerto Rico is not a country: it is a territory of the United States, and Puerto Ricans are US
citizens by birth, with their own Spanish-speaking culture. That's why this lesson says "three
places" rather than "three countries".

## The three lives side by side

| | Mario Molina | Gabriela Mistral | Roberto Clemente |
|---|---|---|---|
| From | Mexico City | Vicuña, Chile | Carolina, Puerto Rico |
| Field | chemistry | poetry and education | baseball |
| Main achievement | showed that CFCs damage the ozone layer | Nobel Prize in Literature, 1945 | 3,000 hits; aid for Nicaragua |
| Tense of the text | preterite | historical present | preterite |

### Example 1: From dates to sentences

A DELE-style task can give you data like this: *1943: nace (Ciudad de México) · 1965: se gradúa
(UNAM) · 1995: Premio Nobel*. Turn each line into a sentence:

1. Choose the tense: preterite (*nació, se graduó, recibió*).
2. Add the date with *en* and no article: *en 1943*; for a full date, *el 19 de marzo de 1943*.
3. Link the sentences: *Mario Molina nació en la Ciudad de México en 1943. Estudió en la UNAM
   y se graduó en 1965. Treinta años después, en 1995, recibió el Premio Nobel de Química.*

### Example 2: From the historical present to the preterite

Retell Gabriela Mistral's fourth paragraph in the preterite.

| Historical present | Preterite |
|---|---|
| *trabaja* | *trabajó* |
| *recibe* | *recibió* |
| *es la primera persona* | *fue la primera persona* |
| *gana* | *ganó* |

Result: *A partir de 1932 trabajó como cónsul de Chile en varias ciudades. En 1945 recibió el
Premio Nobel de Literatura: fue la primera persona de América Latina que ganó ese premio.* *Es*
becomes *fue*: in a finished life, "she was the first" is a fact about the past.

### Example 3: Writing your own

Plan with a timeline like the one above (birth, studies, work, family, today), then write about
70 words, as in the exam. This model is about an invented grandmother (68 words):

> Mi abuela Carmen nació en Morelia en 1952. De niña vivía en el campo y le encantaba leer. A los dieciocho años se mudó a la Ciudad de México para estudiar Enfermería. Trabajó treinta años en un hospital público y se dedicó a cuidar a niños enfermos. Se casó en 1978 y tuvo tres hijos. Hoy está jubilada, vive en Morelia y todavía lee un libro cada semana.

The preterite tells the events (*nació, se mudó, trabajó*), the imperfect the background (*vivía,
le encantaba*), and the present the situation now (*está jubilada, vive*).

## Pronunciation

- Years are read as full numbers: *1943* = *mil novecientos cuarenta y tres*; *2020* = *dos mil
  veinte*.
- *Mistral*: mees-TRAL; *Clemente*: kle-MEN-te; *Molina*: mo-LEE-na.
- *Pittsburgh* is usually said roughly as in English; *Piratas* is pee-RA-tas.

## Common mistakes

- ~~Fue nacido en 1943~~ → *Nació en 1943*. Spanish uses the active verb *nacer*.
- ~~En 15 años~~ for an age → *a los 15 años*.
- *El primer mexicano que ganó* (or *en ganar*) the prize: after *el primero / la primera* use
  *que* + verb or *en* + infinitive.
- Mixing the historical present and the preterite in one text. Choose one and keep it.
- *se murió* is everyday speech; a written biography says *murió*.

## Key points

- A short biography moves through birth, studies, work, achievement, death and legacy, carried
  by dates: *en 1943, a los quince años, a partir de 1932, desde 1973*.
- Preterite for events, imperfect for background, present for "today".
- The **[[historical present]]** (*nace, gana, recibe*) is common in biographies; read it as past.
- *Convertir A en B* = to turn A into B; *convertirse en* = to become.
- New words: *el poeta, la poesía, dedicarse, convertirse, la investigación, el
  investigador, el químico, la capa de ozono, el terremoto, la ayuda, el homenaje, reconocer, la
  medalla, la temporada*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Escuchar: radio, podcasts and announcements
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Listening is often the hardest skill at A2: you can't go back, the speaker doesn't slow down,
and the words run together. The DELE A2 listening test uses short everyday conversations,
short radio items, a longer conversation and recorded messages. This lesson trains you on the
same kinds of sound: a radio news bulletin, an ad, announcements at a bus station and an
airport, and a short podcast conversation, all original scripts written for this course. The
station, the bakery, the airline and the podcast are invented.

Every script below is in a player: press 🔊 for one line or "Play all", and turn on "Hide
the words" to listen before you read. The voice is your device's, which speaks clearly; real
radio is faster, so the lesson also shows you what fast speech does to words.

## A plan for listening

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A plan for listening to a recording
  accDescr: Before you listen, look at the situation and the questions, and predict the words you'll hear. On the first listen, catch the general idea: who is speaking, where, and why. On the second listen, catch the key words and the numbers: times, prices, gates, platforms. Then check your answers against the transcript and listen once more to the parts you missed.
  A["Before: what's the situation? Predict the words"] --> B["Listen 1: the general idea (who, where, why)"]
  B --> C["Listen 2: key words and numbers (times, prices, gates)"]
  C --> D["Check with the transcript"]
  D --> E["Listen again to the parts you missed"]
```

- Predict. A station announcement will have *andén, salida, retraso*; a forecast *grados,
  lluvia, soleado*. Thinking of them first makes them easier to hear.
- First listen for the **[[gist]]**: the general idea, not the details. Who's talking, and why?
- Then listen for key words: the stressed ones carry the meaning, and numbers matter most.
- Don't stop at a word you missed. The next sentence often explains it.

## 1. Un boletín de noticias

A *boletín* is a short news bulletin; a longer news program is *un noticiero* in Mexico (Spain:
*un informativo*). The presenter is *el locutor* or *la locutora*; the listeners are *los
oyentes*. Radio Sol is an invented *emisora* (radio station).

```dialogue lang=es-MX
# Radio Sol: el boletín de las ocho
Locutora: Buenos días, queridos oyentes. Son las ocho de la mañana y esto es Radio Sol, noventa y nueve punto cinco. Les saluda Andrea Ruiz con el boletín de las ocho.
= Good morning, dear listeners. It's eight a.m. and this is Radio Sol, 99.5. Andrea Ruiz here with the eight o'clock bulletin.
Locutora: En la ciudad, el tráfico está muy lento en la avenida Juárez por un choque entre dos camiones. No hay heridos, pero la policía recomienda tomar otra ruta.
= In the city, traffic is very slow on Avenida Juárez because of a crash between two trucks. Nobody is hurt, but the police recommend taking another route.
Locutora: Buenas noticias para los lectores: este sábado empieza la Feria del Libro en la plaza principal. La entrada es gratis, y el sábado y el domingo habrá talleres para niños de diez a dos.
= Good news for readers: the Book Fair starts this Saturday in the main square. Entry is free, and on Saturday and Sunday there will be workshops for children from ten to two.
Locutora: En deportes, los Halcones ganaron anoche dos a uno, y el domingo juegan la final en casa. Nosotros vamos a transmitir el partido en vivo desde el estadio.
= In sports, the Halcones won two to one last night, and on Sunday they play the final at home. We're going to broadcast the game live from the stadium.
Locutora: Y el clima: hoy tendremos una mañana soleada, con una máxima de veintiséis grados, pero por la tarde se esperan lluvias fuertes. Lleven paraguas.
= And the weather: today we'll have a sunny morning with a high of twenty-six degrees, but heavy rain is expected in the afternoon. Take an umbrella.
Locutora: Son las ocho y cinco. Seguimos con música, aquí en Radio Sol.
= It's five past eight. Music next, here on Radio Sol.
```

Listen for the radio's own phrases: *Les saluda…* (literally "… greets you"), *En deportes*,
*Y el clima*, *Seguimos con…* They mark where each item starts. *Lleven paraguas* is an
*ustedes* command (lesson 16), the radio talking to all its listeners.

## 2. Un anuncio

```dialogue lang=es-MX
# Panadería La Espiga
Voz: ¿Quieres pan recién hecho para el desayuno? Ven a Panadería La Espiga.
= Do you want freshly baked bread for breakfast? Come to La Espiga bakery.
Voz: Tenemos conchas, bolillos y pasteles desde las siete de la mañana.
= We have conchas, bolillos and cakes from seven in the morning.
Voz: Y solo este mes, los martes son de promoción: compras dos conchas y te llevas tres.
= And this month only, Tuesdays are special-offer days: buy two conchas and take home three.
Voz: Estamos en la calle Hidalgo número cuarenta y cinco, frente al jardín. Abrimos de lunes a sábado, de siete a nueve.
= We're at 45 Hidalgo Street, opposite the town square. We're open Monday to Saturday, seven to nine.
Voz: Panadería La Espiga: ¡el pan de tu colonia!
= La Espiga bakery: your neighborhood's bread!
```

Ads talk to *tú* and use commands (*Ven*), questions and short phrases. The facts you need are
always the same: what, where, when, how much. *Recién hecho* = freshly made; *el jardín* is
here the town square, as in many Mexican towns; a *concha* is a sweet bun and a *bolillo* a
crusty roll.

## 3. Avisos: the bus station and the airport

Announcements (*avisos*) use a formal, fixed language. Two phrases appear in almost every one:
*con destino a* (going to, bound for) and *procedente de* (coming from). And in Mexico and other
parts of Latin America you'll hear *favor de* + infinitive for a polite instruction: *Favor de
abordar*, please board; *Favor de no fumar*, please don't smoke.

```dialogue lang=es-MX
# En la central de autobuses
Altavoz: Pasajeros con destino a Querétaro, favor de abordar el autobús de las catorce treinta en el andén siete.
= Passengers for Querétaro, please board the 14:30 bus at platform seven.
Altavoz: Se informa a los pasajeros procedentes de Guadalajara que el autobús llegará con veinte minutos de retraso.
= Passengers arriving from Guadalajara are informed that the bus will arrive twenty minutes late.
```

```dialogue lang=es-MX
# En el aeropuerto
Altavoz: Aerolínea Halcón informa a los pasajeros del vuelo cuatro ochenta y dos con destino a Cancún que la salida tiene un retraso. La nueva hora de salida es a las dieciséis cuarenta y cinco, por la puerta doce.
= Halcón Airlines informs passengers on flight 482 to Cancún that the departure is delayed. The new departure time is 16:45, from gate twelve.
Altavoz: Último aviso para el pasajero Julián Reyes Mora, con destino a Monterrey: favor de presentarse de inmediato en la puerta ocho.
= Final call for passenger Julián Reyes Mora, traveling to Monterrey: please go to gate eight immediately.
```

![An airport departures board titled Salidas, with five columns: Vuelo, Destino, Hora, Puerta, Estado. AH 482 to Cancún at 15:20, gate 12, Retrasado 16:45. AH 215 to Monterrey at 15:35, gate 8, Última llamada. AH 760 to Oaxaca at 15:50, gate 14, A tiempo. AH 133 to Tijuana at 16:05, gate 3, Cancelado. AH 904 to Mérida at 16:10, gate 10, A tiempo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Announcements give times on the 24-hour clock (*las dieciséis cuarenta y cinco* = 4:45 p.m.),
and flight numbers are often read in groups (*cuatro ochenta y dos* for 482), though you'll
also hear *cuatrocientos ochenta y dos*.

## 4. Un pódcast

A *pódcast* (the Spanish spelling, with an accent; plural *los pódcast*; you'll also see
*podcast*) comes in *episodios*, and listeners *se suscriben* (subscribe).

```dialogue lang=es-MX
# Palabras al aire, episodio 12
Diego: ¡Hola, hola! Bienvenidos a «Palabras al aire», el pódcast para gente que aprende idiomas. Yo soy Diego.
= Hello, hello! Welcome to "Palabras al aire", the podcast for people learning languages. I'm Diego.
Lupita: Y yo soy Lupita. Hoy hablamos de algo que nos preguntan mucho: ¿cómo podemos escuchar mejor en otro idioma?
= And I'm Lupita. Today we're talking about something people ask us a lot: how can we listen better in another language?
Diego: Mira, cuando yo empecé a aprender inglés, no entendía nada en la radio. Hablaban rapidísimo, y yo terminaba cansadísimo.
= Look, when I started learning English I didn't understand anything on the radio. They talked super fast, and I ended up exhausted.
Lupita: ¡A todos nos pasa! Mi consejo número uno: antes de escuchar, piensa en el tema. Si es el pronóstico del tiempo, ya sabes qué palabras vas a oír.
= It happens to all of us! My tip number one: before you listen, think about the topic. If it's the weather forecast, you already know what words you're going to hear.
Diego: Y el número dos: primero escucha la idea general. No necesitas entender todas las palabras.
= And number two: first listen for the general idea. You don't need to understand every word.
Lupita: Exacto. Y después, escucha los detalles: números, nombres, horas.
= Exactly. And after that, listen for the details: numbers, names, times.
Diego: Yo escuchaba el mismo episodio muchas veces. La primera vez entendía un treinta por ciento; la quinta vez, casi todo.
= I used to listen to the same episode lots of times. The first time I understood about thirty percent; the fifth time, almost everything.
Lupita: Bueno, eso es todo por hoy. Si les gustó, suscríbanse y compártanlo con sus amigos.
= Well, that's all for today. If you liked it, subscribe and share it with your friends.
Diego: ¡Nos escuchamos la próxima semana!
= Talk to you next week!
```

*Suscríbanse* and *compártanlo* are *ustedes* commands with pronouns attached (lesson 16): the
hosts speak to all their listeners. *Nos escuchamos* (literally "we'll hear each other") is the
podcast and radio version of *nos vemos*.

## The sounds of fast speech

Real speakers don't pronounce every sound. This is **[[connected speech]]**: words join, vowels
merge and some sounds get weaker. Recognize these; you don't need to copy them.

| Careful | Fast | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| *los otros* | *lo-so-tros* | a final consonant joins the next vowel |
| *va a ir* | *vair* (almost one word) | the same vowels merge |
| *mi hermano* | *mier-MA-no* | two vowels across words share a syllable |
| *para, para el* | *pa', pa'l* | very common in casual speech |
| *cansado* | *cansao* | the *d* of *-ado* weakens or disappears |
| *usted, verdad* | *usté, verdá* | a final *d* is soft or silent |

The Spanish academies' *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* describes the lost *d* in *-ado* as
frequent in relaxed speech, especially in Spain, Puerto Rico, Paraguay and Chile, and advises
against it in careful speech. Recognize it wherever you hear it, and keep the *d* yourself.

### Example 1: Predicting an announcement

You're at gate 12 for flight AH 482 and the board says *Retrasado*. An announcement starts.

1. Predict the words: *vuelo, Cancún, retraso, nueva hora, puerta*.
2. Listen 1: is it your flight? You hear *vuelo cuatro ochenta y dos con destino a Cancún*:
   yes.
3. Listen 2: the numbers. *Dieciséis cuarenta y cinco* = 16:45; *puerta doce* = gate 12.
4. Conclusion: same gate, new time, 4:45 p.m. It matches the board.

### Example 2: Catching numbers

Numbers fly past in fast speech. Break them into the parts you know.

| You hear | Parts | Write |
|---|---|---|
| *noventa y nueve punto cinco* | 99 + *punto* + 5 | 99.5 |
| *las catorce treinta* | 14 + 30 | 14:30 |
| *calle Hidalgo número cuarenta y cinco* | 45 | Hidalgo 45 |
| *un treinta por ciento* | 30 + percent | 30% |

Spanish usually puts an article before a percentage (*el 30 %, un 30 %*), where English has
none: *entendía un treinta por ciento* = I understood thirty percent. Diego's figure is a rough
one, so the translation says "about".

### Example 3: Decoding fast speech

A friend leaves you a voice note: *"Toy cansao, voy pa' la casa."*

1. *Toy*: the *es-* of *estoy* has fallen off in very casual speech: *estoy*.
2. *cansao*: the *d* of *-ado* has gone: *cansado*.
3. *pa'*: *para*.
4. Careful form: *Estoy cansado, voy para la casa.* (I'm tired, I'm heading home.)

## Pronunciation

- Shadow the scripts: play one line, pause, and repeat it at the same speed.
- In announcements, the stress falls hard on the key words: *an-DÉN SIE-te, PUER-ta DO-ce*.
- *pódcast* is stressed on the first syllable (POD-kast), as the accent shows.

## Common mistakes

- Trying to understand every word on the first listen. Get the gist first.
- Mixing up *con destino a* (going to) and *procedente de* (coming from).
- Writing 24-hour times as 12-hour ones without changing them: *las dieciséis* is 4 p.m., not
  6 o'clock.
- Copying fast-speech forms in writing: write *para* and *cansado*.

## Key points

- Listen in stages: predict, the **[[gist]]**, then key words and numbers, then check.
- Radio: *el locutor, los oyentes, la emisora, el boletín, el noticiero, transmitir en vivo*.
- Announcements: *con destino a, procedente de, favor de* + infinitive, *último aviso*, the
  24-hour clock.
- Podcasts: *el pódcast, el episodio, suscribirse*.
- **[[Connected speech]]**: *pa', cansao, usté*. Recognize them; write and speak the careful forms.
- New words: *el locutor, el oyente, la emisora, el noticiero, el boletín, en vivo, transmitir,
  el pódcast, el episodio, el pasajero, con destino a, procedente de, favor de, el aviso,
  suscribirse*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: Planes, viajes y tiempo libre (plans, travel and free time)
Trabajo, estudios y servicios (work, studies and services)
Noticias, opiniones y el DELE A2 (news, opinions and the A2 exam)
Honors: Leer y escuchar (reading and listening)

questions.stem: In part 1, don Ernesto says "Algunas cosas no se arreglan con herramientas." What does the end of the story show he was thinking about?
choices: He didn't have the right tools for such a big clock.
The priest didn't allow anyone into the tower.
His sadness after his wife's death, when he stopped the clock himself.
The clock was too old to be repaired.
questions.explanation: In part 5 he explains that his wife Rosario died at 4:10 and that he took out the part that day: "No quería oír las horas sin ella." The clock could be fixed with tools (Mateo and Sofía fix it in part 4); what couldn't be fixed with tools was his grief. Nothing in the story says the priest or the clock's age was the problem.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they really happened (not the order the story tells them).
choices: Rosario muere y don Ernesto quita la pieza del reloj.
Mateo ayuda a don Ernesto en el taller los sábados.
Don Ernesto se siente mal y va al hospital.
Laura le da a Mateo una caja de madera.
La campana de la torre suena otra vez.
Don Ernesto le cuenta su secreto a Mateo en la plaza.
questions.explanation: Rosario's death comes first, thirty years before the story, even though it is told last (a flashback in part 5). Then: the Saturdays in the shop (part 1), the hospital (part 2), the box weeks later (part 2), the bell (part 4), and the secret two months later (part 5).

questions.stem: Part 1: "Sus manecillas marcaban siempre las cuatro y diez." From the context, what are "las manecillas" of a clock?
questions.explanation: The manecillas belong to the clock and "marcaban" (showed) a time: those are the hands. Part 4 confirms it: "las manecillas se movieron" and "Las pusimos en las doce." The bell is "la campana" and the wheels are "las ruedas".

questions.stem: Todas las tardes, después de la escuela, yo ___ la puerta y esperaba.
questions.explanation: "Todas las tardes" (every afternoon) is a repeated action in the past, so the imperfect: "miraba", like "esperaba" in the same sentence. "Miré" is one finished look, "he mirado" is the present perfect, and "mirando" is a gerund, not a conjugated verb.

questions.stem: Un sábado de marzo ___ la calle como siempre, pero la puerta del taller estaba cerrada.
questions.explanation: One particular Saturday, a single event that moves the story: the preterite "crucé". The z of cruzar becomes c before e (crucé, like empecé). "Cruzaba" would be a habit or background, "cruzo" is the present, and "cruzé" is a spelling mistake.

questions.stem: Type the preterite of abrir (él/ella): Toqué varias veces. Nadie ___.
questions.explanation: One event in the story, so the preterite: "Nadie abrió" (Nobody opened). Abrir is regular in the preterite: abrí, abriste, abrió. (Only its participle, abierto, is irregular.)

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the church tower.

image.alt: A cross-section of a church bell tower with a bell at the top, a clock face showing ten past four, gear wheels and a crank inside, a staircase and a wooden door at the bottom. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the bell (la campana), 2 the hands of the clock (las manecillas), 3 the gear wheels (las ruedas), 4 the narrow staircase (la escalera) and 5 the door (la puerta). The flashlight (la linterna) and the dust (el polvo) are in the story but not in the picture.

questions.stem: Father Tomás: "¡La llave de la torre! La buscamos durante años." What does "La" in "La buscamos" refer to?
questions.explanation: "La" is a direct object pronoun that replaces the feminine noun just mentioned: "buscamos la llave" (we looked for the key). The tower, the church and the bell were never lost.

questions.stem: Mateo asks don Ernesto: "¿Y por qué me la dio a mí?" What does "la" mean here?
questions.explanation: In part 5 they are talking about the part: "Usted tenía la pieza." "Me la dio" = "me dio la pieza" (you gave it to me). "Me" is the indirect object (to me) and "la" the direct object (it = la pieza).

questions.stem: Match each word from the story to its meaning.
questions.explanation: El taller is don Ernesto's workshop, las herramientas his tools, la linterna Sofía's flashlight, el polvo the dust in the tower, and la campana the bell. "Drawer" is el cajón, which isn't in the list.

questions.stem: Which of these words from the lesson can you safely guess from English? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: El mecanismo (mechanism), exactamente (exactly) and el hospital (hospital) are cognates. La escoba (broom) and el cajón (drawer) don't look like their English meanings, and la librería is a false friend: it means bookshop, not library.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Laura gave it (the box) to me.
questions.explanation: Two pronouns go before the conjugated verb, indirect first: "me la dio" (to me, it). "La" agrees with "la caja". The subject can come first or last: "Me la dio Laura" is also correct. "Le" is wrong here: the box was given to me, not to him or her.

questions.stem: What does the last paragraph tell us about Mateo today?
choices: He sold the shop and moved to Puebla.
He is a clockmaker, and a boy from across the street helps him.
He still doesn't know why the clock stopped.
He never climbed the tower again.
questions.explanation: "Hoy tengo veinticinco años y soy relojero. Los sábados, un niño de la casa de enfrente me ayuda": Mateo now does what don Ernesto did, and a new boy helps him, just as he once helped. Laura didn't sell the shop, and don Ernesto told Mateo why the clock stopped.

questions.stem: You read "Unas palomas salieron volando cuando abrimos la puerta de arriba" and you don't know "palomas". What is the best strategy here?
choices: Stop and look up every word in the paragraph.
Read the whole part again from the beginning.
Skip it: "some ___ flew out" is enough to follow the story.
questions.explanation: The sentence makes sense without the word: something flew out when they opened the door. Skipping keeps you in the story. (Palomas are pigeons.) Looking up every word loses the thread, and "palm" is a false guess.

questions.stem: Scan the Bogotá entry. How high is Bogotá?
questions.explanation: "Bogotá está a unos 2,600 metros de altura." The 14 is the average temperature in degrees, 2,240 m is Mexico City's height (not in the blog), and 1913 is the year Buenos Aires opened its subway.

questions.stem: Why was it cold in Buenos Aires when Valeria arrived in July?
choices: Because the city is very high, like Bogotá.
Because it is in the southern hemisphere, where July is winter.
Because it rained every day that week.
Because the city is near the Andes.
questions.explanation: "Argentina está en el hemisferio sur, y en julio es pleno invierno." South of the equator the seasons are reversed. Buenos Aires is low, on the Río de la Plata, far from the Andes, and the blog says nothing about rain there.

questions.stem: At her hotel in Bogotá, the receptionist tells Valeria "Tómese un tinto". What is "un tinto" there?
questions.explanation: In Colombia (and Ecuador) un tinto is a small black coffee; Valeria explains "Aquí un tinto no es vino". Everywhere, "vino tinto" is red wine, which is the trap.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on the map.

image.alt: A map of South America with three red city dots and the Andes drawn as a line of small peaks. Six places are numbered: three cities, two oceans and the mountains.

questions.explanation: 1 Bogotá, high in the Andes in the north-west; 2 Lima, on the Pacific coast; 3 Buenos Aires, on the Río de la Plata by the Atlantic; 4 the Pacific Ocean to the west; 5 the Atlantic to the east; 6 the Andes, running down the west of the continent. Mexico City and the Caribbean Sea are off this map.

questions.stem: Martín speaks with vos. Match each of his forms to the tú form you would use.
questions.explanation: Vos present forms stress the ending and don't change the stem: sos (eres), querés (quieres), tenés (tienes). Vos commands are the infinitive without -r, stressed at the end: mirá (mira), vení (ven). "Vienes" is the tú present of venir (you come), not a command.

questions.stem: Martín asks "¿Querés un mate?" Say it with tú: ¿___ un mate?
questions.explanation: Querer changes e → ie for tú: quieres. The vos form querés keeps the e and stresses the ending.

questions.stem: Which statements does the lesson's comparison table support? Select all that apply.
choices: Bogotá es la más alta de las tres ciudades.
Lima tiene más habitantes que Bogotá.
La ciudad de Buenos Aires tiene más habitantes que Lima.
En Buenos Aires, julio es invierno.
Bogotá está en la costa del Pacífico.
questions.explanation: Bogotá (about 2,600 m) is the only high city; Lima has about 10.4 million people against Bogotá's 8.0 million; and Buenos Aires has winter from June to August. The city of Buenos Aires has about 3.1 million, fewer than Lima (only Greater Buenos Aires is larger), and Bogotá is in the mountains, not on the coast.

questions.stem: Martín says: "Che, ¿bailamos?" What does "che" do in this sentence?
choices: It gets a friend's attention, like "hey".
questions.explanation: Che is a friendly call for attention in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia, like "hey" or "say". It is informal, not formal, and has nothing to do with tango or time.

questions.stem: In Lima, Valeria ordered "una ensalada con palta". What would she ask for at home in Monterrey?
questions.explanation: Palta is avocado in Peru, Chile, Argentina and Uruguay; Mexico says aguacate. The blog says so: "Era aguacate, claro." In Peru the chili pepper is ají, not palta.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Bogotá is the highest of the three.
questions.explanation: The superlative is "la más" + adjective + "de" for the group: la más alta de las tres. "Que" is for comparing two things (más alta que Lima). "La más alta de las tres es Bogotá" and "De las tres, Bogotá es la más alta" are also correct.

questions.stem: In Bogotá Valeria writes: "Arriba hacía todavía más frío, pero la vista era increíble." Why are "hacía" and "era" in the imperfect?
choices: They describe what it was like up there, the background to her visit.
They are actions that happened many times.
They are events that finished at a moment.
The imperfect is always used for the weather.
questions.explanation: The imperfect describes the scene: the cold and the view at the top. The event itself, going up, is preterite ("subí"). The weather can take the preterite too when it's a finished event (Ayer llovió tres horas), so "always" is wrong.

questions.stem: Skim the Buenos Aires entry. Which title fits it best?
choices: A week of rain on the coast
Winter, mate and a first tango
Climbing a mountain by cable car
questions.explanation: Skimming the first lines and the words that repeat gives cold weather (invierno, bufanda), Martín's mate and the tango at San Telmo. Nobody gets lost, the rain belongs to no entry, and the cable car is in Bogotá.

questions.stem: Put these moments of Valeria's trip in order.
choices: Se compra una chamarra más gruesa.
Sube en teleférico al cerro de Monserrate.
Da un paseo en bicicleta en la Ciclovía.
questions.explanation: Bogotá: the thicker jacket on Wednesday, Monserrate on Saturday, the Ciclovía on Sunday. Then Lima (the ceviche). In Buenos Aires Martín offers her a mate on the first day, and she dances tango on Sunday.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence from the blog: Lima está en la costa del ___ Pacífico.
questions.explanation: El océano Pacífico, the Pacific Ocean. Océano carries an accent on the e: o-CÉ-a-no.

questions.stem: When did Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland publish their article on CFCs and the ozone layer?
questions.explanation: "En 1974 publicaron un artículo muy importante." In 1972 Molina finished his doctorate, in 1987 countries signed the Montreal Protocol, and in 1995 he received the Nobel Prize.

questions.stem: Complete Mario Molina's timeline: match each numbered year to its event.

image.alt: A vertical timeline titled Mario Molina, 1943 to 2020, with seven years (1943, 1965, 1972, 1974, 1987, 1995, 2020) and a box beside each. The 1972 box says Doctorado en Berkeley; the other six are empty and numbered.

choices: Nace en la Ciudad de México
Artículo sobre los CFC y el ozono
Muere en la Ciudad de México
questions.explanation: 1943 birth in Mexico City; 1965 graduation from the UNAM; 1974 the article on CFCs and ozone; 1987 the Montreal Protocol; 1995 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry; 2020 his death in Mexico City. The poetry competition belongs to Gabriela Mistral (1914).

questions.stem: Gabriela Mistral's biography says "En 1945 recibe el Premio Nobel de Literatura." Why is "recibe" in the present?
choices: She is still receiving the prize today.
It is the historical present: past events told in the present tense.
The present is used for every prize in Spanish.
questions.explanation: Biographies and timelines often use the historical present; the date (1945) makes it clear that it's past. Read it as the preterite "recibió". "Recibía" (imperfect) would describe a background or habit, not a single event.

questions.stem: Retell in the preterite: "Gabriela Mistral nace en 1889." → Gabriela Mistral ___ en 1889.
questions.explanation: Nacer is regular in the preterite: nací, naciste, nació. Birth is a single past event, so the preterite (not "nacía").

questions.stem: What did Gabriela Mistral do in Mexico, according to the text?
choices: She studied chemistry at the UNAM.
She published Desolación in Mexico City.
She received the Nobel Prize there.
She worked with José Vasconcelos on the reform of education.
questions.explanation: "En 1922 el gobierno de México la invita a colaborar en la reforma de la educación, y allí trabaja con José Vasconcelos." Desolación was published in New York, the Nobel came in 1945, and the UNAM chemist is Mario Molina.

questions.stem: Why did Roberto Clemente board the plane on 31 December 1972?
choices: To take food and medicine to earthquake victims in Nicaragua.
To play a game in Nicaragua.
To go to the Hall of Fame ceremony.
To return to Pittsburgh after the season.
questions.explanation: "Hubo un terremoto terrible en Nicaragua. Clemente organizó la ayuda para las víctimas… decidió viajar en uno de los aviones con comida y medicinas." He entered the Hall of Fame after his death, in 1973.

questions.stem: Match each person to what the text connects them with.
questions.explanation: Molina studied how CFCs destroy the ozone layer, Mistral was a poet and teacher, and Clemente a baseball player. None of the three is connected with music in the texts.

questions.stem: Which of these are true of Roberto Clemente, according to the text? Select all that apply.
choices: He played his whole career with the Pittsburgh Pirates.
He was the first Latin American-born player in the Hall of Fame.
He died in an earthquake in Nicaragua.
He was born in San Juan.
questions.explanation: The text says he played "con ese equipo toda su carrera", was "el primer jugador nacido en América Latina en el Salón de la Fama", and won two World Series (1960 and 1971). He died when his plane fell into the sea after leaving San Juan, and he was born in Carolina, Puerto Rico.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: He became a hero.
questions.explanation: Convertirse en = to become: "Se convirtió en un héroe." The reflexive pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, and the preposition is "en", not "a".

questions.stem: "A los quince años ya trabaja como ayudante en una escuela." What does "a los quince años" mean?
questions.explanation: A los + number + años gives an age: at fifteen. "In fifteen years" is dentro de quince años, "fifteen years ago" is hace quince años, and "for fifteen years" is durante quince años.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct Spanish for "He was born in 1943"?
questions.explanation: Spanish uses the active verb: nació, with "en" before a year. "Fue nacido" copies English, "a 1943" has the wrong preposition, and the present perfect "ha nacido" doesn't fit a finished date in the past.

questions.stem: Put the parts of a short biography in the usual order this lesson describes.
questions.explanation: Short biographies usually go from birth and childhood to studies, then work and the main achievement, then later life and death, and end with the person's legacy today (a banknote, a prize in their name).

questions.stem: Molina fue el primer mexicano que ___ el Nobel de Química.
questions.explanation: "El primer … que" + a finished past event: the preterite ganó. (You can also say "el primer mexicano en ganar".) "Ganaba" is a habit or background, "gana" is the present, and the gerund "ganando" can't follow "que" here.

questions.stem: Type the preterite of mudarse (ella): Mi abuela ___ a la Ciudad de México a los dieciocho años.
questions.explanation: A single event in a life story: the preterite. Mudarse is reflexive, so the pronoun goes first: se mudó (she moved).

questions.stem: Listen to the announcement. What should these passengers do?

audio.text: Pasajeros con destino a Querétaro, favor de abordar en el andén siete.

choices: Board the bus to Querétaro at platform 7.
Wait for the bus arriving from Querétaro at platform 7.
Board the bus to Querétaro at platform 17.
Board the bus to Guadalajara at platform 7.
questions.explanation: "Con destino a Querétaro" = going to Querétaro, "favor de abordar" = please board, "el andén siete" = platform 7. A bus arriving from somewhere would be "procedente de"; seventeen is diecisiete.

questions.stem: Listen and look at the departures board. Which flight is the announcement about?

image.alt: A departures board for Aerolínea Halcón. AH 482 to Cancún, 15:20, gate 12, delayed to 16:45. AH 215 to Monterrey, 15:35, gate 8, final call. AH 760 to Oaxaca, 15:50, gate 14, on time. AH 133 to Tijuana, 16:05, gate 3, cancelled. AH 904 to Mérida, 16:10, gate 10, on time.

audio.text: Último aviso para los pasajeros del vuelo con destino a Monterrey: favor de presentarse en la puerta ocho.

questions.explanation: Monterrey and gate 8 (puerta ocho) point to AH 215, whose status is "Última llamada": "último aviso" is the final call. AH 482 goes to Cancún, AH 904 to Mérida, and AH 133 to Tijuana.

questions.stem: Listen and type what you hear: ___
questions.explanation: "Favor de no fumar": please don't smoke. Favor de + infinitive is a polite instruction heard in Mexico and other parts of Latin America; "no" goes before the infinitive.

questions.stem: Listen to the weather report. What will the afternoon be like?

audio.text: Hoy tendremos una mañana soleada, con una máxima de veintiséis grados, pero por la tarde se esperan lluvias fuertes.

questions.explanation: "Por la tarde se esperan lluvias fuertes": heavy rain is expected in the afternoon. The sunny morning with a high of 26 degrees comes first: listen for the time words (la mañana, por la tarde).

questions.stem: An announcement gives "las dieciséis cuarenta y cinco". What time is that?
questions.explanation: Announcements use the 24-hour clock: dieciséis = 16 = 4 p.m., and cuarenta y cinco = 45 minutes. So 16:45 = 4:45 p.m. 6 p.m. would be las dieciocho.

questions.stem: Match each phrase from the announcements to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Con destino a = going to, bound for; procedente de = coming from; favor de + infinitive = please …; último aviso = final call. "Delayed" is retrasado (or con retraso).

questions.stem: In fast casual speech you may hear these forms. Match each to its careful form.
questions.explanation: Pa' and pa'l are para and para el; cansao loses the d of -ado; usté loses its final d. Recognize them, but write and say the careful forms.

questions.stem: Before an airport announcement starts, which words should you expect to hear? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Predicting helps you hear: an airport announcement talks about a flight (el vuelo), a gate (la puerta), a destination (con destino a) and often a delay (el retraso). A recipe and a cake belong to a cooking show or an ad.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the lesson's listening plan in order.
choices: Look at the situation and predict the words
Listen for key words and numbers
Check your answers with the transcript
questions.explanation: Predict first, then listen for the gist (who, where, why), then for the details (numbers, names, times), and only then check with the transcript and replay what you missed.

questions.stem: In the ad for Panadería La Espiga, what is the Tuesday offer?
choices: Buy two conchas and take home three.
questions.explanation: "Los martes son de promoción: compras dos conchas y te llevas tres." The bakery opens at seven, Monday to Saturday, so that isn't the Tuesday offer, and nothing is free or half price.

questions.stem: In the podcast, what does Diego say about learning English?
choices: He understood almost everything from the start.
At first he understood nothing on the radio, and he listened to the same episode many times.
He only learned by reading the transcripts.
He stopped listening to the radio because it was too fast.
questions.explanation: "No entendía nada en la radio… Yo escuchaba el mismo episodio muchas veces. La primera vez entendía un treinta por ciento; la quinta vez, casi todo." He kept listening; he didn't give up.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Please board through gate eight.
questions.explanation: Favor de + infinitive: "Favor de abordar por la puerta ocho." "Por favor de" mixes two phrases: say "por favor" alone or "favor de" + infinitive. Announcements sometimes put the place first: "Por la puerta ocho, favor de abordar."

questions.stem: Listen and write the new departure time in figures, on the 24-hour clock (like 09:30): ___

audio.text: La nueva hora de salida es a las dieciséis cuarenta y cinco.

questions.explanation: Dieciséis cuarenta y cinco = 16:45 (4:45 p.m.). Break the number into parts: dieciséis (16), cuarenta y cinco (45).

questions.stem: Who reads the news on the radio?
questions.explanation: El locutor (la locutora) is the presenter or announcer. El oyente is the listener, el pasajero a passenger, and el episodio an episode of a podcast or a series.

questions.stem: Choose the preterite of "andar": Ayer ___ por el centro con mis amigos.
questions.explanation: "Andar" has a strong preterite: stem anduv- with the endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron and no written accents, so "anduve". "Andé" treats it as a regular verb (heard in casual speech, but not standard), "andó" is the regular él form, and "anduví" adds an accent and the wrong ending.

questions.stem: Mis abuelos ___ muchos regalos de Guadalajara. (traer)
questions.explanation: "Traer" has the strong stem traj-. After a j, the ellos ending is -eron, not -ieron: "trajeron" (like "dijeron"). "Trajieron" is the most common mistake; "traieron" and "traeron" ignore the new stem.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Hubieron dos bodas en mi familia el año pasado.
Tuvo dos bodas en mi familia el año pasado.
Hubo dos bodas en mi familia el año pasado.
Hay dos bodas en mi familia el año pasado.
questions.explanation: "Hubo" (there was, there were) reports events, and it never becomes plural: "Hubo dos bodas". "Hubieron" isn't standard, "tuvo" means "he/she had", and "hay" is present, which clashes with "el año pasado".

questions.stem: Mi hermano ___ la biografía de Juan Rulfo en dos días. (leer)
questions.explanation: Between two vowels the i of -ió is written y: le + ió → "leyó" (like "oyó, creyó, cayó, construyó"). "Leió" keeps the i, "lió" drops the e of the stem, and "leyió" has both y and i.

questions.stem: Mi abuela ___ en 2019, a los noventa años. (morir)
questions.explanation: -ir stem changers change o → u in the él and ellos preterite: "murió, murieron" (like "durmió"). "Morió" ignores the change, "muerió" uses the present-tense change (muere), and "murí" changes the yo form, which stays regular (morí) and is the wrong person anyway.

questions.stem: How do you say the year 1985 in Spanish?
choices: mil novecientos y ochenta y cinco
questions.explanation: Spanish reads a year as one number: mil (1000) + novecientos (900) + ochenta y cinco (85). It is never split into pairs as in English ("nineteen eighty-five"). 900 is "novecientos", not "nuevecientos", and "y" goes only between the tens and units.

questions.stem: Which is the natural way to say "She got married at 25"?
questions.explanation: An age at which something happened is "a los … años": "Se casó a los 25 años". Leaving out "los" sounds wrong, "en los 25 años" isn't used for an age, and "por 25 años" would mean "for 25 years".

questions.stem: Read: "Rafael nació en Tijuana en 1970. A los dieciocho años se mudó a Guadalajara para estudiar la carrera de medicina. Consiguió su título en 1994 y se casó dos años después." In what year did Rafael get married?
questions.explanation: He got his degree (título) in 1994 and married "dos años después", two years later: 1996. 1988 is when he moved to Guadalajara (1970 + 18).

questions.stem: Which of these preterite forms are spelled correctly? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Pidió" and "consiguieron" show the e → i change of -ir stem changers in the él and ellos forms, and "tuvo" is a strong preterite with no accent. "Durmí" is wrong because the yo form doesn't change (dormí), and "sentió" is wrong because él does change (sintió).

questions.stem: Write the preterite of "conseguir" (ella): Mi hermana ___ trabajo en una escuela de idiomas.
questions.explanation: "Conseguir" is an -ir stem changer: e → i in the él/ella preterite, "consiguió" (and "consiguieron"). The gu stays to keep the g hard before i.

questions.stem: Match each verb with its yo preterite.
questions.explanation: All five are strong preterites: a new stem (anduv-, pus-, dij-, sup-, vin-) and the ending -e, with no accent. "Vení" and "sabí" are made as if the verbs were regular.

questions.stem: These pictures show events in Rosa's life. Choose the verb for each numbered picture.

image.alt: A timeline titled La vida de Rosa Medina with six pictures above the years 1958, 1964, 1980, 1983, 1990 and 2018: a baby, a school, a graduation cap, two wedding rings, a moving box with an arrow to a house, and a rocking chair. Five pictures are numbered.

questions.explanation: The baby is her birth (nació, 1958), the cap her graduation (se graduó, 1980), the rings her wedding (se casó, 1983), the box and house a move (se mudó, 1990) and the rocking chair her retirement (se jubiló, 2018). The school in 1964 isn't numbered.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: What year did you graduate?
questions.explanation: The question phrase comes first, and the pronoun "te" goes right before the verb: "¿En qué año te graduaste?" "Se" is for él, ella or usted (¿En qué año se graduó?), which doesn't match "graduaste".

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: What did they tell you at the wedding?
questions.explanation: "Decir" has the strong stem dij-, and after j the ellos ending is -eron: "dijeron". The question word goes before the verb: "¿Qué te dijeron en la boda?" (In conversation you can also put the place first: "¿En la boda qué te dijeron?")

questions.stem: De niños, mis hermanos y yo ___ en la calle todas las tardes. (jugar)
questions.explanation: A habit in the past takes the imperfect. The nosotros form of an -ar verb has a written accent: "jugábamos". "Jugabamos" is missing the accent, "jugábanos" has the wrong ending, and "jugaban" is the ellos form, but the subject includes "yo".

questions.stem: Cuando era niña, ___ caricaturas todos los sábados. (ver, yo)
questions.explanation: "Ver" is one of the three irregular imperfects: it keeps the e of the infinitive, "veía". "Vía" drops it, "veo" is the present, and "veí" isn't a form of ver.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes a past habit?
choices: El verano pasado fuimos a la playa una vez.
Voy a ir a la playa.
Cada verano íbamos a la playa.
questions.explanation: "Cada verano" (every summer) and the imperfect "íbamos" describe something that happened again and again. "Ayer fui" and "fuimos … una vez" are single finished events (preterite), and "voy a ir" is a plan.

questions.stem: De niño, en mi escuela ___ dos columpios y un patio muy grande.
questions.explanation: "Había" (there was, there were) describes what existed in the past, and it stays singular even before a plural noun. "Hubo" reports an event, "habían" isn't standard for "there were", and "hay" is the present, which doesn't fit "De niño".

questions.stem: What does "De joven solía correr todos los días" mean?
choices: When I was young I used to run every day.
When I was young I ran once.
I usually run every day now.
When I'm older I'll run every day.
questions.explanation: "Solía" is the imperfect of soler: "used to". With "de joven" (when I was young) it describes a past habit. The present "suelo correr" would be "I usually run".

questions.stem: Antes ___ en un departamento pequeño; ahora vivo en una casa.
questions.explanation: "Antes" alone means "before, in the past", and with the imperfect it gives "used to": "Antes vivía…" (I used to live). "Antes de" needs an infinitive or a noun and would leave the sentence without a main verb; "vivo" is the present.

questions.stem: Read: "De niña, Teresa vivía en un pueblo. La escuela estaba lejos y caminaba una hora todas las mañanas. No tenía muchos juguetes, pero tenía tres hermanos y siempre jugaban a las escondidas." Which statement is true?
choices: She had a lot of toys.
She walked to school every morning.
She went to school by bus.
questions.explanation: "Caminaba una hora todas las mañanas": she walked for an hour every morning. She didn't have many toys ("No tenía muchos juguetes") and she had three siblings.

questions.stem: How do you say "I don't watch cartoons anymore"?
questions.explanation: "Ya no" (not anymore) goes before the verb: "Ya no veo caricaturas." "Todavía veo" means "I still watch", "Ya veo" means "now I see" or "I already watch", and the last choice repeats "no".

questions.stem: Write the imperfect of "ser": De niño, yo ___ muy travieso.
questions.explanation: "Ser" is irregular in the imperfect: era, eras, era, éramos, eran. A description of what you were like as a child takes the imperfect.

questions.stem: Match each verb with its nosotros imperfect.
questions.explanation: "Ser", "ir" and "ver" are the only irregular imperfects (éramos, íbamos, veíamos). "Tener" and "jugar" are regular here: -íamos for -er/-ir, -ábamos for -ar. "Vimos" and "fuimos" are preterites.

questions.stem: Which of these are imperfect forms? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Comía", "éramos" (ser), "iba" (ir) and "veía" (ver) are imperfects. "Comí" and "fuimos" are preterites.

questions.stem: Name the numbered things and people in this schoolyard.

image.alt: A schoolyard at recess in front of a primary school. Numbered: the seat of a swing with a child on it, a boy's white shirt, tie and navy trousers, a ball on the ground, a small doll held by a girl, and a tall woman near the school door.

questions.explanation: The child sits on a swing (el columpio), the boy wears a school uniform (el uniforme), there is a ball (la pelota) by his foot, the girl holds a doll (la muñeca) and the woman by the door is the teacher (la maestra).

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: On Sundays we used to eat at my grandmother's house.
questions.explanation: A habit ("used to") takes the imperfect, "comíamos"; "comimos" is the preterite for one meal. "Los domingos" can go first or last, or right after the verb, and the place can also start the sentence.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Was your teacher strict?
questions.explanation: A description in the past takes the imperfect of ser, "era", and the adjective agrees with "maestra": "estricta". Spanish questions can keep the order of a statement or put the verb first: "¿Tu maestra era estricta?", "¿Era estricta tu maestra?", "¿Era tu maestra estricta?"

questions.stem: Ayer ___ por la calle cuando ___ un ruido muy raro.
questions.explanation: The walk was going on (imperfect "caminaba") when one event interrupted it (preterite "oí"). With "ayer" and a single noise, "oía" would make the noise background or a habit, and "caminé … cuando oí" lists two events as if the walk started because of the noise.

questions.stem: Anoche dormía cuando ___ el teléfono.
questions.explanation: The sleeping was in progress (imperfect), and the phone ringing is the single event that interrupted it: preterite "sonó". "Sonaba" would make it background too, and "ha sonado" and "suena" don't fit a story about last night.

questions.stem: How do you say "I met my wife in 2015"?
questions.explanation: "Conocer" in the preterite means "to meet (for the first time)": "Conocí a mi esposa". A person after conocer needs the personal a. "Conocía" means "I knew", and saber isn't used for people.

questions.stem: What does "No quise ir a la fiesta" mean?
choices: I refused to go to the party.
I couldn't go to the party.
I didn't know about the party.
questions.explanation: In the preterite, "no quise" means "I didn't want to, and I didn't": I refused. "I couldn't go" would be "No pude ir", and "I didn't know" would be "No sabía".

questions.stem: Mientras yo ___, mi hermano ponía la mesa.
questions.explanation: "Mientras" (while) usually takes the imperfect for something going on, and here both actions are background happening at the same time: "Mientras yo cocinaba, mi hermano ponía la mesa."

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Ayer me robaron la cartera en el metro." Which reaction fits?
questions.explanation: "¡No me digas!" shows surprise and "¡Qué mala suerte!" sympathy. "¡Qué bueno!" (good!) and "¡Felicidades!" (congratulations) are for good news, and "¡Buen provecho!" is said to people eating.

questions.stem: Read: "El sábado iba en bicicleta al mercado. Hacía mucho viento y había muchos carros. De repente, un perro cruzó la calle y me caí. Afortunadamente, llevaba casco." What was the weather like?
questions.explanation: "Hacía mucho viento" means it was very windy: background in the imperfect. The events (the dog crossing, the fall) are in the preterite. (El casco = helmet.)

questions.stem: Which of these usually introduce an event in the preterite? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "De repente" (suddenly), "en ese momento" (at that moment) and "al final" (in the end) announce something happening, so the verb is usually preterite. "Mientras" usually goes with the imperfect, and "todos los días" points to a habit (imperfect).

questions.stem: Write the preterite of "caerse" for él (he fell): Mi abuelo ___ en la escalera.
questions.explanation: "Caerse" changes i to y between vowels in the él preterite: "se cayó" (and "se cayeron"). The pronoun "se" goes before the verb.

questions.stem: Match each preterite with its meaning.
questions.explanation: The preterite shows a single moment: meeting someone (conocí), finding something out (supe), refusing (no quise), managing (pude), and having to do something and doing it (tuve que). "I used to know" would be the imperfect "conocía" or "sabía".

questions.stem: Put the story in order.
choices: El domingo caminaba por el parque con mi perro.
De repente, el perro vio un gato y se escapó.
Busqué al perro por todo el parque durante una hora.
Entonces regresé a casa muy triste.
Al final, ¡el perro estaba en la puerta de mi casa!
questions.explanation: The story opens with the scene (caminaba, imperfect), then the events in order: the dog escapes, the search, going home, and the surprise at the end. "Al final" closes the story.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I was walking home when I saw an accident.
questions.explanation: The action in progress takes the imperfect ("caminaba"), and the interrupting event the preterite ("vi"). Either clause can come first: "Caminaba a casa cuando vi un accidente", "Vi un accidente cuando caminaba a casa", "Cuando caminaba a casa, vi un accidente". "Caminé" would turn the walk into a finished event.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Fortunately, nobody fell.
