vocab.example: Los nombres empiezan con mayúscula.
vocab.exampleEn: Names start with a capital letter.

vocab.note: A woman is la examinadora.
vocab.example: La examinadora fue muy amable conmigo.
vocab.exampleEn: The examiner was very kind to me.

vocab.example: Mi monólogo duró casi tres minutos.
vocab.exampleEn: My talk lasted almost three minutes.

vocab.note: Words like bueno, pues, este…, o sea.
vocab.example: Uso demasiadas muletillas cuando estoy nervioso.
vocab.exampleEn: I use too many filler words when I'm nervous.

vocab.example: Llego pasado mañana, es decir, el jueves.
vocab.exampleEn: I arrive the day after tomorrow, that is, on Thursday.

vocab.note: Informal, very common in Mexico; don't overuse it.
vocab.example: Es mi tía, o sea, la hermana de mi mamá.
vocab.exampleEn: She's my aunt, I mean, my mom's sister.

vocab.note: Often after por un lado (on the one hand).
vocab.example: Por un lado, es caro; por otro lado, es muy cómodo.
vocab.exampleEn: On the one hand, it's expensive; on the other hand, it's very comfortable.

vocab.example: En cuanto a la comida, todo estuvo delicioso.
vocab.exampleEn: As for the food, everything was delicious.

readingList.title: Un poco de amor y amistad (Serie de lecturas graduadas de español para extranjeros, Español 2)
readingList.author: Sandra Luz Cruz Iturribarri
readingList.publisher: UNAM, Centro de Enseñanza para Extranjeros (CEPE)
readingList.note: The A2 volume of the free graded-reader series from the National University of Mexico, the series whose first volume (La ciudad) is on the A1 list. Title, author and level are confirmed in the series list printed in volume 1; look for it on the CEPE publications site. Like volume 1, it is written for UNAM's own students in Mexico City.

readingList.title: Esperanza
readingList.author: Carol Gaab
readingList.note: Based on a true story from Guatemala's civil war. A city worker organizes a union, his family is put on a government list, and they have to flee. Told with about 200 different words (about 7,000 in all). Its subject includes political violence.

readingList.title: Robo en la noche
readingList.note: A fifteen-year-old moves to Costa Rica with her father and gets caught up in an illegal trade in endangered macaws. About 240 different words, told in the past; a good first book after module 1.

readingList.title: Cabello que baila: el Carnaval de Coyolillo
readingList.author: Michelle Maria Nicola and Daniela López Carreto
readingList.note: Maya, proud of her Afro-Mexican heritage, finds her name on the list of candidates for Carnaval queen in the Mexican town of Coyolillo and has to work out how she sees herself. About 220 different words.

readingList.title: La llorona de Mazatlán
readingList.author: Katie Baker
readingList.note: A girl goes to Mazatlán to play soccer and starts hearing crying at night and seeing a woman in a long white dress whom no one else notices. A modern ghost story built on the legend of La Llorona.

readingList.title: Fiesta fatal
readingList.author: Mira Canion
readingList.note: A mean-spirited teenager's quinceañera goes wrong when she becomes a target and a drug cartel turns up. Only about 140 different words in some 4,750, with the preterite and the imperfect side by side; read it after lesson 03.

readingList.title: Los bucaneros y el Templo del Jaguar
readingList.author: Mira Canion
readingList.note: Pirates steal an emerald in 1741, in a story that moves from the Colombian jungle to the high seas, and a girl with fang-like teeth, feared by her village, is pulled into the chase. About 240 different words.

readingList.title: Me perdí en Medellín
readingList.author: Adriana Ramírez
readingList.note: A Canadian tourist in Medellín, with no phone data and little money or Spanish, gets lost, and a local who offers to take him to his hotel runs a few errands first. Everyday Colombian Spanish; pairs well with module 4.

readingList.title: Una desaparición misteriosa
readingList.author: Theresa Marrama
readingList.note: Ana's best friend disappears, and an old Peruvian legend may be coming true. About 350 different words, in several tenses.

readingList.title: Short Stories in Spanish for Beginners
readingList.author: Olly Richards
readingList.note: Eight stories in different genres (science fiction, crime, history, thriller) with a glossary, summaries and comprehension questions after each chapter. The publisher maps it to A2–B1 and doesn't say which variety of Spanish it uses, so expect some words from Spain.

readingList.title: Planetas y humanos (Serie de lecturas graduadas de español para extranjeros, Español 3)
readingList.author: Moisés López Olea
readingList.publisher: UNAM, Centro de Enseñanza para Extranjeros (CEPE)
readingList.note: Two science-fiction love stories set in Mexico City and on a distant planet, each with exercises, answers and a glossary. A free PDF from the publisher and the natural next book once you've finished the course.

readingList.title: Easy Spanish (video series)
readingList.note: Weekly videos with street interviews filmed in Mexico and Spain, with Spanish and English subtitles, plus "Super Easy" episodes on grammar and vocabulary for beginners and lower-intermediate learners. Good listening practice for real, unscripted speech.

readingList.title: DELE A2 exam guide
readingList.note: The official description of every part of the DELE A2, with the timing and the scoring rules. The Instituto Cervantes also publishes a free A2 model exam. Save both for lesson 24.
